Part 1

Computer Components

Inside desktops and laptops: processors, boards, memory, graphics, storage (incl. SATA vs mSATA vs M.2), power, cooling, cases, buses, ports, networking and peripherals.

#CPUs — core concepts

The CPU (central processing unit) runs program instructions. These cards cover the ideas you'll see on every spec sheet.

#Cores & threads

Current

A core is an independent processor inside the chip. Threads are instruction streams the core can juggle. With SMT (Intel calls it Hyper-Threading), one core runs two threads at once, so an 8-core/16-thread chip can work on 16 streams.

Typical desktop6–24 cores
Typical phone6–10 cores
Server64–192+ cores

Commonly confused with: More cores doesn't automatically mean faster. Games often care more about single-core speed.

#Clock speed (GHz)

Current

How many cycles per second a core runs. A base clock is guaranteed and a boost clock is reached briefly under good cooling. Comparing GHz only makes sense within the same architecture.

1971 (4004)740 kHz
2000 (Pentium 4)1.5 GHz
Today4–6+ GHz boost

Fun fact: Clocks stalled near 4 GHz for years after 2005 because of heat (the 'power wall'). Chipmakers turned to more cores instead.

#IPC (instructions per clock)

Current

How much work a core finishes per clock tick. Performance ≈ IPC × clock speed. New architectures usually raise IPC, which is how a 4 GHz chip from 2024 crushes a 4 GHz chip from 2012.

#Cache (L1 / L2 / L3)

Current

Small, very fast memory on the CPU itself. L1 is tiny and fastest, L3 is larger and shared by all cores. More cache means fewer slow trips to RAM.

L132–192 KB per core
L2512 KB–3 MB per core
L38–128 MB shared

Fun fact: AMD's 3D V-Cache stacks extra L3 directly on top of the chip. That's why X3D Ryzen chips are top gaming CPUs.

#TDP / PPT / PL1 / PL2

Current

TDP (Thermal Design Power) is roughly the heat a cooler must handle. Real power draw can go well above it. Intel uses PL1/PL2 (long and short boost limits), AMD uses PPT (package power tracking).

Commonly confused with: TDP is not the maximum power draw. A '125 W' chip can pull 250 W+ while boosting.

#Process node (nm)

Current

The manufacturing generation, e.g. TSMC N3 or Intel 18A. Smaller nodes usually mean more transistors, lower power and higher speed. Today 'nm' names are marketing labels, not real physical sizes.

Big foundriesTSMC, Samsung, Intel Foundry
197110 µm
2025'3 nm' / '2 nm' class

#Chiplets / tiles

2017→ Current

Rather than one big die, the CPU is built from several smaller dies linked together: compute chiplets plus an I/O die. AMD Ryzen popularised it, and Intel's Core Ultra uses 'tiles'. Smaller dies cost less to make and waste less silicon.

Fun fact: AMD's first-gen EPYC (2017) used four dies in one package, a big reason it competed so well on core count.

#Hybrid architecture (P-cores / E-cores)

2021→ Current

A mix of big performance cores and small efficiency cores. ARM called it big.LITTLE (2011). Intel brought it to desktops with 12th-gen Alder Lake (2021), and Apple Silicon uses it too. The OS scheduler decides which core gets which task.

#iGPU (integrated graphics)

Current

A graphics processor built into the CPU package. Fine for desktop work and video, and recent ones (AMD Radeon 780M/890M, Intel Arc iGPU, Apple M-series) can run games at lower settings.

Identify it: Intel chips ending in F (e.g. i5-12400F) have no iGPU. Most AMD chips with a G suffix are APUs with strong iGPUs.

#NPU (neural processing unit)

2017→ Current

A dedicated block for AI/ML maths at low power. It appeared first in phones (Apple Neural Engine 2017, Huawei Kirin 970) and came to PCs with Intel Core Ultra, AMD Ryzen AI and Snapdragon X. Measured in TOPS (trillion operations per second).

Fun fact: Microsoft's 'Copilot+ PC' label requires an NPU of 40+ TOPS.

#Instruction set architecture (ISA)

Current

The 'language' a CPU understands. x86-64 (Intel/AMD PCs), ARM (phones, Apple Silicon, Snapdragon PCs), RISC-V (open standard, growing), plus historic ones: PowerPC, SPARC, MIPS, Alpha, 68k.

Commonly confused with: 'x64', 'AMD64', 'x86-64' and 'Intel 64' all mean the same 64-bit x86 instruction set.

#CISC vs RISC

Current

CISC (Complex Instruction Set, e.g. x86) has many complex instructions. RISC (Reduced, e.g. ARM, RISC-V) uses simpler instructions that are easier to pipeline. Modern x86 chips translate CISC into RISC-like micro-ops internally.

#Overclocking & unlocked CPUs

Current

Running a CPU above its rated speed. Intel 'K' chips and nearly all AMD Ryzen chips are unlocked, and the motherboard chipset has to allow it too (Intel Z-series, AMD B/X-series).

Identify it: Intel suffixes: K = unlocked, F = no iGPU, KF = both, T = low power, H/HX/U/P = laptop classes.

#Thermal throttling

Current

When a CPU gets too hot (usually ~95–105 °C), it cuts its own clock speed to protect itself. Constant throttling usually points to dried thermal paste, a bad cooler or poor airflow.

#CPU sockets & packages

How the CPU physically attaches to the motherboard. A CPU only fits sockets of its own generation.

#PGA (Pin Grid Array)

1970s→2022 (desktop) Legacy

The pins are on the CPU and drop into holes in the socket. Used by most AMD desktop CPUs up to AM4, and older Intel chips. A ZIF (zero insertion force) lever clamps it down.

Identify it: Flip the CPU: hundreds of gold pins = PGA.

Commonly confused with: LGA, where the pins are in the socket instead.

Fun fact: Bent PGA pins can often be straightened with a mechanical pencil tube or a credit card.

#LGA (Land Grid Array)

2004→ Current

The pins are in the socket and the CPU has flat gold pads ('lands'). Intel since LGA775 (2004), AMD since AM5 (2022), and nearly all server CPUs.

Identify it: The CPU has flat gold dots, and the motherboard socket has a field of tiny springy pins under a metal load plate.

Commonly confused with: PGA. With LGA, bent pins are on the (more expensive) motherboard.

#BGA (Ball Grid Array)

Current

The chip is soldered straight to the board with tiny solder balls. Used by nearly every laptop CPU since ~2013, plus phones, consoles and Apple Silicon. You can't upgrade it.

Identify it: No socket and no lever, just a chip flush with the board under the heatsink.

#Slot 1 / Slot A (cartridge CPUs)

1997–2000 Obsolete

Intel Pentium II/III (Slot 1) and AMD Athlon (Slot A) came as cartridges that plugged in vertically like expansion cards. They held the CPU plus off-die L2 cache chips, which were hard to put on the die back then.

Identify it: A black plastic 'SECC' cartridge about the size of a cassette tape, plugged into a long slot.

Fun fact: Once L2 cache moved onto the die (Coppermine, Thunderbird), CPUs went back to sockets (Socket 370, Socket A).

#Socket 7 / Super Socket 7

1995–2000 Obsolete

A shared PGA socket that Intel Pentium (P54C/MMX), AMD K5/K6, Cyrix 6x86 and IDT WinChip chips could all use. It was the last time Intel and AMD CPUs could go in the same board.

#Major Intel desktop sockets

1989→ Current

Socket 1–3 (486) → Socket 5/7 (Pentium) → Slot 1 → Socket 370 → Socket 423/478 (Pentium 4) → LGA775 (2004, Core 2) → LGA1156/1366 → LGA1155 → LGA1150 → LGA1151 → LGA1200 → LGA1700 (12th–14th gen) → LGA1851 (Core Ultra 200S, 2024).

Commonly confused with: LGA1151 came in two versions (Skylake/Kaby Lake vs Coffee Lake) that aren't cross-compatible even though the socket is physically the same.

#Major AMD desktop sockets

1999→ Current

Slot A → Socket A/462 (Athlon XP) → Socket 754/939 (Athlon 64) → AM2/AM2+ → AM3/AM3+ (FX) → FM1/FM2 (APUs) → AM4 (2017–2022, PGA 1331) → AM5 (2022→, LGA 1718).

Fun fact: AM4 supported five Ryzen generations across 2017–2022, an unusually long run. AMD has pledged similar longevity for AM5.

#HEDT & server sockets

Current

Large sockets for workstation chips: Intel LGA2011/2066/4677/4710/7529 (Xeon), AMD TR4/sTRX4/sTR5 (Threadripper) and SP3/SP5/SP6 (EPYC). Some EPYC/Threadripper packages are huge, about 75 × 75 mm.

#Intel CPU lineage

From the first commercial microprocessor to Core Ultra.

#Intel 4004

1971 Obsolete

The first commercially available single-chip microprocessor: 4-bit, 2,300 transistors, 740 kHz. It was designed for Busicom calculators.

Transistors2,300
Process10 µm

Fun fact: Intel bought back the rights from Busicom for about $60,000. It may be the best deal in tech history.

#Intel 8080 / 8085

1974 / 1976 Obsolete

8-bit CPUs that powered early microcomputers like the Altair 8800 (1975), the machine that inspired Microsoft's founding.

#Intel 8086 / 8088

1978 / 1979 Obsolete

The 16-bit chips that started x86. The 8088 (8-bit external bus) went into the IBM PC 5150 in 1981, which locked x86 in as the PC standard.

Clock4.77–10 MHz
Transistors~29,000

Fun fact: Almost every Windows PC today can still, in principle, boot in the 8086's 'real mode'.

#Intel 80286

1982 Obsolete

Added protected mode and up to 16 MB of addressable RAM. It powered the IBM PC/AT (1984) and its clones.

#Intel 80386 (i386)

1985 Obsolete

The first 32-bit x86 chip, with paging/virtual memory. This is the base design modern 32-bit x86 still follows. The SX variant had a 16-bit bus.

Fun fact: Compaq beat IBM to market with a 386 PC (Deskpro 386, 1986), a turning point that loosened IBM's grip on the PC standard.

#Intel 80486 (i486)

1989 Obsolete

Built-in floating-point unit (DX models) and L1 cache. The DX2/DX4 introduced clock multipliers.

Commonly confused with: 486SX had its FPU disabled, while 486DX had it enabled.

#Pentium (P5)

1993 Obsolete

Intel switched to a trademarkable name because numbers like '586' couldn't be trademarked. Superscalar design (2 pipelines). MMX models (1997) added multimedia instructions.

Fun fact: The 1994 FDIV bug made some divisions slightly wrong. Intel recalled chips at a cost of about $475 million.

#Pentium Pro / II / III

1995–2001 Obsolete

The P6 architecture: out-of-order execution. Pentium II/III came as Slot 1 cartridges, later as Socket 370. P6 is the ancestor of today's Core line.

#Pentium 4 (NetBurst)

2000–2008 Obsolete

Very long pipeline built for high GHz (up to 3.8 GHz), but it ran hot and had low IPC. Hyper-Threading debuted on desktops here (2002).

Fun fact: Intel planned for NetBurst to reach 10 GHz. Heat killed that plan, and Intel went back to the P6-derived Pentium M design.

#Pentium M / Centrino

2003–2006 Obsolete

An efficient laptop chip derived from P6. The 'Centrino' brand bundled it with Intel Wi-Fi. Its design led directly to Core and Core 2.

#Core 2 (Duo / Quad / Extreme)

2006–2011 Obsolete

Intel's comeback architecture: efficient, fast, and the end of AMD's Athlon 64 lead. Socket LGA775.

SocketLGA775
Cores2–4

#Core i3 / i5 / i7 / i9

2008–2023 Legacy

The 'good/better/best' naming started with Nehalem (2008). The generation is the first digit(s) of the model number: i7-2600K is 2nd gen (Sandy Bridge), i9-14900K is 14th gen (Raptor Lake Refresh).

Identify it: i5-12400F = 12th gen, mid-tier, no iGPU.

Fun fact: Intel was on '14 nm' from 2014 to 2021 (Skylake through Rocket Lake), the '14nm+++' meme era.

#Core Ultra (Series 1 / 2 / 3)

2023→ Current

New branding with tile-based designs and built-in NPUs. Meteor Lake (laptops 2023), Lunar Lake & Arrow Lake (2024, Series 2), Panther Lake (Core Ultra Series 3, launched at CES in January 2026, Intel's first chips made on its 18A process).

TiersUltra 5 / 7 / 9
NPUYes

Source: The Register: Intel unleashes Panther Lake, first on 18A (Jan 2026)

#Celeron & Pentium (budget)

1998–2023 Legacy

Budget brands with cut-down cache and features. Intel retired both names in 2023 for plain 'Intel Processor' (e.g. N100).

#Atom

2008→ Legacy

Low-power x86 chips for netbooks, tablets, phones (briefly) and embedded devices. The engine of the 2008–2011 netbook craze.

Fun fact: Intel paid billions in 'contra revenue' subsidies to get Atom into Android tablets, then quit phones in 2016.

#Xeon

1998→ Current

Intel's server and workstation line: ECC memory support, more cores, more PCIe lanes. Current branding: Xeon 6 (P-core and E-core variants).

#Itanium (IA-64)

2001–2021 Obsolete

A 64-bit non-x86 architecture built with HP. AMD's x86-64 overtook it, and it earned the nickname 'Itanic'. Final shipments were in 2021.

Commonly confused with: IA-64 (Itanium) isn't the same as Intel 64 / x86-64.

#AMD CPU lineage

From Intel second-source to Ryzen.

#Am286 / Am386 / Am486

1982–1995 Obsolete

AMD first made x86 chips as a licensed second source for Intel (IBM required one). Later clones led to years of lawsuits.

#K5 / K6 / K6-2 / K6-III

1996–2000 Obsolete

AMD's first in-house x86 designs. The K6-2 added 3DNow! SIMD and was a budget favourite on Super Socket 7.

#Athlon (K7)

1999–2005 Obsolete

Beat Intel to 1 GHz in March 2000. It started on Slot A, then Socket A (Athlon XP, Duron).

Fun fact: Athlon XP chips could be unlocked with a pencil: drawing over the L1 bridges on the package let you change the multiplier.

#Athlon 64 / Opteron (K8)

2003–2009 Obsolete

Introduced x86-64 (AMD64), the 64-bit extension the whole PC industry adopted, Intel included. The memory controller moved onto the CPU. The Athlon 64 X2 brought dual-core chips to consumers.

#Phenom / Phenom II

2007–2012 Obsolete

AMD's first native quad-core chips. Some Phenom II X2/X3 chips could 'unlock' disabled cores.

#FX (Bulldozer / Piledriver)

2011–2017 Obsolete

A 'module' design where pairs of cores shared resources. It ran hot with weak single-thread performance, and in 2019 AMD settled a class action over its '8-core' marketing.

Fun fact: An FX-8370 reached ~8.72 GHz on liquid nitrogen in 2014, a world CPU frequency record that stood for about a decade.

#A-Series APUs

2011–2019 Legacy

CPU + Radeon graphics on one die (AMD 'Fusion'). Common in budget laptops and also the basis of PS4/Xbox One chips.

#Ryzen (Zen)

2017→ Current

The Zen architecture brought AMD back to the high end. Tiers: Ryzen 3/5/7/9. Desktop generations: 1000 → 2000 → 3000 → 5000 (AM4) → 7000 → 9000 (AM5). Laptop chips are now 'Ryzen AI'.

Identify it: Suffixes: X = higher clocks, X3D = 3D V-Cache (gaming), G = has strong iGPU, U/HS/HX = laptop power classes.

#Ryzen Threadripper

2017→ Current

HEDT/workstation chips with up to 96 cores (7995WX) on sTR5. Used by 3D artists, engineers and video editors.

#EPYC

2017→ Current

AMD's server line, now up to 192 cores (Zen 5c 'Turin'). Took major data-centre market share from Xeon.

#Other CPU families (historic & modern)

Chips beyond Intel and AMD that shaped computing.

#MOS 6502

1975 Obsolete

A cheap 8-bit CPU (about $25, against ~$179 for rivals) that powered the Apple I/II, Commodore 64 (6510 variant), Atari 2600 (6507) and NES (Ricoh 2A03).

Fun fact: Bender in Futurama and the T-800 in The Terminator both 'run' 6502 code on screen.

#Zilog Z80

1976 Obsolete

An 8-bit 8080-compatible CPU used in the TRS-80, ZX Spectrum, MSX, Game Boy (a Sharp variant) and countless embedded devices. Production finally ended in 2024.

#Motorola 68000 (68k)

1979 Obsolete

32-bit internal design that powered the original Macintosh (1984), Amiga, Atari ST, Sega Genesis/Mega Drive and early Sun workstations.

#PowerPC

1991–2006 (Mac) Legacy

Built by the AIM alliance (Apple, IBM, Motorola). Powered Macs from 1994 to 2006 (G3, G4, G5), plus the GameCube, Wii, Xbox 360 and PS3 (Cell, PowerPC-based).

Fun fact: Apple moved Macs to Intel in 2006 because IBM couldn't fit a G5 in a laptop. Apple then left x86 for its own chips in 2020.

#ARM

1985→ Current

A RISC architecture that started at Acorn Computers (UK). ARM Holdings licenses the designs, and others (Apple, Qualcomm, Samsung, MediaTek) build the chips. It runs about 99% of smartphones and is spreading into PCs and servers.

Fun fact: The first ARM chip (ARM1, 1985) used so little power it ran on leakage current while its supply line was unplugged during a test.

#Apple Silicon (M-series)

2020→ Current

Apple's ARM chips for Mac and iPad: M1 (2020), M2, M3, M4, M5, each with Pro/Max (and sometimes Ultra) variants. Unified memory sits on the package. Rosetta 2 translates x86 apps.

ArchitectureARM64
MemoryUnified, on-package

Identify it: Mac model years 2020+ (except some early 2020 models that had Intel).

#Qualcomm Snapdragon X (PC)

2024→ Current

ARM laptop chips (X Elite / X Plus, then X2) using Oryon cores, which came from Qualcomm's purchase of Nuvia. They launched the Copilot+ PC wave for Windows on ARM.

#RISC-V

2010→ Current

An open-source, royalty-free instruction set from UC Berkeley. Common in microcontrollers and growing in SBCs and AI accelerators. Chips from SiFive, StarFive, Espressif, Alibaba T-Head.

#Cyrix

1988–1999 Obsolete

Made x86 clones (6x86, MII) and math coprocessors. Bought by National Semiconductor in 1997, and its designs later went to VIA.

#VIA (C3, C7, Nano) / Zhaoxin

1999→ Legacy

Taiwan's VIA held an x86 licence through its Cyrix/Centaur purchases. It made low-power chips (Mini-ITX was VIA's invention). Its x86 work continues in China through the Zhaoxin joint venture.

#Transmeta Crusoe

2000–2009 Obsolete

Low-power chips that translated x86 code in software ('code morphing'). Linus Torvalds worked there from 1997 to 2003.

#IBM POWER

1990→ Current

IBM's server RISC architecture (POWER1 through POWER11). Used in IBM Power Systems and mainframe-class servers. It's PowerPC's big sibling.

#SPARC (Sun)

1987→ Legacy

Sun Microsystems' RISC architecture for Solaris workstations and servers. Oracle bought Sun in 2010 and wound SPARC development down by 2017.

#DEC Alpha

1992–2004 Obsolete

A 64-bit RISC chip from Digital Equipment Corp, famous for its speed. It was the first commercial chip to pass 500 MHz. Compaq and then HP killed it in favour of Itanium.

#MIPS

1985→ Legacy

A RISC design in SGI workstations, the Nintendo 64 and PlayStation 1/2/PSP, and many routers. Now mostly replaced by ARM and RISC-V.

#Motherboards

The main circuit board. It connects the CPU, RAM, storage, expansion cards and ports.

#ATX

1995→ Current

Intel's standard that set the modern PC layout: rear I/O panel, soft power, 24-pin main power. Up to 7 expansion slots.

Size305 × 244 mm
Slotsup to 7
Mounting holes9

Identify it: Full-size board, usually 4 RAM slots and several PCIe slots.

#Micro-ATX (mATX)

1997→ Current

A shorter ATX that keeps the same mounting holes and I/O position. Up to 4 slots. Very common in budget and office PCs.

Size244 × 244 mm (max)

#Mini-ITX

2001→ Current

A tiny square board designed by VIA. One PCIe slot, usually 2 RAM slots. The heart of small-form-factor (SFF) gaming builds.

Size170 × 170 mm

#E-ATX / XL-ATX / SSI-EEB

Current

Oversized boards for HEDT/workstations and dual-CPU servers. 'E-ATX' sizes vary by vendor (often 305 × 330 mm), so check your case.

#Nano-ITX / Pico-ITX / Mini-STX

2004→ Current

Very small embedded/mini-PC boards: Nano-ITX 120×120 mm, Pico-ITX 100×72 mm, Mini-STX 147×140 mm (Intel, 2015, uses an external power brick).

#AT / Baby AT

1984–late 1990s Obsolete

IBM PC/AT-era format. It used a hard power switch wired to the PSU and two 6-pin power plugs (P8/P9). A DIN-5 keyboard port was the only built-in rear port.

Identify it: Two side-by-side 6-pin power plugs. Getting them backwards could fry the board (rule: black wires together in the middle).

Fun fact: On AT systems, 'shut down' left you at a screen saying 'It is now safe to turn off your computer'.

#LPX / NLX

1990s Obsolete

Slimline formats with a riser card where expansion cards plugged in sideways. Common in Packard Bell, Compaq and other prebuilt desktops.

#BTX

2004–~2008 Obsolete

Intel's proposed ATX replacement, designed to cool the hot Pentium 4 with a front-to-back wind tunnel. Mostly Dell and Gateway used it before it died.

Identify it: A mirror-image layout: the I/O panel on the left as seen from the back, and a big front intake duct over the CPU.

#Proprietary OEM boards

Current

Dell, HP, Lenovo and Apple often use custom shapes, power connectors (e.g. 8-pin or 10-pin ATX12VO-style) and front-panel pinouts. Swapping cases or PSUs can be difficult.

#Back-connector boards (BTF / Project Zero)

2023→ Current

Boards with power and data headers on the back side for hidden cables (ASUS BTF, MSI Project Zero, Gigabyte Stealth). They need a compatible case.

#Chipset

Current

A support chip that handles extra USB, SATA and PCIe lanes and sets the board's feature level. Intel: H (basic), B (mainstream), Z (overclocking). AMD: A, B, X (e.g. B650, X870E).

Commonly confused with: Chipset ≠ socket. A B760 and a Z790 board share socket LGA1700, but only the Z790 overclocks.

#Northbridge & Southbridge

1990s–~2011 Legacy

Older two-chip chipsets. The northbridge handled CPU, RAM and AGP/graphics, the southbridge handled slower I/O. Once memory controllers moved into CPUs, only the southbridge was left. Today it's the 'PCH'.

#VRM (voltage regulator module)

Current

The power stages around the socket that turn the PSU's 12 V into ~1 V for the CPU. Count the 'phases' and look for heatsinks: weak VRMs throttle high-end chips.

Identify it: A row of small square chokes (inductors) with MOSFETs beside them, around the CPU socket.

#BIOS vs UEFI

1981 → 2010s Current

Firmware that starts the PC. Legacy BIOS dates to the IBM PC. UEFI (2005+, mainstream ~2011) adds a mouse-driven GUI, Secure Boot, drives over 2 TB (GPT) and faster boot.

Commonly confused with: People still say 'BIOS' when they mean the UEFI setup screen.

Fun fact: 'BIOS flashback' buttons let you update firmware with no CPU or RAM installed.

#UEFI: what it means

Components · 2005→ Current

UEFI = Unified Extensible Firmware Interface. Firmware is the small program stored in a chip on the motherboard that runs first when you press power: it checks the hardware, then finds and starts the operating system. Unified because one standard is shared by Intel, AMD, Arm, Microsoft, Apple and PC makers through the UEFI Forum (founded 2005). Extensible because it can load add-on drivers and programs (graphics cards and network cards carry their own UEFI drivers). Interface because it is a defined way for the firmware and the operating system to talk to each other. It grew out of Intel's EFI (late 1990s, for Itanium servers) and replaced the 1981-style BIOS in most PCs by about 2011–2012.

Boots fromThe EFI System Partition (ESP): a small FAT32 partition holding .efi boot files, e.g. \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi
Disk styleGPT (drives over 2 TB, 128 partitions)
SecuritySecure Boot (only signed boot loaders), works with TPM
ExtrasMouse-driven setup screen, network boot, firmware updates from Windows ('capsule updates'), fast boot
Old modeCSM (Compatibility Support Module) imitates a BIOS for old OSes; Intel planned to drop it from 2020 and many new boards no longer include it

Identify it: In the setup screen you'll see 'UEFI', 'Boot mode: UEFI / Legacy (CSM)', 'Secure Boot', and boot entries such as 'Windows Boot Manager' or 'UEFI: USB drive'

Commonly confused with: People still call the UEFI setup screen 'the BIOS', and motherboard makers label it that way too. Also: UEFI ≠ Secure Boot (Secure Boot is one feature of UEFI that can be turned off)

Fun fact: Windows 11 requires a PC that boots in UEFI mode with Secure Boot capability. A USB installer made in 'MBR/BIOS' mode won't show up when the PC is set to UEFI-only.

#CMOS battery (CR2032)

Current

A coin cell that keeps the clock and BIOS settings while the PC is unplugged. When it dies, the date resets to the BIOS release date and you get 'CMOS checksum' errors.

Identify it: A shiny coin battery about the size of a nickel, usually near the PCIe slots.

#Front-panel & internal headers

Current

Pin rows on the board: F_PANEL (power switch, reset, LEDs), USB 2.0 (9-pin), USB 3.x (19/20-pin blue), USB-C (Key-A), HD Audio, CPU_FAN / SYS_FAN (4-pin PWM), TPM, COM.

Commonly confused with: RGB (12 V, 4-pin) vs ARGB (5 V, 3-pin). Plugging ARGB into a 12 V header can burn out the LEDs.

#TPM (Trusted Platform Module)

2009→ Current

A security chip for keys and encryption (BitLocker, Windows Hello). Windows 11 requires TPM 2.0. Modern CPUs build it in as firmware TPM (AMD fTPM / Intel PTT).

#I/O shield

Current

The metal plate in the rear port opening. Many mid- and high-end boards now have it pre-attached.

Fun fact: Forgetting the I/O shield before installing the board is a famous PC-builder rite of passage.

#POST & beep codes / debug LEDs

Current

On power-up, the Power-On Self-Test checks the hardware. Failures show as beep patterns (AMI/Award/Phoenix differ), 2-digit Q-codes, or four debug LEDs (CPU / DRAM / VGA / BOOT).

Motherboard form factors — to scale (1 px = 1 mm), anchored at the I/O corner

Every board shares the rear I/O corner (bottom-left here), which is why smaller boards fit in larger cases.

#Memory (RAM)

Fast, temporary working memory that's wiped when power is lost. The type and generation must match the motherboard.

#DRAM vs SRAM

Current

DRAM stores bits in capacitors that must be refreshed constantly. It's dense and cheap, and used for system RAM. SRAM uses flip-flops: fast, expensive, and used for CPU cache.

#SIMM (30-pin / 72-pin)

1983–late 1990s Obsolete

Single In-line Memory Module. Contacts on both sides carry the same signal. 30-pin SIMMs (8-bit) had to be installed in sets of 4 on 386/486 systems, and 72-pin (32-bit) in pairs on Pentiums.

Identify it: Short sticks with one notch on the corner, installed at an angle and then tilted upright.

#FPM / EDO RAM

1990–1997 Obsolete

Asynchronous DRAM types on SIMMs. EDO (Extended Data Out) was ~10–15% faster than FPM (Fast Page Mode).

#SDR SDRAM

1996–2003 Obsolete

Synchronous DRAM clocked to the system bus. 168-pin DIMMs, 3.3 V. Speeds PC66 / PC100 / PC133.

Identify it: Two notches in the gold edge.

#RDRAM / RIMM (Rambus)

1999–2003 Obsolete

High-bandwidth memory Intel pushed for the Pentium III/4. Expensive and hot, with heat spreaders. Empty slots needed CRIMM continuity dummy sticks.

Fun fact: The PlayStation 2 and Nintendo 64 used Rambus memory.

#DDR SDRAM

2000 Obsolete

Double Data Rate: transfers on both clock edges. 184-pin, 2.5 V.

Speed200–400 MT/s

#DDR2

2003 Obsolete

240-pin, 1.8 V.

Speed400–1066 MT/s

#DDR3 / DDR3L

2007 Legacy

240-pin DIMM / 204-pin SO-DIMM. 1.5 V (DDR3L 1.35 V). The mainstream for a decade.

Speed800–2133 MT/s (JEDEC)

Commonly confused with: DDR3L sticks usually work in DDR3 slots, but some laptops require DDR3L.

#DDR4

2014 Current

288-pin DIMM / 260-pin SO-DIMM, 1.2 V. The edge is slightly curved to make insertion easier.

Speed2133–3200 MT/s JEDEC, 4000+ with XMP

#DDR5

2021 (consumer) Current

288-pin, 1.1 V. Each stick has two independent 32-bit sub-channels, a built-in PMIC (power chip), and on-die ECC (inside the chip, not full ECC).

Speed4800–6400 MT/s JEDEC, 8000+ with XMP/EXPO

Commonly confused with: DDR4 and DDR5 are both 288-pin, but the notch is in a different spot, so they won't fit each other's slots.

Fun fact: First boot on DDR5 can take a minute or more while the board 'trains' the memory. That's normal.

#SO-DIMM

Current

Small Outline DIMM for laptops, mini PCs and some routers. About half the length of a DIMM.

PinsDDR3 204 · DDR4 260 · DDR5 262

#LPDDR (Low-Power DDR)

2006→ Current

A mobile memory type that's almost always soldered: phones, tablets, thin laptops, Apple Silicon. LPDDR4X, LPDDR5, LPDDR5X (up to ~10,700 MT/s).

Commonly confused with: LPDDR5 ≠ DDR5. They're different standards and aren't interchangeable.

#CAMM2 / LPCAMM2

2023→ Current

A flat, screw-down memory module that replaces SO-DIMM in thin laptops. LPCAMM2 makes LPDDR5X upgradeable again. Dell first built the idea (CAMM).

Identify it: A flat rectangular module held by screws over a compression connector, rather than a stick in a slot.

#CUDIMM / CSODIMM

2024→ Current

DDR5 modules with an on-board clock driver (CKD) for stability at very high speeds (8000+ MT/s). Supported from Intel Core Ultra 200S.

#ECC memory

Current

Error-Correcting Code: extra chips detect and fix single-bit errors. Needed for servers and workstations. Consumer Ryzen often supports unbuffered ECC unofficially or partly.

Identify it: 9 chips per side instead of 8 on older DIMMs, and 'ECC' on the label.

#Registered / buffered (RDIMM, LRDIMM)

Current

Server memory with a register chip that buffers signals so a system can hold far more RAM (TBs). Won't work in consumer boards.

Commonly confused with: RDIMM vs UDIMM (unbuffered, consumer). They aren't interchangeable.

#XMP / EXPO profiles

2007→ Current

Factory overclock profiles stored on the stick. Intel XMP and AMD EXPO. Without enabling them in BIOS, your '6000 MT/s' kit runs at the JEDEC default (e.g. 4800).

#Dual / quad channel

Current

Using matched sticks in the right slots (usually A2 + B2) doubles bandwidth. A single stick costs noticeable iGPU and gaming performance.

Identify it: Check the motherboard manual for slot priority. It's usually the 2nd and 4th slots from the CPU.

#CAS latency & timings

Current

Numbers like CL30-36-36-76. Lower = faster response. Real latency (ns) ≈ CL × 2000 ÷ speed in MT/s, so DDR5-6000 CL30 = 10 ns.

RAM modules: notch positions (schematic)

The notch stops you from fitting the wrong generation. DDR4 and DDR5 have the same pin count but different notch positions, so neither fits the other's slot.

#Every type of RAM

Desktop sticks, laptop and phone memory, graphics memory, AI memory, module shapes, soldered memory, and the old and odd types.

#How to read a RAM name

Concept

DDR = Double Data Rate (data moves twice per clock tick). The number after it is the generation (DDR4, DDR5). LP = Low Power (phones and thin laptops, usually soldered). G = Graphics (GDDR, on graphics cards). HBM = High Bandwidth Memory (stacked chips next to AI and data-centre GPUs). Speed is written in MT/s (mega-transfers per second, often wrongly called 'MHz'), e.g. DDR5-6000 = 6,000 MT/s. The module name in GB/s is speed × 8: DDR4-3200 = PC4-25600 (25.6 GB/s).

Rule 1Generations are never interchangeable: a DDR4 stick physically won't fit a DDR5 slot (the notch is in a different place)
Rule 2LPDDR and GDDR can't be bought as sticks for normal slots; they're soldered (except LPCAMM2/SOCAMM modules)
Rule 3More channels (dual, quad) multiply bandwidth

Commonly confused with: MT/s vs MHz: DDR5-6000 actually runs a 3,000 MHz clock, transferring twice per tick

Fun fact: Every 'G' (GDDR) generation is built on the same ideas as the DDR before it, but tuned for bandwidth instead of low latency.

#Which RAM should I buy?

Guide

Check your motherboard or laptop manual first: it lists the type (DDR4 or DDR5, UDIMM or SO-DIMM), maximum size and supported speeds. For a 2026 desktop: DDR5-6000 CL30, 2 × 16 GB is the sweet spot for AMD Ryzen; Intel Core Ultra likes 6400–8000 (CUDIMM for the top speeds). Buy matched kits rather than mixing sticks, put two sticks in the slots the manual recommends (usually A2 and B2), and turn on XMP/EXPO in the BIOS. For laptops with soldered memory, choose 16 GB minimum, 32 GB for heavy work or local AI.

Commonly confused with: A 'DDR5-6000' kit runs at 4800 until you enable XMP/EXPO in the BIOS: many people never do.

#Graphics cards (GPUs)

Graphics processors render images, and they now also run AI, video encoding and scientific computing.

#Integrated vs dedicated GPU

Current

Integrated graphics live in the CPU and share system RAM. A dedicated (discrete) GPU has its own chip and VRAM, on a card or a laptop board.

Identify it: Dedicated: a graphics card in the PCIe slot, and the monitor plugs into its ports, not the motherboard's.

Fun fact: A classic beginner mistake: plugging the monitor into the motherboard port and gaming on the iGPU.

#VRAM (video memory)

Current

The GPU's own memory for textures and frame buffers. Types: GDDR5, GDDR5X, GDDR6, GDDR6X (NVIDIA), GDDR7 (2025), and HBM (stacked, high-bandwidth, used in data-centre GPUs).

Budget card8 GB
Mid/high12–16 GB
Flagship24–32 GB

#PCIe graphics slot

2004→ Current

Modern GPUs use a PCIe ×16 slot (PCIe 3.0 / 4.0 / 5.0). Earlier: AGP (1997–2004), before that PCI and ISA/VLB.

Commonly confused with: PCIe ×16 physical slot vs ×16 electrical. Lower slots are often wired ×4.

#GPU power connectors

Current

Up to 75 W comes from the slot. Beyond that: PCIe 6-pin (75 W), 8-pin (150 W), 12VHPWR (2022, 600 W) and its revision 12V-2x6 (2023).

Fun fact: 12VHPWR made headlines for melting when not fully seated. 12V-2x6 shortened the sense pins to help prevent it.

#MXM (Mobile PCI Express Module)

2004→ Legacy

A swappable laptop GPU module standard (MXM 3.0 Type A/B). It used to let gaming laptops upgrade GPUs. Now rare, since most laptop GPUs are soldered.

#eGPU (external GPU)

2017→ Current

A desktop graphics card in an enclosure, connected by Thunderbolt/USB4 (or OCuLink). Turns a thin laptop into a gaming rig, losing roughly 10–30% performance to bandwidth (it depends on the game and the connection).

#Ray tracing & upscaling

2018→ Current

Ray tracing simulates light paths for realistic reflections and shadows (RT cores). Upscalers render at lower resolution and reconstruct it with AI: NVIDIA DLSS, AMD FSR, Intel XeSS. Frame generation inserts AI-made frames.

#Video output ports on GPUs

Current

Current cards: HDMI 2.1 and DisplayPort 1.4a/2.1. Older cards: DVI-D, DVI-I, VGA (analog), S-Video/composite (TV-out). See Ports & Cables.

#Multi-GPU: SLI & CrossFire

2004–~2020 Obsolete

Linking 2–4 cards for more performance. NVIDIA SLI (with bridge connectors) and AMD CrossFire. Gone for gaming because of micro-stutter and poor support.

Fun fact: The name SLI came from 3dfx's 'Scan-Line Interleave' (1998). NVIDIA bought 3dfx and kept the initials as 'Scalable Link Interface'.

#3dfx Voodoo

1996–2000 Obsolete

The card that started 3D gaming on the PC. The original Voodoo was a 3D-only add-on that needed a pass-through VGA cable from your 2D card. Its Glide API ruled until DirectX/OpenGL took over.

Fun fact: NVIDIA bought 3dfx's assets in December 2000.

#NVIDIA GeForce

1999→ Current

GeForce 256 (1999) was marketed as the 'world's first GPU'. Then GeForce 2–9, GTX 200–900, GTX 10 (Pascal), RTX 20 (Turing, 2018, first ray tracing), RTX 30 (Ampere), RTX 40 (Ada Lovelace), RTX 50 (Blackwell, 2025).

Identify it: RTX 5070 = 50-series, '70' tier. Ti / SUPER = in-between upgrades.

#NVIDIA workstation & data-centre

Current

Quadro (1999–2020) → RTX A-series → RTX PRO (Blackwell). Data centre: Tesla → A100 → H100/H200 → B200/GB200 (Blackwell), the engines of the AI boom.

#ATI / AMD Radeon

1985 / 2000→ Current

ATI (Canada) made Rage and then Radeon (2000). AMD bought ATI in 2006. Generations: HD 2000–7000, R7/R9, RX 400/500 (Polaris), Vega, RX 5000 (RDNA), 6000 (RDNA 2), 7000 (RDNA 3), RX 9000 (RDNA 4, 2025).

Fun fact: The PS4, PS5, Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S all use AMD Radeon graphics.

#Intel Arc

2022→ Current

Intel's dedicated GPUs: Alchemist (A380/A750/A770, 2022), Battlemage (B570/B580, Dec 2024). Also inside Core Ultra iGPUs.

Fun fact: Intel's earlier dedicated card, the i740 (1998), used AGP. Its next one was Arc, 24 years later.

#Matrox

1976→ Legacy

A Canadian GPU maker famous for the Millennium and the G400 'DualHead' multi-monitor cards. Today it focuses on video walls and broadcast.

#S3, Trident, Cirrus Logic, Tseng Labs

1980s–2000s Obsolete

2D/early 3D chipmakers that equipped most 1990s PCs (S3 ViRGE, Trident TVGA, Cirrus GD54xx, Tseng ET4000).

Fun fact: The S3 ViRGE (1995) was nicknamed a '3D decelerator' because 3D often ran slower on it than in software.

#PowerVR (Imagination)

1996→ Current

A tile-based GPU design used in the Sega Dreamcast and, for years, in iPhones/iPads (until Apple's in-house GPUs in 2017).

#Mobile GPUs (Adreno, Mali, Apple GPU)

Current

Phone/tablet graphics built into SoCs: Qualcomm Adreno (once ATI's mobile unit, an anagram of 'Radeon'), ARM Mali / Immortalis, Apple's custom GPUs, Samsung Xclipse (AMD RDNA-based).

#Storage — core concepts

Where your files live when the power is off. The key thing to keep straight: form factor (shape), interface (SATA / NVMe) and media (spinning disk / flash) are three separate things.

#HDD vs SSD

Current

An HDD stores data magnetically on spinning platters read by a moving head: cheap per TB, but slow and fragile. An SSD uses NAND flash chips with no moving parts. It's 5–100× faster at random access, silent and shock-resistant.

HDD random reads~0.5–2 MB/s (4K)
SATA SSD~550 MB/s sequential
PCIe 5.0 NVMe~14,000 MB/s sequential

Fun fact: Swapping an old laptop's HDD for an SSD is still the single best upgrade for an aging PC.

#Form factor vs interface vs protocol

Current

Form factor = physical shape (2.5", mSATA, M.2 2280). Interface/bus = the electrical link (SATA, PCIe). Protocol = the command language (AHCI for SATA, NVMe for PCIe). One M.2 slot might support SATA, NVMe, or both.

Commonly confused with: 'M.2' is NOT a speed. An M.2 SATA SSD is no faster than a 2.5" SATA SSD.

#NAND flash types (SLC / MLC / TLC / QLC / PLC)

Current

How many bits each flash cell stores: SLC 1, MLC 2, TLC 3, QLC 4, PLC 5 (experimental). More bits = cheaper and denser, but slower and less durable.

Typical consumerTLC
Budget/high-capacityQLC
Endurance (P/E cycles)SLC ~100k → QLC ~1k (approx.)

Fun fact: Most SSDs use part of their TLC/QLC as a fast 'SLC cache'. Once it fills on a big copy, write speed can drop sharply.

#3D NAND (V-NAND)

2013→ Current

Flash cells stacked vertically in layers (now 200–300+). Samsung's V-NAND was first in mass production. Stacking is how SSD capacity kept growing.

#DRAM cache vs DRAM-less (HMB)

Current

Many SSDs carry a DRAM chip that holds the mapping table. Cheaper DRAM-less NVMe drives borrow a slice of system RAM via HMB (Host Memory Buffer). DRAM-less SATA drives tend to suffer most.

#TBW / DWPD (endurance)

Current

TBW = terabytes written before warranty wear-out (e.g. 600 TBW for a 1 TB TLC drive). DWPD = drive writes per day, a server metric. Normal users rarely get anywhere near TBW.

#TRIM & garbage collection

Current

TRIM lets the OS tell the SSD which blocks are free, which keeps write speed up. Defragmenting an SSD is unnecessary, and Windows runs 'Optimize' (TRIM) on SSDs instead.

#AHCI vs NVMe

2004 / 2011→ Current

AHCI was designed for spinning disks: one queue of 32 commands. NVMe was designed for flash over PCIe: up to 65,535 queues × 65,536 commands. That's why NVMe drives have much lower latency.

Commonly confused with: An NVMe drive won't show up if the BIOS slot is set to SATA-only, and vice versa.

#MBR vs GPT partitioning

1983 / 2000s Current

MBR (old BIOS style) allows up to 4 primary partitions and 2 TB disks. GPT (UEFI) allows 128 partitions and practically unlimited size. Windows 11 needs GPT + UEFI to boot.

#RAID

1987→ Current

Combining drives: RAID 0 (striping, fast, no redundancy), 1 (mirror), 5 (parity, survives 1 failure), 6 (survives 2), 10 (mirrored stripes). RAID is not a backup.

Fun fact: RAID once stood for 'Redundant Array of Inexpensive Disks'. The industry later changed it to 'Independent'.

#NAS & DAS

Current

NAS (Network Attached Storage) is a box of drives on your network (Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS). DAS (Direct Attached) connects straight to one computer by USB/Thunderbolt.

#Hard disk drives (HDD)

Spinning magnetic storage, from refrigerator-sized cabinets to matchbook-sized Microdrives.

#IBM 350 RAMAC

1956 Obsolete

The first commercial hard drive. Fifty 24-inch platters stored about 3.75 MB. Leased for roughly $3,200/month and weighed about a ton.

Fun fact: It was shipped by forklift and plane. A 1 TB microSD card holds more than 250,000× as much.

#5.25" hard drives

1980–late 1990s Obsolete

The ST-506 (Seagate, 1980, 5 MB) brought hard drives to PCs. Full-height and half-height 5.25" drives filled early IBM PC/XT/AT machines.

Fun fact: The Quantum Bigfoot (1996–1999) was a late 5.25" consumer drive found in cheap Compaq and Packard Bell PCs.

#3.5" HDD (desktop)

1983→ Current

The standard desktop/NAS hard drive. Spins at 5,400–7,200 RPM (consumer) or 10K–15K RPM (old enterprise). Capacities now exceed 30 TB.

Size101.6 × 147 × 26.1 mm
PowerSATA (12 V + 5 V)
Weight~450–700 g

Identify it: A heavy metal brick about the size of a paperback, with SATA data and power ports on one end.

#2.5" HDD (laptop)

1988→ Current

The laptop-size drive, also used in USB portable drives and consoles. Common thicknesses: 9.5 mm and 7 mm (thin laptops), with 12.5/15 mm for high-capacity models.

Size69.85 × 100 mm
RPM5,400 / 7,200
Power5 V only

Commonly confused with: A 9.5 mm drive won't fit a 7 mm bay. A 7 mm drive fits a 9.5 mm bay with a spacer.

#1.8" drives

~2003–2012 Obsolete

Tiny drives for iPod Classic, ultraportables (early MacBook Air), and some Dell/HP business laptops. Interfaces: ZIF/LIF ribbon connectors, later micro-SATA. Toshiba and Samsung made most of them.

#1" Microdrive (IBM / Hitachi)

1999–~2008 Obsolete

A tiny hard disk built into a CompactFlash Type II card, 170 MB to 8 GB. Used in cameras and the iPod mini.

Fun fact: The iPod mini's 4 GB drive was a Microdrive, and people pulled them out to use as cheap CF cards.

#RPM (spindle speed)

Current

5,400 RPM: quiet, low-power, cool (laptops, NAS 'green' drives). 7,200: mainstream desktop. 10,000–15,000: old enterprise SAS/SCSI and the WD Raptor/VelociRaptor enthusiast line.

#CMR vs SMR

2010s→ Current

CMR (Conventional Magnetic Recording) writes tracks side by side. SMR (Shingled) overlaps them like roof shingles: more capacity, but very slow sustained rewrites, which is bad for RAID/NAS.

Fun fact: In 2020 WD was caught selling SMR drives in its 'Red' NAS line without saying so. Red Plus now marks the CMR models.

#Helium-filled drives

2013→ Current

Sealed drives filled with helium, which has less drag than air, so more platters fit (up to 10–11). HGST launched them. Nearly all 12 TB+ drives use helium.

#HAMR / MAMR

2020s→ Current

Energy-assisted recording that allows denser data: HAMR (heat, Seagate Mozaic 3+, 30 TB+) and MAMR (microwave, Toshiba/WD ePMR variants).

#Head crash, click of death & head parking

Current

A head crash is the read head touching the platter, usually terminal. The 'click of death' is a failing drive's repeated head-seek clicking. Heads park off the platters when idle or powered down.

#Hybrid drives (SSHD) & Fusion Drive

2010–~2020 Legacy

HDDs with a small flash cache (8–32 GB) for frequently used files: Seagate Momentus XT / FireCuda. Apple's Fusion Drive paired a separate SSD with an HDD in software.

#Storage interfaces & connectors

How drives talk to the computer. This is where SATA vs mSATA vs M.2 gets confusing, so the diagrams below show them side by side.

Storage form factors — drawn to scale (2 px = 1 mm)

mSATA is a bare card, about 30 mm wide. An M.2 card is 22 mm wide, and the 4-digit name gives width then length (2280 = 22 mm × 80 mm).

mSATA vs Mini PCIe vs M.2 — drawn at 3 px = 1 mm

mSATA and Mini PCIe use the same card shape and the same connector, but they carry different signals. An mSATA SSD only works in a slot wired for mSATA. M.2 is longer and narrower, and its connector isn't compatible with either.

#ST-506 / ST-412 (MFM & RLL)

1980–~1990 Obsolete

The first PC hard-drive interface. A separate controller card connected to the drive with two ribbon cables (34-pin control, 20-pin data). MFM vs RLL were encoding schemes, and RLL squeezed out about 50% more capacity.

Fun fact: You had to type the drive's geometry (cylinders, heads, sectors) into BIOS by hand, often off a sticker on the drive.

#ESDI

1983–early 1990s Obsolete

A faster successor to ST-506 for high-end PCs and workstations. Same two-cable idea. IDE and SCSI replaced it quickly.

#PATA / IDE / ATA

1986–~2008 Obsolete

Parallel ATA, also called IDE (Integrated Drive Electronics, because the controller sat on the drive). A wide 40-pin ribbon cable, two devices per cable, a 4-pin Molex for power. Speeds from ATA-33 to ATA-133 (UDMA/133).

Cable40-pin, 40-wire (old) or 80-wire (UDMA/66+)
Max133 MB/s
Devices/channel2 (Master + Slave)

Identify it: A flat grey ribbon cable about 5 cm wide, often with a red stripe marking pin 1.

Commonly confused with: PATA vs SATA: SATA is the thin serial cable that replaced it in the mid-2000s.

#Master / Slave / Cable Select jumpers

1986–~2008 Obsolete

Each IDE channel had two drives: one set Master, one Slave by a small plastic jumper on the drive's pins. CS (Cable Select) let the cable position decide. Two Masters on one cable = neither drive detected.

Fun fact: A huge share of 1990s 'my new drive doesn't show up' problems came down to one jumper.

#EIDE / ATAPI / CompactFlash-IDE

1994→ Obsolete

EIDE (Western Digital) added a second channel (4 devices total) and support for bigger drives. ATAPI let CD-ROMs share the IDE bus. CompactFlash is electrically IDE-compatible, so CF-to-IDE adapters make cheap SSDs for retro PCs.

#SCSI

1986–2000s Legacy

Small Computer System Interface (said 'scuzzy'). A daisy chain of up to 7 or 15 devices, each needing a unique ID and the chain needing termination at the end. Used in servers, Macs (until 1998) and scanners.

VariantsSCSI-1 → Fast → Wide → Ultra → Ultra2 → Ultra160 → Ultra320
Connectors50-pin Centronics, DB-25 (Mac), HD50, HD68, SCA-80

Fun fact: SCSI troubleshooting was so painful that people joked about 'SCSI voodoo' and sacrificing a goat to the termination gods.

#SAS (Serial Attached SCSI)

2004→ Current

The serial successor to SCSI for servers: 3/6/12/24 Gb/s, dual-port for redundancy. SAS controllers accept SATA drives, but SATA controllers can't run SAS drives.

Identify it: Like a SATA drive, but the data and power connectors are joined by a bridge of plastic (no gap).

#SATA (Serial ATA)

2003→ Current

The thin 7-pin data cable that replaced IDE. One drive per cable, and hot-swap capable. Revisions: SATA I (1.5 Gb/s ≈ 150 MB/s), SATA II (3 Gb/s ≈ 300 MB/s), SATA III (6 Gb/s ≈ 600 MB/s, ~550 MB/s real).

Data plug7-pin L-shaped
Power plug15-pin L-shaped (3.3/5/12 V)
Used by2.5"/3.5" drives, optical drives

Identify it: Two L-shaped connectors on the drive edge: a short one (data) and a long one (power).

Commonly confused with: 'SATA 3' (6 Gb/s revision) vs 'SATA 3.x' (spec versions). Also: SATA cables and SATA power are different plugs.

#mSATA (mini-SATA)

2009–~2015 Legacy

A bare-card SATA SSD with no case, using the Mini PCIe card shape and its 52-pin edge connector, but carrying SATA signals. Found in ultrabooks (~2011–2013), early Lenovo ThinkPads (as cache drives), Dell/HP business laptops, mini-PCs and industrial boxes.

Size (full)30 × 50.95 mm (half-size ~30 × 26.8 mm)
InterfaceSATA (up to SATA III, ~550 MB/s)
ConnectorMini PCIe-style 52-pin edge, single notch
Mounting2 screws at the far corners

Identify it: A small green card about 3 × 5 cm with gold contacts on one short edge. It's wider and shorter than M.2, with two screw cut-outs (M.2 has one). Labels usually say 'mSATA'.

Commonly confused with: Mini PCIe cards (Wi-Fi, WWAN) are physically identical but carry PCIe/USB signals. Some slots support both, many don't. M.2 is narrower (22 mm), longer and uses a different connector, so it doesn't fit an mSATA slot without an adapter.

Fun fact: mSATA lasted only a few years: M.2 (2013–2014) replaced it because it was thinner and could also carry PCIe/NVMe.

#Regular SATA SSD (2.5")

2008→ Current

The same SATA interface as mSATA in a 2.5" plastic/metal case with standard SATA data + power connectors. It's the drop-in HDD replacement.

Speed~550 MB/s (same ceiling as mSATA)
Thicknessusually 7 mm (+2.5 mm spacer)

Commonly confused with: 2.5" SATA SSD vs mSATA: same speed and same protocol, different shape and connector. An mSATA→2.5" adapter enclosure exists.

#eSATA / eSATAp

2004–~2015 Obsolete

eSATA = external SATA for docks and external drives, with a shielded connector and no power. eSATAp ('Power over eSATA', also eSATA/USB combo) combined eSATA with a USB port that also carried power.

Identify it: It looks like a flattened USB port but without the inner tongue. eSATAp ports often say 'eSATA/USB'.

Fun fact: USB 3.0 (2008) ended eSATA's speed advantage almost overnight.

#SATA Express

2013–~2016 Obsolete

A short-lived connector combining two SATA ports with PCIe ×2 lanes for faster drives. Almost no drives were ever sold for it, and M.2 won.

Identify it: On some 2014–2016 motherboards: two SATA ports with a small extra connector beside them.

#SATA DOM (Disk on Module)

2000s→ Legacy

A tiny SSD that plugs straight into a SATA port with no cable, powered by pin 7 (on supporting boards) or a small power lead. Used in servers, firewalls and embedded/industrial boxes as boot drives.

Identify it: A thumb-sized module sticking straight up from a SATA port.

Commonly confused with: It's not a USB stick, even though it looks like one.

#M.2 (NGFF)

2013→ Current

The 'Next Generation Form Factor': a slim bare card that can carry SATA, PCIe/NVMe, USB or other signals. Used for SSDs, Wi-Fi cards and modems. The size code is width + length in mm: 2230, 2242, 2260, 2280 (most common), 22110.

Width22 mm (almost always)
Lengths30 / 42 / 60 / 80 / 110 mm
KeysB, M, B+M (storage); A, E (Wi-Fi)
Mountingone screw or latch at the end

Identify it: A long thin stick of gum with chips on it, one notched gold edge, and a half-circle screw notch at the other end.

Commonly confused with: M.2 SATA (B+M key, ~550 MB/s) vs M.2 NVMe (M key, 2,000–14,000 MB/s). Same shape, very different speed. Check which your slot supports.

#M.2 2230 / 2242 (short M.2)

Current

Short M.2 drives used in the Steam Deck, ROG Ally, Microsoft Surface, many thin laptops and mini PCs.

Fun fact: The Steam Deck made 2230 NVMe drives a popular retail product almost overnight.

#NVMe SSD

2011 (spec) / ~2015 consumer Current

Flash storage speaking NVMe over PCIe lanes, usually in M.2 form. Generations follow PCIe: Gen3 ×4 ≈ 3.5 GB/s, Gen4 ≈ 7 GB/s, Gen5 ≈ 14 GB/s.

Fun fact: Samsung's 950 Pro (2015) was one of the first widely sold consumer M.2 NVMe drives.

#PCIe add-in-card (AIC) SSD

2010s→ Legacy

An SSD shaped like an expansion card that plugs into a PCIe slot (OCZ RevoDrive, Intel 750, Optane 905P). Also: passive M.2-to-PCIe adapter cards.

#U.2 (SFF-8639)

2015→ Current

A 2.5" enterprise NVMe drive with a combined connector that also accepts SATA/SAS. Hot-swappable in servers. Also in a few prosumer drives (Intel 750 U.2).

Identify it: A 2.5" drive, usually 15 mm thick, with a connector that has an extra row of pins on the back of the key bridge.

#U.3

2019→ Current

A tri-mode revision of U.2: one backplane bay handles SAS, SATA or NVMe.

#EDSFF (E1.S, E1.L, E3.S, E3.L)

2017→ Current

'Ruler' data-centre SSD formats built for density and airflow. E1.L 'rulers' are 318 mm long. Intel started it, and it's now an industry standard replacing U.2.

#Intel Optane (3D XPoint)

2017–2022 Obsolete

Non-NAND memory (Intel & Micron) with extremely low latency and huge endurance. Sold as M.2 cache modules (16/32 GB), SSDs (900P/905P, P5800X) and Optane DIMMs (persistent memory). Discontinued in 2022.

Commonly confused with: 'Intel Optane memory' modules were small caches for a hard drive, not RAM and not a normal SSD.

#NVMe-oF / Thunderbolt NVMe enclosures

Current

External NVMe: USB 3.2 (~1,000 MB/s), USB 3.2 2×2 (~2,000), USB4 / Thunderbolt 3/4/5 (~3,000–6,000+ MB/s).

M.2 edge connectors: where the notch ("key") sits

Schematic: the gold edge, the 75 pin positions, and the pins removed for each key. A card's notches have to match the socket's key. B+M cards are usually SATA, and M-only cards are usually NVMe.

SATA connectors (face view, schematic)

A 2.5" or 3.5" SATA drive takes two plugs: the narrow L-shaped data plug and the wide L-shaped power plug. mSATA and M.2 cards get both through their edge connector, so they need no cables.

#Optical drives & discs

Data read by laser from pits on a spinning disc.

#CD-ROM

1985 (PC) Obsolete

Compact Disc Read-Only Memory: ~650–700 MB. '1×' = 150 KB/s, drives reached 52×. Before ATAPI, drives often hung off a sound card (Sound Blaster/Panasonic/Mitsumi interfaces).

Fun fact: Encyclopedias, Myst (1993) and Encarta made the CD-ROM essential, a 'multimedia PC' requirement.

#CD-R / CD-RW

1990s Obsolete

Recordable (once) and ReWritable CDs. 'Burning' was huge in the 2000s. Buffer underruns ruined discs (coasters) until BURN-Proof technology.

#DVD (±R, ±RW, RAM, DL)

1996→ Legacy

4.7 GB single-layer, 8.5 GB dual-layer. Rival recordable formats DVD-R (Pioneer/DVD Forum) and DVD+R (Philips/Sony) were both settled by 'DVD±RW' drives. DVD-RAM was used in cartridges and camcorders.

1×1.385 MB/s
Max drive speed~24×

#Blu-ray (BD)

2006→ Current

Blue-violet 405 nm laser: 25 GB per layer, up to 100–128 GB (BDXL). Ultra HD Blu-ray for 4K. Won the format war against HD DVD in 2008.

Fun fact: The PS3's built-in Blu-ray drive is widely credited with winning the format war.

#HD DVD

2006–2008 Obsolete

Toshiba's Blu-ray rival: 15 GB per layer. Discontinued in February 2008 after Warner Bros. went Blu-ray-only. Microsoft sold an Xbox 360 add-on drive.

#Slim, slot-load & ultra-slim drives

Legacy

Laptop drives: 12.7 mm slim and 9.5 mm ultra-slim, with tray or slot-loading. A 'caddy' adapter lets you swap the drive for a 2.5" SSD/HDD.

Identify it: Slim drives use a single compact slimline SATA (or older 50-pin slim IDE) connector.

#LightScribe / LabelFlash

2004–~2013 Obsolete

Drives that could laser-etch a grayscale label on special discs. Slow, but beloved for mixtapes.

#Magneto-optical (MO) & MiniDisc data

1985–2000s Obsolete

Rewritable optical cartridges (128 MB–9.1 GB) used in Japan and in archiving. The NeXT Computer (1988) used a 256 MB MO drive as its main storage.

Fun fact: Sony's Hi-MD MiniDisc (2004) could store 1 GB of computer data.

#Floppies, removable drives & tape

The sneakernet era: moving data on things you could put in your pocket (or a truck).

#Punched cards

1890–1980s Obsolete

80-column IBM cards stored programs and data, one line per card. Herman Hollerith's punch cards ran the 1890 US Census, and his company later became part of IBM.

Fun fact: The 80-character line width of many terminals and coding styles comes from the 80-column card.

#8" floppy disk

1971–1980s Obsolete

IBM's original floppy (80 KB, read-only at first, later ~1.2 MB). Used on CP/M machines and word processors.

Fun fact: The US nuclear command system used 8" floppies until 2019.

#5.25" floppy

1976–1990s Obsolete

The truly 'floppy' disk: 160/180/360 KB (DD) up to 1.2 MB (HD). Write-protect by covering a notch with a sticker. People cut a second notch to make 'flippy' double-sided disks.

#3.5" floppy

1982–2010s Obsolete

Hard plastic shell with a metal shutter. 720 KB DD and 1.44 MB HD (most common), plus a rare 2.88 MB ED. The Mac (1984) helped popularise it.

Identify it: A square about 9 × 9 cm. HD disks have a second hole opposite the write-protect slider.

Fun fact: The 'Save' icon is still a 3.5" floppy. Sony made the last ones in 2011.

#Floppy drive interface (34-pin)

Obsolete

PC floppy drives used a 34-pin ribbon cable with a twist in it: the drive after the twist became A:, before the twist B:. Power came from the small 4-pin Berg connector.

#Iomega Zip drive

1994–2003 Obsolete

Removable 100 MB disks (later 250/750 MB) in parallel, SCSI, IDE and USB versions. Hugely popular for moving files around.

Fun fact: The 'Click of Death' (a drive repeatedly clicking and then ruining disks) led to a class action lawsuit.

#Iomega Jaz

1995–2002 Obsolete

A removable 1 GB / 2 GB hard-disk cartridge for graphic designers and video editors. SCSI-only. Notoriously unreliable.

#SyQuest cartridges

1982–1998 Obsolete

Removable hard-disk cartridges (44/88/200 MB, EZ135, SyJet) that ruled pre-press and design studios before Zip and Jaz.

#SuperDisk LS-120 / LS-240

1997–2003 Obsolete

120 MB (later 240 MB) magnetic disks whose drives could also read regular 1.44 MB floppies. Imation/Panasonic, found in some Compaq and Gateway PCs.

#Iomega Clik! / PocketZip

1999–2003 Obsolete

Tiny 40 MB disks for cameras and handhelds, about the size of a matchbook.

#Iomega REV

2004–2010 Obsolete

Removable 35–120 GB hard-disk cartridges for small-business backup.

#Tape drives (QIC, Travan, DAT/DDS, DLT, AIT)

1970s–2000s Obsolete

Cartridge tape for backups. QIC/Travan for PCs, DAT/DDS (4 mm digital audio tape), DLT and AIT for servers. Slow sequential access but cheap per GB.

#LTO (Linear Tape-Open)

2000→ Current

Modern enterprise tape: LTO-9 holds 18 TB native (45 TB compressed) per cartridge. Used by hyperscalers and film studios for archive and ransomware-proof air-gapped backup.

Fun fact: Tape is still the cheapest per TB for long-term cold storage and lasts ~30 years on a shelf.

#Cassette tape (home computers)

1977–1980s Obsolete

Commodore Datasette, ZX Spectrum and TRS-80 loaded programs from ordinary audio cassettes, with loading times measured in minutes.

#Memory cards (SD, microSD, CompactFlash…)

Removable flash cards for cameras, phones, consoles and computers. USB flash drives have their own section below.

#CompactFlash (CF)

1994→ Legacy

SanDisk's card format: Type I (3.3 mm) and Type II (5 mm). Electrically IDE-compatible, so it's a cheap SSD for retro PCs. Long-time pro DSLR standard.

Size43 × 36 mm

#SmartMedia

1995–2002 Obsolete

A thin card with no controller (raw NAND). Max 128 MB. Used by Olympus and Fujifilm cameras before xD.

#MultiMediaCard (MMC)

1997→ Obsolete

SD's predecessor, the same size but thinner. Most SD slots still accept MMC.

#On-board eMMC chip (embedded MultiMediaCard)

Storage · 2006→ Legacy

eMMC puts the MMC memory-card idea into one chip soldered onto the motherboard: NAND flash plus its own small controller in a single BGA package, talking over a simple 8-bit parallel bus. It's cheap and small, so it's used in budget laptops and Chromebooks, cheap tablets, Android TV boxes, smart TVs, routers, car infotainment systems, single-board computers (Raspberry Pi Compute Module, Orange Pi) and older or budget phones. The catch: it's slow compared with an SSD (eMMC 5.1 reads at about 250–400 MB/s and writes far slower, with weak random speed), it usually can't be upgraded, and when it wears out or dies the device often won't boot at all.

StandardJEDEC eMMC 4.x → 5.1 (2015, latest common)
Bus8-bit parallel, HS400 mode (up to ~400 MB/s)
Typical sizes16–256 GB
PackageSmall BGA chip, e.g. 11.5 × 13 mm (153 or 169 balls)
SuccessorUFS (phones), NVMe/BGA SSD (laptops)

Identify it: A small black square chip on the board, often near the CPU, printed with a maker and part number: Samsung KLM…, SanDisk/WD SDIN… or SDINBDG4…, Kioxia/Toshiba THGB…, SK hynix H26M…, Kingston EMMC…, Micron MTFC…. There's no M.2 slot or SATA connector.

Commonly confused with: eMMC vs SSD (an SSD has a fast PCIe/SATA controller and many flash chips in parallel) · eMMC vs UFS (UFS is a faster serial successor in phones) · eMMC vs microSD (removable card, also slow)

Fun fact: Some boards (Odroid, Pine64, Radxa) use removable eMMC modules on a tiny connector, which are faster and more reliable than microSD. If a cheap laptop says 'Storage: 64 GB', check whether it's eMMC: Windows updates alone can fill it.

#SD / SDHC / SDXC / SDUC

1999→ Current

Secure Digital cards. SD ≤ 2 GB, SDHC ≤ 32 GB, SDXC ≤ 2 TB, SDUC ≤ 128 TB. Bus speeds: Default, High Speed, UHS-I, UHS-II (extra row of pins), UHS-III, SD Express (PCIe/NVMe).

Size32 × 24 × 2.1 mm

Commonly confused with: An SDXC card needs an SDXC-capable reader. Old SD-only readers won't see it.

#miniSD

2003–~2008 Obsolete

A middle size (21.5 × 20 mm) used in mid-2000s phones. microSD replaced it quickly.

#microSD (TransFlash)

2005→ Current

Fingernail-sized flash (15 × 11 mm) from SanDisk's TransFlash. Used in phones, Nintendo Switch, drones, action cams and Raspberry Pi. Up to 2 TB.

Identify it: Look for rating symbols: C10, U1/U3, V30/V60/V90 (video), A1/A2 (app performance).

#SD speed classes

Current

Class 2/4/6/10 (MB/s minimum), UHS U1 (10 MB/s) / U3 (30 MB/s), Video V6–V90 (MB/s), A1/A2 (random IOPS for running apps).

#Memory Stick (Sony)

1998–~2010 Obsolete

Sony's proprietary family: Memory Stick, Pro, Duo, Pro Duo, Pro-HG, and the tiny Micro (M2). Used in PSP, Cyber-shot cameras and Sony Ericsson phones.

Fun fact: Sony gave in and added microSD support to its phones and cameras from about 2010.

#xD-Picture Card

2002–~2010 Obsolete

Olympus and Fujifilm's proprietary card. Small and slow, max 2 GB in practice.

#CFast

2008→ Legacy

CompactFlash shape with a SATA interface. Used in cinema cameras (Blackmagic, Canon C300 II).

#XQD

2012→ Legacy

A Sony/SanDisk/Nikon PCIe-based card. Nikon Z and Sony pro cameras. CFexpress Type B uses the same shape.

#CFexpress (Type A / B / C)

2017→ Current

Current pro camera cards built on PCIe + NVMe. Type A (Sony, small), Type B (XQD-sized, most common), Type C (large). Up to ~3,500 MB/s.

Commonly confused with: A CFexpress Type B card fits XQD slots (with a firmware update) but not CompactFlash slots.

#UFS card

2016–~2020 Obsolete

A Samsung removable UFS card, faster than microSD. It never caught on.

#USB flash drives (thumb drives, pen drives, USB sticks)

The pocket-sized drive everyone owns. Also called a flash disk, memory stick or, in Arabic, فلاشة / فلاش ميموري. How they work, how fast they really are, and how to avoid fakes and data loss.

#USB flash drive

2000→ Current

Flash memory (NAND) plus a small controller chip with a USB plug, in one tiny case. It needs no power supply and works in almost any computer, TV, car stereo or console. Capacities run from a few GB to 1–2 TB, with USB-A, USB-C or both plugs.

InsideUSB controller + NAND flash chip(s) + crystal
PlugsUSB-A, USB-C, dual A+C, micro-USB, Lightning
Typical sizes32 GB – 1 TB

Identify it: A blue plastic tongue inside a USB-A plug usually means USB 3.x. Black or white usually means USB 2.0.

Commonly confused with: Not the same as a portable SSD. Flash drives are smaller and cheaper, but usually much slower at writing and less durable.

#Who invented it?

1999–2000 Concept

Several companies filed early patents and claim it: Israel's M-Systems (the DiskOnKey, sold by IBM in 2000 with 8 MB), Singapore's Trek 2000 (the ThumbDrive, also 2000), and China's Netac. 8 MB was more than five floppy disks, and within a few years flash drives killed the floppy (see 'Floppies, removable drives & tape' above).

Fun fact: M-Systems was bought by SanDisk in 2006, and SanDisk later by Western Digital. SanDisk was spun off again as a separate company in 2025.

#Fake-capacity flash drives

Guide

A very common scam: a drive sold as 1 TB or 2 TB for a tiny price has a hacked controller that reports the big size but really holds 8–64 GB. Files seem to copy fine, but anything beyond the real size silently overwrites earlier data, and you only find out when files won't open. Test every new drive by filling it completely and reading it back with H2testw (Windows) or F3 (Mac/Linux). Buy from the brand's official store or a reputable shop.

Identify it: Red flags: a famous brand at a fraction of the normal price, odd brand names, '2TB' drives costing less than a meal, and sellers with no reviews.

#Do I need to 'Safely Remove' or eject?

Guide

Windows: since Windows 10 version 1809, drives use 'Quick removal' by default (no write caching), so once copying has finished you can usually just pull the drive out. Mac and Linux: eject first, because they may still be writing data in the background. Everywhere: never pull a drive while its light is blinking or a copy is running, as that can corrupt files or the whole drive.

Sources: Neowin: Microsoft says safe removal is no longer needed (1809) · gHacks: Quick Removal is the new default in Windows 10 1809

#Security: never plug in a USB drive you found

Guide

Flash drives can carry malware, and a malicious device can pretend to be a keyboard and type commands (BadUSB, shown in 2014). The Stuxnet worm spread via USB drives into isolated industrial networks. In a 2016 University of Illinois study, researchers dropped 297 drives on campus and found that people picked up and plugged in an estimated 45–98% of them, the first within minutes. Hand found drives to IT or lost-and-found instead. At work, follow your organisation's USB policy.

Sources: Tischer et al., 'Users Really Do Plug in USB Drives They Find' (IEEE S&P 2016) · Sophos: almost half of dropped USB sticks get plugged in

#Encrypting a flash drive

Guide

Flash drives get lost, so encrypt anything private. Windows: BitLocker To Go (right-click the drive → Turn on BitLocker). Pro editions can encrypt drives, and Home can unlock them. Mac: erase the drive as an encrypted APFS volume in Disk Utility, or right-click it in Finder → Encrypt. Any system: VeraCrypt (free). Hardware-encrypted drives with a keypad (Kingston IronKey, Apricorn Aegis) need no software at all.

#Lifespan, reliability & recovery

Guide

Flash cells wear out with writing, and cheap drives use low-grade chips and controllers that fail without warning. A drive left in a drawer can also lose data over the years, because flash is not an archive. Keep important files in at least two other places (the 3-2-1 backup rule: see Part 12). Deleted files can often be recovered with free tools like PhotoRec or Recuva if you stop using the drive right away. A drive that is physically broken, or no longer detected at all, needs a professional data-recovery lab.

#Buying a flash drive

Guide

Stick to known brands (SanDisk, Samsung, Kingston, Lexar, PNY, Transcend, Corsair) from official or reputable sellers, and check write speed in reviews, not just read speed. Get USB-C or dual-plug if you use an iPhone 15 or later, an Android phone or a modern laptop. iPhones open USB-C drives in the Files app. For car stereos and TVs, a small 32–64 GB drive formatted FAT32 is the most compatible. Run H2testw or F3 once on any new drive.

#Power supplies (PSU)

These convert wall AC into the DC voltages the components need: 12 V, 5 V and 3.3 V.

#ATX PSU

1995→ Current

The standard desktop power supply: 150 × 86 mm face, depth 140–200 mm. Supports soft power (the motherboard switches it on). Current spec: ATX 3.0/3.1 (2022→) with 12V-2x6 GPU power and better handling of power spikes.

Identify it: The metal box at the back (or bottom) of the case with the AC socket and a rocker switch.

#SFX / SFX-L

2000s→ Current

A small PSU for Mini-ITX builds: 125 × 63.5 × 100 mm (SFX-L is 130 mm deep with a larger, quieter fan).

#TFX / Flex ATX (1U)

Current

Long, thin PSUs for slim office desktops (TFX) and tiny cases or servers (Flex ATX).

#AT PSU

1984–late 1990s Obsolete

IBM AT-era PSU with a hard power switch wired to the case front and two 6-pin P8/P9 board connectors, plus -5 V and -12 V rails.

#ATX12VO

2019→ Current

Intel's 12 V-only spec: the PSU outputs only 12 V and the motherboard makes 5 V/3.3 V. A 10-pin board connector. Mostly used in OEM PCs (Dell, HP, Lenovo).

#80 PLUS efficiency tiers

2004→ Current

Certification for how much wall power reaches components rather than turning to heat. White (80%) → Bronze → Silver → Gold → Platinum → Titanium (~94% at 50% load, 115 V). Cybenetics (ETA/LAMBDA) is a newer, stricter rating that also covers noise.

Commonly confused with: An efficiency rating says nothing about quality or safety. Plenty of bad Gold units exist.

#Modular / semi-modular / non-modular

Current

Modular units let you detach every cable. Semi-modular fixes the 24-pin and CPU cables. Non-modular has everything permanently attached.

Commonly confused with: Never mix modular cables between brands, or even between models of the same brand. Pinouts differ, and it can destroy drives.

#24-pin ATX (main) connector

Current

The motherboard's main power plug. It started as 20-pin, and many PSUs ship a 20+4 split plug for old boards.

Fun fact: Shorting the green PS_ON wire to any black ground with a paperclip turns a PSU on for testing.

#EPS 8-pin / 4+4 CPU power

Current

Feeds the CPU VRMs. High-end boards have 8+8 or 8+4 pins. Older 4-pin 'P4' (ATX12V) connectors date from Pentium 4.

Commonly confused with: 8-pin EPS (CPU) and 8-pin PCIe (GPU) look similar but are keyed differently. Forcing the wrong one in can short the rails.

#PCIe 6-pin / 8-pin (6+2)

2004→ Current

GPU power: 6-pin = 75 W, 8-pin = 150 W. A 6+2 plug fits both kinds of socket.

#12VHPWR / 12V-2x6

2022→ Current

A 16-pin (12 power + 4 sense) GPU connector rated up to 600 W. 12V-2x6 (2023) is the safer revision. Push it in fully and avoid tight bends right at the plug.

#Molex (4-pin peripheral)

1980s→ Legacy

Big 4-pin plug (12 V yellow, 5 V red, two grounds) for IDE drives, fans and old GPUs. Hard to push in and pull out.

Fun fact: Common joke: 'Molex to SATA, lose all your data', because cheap moulded adapters can melt and catch fire.

#Berg (floppy) connector

1980s→ Obsolete

The small 4-pin plug for 3.5" floppy drives. Still found on some PSUs and fan controllers.

#SATA power

2003→ Current

15-pin L-shaped plug with 3.3, 5 and 12 V. Feeds SSDs, HDDs, optical drives and hubs.

#Laptop power: barrel jacks

1990s→ Legacy

Round DC plugs that vary by size and voltage (commonly 19–20 V). Dell, HP and Lenovo use a centre ID pin so the laptop can recognise the charger. Lenovo also used a rectangular 'slim tip'.

Commonly confused with: Same size barrel ≠ same voltage or polarity. Check the label.

#Apple MagSafe

2006→ Current

Magnetic laptop charging plugs that pop off when tripped over. MagSafe 1 (L or T plug) → MagSafe 2 (2012, thinner) → dropped for USB-C (2016) → MagSafe 3 (2021).

Commonly confused with: iPhone 'MagSafe' (2020→) is a magnetic wireless charging ring, a different product.

#USB-C Power Delivery (PD)

2014→ Current

USB PD negotiates voltage over USB-C: 5/9/15/20 V up to 100 W, and PD 3.1 EPR up to 48 V / 240 W. It's now the universal laptop and phone charging standard (and EU law for phones).

Identify it: Look for 'PD' and the wattage on the charger. 100 W+ needs a 5 A e-marked cable.

#UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply)

Current

A battery box that keeps a PC running through brief outages and gives you time to shut down. Types: standby, line-interactive and online (double-conversion). Pure sine-wave output is best for active-PFC PSUs.

#Cooling

Moving heat away from hot chips. The next four sections go deeper: heat spreaders (IHS), every kind of cooler, fans, and paste & temperatures.

#Air tower cooler

Current

Heat pipes carry heat from the base to a stack of fins with a fan blowing through. Quiet, reliable and nothing to leak (e.g. Noctua NH-D15, Thermalright Peerless Assassin).

#Top-down / low-profile cooler

Current

The fan blows down onto the board, which also cools the VRMs. Used in small cases (e.g. Noctua NH-L9).

#Stock cooler

Current

The cooler bundled with a CPU (Intel Laminar, AMD Wraith). Adequate for mid chips, loud on high-end ones.

#AIO liquid cooler

2008→ Current

All-in-one closed loop: pump + cold plate on the CPU, tubes to a radiator with fans. Sizes: 120 / 240 / 280 / 360 / 420 mm.

Fun fact: Mounting an AIO with the pump as the highest point traps air, which causes gurgling and early pump wear.

#Custom water loop

Current

A user-built loop of reservoir, pump, CPU/GPU blocks, radiators, fittings and coolant. Peak cooling and looks, but needs maintenance.

#Thermal paste / pads / liquid metal / PTM

Current

Thermal paste fills microscopic gaps between chip and cooler. Liquid metal (gallium-based) conducts much better but is electrically conductive and eats aluminium. Pads suit uneven gaps (VRAM, VRMs). PTM7950 is a phase-change pad that melts into place.

Fun fact: A pea-sized dot of paste is plenty. The cooler's pressure spreads it out.

#Fans: 3-pin DC vs 4-pin PWM

Current

3-pin fans change speed by voltage. 4-pin PWM fans switch on and off rapidly at full voltage, which controls them more precisely. Sizes: 80, 92, 120, 140, 200 mm. Fans differ in airflow vs static pressure (pressure matters for radiators).

Fun fact: Noctua's beige-and-brown fan colour scheme is famously 'ugly' yet so loved that their later all-black chromax line was a major event.

#Airflow: positive vs negative pressure

Current

More intake than exhaust (positive) keeps dust out because air leaves through every gap. Negative pressure pulls dust in through unfiltered cracks.

#Vapor chamber

Current

A flat, sealed heat pipe that spreads heat across a wide area. Used in GPUs, gaming laptops and flagship phones.

#Peltier / TEC & phase-change

Legacy

Thermoelectric and refrigeration coolers that can go below room temperature. Risk of condensation. Mostly extreme overclocking (along with LN2).

#Heat spreaders (IHS), delidding & the heat path

How heat gets from the chip into the air, and what the metal lid on a CPU is for.

#IHS (Integrated Heat Spreader)

2000→ Current

The metal lid on top of a desktop CPU, the part with the brand and model printed on it. It's nickel-plated copper. Under it sits the tiny silicon die that actually makes the heat. The IHS protects the die from cracking when you tighten a cooler and spreads the heat from a small hot spot over a bigger area the cooler can grab. Between die and IHS is TIM1 (solder or paste, done at the factory); between IHS and cooler is TIM2, the paste you apply.

MaterialNickel-plated copper
Under itTIM1: indium solder (most modern AMD and Intel K chips) or polymer paste (cheaper chips, Intel 2012–2018)
Without oneLaptop CPUs, GPUs, phone chips and Apple M-series are 'bare die' (the cooler touches the chip directly)
AMD AM5 shape'Octopus' lid with cut-outs for capacitors, kept the same height as AM4 so old coolers fit

Identify it: The shiny silver square on top of a desktop CPU with the logo and model number etched on it

Commonly confused with: The die (the silicon underneath) and the cooler's base (the copper plate that touches the IHS)

Fun fact: Before heat spreaders, Athlon XP and Pentium III owners cracked the corners of bare dies by tightening coolers unevenly, so people sold copper 'shims' to protect them.

#Soldered vs pasted IHS (TIM1)

Concept

Solder (indium) between die and lid conducts heat very well and lasts for the life of the chip. Polymer paste is cheaper but conducts worse. Intel used paste on its mainstream chips from Ivy Bridge (3rd gen, 2012) to 8th gen, which made them run hot and started the delidding craze; the i9-9900K (2018) and later K-series went back to solder. AMD Ryzen desktop CPUs are soldered (some early APUs used paste).

Commonly confused with: TIM1 (factory, under the lid) vs TIM2 (your paste, on top of the lid)

#Delidding

2012→ Guide

Removing the IHS to replace the TIM1 with liquid metal, or to cool the die directly. On pasted Intel chips it dropped temperatures by 10–20 °C. You use a special delid tool (a vice that slides the lid off) rather than a razor blade. It voids the warranty, and on soldered chips it's far riskier and gains much less. Today it's mostly for extreme overclockers.

Commonly confused with: Delidding (removing the lid) vs 'direct-die' cooling (running the cooler on the bare die afterwards, with a special frame)

#Bare die / direct-die

Current

Chips with no IHS: laptop CPUs, graphics cards, consoles, phones and Apple Silicon. The cooler touches the silicon directly, which cools better but means mounting pressure must be even. That's why GPU and laptop coolers use spring screws in a set order.

Identify it: A shiny dark rectangle of silicon (sometimes several) sitting on a green or brown board, with small components around it

#Contact frames & CPU bending (LGA1700 / LGA1851)

2021→ Guide

On Intel 12th–14th gen and Core Ultra boards, the socket's stock clamp (the ILM) can press unevenly and slightly bend the long CPU, leaving a gap in the middle of the IHS and raising temperatures a few degrees. A cheap aftermarket contact frame replaces the clamp and spreads the pressure evenly. Install carefully and check your warranty.

#Lapping

Legacy

Sanding the IHS or cooler base perfectly flat and mirror-smooth on fine sandpaper. It can gain a couple of degrees but removes the printing and the warranty. Rarely worth it with modern coolers.

#Every kind of cooler

From the free cooler in the CPU box to custom water loops, plus coolers for GPUs, laptops, phones, servers, SSDs and RAM.

#Heatsinks & heat pipes

Concept

A heatsink is a block of metal with many thin fins to give lots of surface to the air. Aluminium is light and cheap; copper conducts heat about 1.7× better but is heavy and pricey, so good coolers use a copper base and heat pipes with aluminium fins. A heat pipe is a sealed copper tube with a little water inside at low pressure and a wick on the inner wall: the water boils at the hot end, the vapour flows to the cool fins and condenses, and the wick pulls the liquid back. It moves heat far better than solid copper. Direct-touch (HDT) coolers press the heat pipes straight onto the CPU; others solder them into a flat copper base.

Fun fact: Heat pipes contain mostly water, yet they work because the low pressure inside makes it boil at well below 100 °C.

#AIO liquid coolers in depth

Guide

Parts: a cold plate + pump on the CPU (some new designs put the pump in the radiator or tubing), two tubes, and a radiator with fans. Coolant slowly escapes through the tubes over the years, so AIOs last roughly 5–7 years. Mount the radiator so the pump isn't the highest point (top-mounted or front-mounted with tubes at the bottom is best). Plug the pump into the AIO_PUMP header or set that header to full speed: a slow pump makes the CPU overheat.

Identify it: Two rubber tubes running from a block on the CPU to a radiator on the top or front of the case

Commonly confused with: AIO cooler (liquid cooler) vs AIO PC (computer built into a monitor)

#Custom water loops

Guide

A loop you build: pump + reservoir (D5 or DDC pumps), water blocks for CPU and GPU, radiators, soft or hard tubing, G1/4" fittings and coolant. Don't mix aluminium with copper/brass in one loop (galvanic corrosion). Leak-test with the PC unplugged for 12–24 hours using only the pump, and plan on draining and cleaning about once a year.

#Laptop & mini-PC cooling tips

Guide

Use it on a hard, flat surface (not a bed or lap), keep the vents clear, and blow out dust every few months. Windows power modes and the maker's app (performance / balanced / quiet) change fan behaviour a lot. Fanless laptops like the MacBook Air have no fan at all: they slow down slightly under long heavy loads instead of getting loud.

#Fans in depth: sizes, connectors, bearings & specs

Everything printed on a fan box, and how to choose and connect fans.

#Fan direction, curves & hubs

Guide

Air blows out of the side with the frame struts (the side with the label). Small arrows on the frame show airflow and spin direction. Set fan curves in the BIOS or software: quiet at idle, faster under load, with a little delay (hysteresis) so fans don't keep revving up and down. Too many fans for your headers? A fan hub or PWM splitter powered from SATA runs several fans from one header.

Commonly confused with: Normal vs reverse-blade fans: reverse fans blow the other way so the nice side faces you (used at the bottom or back of glass cases)
