Fun fact: GPUs often stop their fans completely at idle ('zero RPM mode'); a still GPU fan on the desktop isn't broken.

#Famous fans

Current

Noctua NF-A12x25 and its 2025 G2 version (the reference for quality; the brown-beige look), Arctic P12 / P14 (cheap, great value), Phanteks T30 (30 mm thick, very strong), be quiet! Silent Wings (quiet), Lian Li UNI FAN (snap together, fewer cables), Corsair and Thermalright RGB fans (looks).

#Thermal paste, temperatures & troubleshooting

Applying paste, what temperatures are normal, and fixing a PC that runs too hot.

#How to apply thermal paste

Guide

1. Clean the old paste off the IHS and cooler with isopropyl alcohol (90%+) and a lint-free cloth. 2. Remove the plastic film from the cooler base (the classic mistake). 3. Apply a pea-sized dot in the centre, or an X or five dots for big CPUs like Threadripper or long Intel chips. 4. Place the cooler straight down and tighten the screws a little at a time in a cross pattern. Too much paste is messy but rarely harmful with non-conductive paste; too little leaves bare spots. Repaste every 3–5 years or if temperatures creep up.

Commonly confused with: Thermal paste vs thermal adhesive (glue that sets permanently: never use it on a CPU)

Fun fact: People really have tried toothpaste and chocolate as thermal paste for videos. It 'works' for a few minutes and then dries out.

#Cooling in hot, dusty climates (Gulf tips)

Guide

In Riyadh-style summers the room can be 30 °C or more even with air conditioning set high, and every degree of room temperature adds a degree to your parts. Fine desert dust clogs fins and filters fast. Use cases with dust filters on every intake and run slight positive pressure; clean filters monthly and blow out the PC every 3–6 months (more after dust storms). Undervolting (in the BIOS for desktops, or with the vendor tool for laptops and GPUs) cuts heat a lot for almost no performance loss. Keep consoles and PCs out of closed TV cabinets.

#Cases & chassis

The enclosure: size, airflow and what fits inside.

#Full tower

Current

Fits E-ATX/XL-ATX, many drives and big radiators. Often 55+ cm tall.

#Mid tower

Current

The most common ATX case (~45–50 cm tall). Fits most GPUs and 360 mm radiators.

#Mini tower / Micro-ATX case

Current

Compact case for mATX boards. Very common in office and prebuilt PCs.

#SFF (small form factor) / ITX cases

Current

Tiny cases for Mini-ITX, roughly 4–20 L (e.g. Dan A4, NR200, Fractal Terra). Often use a PCIe riser cable to mount the GPU sandwich-style.

Fun fact: SFF builders measure cases in litres, and anything under 10 L counts as impressive.

#Desktop / slim / pizza box

1980s→ Legacy

Horizontal cases that the monitor sits on. The IBM PC, early Macs (e.g. Mac LC 'pizza box'), Sun SPARCstations and office slimlines.

#All-in-one (AIO) PC

1977→ Current

Computer and screen in one unit: Commodore PET (1977), the original Macintosh, iMac (1998→), HP/Dell/Lenovo AIOs.

Commonly confused with: An 'AIO' PC is not an 'AIO' liquid cooler.

#HTPC case

Legacy

Home Theater PC cases shaped like AV components to sit under the TV.

#Rackmount (1U / 2U / 4U)

Current

Server chassis for 19" racks. 1U = 1.75 in (44.45 mm) tall. Deep, loud and built for front-to-back airflow.

#Open-frame / test bench

Current

No panels at all, for testing parts or showing off a build.

#Dual-chamber / 'fish tank' cases

2020→ Current

Glass-front, no-pillar cases with the PSU and drives in a rear chamber (e.g. Lian Li O11, Hyte Y60). Built to show off RGB.

#Drive bays (5.25" / 3.5" / 2.5")

Legacy

External 5.25" bays held optical drives and front-panel gadgets. Most modern cases have dropped them, and sometimes 3.5" bays too.

#Expansion buses & slots

Slots for adding cards (graphics, sound, network and more), from the IBM PC to PCIe 6.0.

#ISA (8-bit / 16-bit)

1981–~2000 Obsolete

Industry Standard Architecture from the IBM PC (8-bit, 1981) and PC/AT (16-bit, 1984). About 8 MHz. Cards needed manual IRQ/DMA/IO jumpers until Plug and Play (PnP ISA) arrived.

Identify it: Long black slots, the 16-bit version with a second short segment.

Fun fact: Sound Blaster settings like 'A220 I5 D1' were ISA resources you set with jumpers and typed into DOS games.

#MCA (Micro Channel Architecture)

1987–mid 1990s Obsolete

IBM's proprietary 32-bit bus in its PS/2 line. Technically ahead (software configuration, bus mastering), but IBM charged licence fees, so clone makers went with EISA instead. A major reason IBM lost control of the PC market.

Fun fact: MCA cards came with 'reference diskettes' holding their configuration files.

#EISA

1988–late 1990s Obsolete

Extended ISA: a 32-bit bus from the 'Gang of Nine' clone makers (Compaq and others) to rival MCA. Backwards-compatible with ISA cards. Mostly servers.

#VLB (VESA Local Bus)

1992–1995 Obsolete

A 32-bit extension tacked onto ISA slots for 486 graphics. It ran at CPU bus speed, which gave fast Windows graphics.

Identify it: A long brown extension behind a black ISA slot, making a very long slot overall.

#NuBus

1987–1995 Obsolete

Apple's expansion bus in the Macintosh II and Quadra series, plus NeXT. Replaced by PCI in Power Macs.

#PCI

1992–2010s Legacy

Intel's Peripheral Component Interconnect: 32-bit, 33 MHz (133 MB/s), shared bus, true plug-and-play. It held nearly every card type from the 1990s to the 2000s.

Identify it: Short white/cream slots (about 8.5 cm long), set back from the board edge.

#PCI-X

1998–2000s Obsolete

64-bit / up to 133 MHz PCI for servers (and the Power Mac G5).

Commonly confused with: PCI-X is not PCIe (PCI Express).

#AGP

1997–2006 Obsolete

Accelerated Graphics Port: a dedicated graphics slot. 1× / 2× / 4× / 8×. Keyed for 3.3 V vs 1.5 V cards, and Universal cards fit both.

Identify it: A single brown slot placed further back than the PCI slots. Most have a retention clip.

Fun fact: Plugging a 3.3 V-only card into a 1.5 V-only board (in the rare cases it physically fit) could kill both.

#AMR / CNR / ACR riser slots

1998–2003 Obsolete

Tiny slots for cheap 'soft' modems and audio cards that let the CPU do the work. Mostly empty in practice.

#PCI Express (PCIe)

2004→ Current

Serial point-to-point lanes in widths ×1 / ×4 / ×8 / ×16. Each generation roughly doubles per-lane speed. Used for GPUs, NVMe, network cards and more. A shorter card fits a longer slot.

Gen 1250 MB/s/lane (2003)
Gen 3~985 MB/s/lane (2010)
Gen 4~1.97 GB/s/lane (2017)
Gen 5~3.9 GB/s/lane (2019)
Gen 6~7.6 GB/s/lane (2022, PAM4)

Identify it: Slots with a small key gap near the front. ×16 slots are long, ×1 slots are short stubs.

Fun fact: Full details, PCIe 7.0/8.0 and a bandwidth calculator: PCI Express in depth.

#Mini-PCI

1999–~2007 Obsolete

Laptop expansion cards (mostly Wi-Fi) that lay flat. Replaced by Mini PCIe.

#Mini PCIe (PCIe Mini Card)

2005–~2016 Legacy

Small laptop cards for Wi-Fi, WWAN modems and TV tuners. It carries PCIe ×1 + USB 2.0. The same physical size and connector as mSATA.

Commonly confused with: An mSATA SSD won't work in a Wi-Fi-only Mini PCIe slot (see Storage → mSATA).

#PCMCIA / PC Card (16-bit)

1990–~2005 Obsolete

Credit-card-sized laptop expansion: modems, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, SCSI, memory. Type I (3.3 mm), Type II (5 mm, most common), Type III (10.5 mm, for tiny hard drives).

Fun fact: The joke expansion of PCMCIA: 'People Can't Memorize Computer Industry Acronyms'.

#CardBus

1995–~2007 Obsolete

The 32-bit PCI-based version of PC Card. Same slot, with a gold grounding strip on the card.

#ExpressCard (/34 & /54)

2003–~2014 Obsolete

PC Card's successor, built on PCIe + USB. /34 is 34 mm wide and /54 is L-shaped (54 mm). Common in ThinkPads and MacBook Pros (until 2012) for USB 3.0, eSATA and FireWire add-ons.

Fun fact: Some enthusiasts used ExpressCard-to-PCIe adapters as early external GPUs.

#OCuLink

2012→ Current

A small cable connector carrying raw PCIe (×4/×8). Used for server drives and, lately, high-bandwidth external GPU docks on mini PCs and handhelds.

#CXL (Compute Express Link)

2019→ Current

A data-centre protocol running over PCIe 5/6 for coherent memory expansion and pooling between CPUs and accelerators.

#PCI Express (PCIe) in depth

The highway inside every modern computer: lanes, generations, slots, and how to avoid slowing down your GPU or SSD.

#What PCIe is

Components · 2003→ Concept

PCI Express connects the CPU to graphics cards, NVMe SSDs, network cards, Wi-Fi, capture cards and more. Instead of one shared bus (like old PCI), each device gets its own private link made of lanes. A lane is two pairs of wires, one sending and one receiving at the same time. Links come in ×1, ×2, ×4, ×8 and ×16 lanes, and each new generation doubles the speed per lane. It's run by the PCI-SIG group (Intel, AMD, Nvidia, Arm and hundreds of others) and has doubled speed about every three years for two decades.

Generations in PCs (2026)PCIe 3.0, 4.0, 5.0
Latest specPCIe 7.0 (June 2025)
In developmentPCIe 8.0, planned for 2028
CompatibilityEvery generation works with every other, at the slower one's speed

Identify it: Long or short slots on the motherboard with a small notch near one end

Commonly confused with: PCIe (PCI Express) vs PCI-X (an old 64-bit server bus) vs PCI (the 1990s shared bus)

Fun fact: A ×16 PCIe 5.0 slot moves about 64 GB/s each way: a whole 50 GB game in under a second, in theory.

Sources: PCI-SIG: PCIe 7.0 specification released, 128 GT/s (Jun 2025) · PCI-SIG: PCIe 8.0 to reach 256 GT/s, planned for 2028 (Aug 2025) · ServeTheHome: PCIe 8.0 draft 0.5 released · TechSpot: PCIe 3.0/4.0 still enough for most consumer devices in 2026

#Calculator: real PCIe bandwidth for any generation and lane count

Concept

Raw speed × lanes × encoding efficiency ÷ 8 bits = GB/s in one direction. This also answers common questions like 'is a PCIe 4.0 SSD wasted in a 3.0 slot?'.

Python
gens = {1: (2.5, 8/10), 2: (5, 8/10), 3: (8, 128/130), 4: (16, 128/130),
        5: (32, 128/130), 6: (64, 242/256), 7: (128, 242/256)}   # GT/s, efficiency

def gbps(gen, lanes):
    gt, eff = gens[gen]
    return gt * eff * lanes / 8

print(f"{'Gen':<5}" + "".join(f"{'x' + str(l):>9}" for l in (1, 4, 8, 16)))
for g in gens:
    print(f"{g}.0  " + "".join(f"{gbps(g, l):>9.1f}" for l in (1, 4, 8, 16)))

print("\nPCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe SSD (~7.0 GB/s) in a 3.0 x4 slot ->", round(gbps(3, 4), 1), "GB/s max")
print("Graphics card 4.0 x8 (budget GPUs) in a 3.0 board ->", round(gbps(3, 8), 1), "GB/s, vs", round(gbps(4, 8), 1), "on 4.0")
Output
Gen         x1       x4       x8      x16
1.0        0.2      1.0      2.0      4.0
2.0        0.5      2.0      4.0      8.0
3.0        1.0      3.9      7.9     15.8
4.0        2.0      7.9     15.8     31.5
5.0        3.9     15.8     31.5     63.0
6.0        7.6     30.2     60.5    121.0
7.0       15.1     60.5    121.0    242.0

PCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe SSD (~7.0 GB/s) in a 3.0 x4 slot -> 3.9 GB/s max
Graphics card 4.0 x8 (budget GPUs) in a 3.0 board -> 7.9 GB/s, vs 15.8 on 4.0

Source: PCI-SIG: PCIe 7.0 specification released, 128 GT/s (Jun 2025)

#PCIe tips & troubleshooting

Guide

Check your link: GPU-Z (Windows) shows 'Bus Interface', e.g. PCIe x16 4.0 @ x16 4.0; on Linux run sudo lspci -vv and look for LnkSta. Graphics cards drop to a lower link speed when idle to save power, so test under load. Bifurcation (BIOS setting) splits one ×16 slot into ×4/×4/×4/×4 for multi-SSD adapter cards. Risers: cheap PCIe 3.0 riser cables can cause crashes or black screens with 4.0/5.0 GPUs; set the slot to Gen 3 in the BIOS or buy a riser rated for your generation. Heavy GPUs sag: use the support bracket. And reseat a card (power off, unplug) before blaming it.

#Ports & cables

Every plug you've wondered about, from the 1981 PC to Thunderbolt 5.

USB & phone connector shapes (face view, not to scale)

The connector shape tells you nothing about speed. A USB-C port can be anything from USB 2.0 to USB4 / Thunderbolt 5.

#USB 1.0 / 1.1

1996 / 1998 Obsolete

Universal Serial Bus replaced serial, parallel and PS/2 ports. Low Speed 1.5 Mb/s, Full Speed 12 Mb/s.

Fun fact: The iMac G3 (1998) was the first mainstream computer to go USB-only, with no floppy or legacy ports, and that pushed the whole industry along.

#USB 2.0 (Hi-Speed)

2000 Current

480 Mb/s (~35–40 MB/s real). Still common for keyboards, mice and cheap flash drives.

Identify it: Black or white plastic inside a USB-A port.

#USB 3.x (naming mess)

2008→ Current

USB 3.0 = 5 Gb/s → renamed USB 3.1 Gen 1 → renamed USB 3.2 Gen 1 → marketed as 'USB 5Gbps'. USB 3.1 Gen 2 / 3.2 Gen 2 = 10 Gb/s. USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 = 20 Gb/s (USB-C only).

Identify it: Blue inside a USB-A port usually means 5 Gb/s, teal/red often 10 Gb/s, and an 'SS' logo means SuperSpeed.

Commonly confused with: The same port can be called three different names depending on the year of the spec sheet.

#USB4 (v1 / v2)

2019 / 2022 Current

Built on the Thunderbolt 3 protocol, USB-C only. USB4 v1: 20 or 40 Gb/s. USB4 v2: 80 Gb/s (up to 120 Gb/s one way). Tunnels PCIe and DisplayPort.

#USB Type-A

1996→ Current

The classic flat rectangular host port. One-way-up (and somehow it's always the wrong way first).

#USB Type-B

1996→ Legacy

Square-ish device plug for printers, scanners and audio interfaces. USB 3.0 Type-B has an extra bump on top.

#Mini-USB (Mini-B)

2000–~2012 Obsolete

Trapezoid plug for cameras, MP3 players, GPS units, PS3 controllers and early BlackBerrys.

#Micro-USB (Micro-B)

2007–~2020 Legacy

Thin trapezoid that was the universal Android/Bluetooth-gadget charging port for a decade. Micro-B USB 3.0 adds a second side lobe and shows up on portable hard drives.

Fun fact: The EU common-charger push of 2009 standardised Micro-USB. In 2022 the EU picked USB-C for the next round.

#USB Type-C

2014→ Current

Small, oval and reversible. Can carry USB 2.0 up to USB4, DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt and up to 240 W of power. Mandatory for phones sold in the EU since Dec 2024.

Commonly confused with: USB-C is a shape, not a speed. A USB-C port might be only USB 2.0 (480 Mb/s), and cables vary just as much.

#Apple Lightning

2012–2023 Legacy

Apple's 8-pin reversible plug for iPhone 5 through iPhone 14/15-era accessories. Replaced by USB-C on iPhone 15 (2023).

Identify it: A flat, solid tab with 8 contacts on each side and no hole in the middle.

#Apple 30-pin dock connector

2003–2012 Obsolete

The wide flat iPod/iPhone/iPad connector before Lightning. A whole ecosystem of speaker docks was built around it.

#Thunderbolt (1 → 5)

2011→ Current

Intel and Apple's high-speed port. TB1/TB2 (10/20 Gb/s) used the Mini DisplayPort shape. TB3 (2015, 40 Gb/s) moved to USB-C. TB4 (2020, 40 Gb/s with stricter minimums). TB5 (2023, 80 Gb/s, 120 Gb/s boost).

Identify it: A lightning-bolt icon next to the port.

Commonly confused with: Every Thunderbolt 3/4/5 port is USB-C shaped, but most USB-C ports are not Thunderbolt.

#FireWire (IEEE 1394)

1995–~2014 Obsolete

Apple-led high-speed serial bus: FireWire 400 (6-pin, or 4-pin unpowered 'i.LINK' on Sony), FireWire 800 (9-pin beta connector). Ruled camcorders (DV), audio interfaces and early iPods.

Fun fact: Target Disk Mode let a Mac boot as an external FireWire drive for another Mac.

#Serial port (RS-232, COM)

1960s–2000s Legacy

DE-9 (9-pin) or DB-25 male connectors for mice, modems and console cables. Still used for network gear, industrial machines and CNC.

Identify it: A 9-pin male D-shaped port, often teal under the PC99 colour code.

#Parallel port (LPT, Centronics)

1970s–2000s Obsolete

DB-25 female port on PCs for printers, Zip drives and scanners. The printer end used a 36-pin Centronics connector. Modes: SPP, EPP, ECP.

Identify it: A 25-hole female D-port, usually pink (PC99 colour code).

#Game port (DA-15)

1981–~2005 Obsolete

A 15-pin joystick/MIDI port, usually on the sound card. Replaced by USB HID.

#PS/2 (mini-DIN 6)

1987→ Legacy

Round keyboard (purple) and mouse (green) ports from IBM's PS/2 line. Some gamers still use them for 'N-key rollover'. Not hot-pluggable in older systems.

Commonly confused with: Purple and green PS/2 ports aren't always interchangeable. A combo port is half purple, half green.

#AT keyboard (DIN-5)

1984–1990s Obsolete

A big round 5-pin keyboard connector from the IBM PC/AT. Passive adapters convert it to PS/2.

#ADB (Apple Desktop Bus)

1986–1998 Obsolete

Apple's 4-pin mini-DIN port for daisy-chaining keyboards and mice. Looks almost exactly like S-Video.

#VGA (DE-15)

1987–2010s Legacy

IBM's analog video connector: 15 pins in 3 rows, usually blue. Image quality fades at high resolutions. Still common on projectors and servers.

#DVI (-A / -D / -I, single/dual link)

1999–2010s Legacy

Digital Visual Interface. DVI-D is digital only, DVI-I adds analog pins (passive VGA adapters work), DVI-A is analog only. Dual-link doubles the pins for 2560×1600 or 144 Hz at 1080p.

Identify it: A white rectangular port with a grid of square holes and a flat blade slot. Four extra holes around the blade mean DVI-I.

#HDMI (1.0 → 2.2)

2002→ Current

The TV/consumer digital video + audio standard. 1.4 (4K30, ARC), 2.0 (4K60), 2.1 (48 Gb/s, 4K120/8K60, VRR, eARC), 2.2 (2025, 96 Gb/s). Plug sizes: Type A (standard), C (Mini), D (Micro).

Commonly confused with: 'HDMI 2.1' ports may support only some 2.1 features. Check for 48 Gb/s 'Ultra High Speed' cables and port specs.

#DisplayPort / Mini DisplayPort

2006 / 2008→ Current

VESA's PC video standard, with daisy-chaining (MST) and adaptive sync. DP 1.2 → 1.4a (HBR3, DSC) → 2.0/2.1 (UHBR up to 80 Gb/s). Mini DP was Apple's (2008), later used for Thunderbolt 1/2.

Identify it: One corner of the plug is cut off, and full-size DP plugs have a latch you press to release.

#Composite / S-Video / Component

1950s–2000s Obsolete

Analog video: composite (one yellow RCA), S-Video (4-pin mini-DIN, separate brightness and colour), component YPbPr (red/green/blue RCAs, up to 1080i). Old GPUs had 'TV-out'.

#SCART / 13W3 / DB13W3

Obsolete

European AV connector (SCART, 21-pin), and Sun/SGI workstation video (13W3: 3 coax pins plus 10 signal pins).

#Audio jacks (3.5 mm TRS/TRRS)

Current

TRS (3 contacts: stereo) and TRRS (4 contacts: stereo + mic, headsets). PC colour codes: green line-out, pink mic, blue line-in, plus orange/black/grey for surround.

Fun fact: Two incompatible TRRS wirings exist: CTIA/AHJ (modern standard) and OMTP (older Nokia). That's why some headsets hum or lose the mic.

#S/PDIF (Toslink optical / coax)

1983→ Legacy

Digital audio out to receivers and soundbars over a red-glowing optical fibre (Toslink) or an RCA coax.

#RJ-45 (Ethernet) & RJ-11 (phone)

Current

RJ-45 = 8-pin Ethernet jack. RJ-11 = smaller 4/6-pin phone/modem jack. Dial-up laptops often had both.

Commonly confused with: An RJ-11 plug fits loosely into an RJ-45 port. It's the wrong cable.

#Docking connectors

1990s→ Legacy

Proprietary under-laptop dock ports (ThinkPad, Dell E-Port, HP), now replaced by USB-C/Thunderbolt docks.

Video connectors (face view, schematic)

DVI-I has the four extra analog pins around the flat blade. DVI-D doesn't. A DisplayPort plug has one clipped corner, while HDMI is symmetrical.

#Networking & wireless

How devices connect to each other and to the internet.

#Ethernet speeds

1983→ Current

10 Mb/s (10BASE-T) → Fast Ethernet 100 Mb/s → Gigabit 1 Gb/s → 2.5G / 5G (multi-gig over existing Cat5e/6) → 10GbE → 25/40/100/400/800G in data centres.

#Ethernet cables (Cat5 → Cat8)

Current

Cat5e: 1 Gb/s, 100 m. Cat6: 10 Gb/s up to ~55 m. Cat6a: 10 Gb/s, 100 m. Cat8: 25/40 Gb/s, short runs in data centres.

Fun fact: Cat7 was never a TIA standard and uses different connectors in its true form.

#Coax / 10BASE2 / Token Ring

1980s–1990s Obsolete

Early LANs: 10BASE2 'thinnet' used coax with BNC T-connectors and 50 Ω terminators. IBM Token Ring (4/16 Mb/s) passed a 'token' around a ring.

#NIC (network interface card)

Current

The network adapter: built into the board, a PCIe card, a USB dongle, or an M.2 module (Wi-Fi).

#Dial-up modem

1960s–2000s Obsolete

Data sent as sound over phone lines: 300 baud → 2400 → 14.4k → 28.8k → 33.6k → 56k (V.90/V.92). Internal ISA/PCI cards, 'Winmodems', or external serial boxes.

Fun fact: The dial-up handshake noise was the two modems negotiating which protocol and speed to use.

#ISDN / DSL / Cable / Fibre

1990s→ Current

ISDN (128 kb/s digital phone), DSL/ADSL/VDSL (over copper phone lines), DOCSIS cable (over TV coax), FTTH fibre (GPON/XGS-PON, up to 10 Gb/s+).

#Wi-Fi generations (802.11)

1997→ Current

Wi-Fi Alliance numbering: Wi-Fi 4 = 802.11n (2009), 5 = ac (2013), 6 = ax (2019), 6E = ax on 6 GHz, 7 = be (2024, 320 MHz channels, MLO), 8 = bn (in development).

Fun fact: Before the numbers, 802.11b (1999, 11 Mb/s) and g (2003, 54 Mb/s) started the home Wi-Fi boom. Apple's 'AirPort' was the first big consumer push.

#Bluetooth versions

1999→ Current

1.x (721 kb/s) → 2.0+EDR (3 Mb/s) → 4.0 (2010, Bluetooth Low Energy) → 5.0 (2016, more range) → 5.x (LE Audio in 5.2) → 6.0 (2024, Channel Sounding for precise distance).

Fun fact: Bluetooth is named after Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson, the 10th-century Danish king who united tribes. Its logo combines his runic initials.

#Laptop Wi-Fi cards (M.2 E-key / CNVi)

Current

Most laptops use an M.2 2230 E-key Wi-Fi card (e.g. Intel AX210, BE200). CNVio cards (Intel AX201) only work with Intel CPUs that have the matching controller.

Commonly confused with: A CNVi card (AX201/AX211/BE201) won't work in an AMD laptop. Use AX210/BE200-class cards instead.

#Cellular modems (WWAN)

Current

LTE/5G modules in laptops (M.2 B-key). Also USB dongles and phone hotspots.

#IrDA (infrared)

1994–2000s Obsolete

Line-of-sight infrared data between laptops, PDAs and phones. Only 9.6 kb/s to 4 Mb/s, but magical in 2001.

#NFC & UWB

2004 / 2019→ Current

NFC: short-range (~4 cm) tap-to-pay and pairing. UWB (Ultra-Wideband): precise location for AirTags, digital car keys and AirDrop direction finding.

#Router, switch, access point, modem

Current

Modem connects to the ISP line. Router directs traffic between networks (NAT, DHCP). Switch connects wired devices on one network. Access point adds Wi-Fi. A home 'router' usually does all four.

Commonly confused with: Hub vs switch: a hub (obsolete) broadcasts everything to every port, while a switch sends traffic only where it needs to go.

#Mesh Wi-Fi

2016→ Current

Several Wi-Fi nodes forming one network for whole-home coverage (eero, Google Wifi, Deco, Orbi).

#Powerline / MoCA

Current

Networking over a home's power wiring (HomePlug/G.hn) or TV coax (MoCA 2.5, up to 2.5 Gb/s).

#Peripherals

Everything you plug in to see, type, click, print and hear.

#Keyboard switch types

Current

Membrane/rubber dome (cheap, mushy), scissor (laptops, short travel), mechanical (Cherry MX and clones: linear red, tactile brown, clicky blue), optical and Hall-effect/magnetic (adjustable actuation, rapid trigger), buckling spring (IBM Model M).

Fun fact: The IBM Model M (1985) is so durable that 30-year-old units still work, and it's still produced by Unicomp.

#Keyboard sizes & layouts

Current

Full-size (100%), TKL (80%, no numpad), 75%, 65%, 60%, 40%. Layouts: ANSI (US, wide Enter) vs ISO (EU, tall Enter) vs JIS. Language layouts: QWERTY, AZERTY, QWERTZ, Dvorak, Colemak, Arabic.

#Mouse sensors (ball → optical → laser)

1968→ Current

Douglas Engelbart showed the first mouse in 1968 (a wooden box with wheels). Ball mice (1980s–2000s, cleaning the rollers!), optical LED (1999, Microsoft IntelliMouse Explorer), laser (2004, Logitech MX1000), modern gaming optical sensors (20,000+ DPI).

Fun fact: Engelbart's 1968 'Mother of All Demos' also showed hypertext, video calls and collaborative editing.

#Trackball & pointing stick

Current

A trackball is an upside-down ball mouse (Logitech, Kensington). A pointing stick is ThinkPad's red TrackPoint (1992) nub, also found on some Dell and HP laptops.

#CRT monitors

1970s–2000s Obsolete

Cathode-ray tube displays: heavy and deep, with near-zero latency and no fixed native resolution. The Sony Trinitron and its FD descendants were legendary.

Fun fact: Some competitive Smash Bros players still use CRTs for their zero input lag.

#LCD panel types (TN / IPS / VA)

Current

TN: fast and cheap, poor viewing angles. IPS: best colour and angles, some 'IPS glow'. VA: high contrast, deep blacks, slower dark transitions. Backlights: CCFL (old) → LED edge-lit → Mini-LED (local dimming).

#OLED & QD-OLED

Current

Self-emissive pixels give perfect blacks and very fast response. WOLED (LG) and QD-OLED (Samsung) monitors. Risk of burn-in from static images.

#Refresh rate & response time

Current

Hz = full screen redraws per second: 60, 75, 120, 144, 165, 240, 360, 480, 500+. Adaptive sync: VESA Adaptive-Sync, AMD FreeSync, NVIDIA G-SYNC. Response time = how fast pixels change (GtG).

#Resolutions

Current

VGA 640×480 → SVGA 800×600 → XGA 1024×768 → 720p 1280×720 → 1080p (FHD) → 1440p (QHD) → 4K UHD 3840×2160 → 5K → 8K. Ultrawide 21:9 (3440×1440) and 32:9 'super ultrawide'.

#Printers (dot-matrix → inkjet → laser)

Current

Dot-matrix (impact pins, tractor-feed paper, still used for multi-part forms), inkjet (thermal = HP/Canon, piezo = Epson, ink tanks = EcoTank/MegaTank), laser (toner + drum, fast and cheap per page), plus thermal (receipts) and 3D printers (FDM, resin).

Fun fact: Inkjet ink has often been priced well above Chanel No. 5, per millilitre.

#Scanners

Current

Flatbed (CCD vs CIS sensors), sheet-fed/ADF document scanners, film scanners, and handheld wands.

#Webcams & capture cards

Current

USB webcams (UVC standard), and HDMI capture cards for streaming consoles or cameras (Elgato, AVerMedia).

#Sound cards & audio interfaces

1987→ Current

AdLib (1987, FM synth) → Creative Sound Blaster (1989), the DOS standard → Sound Blaster Live!/Audigy (EAX) → onboard audio (Realtek, AC'97 → HD Audio) → USB DACs and audio interfaces (Focusrite, Universal Audio) for creators.

Fun fact: 'Sound Blaster compatible' was such a must that clone cards emulated its exact I/O addresses.

#Speakers & headsets

Current

PC speakers (2.0, 2.1, 5.1), USB/3.5 mm/2.4 GHz wireless/Bluetooth headsets, and the PC's internal beeper (POST beeps!).

#Game controllers

Current

Gameport joysticks → USB gamepads → XInput (Xbox 360 standard on PC) → DualShock/DualSense, Switch Pro. Plus flight sticks (HOTAS), racing wheels and arcade sticks.

#Graphics tablets & pen displays

Current

Wacom (since 1983), Huion, XP-Pen. Pressure-sensitive pens, screenless (Intuos) or pen displays (Cintiq).

#KVM switches

Current

Keyboard-Video-Mouse switches let one set of peripherals control several computers.

Part 2

Laptops

Classes of portable computers, from 1981 luggables to AI PCs, and the parts that make laptops different.

#Laptop classes & categories

The kinds of portable computer, from luggables to Copilot+ PCs.

#Luggable / portable

1981–late 1980s Obsolete

Suitcase-sized computers with built-in CRTs that ran on mains power. The Osborne 1 (1981, 10.7 kg, 5" screen) and the Compaq Portable (1983, the first 100% IBM-compatible clone).

Fun fact: Osborne announced its next model too early, buyers stopped buying the current one, and the company went bankrupt. That's now called the 'Osborne effect'.

#Laptop / notebook (early)

1982–1990s Obsolete

Battery-powered clamshells: GRiD Compass (1982, flew on the Space Shuttle), Toshiba T1100 (1985), Apple PowerBook (1991, palm rest + trackball layout), IBM ThinkPad 700C (1992).

#Subnotebook / ultraportable

1990s→ Current

Small, light laptops (under ~1.5 kg): Toshiba Libretto, Sony VAIO X505/X/Z, Panasonic Let's Note.

#Netbook

2007–~2012 Obsolete

Cheap, small (7–12") laptops for web and email, usually Intel Atom + Windows XP/Linux. ASUS Eee PC 701 (2007) started the craze, and Acer Aspire One, MSI Wind and Dell Mini followed. Tablets and Chromebooks ended it.

Fun fact: Microsoft extended Windows XP sales mainly because netbooks were too weak for Vista.

#Ultrabook

2011→ Current

Intel's spec/brand for thin, light, SSD-equipped Windows laptops, launched in response to the MacBook Air (2008). The name is mostly retired, but the category is mainstream.

#Gaming laptop

Current

Laptops with dedicated GPUs, high-refresh screens and strong cooling. Thick 'desktop replacements' (Alienware, ASUS ROG, MSI) and thin-and-light gaming models (Razer Blade, ROG Zephyrus).

Commonly confused with: A laptop 'RTX 4070' isn't the same as the desktop card. It runs at much lower power (TGP), so check the wattage.

#Mobile workstation

Current

Pro laptops with certified pro GPUs (NVIDIA RTX PRO), ECC RAM support and ISV certifications: Dell Precision, HP ZBook, Lenovo ThinkPad P-series.

#2-in-1 / convertible / detachable

2012→ Current

Convertibles fold 360° into tablet mode (Lenovo Yoga, HP x360). Detachables separate the screen from the keyboard (Microsoft Surface Pro, Surface Book).

#Chromebook

2011→ Current

Laptops running Google's ChromeOS: cheap, secure, cloud-centred, hugely popular in schools. Can run Android and Linux apps. Chromebook Plus (2023) sets a higher hardware floor.

Fun fact: Each Chromebook has an 'Auto Update Expiration' date, now 10 years for models from 2019 onward.

#Rugged laptop

Current

Drop-, water- and dust-proof machines (MIL-STD-810H, IP65) for military and field work: Panasonic Toughbook, Dell Latitude Rugged, Getac, Durabook.

#Copilot+ PC / AI PC

2024→ Current

Windows laptops with an NPU of 40+ TOPS (Snapdragon X, AMD Ryzen AI 300, Intel Core Ultra 200V) that unlock on-device AI features (Recall, Live Captions translation, Cocreator).

#Pen computer & tablet PC

1989–2000s Obsolete

Stylus-driven laptops: GRiDPad (1989), Windows for Pen Computing, Windows XP Tablet PC Edition (2002), ThinkPad X41 Tablet swivel convertibles. See Part 4.

#Handheld PC / palmtop

1989–2000s Obsolete

Pocket clamshells with keyboards: Atari Portfolio (1989), HP 95LX/200LX, Psion Series 5, Windows CE Handheld PCs (HP Jornada), Sony VAIO UX/P, OQO.

Fun fact: The Atari Portfolio was the 'hacking' computer in Terminator 2.

#Gaming handheld PC

2022→ Current

x86 PCs shaped like game consoles: Valve Steam Deck (2022), ASUS ROG Ally, Lenovo Legion Go, MSI Claw, GPD Win.

#Laptop-specific parts

What's different inside a laptop compared with a desktop.

#Soldered vs socketed RAM

Current

Many thin laptops solder LPDDR to the board (fast, efficient, not upgradeable). Others use SO-DIMM slots or LPCAMM2. Some have both (one soldered bank plus one slot).

Identify it: Check the spec sheet for 'onboard' (soldered) vs 'SO-DIMM' slots, or open the bottom panel.

#Soldered vs socketed storage

Current

Most laptops use an M.2 2230/2242/2280 SSD. Some soldered NAND directly (older MacBooks, cheap eMMC laptops). Apple's 2023+ Mac Studio/Pro use removable but proprietary modules.

#eMMC storage

2010s→ Legacy

Embedded flash on budget laptops and Chromebooks: usually 32–128 GB, slow (~250 MB/s at best), soldered.

Commonly confused with: '128 GB eMMC' isn't the same as a 128 GB SSD. eMMC is much slower.

#Laptop display panels & connectors

Current

LVDS (old, 30/40-pin, up to ~1080p) → eDP (Embedded DisplayPort, 30/40-pin) on modern laptops. Panel IDs (e.g. LP140WF6) tell you the exact replacement part.

Identify it: The panel model number is printed on its rear sticker, so check it before you order a replacement.

#Laptop panel tech

Current

TN (cheap), IPS (most common), OLED (vivid, deep blacks), Mini-LED (bright HDR, MacBook Pro), plus matte vs glossy finishes, touch and pen (Wacom AES / MPP).

#Batteries (internal vs removable)

Current

Old laptops had removable packs that slid out. Most modern ones are internal, screwed or glued in. Chemistry: NiCd → NiMH (1990s) → Li-ion → Li-polymer (thin, shaped). Capacity is in Wh (100 Wh is the airline carry-on limit).

Fun fact: ThinkPads with 'Power Bridge' (T440–T480) had an internal battery plus a hot-swappable external one.

#Battery health & cycles

Current

Li-ion degrades with charge cycles and heat. Expect roughly 80% capacity after 300–1,000 cycles. Limiting the charge to 80% (Lenovo Vantage, ASUS, macOS 'Optimised') slows ageing.

#Swollen battery

Current

A failing Li-ion cell can expand: a lifting trackpad, a bulging case. Stop using it, don't puncture it, and recycle it properly. It's a fire risk.

Identify it: The trackpad stops clicking, the bottom case rocks on a table, or there's a gap at the keyboard edge.

#Keyboards: chiclet, butterfly, scissor

Current

Island-style 'chiclet' keys became standard ~2008. Apple's thin butterfly keyboard (2015–2019) was prone to failure and led to a repair programme and lawsuit, and Apple went back to scissor switches ('Magic Keyboard').

#Trackpads

Current

Mechanical-click pads, 'clickpads' (the whole surface clicks), Force Touch haptic pads (Apple 2015, now also Windows haptic pads). Windows Precision Touchpad drivers improved PC gestures a lot.

#Pointing stick (TrackPoint)

1992→ Current

The red nub in ThinkPad keyboards (IBM's invention by Ted Selker). Also on Dell Latitude and HP EliteBook (a few models).

#Hinges

Current

Clamshell, 360° convertible, dual-hinge, 'Dynamic' (Surface Book's fulcrum hinge), and folding OLED screens (ASUS Zenbook 17 Fold, Lenovo X1 Fold).

#Docking stations & port replicators

Current

Proprietary under-laptop docks (ThinkPad, Dell E-Port, HP) → USB-C/Thunderbolt docks with one cable for power, displays, Ethernet and USB.

Commonly confused with: A DisplayLink USB dock uses software video compression. It's fine for office work, not for gaming.

#Laptop cooling

Current

Heat pipes + blower fans + fin stacks. Some use vapor chambers or liquid metal paste. Fanless designs (MacBook Air M-series) rely on passive spreading.

#Laptop power classes (U / P / H / HX)

Current

Intel/AMD suffixes give the power target: U (~15 W ultraportable), P (28 W), H/HS (35–45 W performance), HX (55 W+ desktop-class). Apple uses base/Pro/Max tiers instead.

#BIOS whitelists & locked hardware

2000s–2010s Legacy

Some laptops (notably older Lenovo and HP) only booted with approved Wi-Fi cards. A 'BIOS whitelist' error (e.g. 1802 on ThinkPads) blocked unapproved cards.

#Right-to-repair / modular laptops

2021→ Current

Framework laptops have swappable ports, mainboards and screens. iFixit repairability scores. EU and US state right-to-repair laws push makers toward replaceable batteries and parts.

Part 3

Phones

From the 1983 brick phone through PDAs and BlackBerry to foldables: history, chips and hardware, then the extremes: tri-folds, luxury phones and rugged camping phones.

#Phone history: brick phones to foldables

Milestones in mobile phones.

#Motorola DynaTAC 8000X

1983 Obsolete

The first commercial handheld cellphone: about 790 g, 30 minutes of talk time, roughly 10 hours to charge, priced at $3,995. Martin Cooper made the first handheld cellular call on a prototype in 1973.

Fun fact: Its nickname was 'the brick'. It shows up in the 1987 film Wall Street.

#1G analog networks (AMPS, NMT, TACS)

1979–2000s Obsolete

Analog voice only, easy to eavesdrop on with a scanner. NMT (Nordic, 1981) was the first multinational system.

#2G: GSM & CDMA

1991→ Legacy

Digital voice + SMS (first text sent 1992: 'Merry Christmas'). GSM (SIM-based, Europe and most of the world) vs CDMA (Qualcomm, US/Korea). GPRS/EDGE ('2.5G') added slow data.

#Feature phones / candybar

1990s→ Current

Non-smartphones: Nokia 3310 (2000, Snake II), Nokia 1100 (~250 million sold, one of the best-selling phones ever), plus modern KaiOS phones.

#Flip & slider phones

1996–2010 Obsolete

Motorola StarTAC (1996, the first clamshell), RAZR V3 (2004, 130 million+ sold), Nokia slider phones, Sony Ericsson Walkman/Cyber-shot phones, Sidekick swivel.

#PDA (Personal Digital Assistant)

1993–~2010 Obsolete

Pocket organisers with styluses: Apple Newton (1993), Palm Pilot (1996, Graffiti handwriting), Pocket PC / Windows Mobile (Compaq iPAQ, HP), Psion. PDAs merged with phones into early smartphones.

#IBM Simon

1994 Obsolete

Often called the first smartphone: a touchscreen, email, fax and apps on a 1994 cellphone. BellSouth sold about 50,000.

Fun fact: The word 'smartphone' wasn't common yet. It was marketed as a 'Personal Communicator'.

#BlackBerry era

1999–2016 Obsolete

RIM's pagers became email phones with physical QWERTY keyboards and BBM. The executive and government standard of the 2000s ('CrackBerry'). The Bold, Curve and Pearl.

Fun fact: President Obama famously fought to keep his BlackBerry in 2009.

#Symbian & Nokia smartphones

1998–2013 Obsolete

Symbian (S60, UIQ) ran Nokia's smartphones: N95 (2007, GPS + 5 MP camera), E-series, N8, and the 808 PureView (41 MP, 2012). It was the top smartphone OS until ~2010.

#Windows Mobile / Windows Phone

2000–2017 Obsolete

Stylus-driven Windows Mobile (Pocket PC) → touch-first Windows Phone 7/8/10 (2010) with Metro 'Live Tiles', mostly on Nokia Lumias. Ended because of an 'app gap'.

#iPhone (original)

2007 Obsolete

Apple's multitouch phone: no keyboard, a full web browser, visual voicemail. 2G (EDGE) only, and no App Store until 2008.

Fun fact: Steve Jobs introduced it as 'an iPod, a phone, and an Internet communicator', then revealed they were one device. Every iPhone model is listed in Old iPhones, Part 22.

#Android (first phone: HTC Dream / T-Mobile G1)

2008 Obsolete

Google's Linux-based OS debuted on the HTC Dream with a slide-out keyboard. Android became the world's most-used OS (~70%+ of phones).

#3G / 4G LTE / 5G

2001 / 2009 / 2019 Current

3G (UMTS/HSPA, CDMA2000): mobile internet. 4G LTE: fast data, the app era. 5G: sub-6 GHz plus mmWave for multi-gigabit speeds and low latency. 2G/3G networks are being shut down worldwide.

#Phablets → large phones

2011→ Current

The Samsung Galaxy Note (2011, 5.3" with S Pen) was mocked as too big. Today almost every phone is 6–6.9".

#Foldables & flips

2019→ Current

Flexible OLEDs that fold: Galaxy Fold/Z Fold (2019→), Z Flip, Motorola razr (2019 revival), Google Pixel Fold, Huawei Mate X, OnePlus Open, Honor Magic V, Huawei Mate XT tri-fold (2024).

#Modular phones

2013–2020 Obsolete

Google Project Ara (cancelled 2016), LG G5 'Friends' modules, Moto Mods (Moto Z). Fairphone continues the repairable idea.

#Phone chips (SoCs)

Phones use a System on a Chip: CPU, GPU, NPU, modem (often), ISP (camera processor) and memory controller on one die.

#Apple A-series / Bionic

2010→ Current

Apple-designed ARM chips: A4 (iPhone 4) → A7 (2013, first 64-bit phone chip) → A11 Bionic (Neural Engine, Face ID) → A17 Pro (3 nm) → A18 / A19 series.

Fun fact: The A7's jump to 64-bit surprised Qualcomm so much that one executive publicly called it a 'marketing gimmick' before walking it back.

#Qualcomm Snapdragon

2007→ Current

The dominant Android flagship chip: Snapdragon S1 → 800 series (800, 820, 835, 845, 855, 865, 888) → 8 Gen 1/2/3 → 8 Elite (2024, custom Oryon cores) → 8 Elite Gen 5. Tiers: 8 (flagship), 7, 6, 4.

Identify it: 'for Galaxy' versions are slightly overclocked Samsung editions.

#Samsung Exynos

2010→ Current

Samsung's own SoCs (Exynos 2400/2500). Galaxy S phones sometimes ship Exynos in some regions and Snapdragon in others, and performance comparisons between them get heated.

#MediaTek Dimensity / Helio

1997 → 2020s Current

Taiwan's MediaTek ships the most phone chips by volume: budget Helio chips and flagship Dimensity (9300/9400 used all-big-core designs).

#Google Tensor

2021→ Current

Google's Pixel chips, built with Samsung (G1–G4) and then TSMC (G5, 2025). Focused on on-device AI and photo processing rather than benchmarks.

#HiSilicon Kirin (Huawei)

2012→ Current

Huawei's in-house SoCs. US sanctions (2020) cut it off from TSMC, but the Kirin 9000S (2023, SMIC 7 nm) brought 5G back to Huawei phones.

#Others: UNISOC, Tegra, OMAP, Snapdragon S4

Legacy

UNISOC (Spreadtrum) powers ultra-budget phones. Historic: NVIDIA Tegra (Tegra 2/3/4 tablets, now the Nintendo Switch), TI OMAP (early Droids), Intel Atom phones (2012–2016).

#Modems & baseband

Current

The radio chip for cellular. Often integrated into the SoC (Snapdragon), or separate (iPhone's Qualcomm modems → Apple's own C1 modem in 2025's iPhone 16e).

#Phone hardware explained

Screens, cameras, storage, batteries, SIMs and charging.

#LCD (TFT / IPS) phone screens

Legacy

Backlit liquid crystal screens: cheaper, no burn-in, greyer blacks. Apple's 'Retina' IPS (iPhone 4, 2010, ~326 PPI). Now mostly on budget phones.

#OLED / AMOLED

2007→ Current

Self-lit pixels: true blacks, thin and flexible. Samsung's AMOLED / Dynamic AMOLED led here. Watch for burn-in from static UI and PWM flicker sensitivity.

#LTPO & refresh rates

2020→ Current

LTPO (low-temperature polycrystalline oxide) backplanes vary refresh from 1 Hz to 120 Hz, which saves battery and enables always-on displays. ProMotion is Apple's name for it.

#Notches, punch-holes & Dynamic Island

2017→ Current

Ways to fit front cameras: the iPhone X notch, waterdrop notches, punch-holes, pop-up cameras (OnePlus 7 Pro), under-display cameras, Apple's Dynamic Island (2022).

#Cover glass (Gorilla Glass, Ceramic Shield)

2007→ Current

Corning Gorilla Glass (first on the iPhone), Victus 2/Armor. Apple Ceramic Shield (with Corning). Sapphire is used on camera lenses and watches.

#Phone cameras

Current

Main (wide), ultrawide, telephoto and periscope (folded) zoom lenses. Pixel binning (e.g. 200 MP → 12.5 MP). Sensor size matters more than megapixels (1-inch-type sensors on some flagships). OIS (optical image stabilisation), computational photography (HDR+, Night mode).

#Storage: eMMC vs UFS vs NVMe

Current

Phone storage is soldered. eMMC (budget, slow) → UFS 2.x/3.x/4.x (fast, Android flagships) → Apple's custom NVMe storage. Some phones still take microSD.

#RAM (LPDDR)

Current

4–24 GB of LPDDR4X/LPDDR5X, packaged right on top of the SoC (PoP). More RAM keeps more apps in memory.

#SIM cards: full → mini → micro → nano

1991→ Current

Full-size (credit card, 1991) → Mini-SIM (25 × 15 mm, '2FF') → Micro-SIM (15 × 12 mm, 3FF, 2010 iPad/iPhone 4) → Nano-SIM (12.3 × 8.8 mm, 4FF, iPhone 5, 2012).

Identify it: The gold chip is the same size on all of them. Only the plastic around it changes, which is why cutting a SIM down could work.

#eSIM / iSIM

2016→ Current

Software-provisioned SIM profiles on an embedded chip. US iPhone 14+ are eSIM-only. iSIM builds it into the SoC. Dual SIM = physical + eSIM, or two eSIMs.

#Batteries (Li-ion / Li-Po / silicon-carbon)

Current

Typical 3,000–6,000+ mAh. Silicon-carbon anodes (2023→, e.g. Honor, OnePlus, Xiaomi) pack more capacity into the same space. Removable batteries largely disappeared ~2015, and EU rules will push replaceability from 2027.

#Wired charging standards

Current

USB PD (universal), Qualcomm Quick Charge, OnePlus/OPPO Warp/SuperVOOC (up to 240 W), Xiaomi HyperCharge, Samsung Super Fast Charging (PD PPS, 25/45 W).

Commonly confused with: Proprietary fast charging only works at full speed with the brand's own charger and cable.

#Wireless charging: Qi, MagSafe, Qi2

2008→ Current

Qi (Wireless Power Consortium, 5–15 W) → Apple MagSafe for iPhone (2020, magnetic, 15–25 W) → Qi2 (2023, MagSafe-based magnetic standard, Qi2 25 W). Also reverse wireless charging.

#Headphone jack removal

2016→ Current

Apple removed the 3.5 mm jack on the iPhone 7 (2016, 'courage'). Most flagships followed. USB-C/Lightning dongles and Bluetooth earbuds (AirPods, 2016) took over.

#Biometrics

Current

Fingerprint (Touch ID 2013, capacitive), in-display optical and ultrasonic readers, face unlock (2D camera vs Face ID 3D structured light, 2017).

#Water resistance (IP ratings)

Current

IP67 = dust-tight + 1 m for 30 min, IP68 = beyond 1 m (maker-specified depth). The first digit is solids (dust), the second liquids.

Commonly confused with: Water-resistant ≠ waterproof, and resistance wears off as seals age.

#Mobile operating systems

Current

Current: Android (with skins like One UI, HyperOS, ColorOS, OxygenOS, Pixel UI), iOS, HarmonyOS NEXT (Huawei, no Android base, 2024). Past: Symbian, BlackBerry OS / BB10, Windows Phone, webOS (Palm), Bada (Samsung), Firefox OS → KaiOS, Tizen, Sailfish, MeeGo.

#Tri-folds & foldables: phones that turn into tablets

Phones that fold once, twice, and cost as much as a laptop.

#Apple iPhone Duo

Phones · 2026 Current

Apple's first foldable iPhone, a book-style foldable announced on 9 September 2026 and on sale from 23 October 2026. Opened, its screen is about 50% larger than the iPhone 18 Pro Max's.

Price (US)$1,999 (256 GB) to $3,199 (2 TB)
TypeBook fold (not a tri-fold)

Commonly confused with: iPhone Duo (folds once) vs tri-folds (fold twice)

Fun fact: At launch it became the most expensive iPhone Apple had ever sold.

Sources: Technology Magazine: iPhone Duo, Apple's first foldable, at $1,999 · Inven Global: iPhone Duo prices by storage

#Luxury & super-expensive phones

When a phone is jewellery: gold, diamonds, alligator leather, and a personal concierge button.

#Vertu

Phones · 1998– Active

The best-known luxury phone brand. Vertu was started in 1998 as a Nokia luxury brand in England, sold off in 2012, and today sells Android phones and foldables wrapped in leather, titanium, gold and gemstones, plus a concierge service. The Vertu Agent Q starts around $5,400, and its top alligator, white-gold and diamond edition is listed at about $109,680. The AlphaFold foldable launched at over $6,800.

MaterialsLeather, titanium, sapphire crystal, gold, diamonds
Typical price$5,000 to over $100,000
SpecsOften behind cheaper flagships

Identify it: Pointed, jewel-like shape, stitched leather back, a big 'V' and a red concierge key on many models

Commonly confused with: Luxury brand (Vertu) vs customised flagships (gold-plated iPhones by firms like Caviar)

Fun fact: Reviewers often note that the processor and cameras in luxury phones are weaker than a normal $1,000 flagship's: you pay for materials and service, not speed.

Sources: Notebookcheck: Vertu AlphaFold launches for over $6,800 · BGR: the $5,400 Vertu Agent Q Android phone · MobileMasr: Vertu Agent Q top edition at $109,680

#Rugged 'camping' phones: thick, bright and weeks of battery

The bricks with blinding lights, giant batteries and power-bank superpowers.

#What a rugged phone is

Concept

A phone built to survive drops, sand, water and heat: rubber-armoured body, screws on the back, IP68/IP69K water and dust rating, and MIL-STD-810H drop and temperature testing. The 'camping' models go further: batteries of 20,000–33,000 mAh (four to six times a normal phone), a 1,000–1,200-lumen camping light on the back, very loud speakers, and reverse charging so the phone works as a power bank. The price is weight and thickness: around 500–700 g and 25–35 mm thick, like carrying two or three phones stacked together.

Commonly confused with: 'Up to a month of battery' figures assume mostly standby. With real use, a 20,000 mAh phone lasts roughly 2 days of heavy use (screen, GPS, camera) up to about a week of light use: see the calculator below.

#What about solar charging?

Concept

A solar panel built into a phone is tiny: in full sun it gives only a trickle of power, it heats the phone, and it sits under the screen or on the back. Companies such as Kyocera and Infinix have shown solar-phone prototypes and concepts, but they haven't become normal products. What campers actually use is a foldable solar panel (20–60 W) or a solar power bank, plugged into the phone's huge battery. The calculator below shows why.

#Calculator: how long does a camping phone last, and can the sun refill it?

Concept

Battery size in mAh × voltage (≈3.87 V) = energy in watt-hours. Compare that with how much power the phone uses, and what a real solar panel delivers in Saudi sunshine (rough averages; real results depend on heat, angle and clouds).

Python
battery_mah = 20_000
wh = battery_mah / 1000 * 3.87                     # ≈ 77 Wh of energy
print(f"Battery energy: {wh:.0f} Wh (a normal phone: about 19 Wh)")

uses = {"Standby, signal on": 0.10, "Light use (calls, WhatsApp)": 0.45,
        "Heavy use (screen, GPS, camera)": 1.6, "Camping light on full": 6.0}   # watts
for name, watts in uses.items():
    hours = wh * 0.9 / watts                        # ~10% lost as heat
    print(f"{name:<33}{hours:>7.0f} h  = {hours / 24:4.1f} days")

sun_hours = 6                                       # good sunshine hours a day in Saudi Arabia
for panel, watts, eff in [("Built-in phone panel (~1 W)", 1, 0.5), ("Foldable panel 28 W", 28, 0.6)]:
    per_day = watts * eff * sun_hours
    print(f"{panel:<33}{per_day:>5.0f} Wh/day -> full refill in {wh / per_day:4.1f} days")
Output
Battery energy: 77 Wh (a normal phone: about 19 Wh)
Standby, signal on                   697 h  = 29.0 days
Light use (calls, WhatsApp)          155 h  =  6.5 days
Heavy use (screen, GPS, camera)       44 h  =  1.8 days
Camping light on full                 12 h  =  0.5 days
Built-in phone panel (~1 W)          3 Wh/day -> full refill in 25.8 days
Foldable panel 28 W                101 Wh/day -> full refill in  0.8 days

Source: TechRadar: Energizer P30K Apex, a 30,000 mAh phone charged once a month

#Camping & desert tech tips

Guide

Download offline maps (Google Maps offline areas, Organic Maps) before you go, and share your location with someone at home. Keep the phone out of direct sun: heat damages batteries faster than anything, and an overheated phone will dim its screen, stop charging and eventually shut itself down. Carry a power bank or foldable solar panel even with a big-battery phone. In emergencies in Saudi Arabia call 911, the unified emergency number. Newer phones with satellite SOS can send emergency messages with no signal where the service is supported.

Part 4

Tablets

Slates, e-readers and pen computers: history, product lines, styluses and keyboards.

#Tablet history

Slate computers, from the 1960s Dynabook concept to the iPad Pro.

#Dynabook concept (Alan Kay)

1968–1972 Obsolete

Alan Kay's vision of a 'personal computer for children of all ages', a thin slate. Never built as described, but it inspired laptops and tablets alike.

Fun fact: The Toshiba laptop brand 'dynabook' (now Dynabook Inc.) borrowed the name.

#GRiDPad

1989 Obsolete

One of the first commercial tablet computers: MS-DOS, pen input, 4.5 lb. Designed by Jeff Hawkins, who went on to create the Palm Pilot.

#Apple Newton MessagePad

1993–1998 Obsolete

Apple's handwriting-recognising pen tablet/PDA, the device that made 'PDA' a household term. Its early handwriting recognition was mocked on The Simpsons and Doonesbury.

Fun fact: Steve Jobs killed the Newton in 1998 shortly after returning to Apple.

#Windows XP Tablet PC Edition

2002–2008 Obsolete

Microsoft's push for pen-based convertible and slate PCs with active Wacom digitizers: Toshiba Portégé, ThinkPad X-Tablets, HP Compaq TC1100, Fujitsu Stylistic.

#UMPC / Origami

2006–2008 Obsolete

Ultra-Mobile PCs: small 7" Windows tablets (Samsung Q1, Sony VAIO UX). Slow, pricey and short on battery.

#iPad (original)

2010 Obsolete

Apple's 9.7" multitouch tablet running iPhone OS. It sold 15 million units in about 9 months and defined the modern tablet category.

Fun fact: Many critics in 2010 dismissed it as 'just a big iPhone'.

#Android Honeycomb tablets

2011 Obsolete

Android 3.0 'Honeycomb' was tablet-only and debuted on the Motorola Xoom. Few tablet-optimised apps meant a weak start.

#HP TouchPad (webOS)

2011 Obsolete

HP's webOS tablet was discontinued after 49 days. The $99 fire sale caused a buying frenzy.

Fun fact: The fire sale made it briefly the second-best-selling tablet on the market.

#BlackBerry PlayBook

2011–2014 Obsolete

RIM's 7" QNX-based tablet. It launched without a native email app, which was a bizarre choice for a BlackBerry.

#Microsoft Surface RT / Pro

2012→ Current

Surface RT (ARM, Windows RT, couldn't run desktop apps) flopped. Surface Pro (x86) created the detachable 2-in-1 'tablet that can replace your laptop' category.

#Nexus 7

2012–2013 Obsolete

Google + ASUS 7" tablet for $199: a beloved, affordable Android tablet that showed what stock Android could do.

#Tablet types & lines

The kinds of tablets you can buy today.

#iPad (base)

2010→ Current

Apple's entry tablet (10th gen 2022, 11th gen 2025 with A16). Works with USB-C Apple Pencil / 1st-gen Pencil, depending on model.

#iPad mini

2012→ Current

The ~7.9–8.3" small iPad. Popular with pilots (EFB charts), doctors and readers.

#iPad Air

2013→ Current

The mid-tier iPad: M-series chips (M1 Air 2022 → M2/M3), offered in 11" and 13" sizes since 2024.

#iPad Pro

2015→ Current

The pro tablet: ProMotion 120 Hz, Face ID, Thunderbolt, LiDAR. The 2024 M4 iPad Pro introduced Tandem OLED and a 5.1 mm body, the thinnest Apple device to date.

#Samsung Galaxy Tab S / A / FE

2010→ Current

Samsung's Android tablets: Tab S flagships (AMOLED, S Pen included, DeX desktop mode), Tab S FE (Fan Edition), Tab A (budget), Active (rugged).

#Amazon Fire tablets

2011→ Current

Very cheap 7/8/10/11" tablets running Fire OS (forked Android, no Google Play by default). Used for media, Kindle reading and kids.

#Android tablets (others)

Current

Lenovo Tab / Legion Tab (gaming), Xiaomi Pad / Redmi Pad, OnePlus Pad, Google Pixel Tablet (2023, speaker dock), Huawei MatePad (HarmonyOS), Honor Pad, TCL NXTPAPER (paper-like matte display).

#Windows tablets / detachables

Current

Microsoft Surface Pro, Lenovo ThinkPad X12/X1 Tablet, ASUS ROG Flow Z13 (gaming tablet), Dell Latitude 7350 Detachable.

#E-readers (E Ink)

2004→ Current

Paper-like electrophoretic (E Ink) displays that are easy on the eyes and last weeks on a charge. Sony Reader (2006), Amazon Kindle (2007), Kobo, Barnes & Noble Nook, PocketBook, colour Kaleido panels.

Fun fact: The first Kindle (2007) had free built-in 3G called 'Whispernet' for buying books anywhere.

#E-ink writing tablets

2017→ Current

Paper-like note-taking tablets: reMarkable 1/2/Paper Pro, Boox (Android E Ink), Kindle Scribe, Supernote, Kobo Elipsa.

#Kids' tablets

Current

Amazon Fire Kids (bumper case, 2-year warranty), LeapFrog LeapPad, VTech, Samsung Galaxy Tab A Kids. Parental controls and rugged cases.

#Rugged & enterprise tablets

Current

Panasonic Toughbook/Toughpad, Samsung Galaxy Tab Active, Zebra, Getac for warehouses, the military and field service.

#Styluses, keyboards & tablet tech

How you interact with a tablet beyond your finger.

#Resistive vs capacitive touch

Current

Resistive screens (PDAs, Nintendo DS, old GPS) respond to pressure from any object and need a stylus. Capacitive screens (iPhone onward) sense your skin's electrical charge and support multitouch.

Fun fact: Capacitive gloves have conductive thread in the fingertips so the screen can sense them.

#Passive vs active styluses

Current

Passive (a rubber nub that mimics a finger, no pressure). Active: EMR (Wacom, Samsung S Pen, needs no battery), AES (Wacom Active ES), MPP (Microsoft Pen Protocol), USI (Chromebooks), Apple Pencil.

#Apple Pencil generations

2015→ Current

1st gen (Lightning cap, charged by plugging into the iPad) → 2nd gen (2018, magnetic charging) → USB-C (2023, no pressure sensitivity) → Pencil Pro (2024, squeeze, barrel roll, haptics).

Commonly confused with: Check compatibility carefully: each iPad model supports only certain Pencils.

#Samsung S Pen

2011→ Current

A Wacom EMR-based pen. Galaxy Note phones, Tab S tablets, and Galaxy S Ultra phones (S22–S25 Ultra). Needs no charging for writing. Some models add Bluetooth 'Air Actions'.

#Keyboard covers & folios

Current

Apple Smart Keyboard, Magic Keyboard (floating cantilever, trackpad), Microsoft Type Cover, Samsung Book Cover Keyboard. They connect through Smart Connector / Pogo pins (magnetic contacts, no pairing).

#Tablet chipsets

Current

iPad: A-series → M-series (Apple Silicon). Android: Snapdragon 8-series (flagship), MediaTek Dimensity/Kompanio, Exynos, Tensor (Pixel Tablet). Amazon Fire: MediaTek.

#Desktop modes on tablets

Current

Samsung DeX, iPadOS Stage Manager and windowed apps (iPadOS 26), Android desktop windowing, which let tablets act like laptops with external displays.

#Computing pioneers & historic brands

The companies that built personal computing, including many that no longer exist. IBM and Apple (Macintosh) are here. Several of them (Apple, HP, Lenovo, Dell) also appear in the laptop and phone sections.

#IBM

Founded 1911 (as CTR; IBM from 1924) · USA Active
HQArmonk, New York
Known forMainframes, the IBM PC 5150 (1981) that set the PC standard, the ThinkPad, PS/2 & Micro Channel, the hard drive, the floppy disk, DRAM, relational databases, Deep Blue, Watson, quantum computers.
Key product linesSystem/360 (1964), IBM PC/XT/AT, PS/2, PCjr, ThinkPad (1992–2005), Aptiva, NetVista, z-series mainframes, POWER servers.
StatusStill active. Sold its PC division to Lenovo (2005) and x86 servers to Lenovo (2014).

Fun fact: IBM built the PC from off-the-shelf parts and an outside OS (Microsoft DOS), so anyone could clone it, and the 'IBM-compatible PC' outgrew IBM itself.

#Apple (Macintosh)

Founded 1976 · USA Active
HQCupertino, California
Known forThe Apple II, the Macintosh (1984), the first mass-market GUI computer with a mouse, then iMac, iPod, iPhone, iPad and Apple Silicon.
Key product linesApple I/II/III, Lisa, Macintosh 128K/Plus/SE/II, PowerBook, Performa, Power Mac, iMac, iBook, MacBook / Air / Pro, Mac mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro, iPhone, iPad, Watch, Vision Pro.

Fun fact: The 1984 Mac launched with the Ridley Scott-directed '1984' Super Bowl ad. Apple Computer, Inc. dropped 'Computer' from its name in 2007.

#Commodore

Founded 1954 (computers from 1977) · Canada → USA Defunct brand
Known forFounded by Jack Tramiel. The Commodore 64 (1982) is often called the best-selling single computer model ever. Also the PET and the Amiga.
Key product linesPET 2001 (1977), VIC-20 (first computer to sell 1 million units), C64, C128, Amiga 500/1000/1200/4000, CD32.
StatusBankrupt 1994. Brand names later licensed for retro hardware.

Fun fact: Commodore went bankrupt in 1994. The Amiga's multitasking and graphics were years ahead of PCs and Macs in 1985.

#Atari

Founded 1972 · USA Active
Known forPong, the Atari 2600 console, Atari 400/800 home computers and the Atari ST (1985), a favourite of musicians thanks to built-in MIDI.
Key product linesPong, 2600, 5200, 7800, 400/800/XL/XE, ST/STE/TT/Falcon, Lynx, Jaguar, Portfolio palmtop.
StatusThe original company split in 1984. The brand now belongs to Atari SA (France), which makes retro consoles and games.

Fun fact: Steve Jobs worked at Atari in 1974, and Steve Wozniak helped design Breakout for it.

#Tandy / RadioShack

Founded 1919 (Tandy) / 1921 (RadioShack) · USA Defunct brand
Known forThe TRS-80 (1977), one of the '1977 Trinity' with the Apple II and Commodore PET. The Tandy 1000 was a popular cheap IBM PC compatible.
Key product linesTRS-80 Model I/III/4, Color Computer ('CoCo'), Model 100 laptop (1983), Tandy 1000/2000.
StatusRadioShack went bankrupt in 2015 and 2017. The brand survives in licensed form.

Fun fact: The TRS-80 was jokingly called the 'Trash-80'. The Model 100 was a favourite of journalists for filing stories from the field.

#Texas Instruments (TI)

Founded 1930 (as GSI) · USA Active
HQDallas, Texas
Known forJack Kilby built the first integrated circuit at TI (1958). The TI-99/4A home computer and the graphing calculators every US student knows.
Key product linesTI-99/4A (1981), TI-83/84/89/Nspire calculators, Speak & Spell, DSPs, OMAP phone chips, analog chips.

Fun fact: TI lost a 1983 price war with Commodore, cutting the TI-99/4A to $49, and left home computers with heavy losses.

#Sinclair Research

Founded 1973 · UK Acquired / merged
Known forSir Clive Sinclair's cheap computers started the UK home-computer boom: the ZX80, ZX81 and the ZX Spectrum (1982) with its rubber keys.
Key product linesZX80, ZX81 (Timex Sinclair 1000 in the US), ZX Spectrum, Spectrum+, QL, C5 electric trike.
StatusSold its computer line to Amstrad in 1986.

Fun fact: The Sinclair C5 electric vehicle (1985) was a famous flop.

#Amstrad

Founded 1968 · UK Acquired / merged
Known forAlan Sugar's budget electronics: the CPC 464 (1984, with a built-in cassette drive), the PCW word processors and the PC1512, a cheap PC clone.
Key product linesCPC 464/664/6128, PCW 8256, PC1512/1640, Sinclair Spectrum +2/+3, satellite receivers.
StatusAcquired by BSkyB in 2007.

Fun fact: Alan Sugar later became famous as the host of the UK version of The Apprentice.

#Acorn Computers

Founded 1978 · UK Defunct brand
Known forThe BBC Micro (1981), used in UK schools, and the Archimedes (1987), the first computer with an ARM processor, which Acorn designed.
Key product linesAtom, BBC Micro, Electron, Archimedes, RiscPC, RISC OS.
StatusBroken up around 1998–2000. Its legacy lives on in ARM Holdings.

Fun fact: ARM began as the 'Acorn RISC Machine'. Acorn spun it off in 1990 with Apple and VLSI, and today ARM chips run almost every phone.

#Compaq

Founded 1982 · USA Acquired / merged
HQHouston, Texas
Known forThe Compaq Portable (1983), the first legally cloned 100% IBM-compatible PC, and the Deskpro 386, which beat IBM to the 386. Once the world's largest PC maker.
Key product linesPortable, Deskpro, Presario, ProLiant servers, Armada and Evo laptops, iPAQ Pocket PC.
StatusBought DEC (1998). Merged into HP in 2002.

Fun fact: Compaq reverse-engineered the IBM BIOS using a 'clean room' process to avoid copyright infringement.

#Gateway (Gateway 2000)

Founded 1985 · USA Acquired / merged
Known forDirect-mail PCs shipped in iconic cow-spotted boxes from South Dakota.
Key product linesGateway 2000 desktops, Solo laptops, Profile all-in-ones, Destination media PCs.
StatusAcquired by Acer (2007). The brand was revived for Walmart-exclusive budget laptops.

Fun fact: Gateway named itself 'Gateway 2000' to sound futuristic, then dropped the '2000' in 1999 as the year arrived.

#Packard Bell

Founded 1926 (PCs from 1986) · USA Defunct brand
Known forA 1990s retail-store PC giant known for cheap home PCs bundled with software (and a reputation for poor quality).
Key product linesLegend, Pack-Mate, Multimedia, later EasyNote laptops (Europe).
StatusNEC took a stake in the 1990s, then Acer acquired it in 2008. The brand was phased out in the 2010s.

Fun fact: It began as a radio maker in Los Angeles. It has no relation to Hewlett-Packard or Bell Labs.

#eMachines

Founded 1998 · USA Defunct brand
Known forSub-$500 PCs that pushed prices down in the late 1990s and 2000s.
Key product lineseTower, eOne (an iMac look-alike that Apple sued over), T-series.
StatusAcquired by Gateway (2004), then Acer. Retired in 2013.

Fun fact: The eOne's resemblance to the iMac G3 led to a lawsuit and a quick redesign.

#Digital Equipment Corp. (DEC)

Founded 1957 · USA Acquired / merged
HQMaynard, Massachusetts
Known forMinicomputers that brought computing to labs and universities: the PDP-8, PDP-11, VAX, plus the Alpha chip and the AltaVista search engine.
Key product linesPDP series, VAX/VMS, DECstation, Alpha, VT100 terminals, AltaVista.
StatusAcquired by Compaq in 1998.

Fun fact: Unix and the C language were developed on DEC PDP-7 and PDP-11 machines at Bell Labs. The VT100's escape codes are still used in today's terminals.

#Sun Microsystems

Founded 1982 · USA Acquired / merged
Known forSPARC/Solaris Unix workstations and servers. Created Java (1995) and NFS. 'The network is the computer.'
Key product linesSPARCstation, Sun Ultra, Sun Fire, Solaris, Java, MySQL (acquired 2008), StarOffice/OpenOffice.
StatusAcquired by Oracle in 2010.

Fun fact: 'SUN' originally stood for Stanford University Network.

#Silicon Graphics (SGI)

Founded 1981 · USA Defunct brand
Known forHigh-end 3D graphics workstations (MIPS/IRIX) used for Jurassic Park, Terminator 2 and NASA. Created OpenGL.
Key product linesIRIS, Indigo, Indy, O2, Octane, Onyx, Origin supercomputers.
StatusBankrupt in 2009. Its assets went to Rackable (renamed SGI), which HPE bought in 2016.

Fun fact: SGI helped design the Nintendo 64's graphics chip.

#NeXT

Founded 1985 · USA Acquired / merged
Known forSteve Jobs's company after he left Apple: the black magnesium NeXT Computer (1988) and the NeXTSTEP OS.
Key product linesNeXT Computer, NeXTcube, NeXTstation, NeXTSTEP, OpenStep, WebObjects.
StatusApple bought NeXT in 1997, and NeXTSTEP became the basis of Mac OS X, iOS and macOS.

Fun fact: Tim Berners-Lee wrote the first World Wide Web browser and server on a NeXT at CERN (1990). Doom was also developed on NeXT machines.

#Wang Laboratories

Founded 1951 · USA Defunct brand
Known forFounded by An Wang. Dedicated word-processing systems that ruled 1970s–80s offices.
Key product linesWang 2200, Wang OIS/VS word processors, Wang PC.
StatusBankrupt 1992. Acquired by Getronics 1999.

Fun fact: At its peak in the 1980s, Wang employed ~30,000 people, then missed the PC shift.

#Osborne Computer

Founded 1980 · USA Defunct brand
Known forThe Osborne 1 (1981), the first commercially successful portable computer, with a bundle of free software.
Key product linesOsborne 1, Executive.
StatusBankrupt in 1983.

Fun fact: Gave its name to the 'Osborne effect': announcing a future product too early kills sales of the current one.

#Kaypro

Founded 1952 (as Non-Linear Systems) · USA Defunct brand
Known forRugged metal CP/M 'luggables' that beat the Osborne on value.
Key product linesKaypro II, 4, 10, Kaypro 2000 laptop.
StatusBankrupt in 1990.

Fun fact: It began as a maker of digital voltmeters.

#Zenith Data Systems

Founded 1979 · USA Defunct brand
Known forHeathkit kit computers and later IBM-compatible desktops and laptops, including a big US government contract.
Key product linesHeathkit H8/H89, Z-100, SupersPort laptops.
StatusSold to Groupe Bull in 1989, later absorbed by Packard Bell NEC.

Fun fact: Heathkit was famous for build-it-yourself electronics kits.

#AST Research

Founded 1980 · USA Defunct brand
Known forStarted with memory expansion cards for IBM PCs and became a top-5 PC maker in the early 1990s.
Key product linesSixPakPlus cards, Bravo, Advantage!, Ascentia laptops.
StatusAcquired by Samsung in 1997, later shut down.

Fun fact: 'AST' came from the founders' initials: Albert Wong, Safi Qureshey, Thomas Yuen.

#MITS

Founded 1969 · USA Defunct brand
Known forMade the Altair 8800 (1975), the kit computer that launched the hobbyist PC revolution.
Key product linesAltair 8800, Altair 680.
StatusSold to Pertec in 1977.

Fun fact: Microsoft's very first product was Altair BASIC, and Microsoft was founded in Albuquerque to be near MITS.

#Xerox PARC

Founded 1970 · USA Active
Known forThe research lab that invented the modern GUI, the Alto (1973), Ethernet, laser printing and object-oriented programming (Smalltalk).
Key product linesXerox Alto, Xerox Star 8010 (1981).
StatusNow 'PARC', an SRI International company (since 2023).

Fun fact: Steve Jobs's 1979 PARC visit inspired the Lisa and Macintosh GUIs.

#Olivetti

Founded 1908 · Italy Active
Known forTypewriters, then the Programma 101 (1965), considered one of the first desktop computers, and the Olivetti M24 PC.
Key product linesProgramma 101, M20, M24, Echos laptops.
StatusNow part of TIM (Telecom Italia), focused on business devices.

Fun fact: NASA used Programma 101s to help plan the Apollo 11 mission.

#NEC

Founded 1899 · Japan Active
HQTokyo
Known forThe PC-98 series, which dominated Japanese PCs for 15 years, plus monitors, the TurboGrafx-16 / PC Engine console and supercomputers.
Key product linesPC-8801, PC-9801 series, Versa laptops, MultiSync monitors, PC Engine.
StatusConsumer PCs now via a joint venture with Lenovo (NEC Personal Computers, 2011).

Fun fact: PC-98 machines used their own architecture, so Japanese PC software long wouldn't run on Western IBM compatibles.

#Fujitsu

Founded 1935 · Japan Active
HQTokyo
Known forMainframes, the FM-7 and FM Towns (one of the first PCs with a built-in CD-ROM, 1989), and Lifebook laptops. Built the Fugaku supercomputer.
Key product linesFM Towns, Lifebook, Stylistic tablets, Esprimo, Celsius, Fugaku.
StatusPC unit (Fujitsu Client Computing) has been majority-owned by Lenovo since 2018.

Fun fact: Fujitsu's K computer and Fugaku have both held the world's #1 supercomputer title.

#Toshiba

Founded 1875 (Toshiba name 1939) · Japan Active
Known forThe T1100 (1985), widely credited as the first mass-market IBM-compatible laptop. Inventor of NAND flash (Fujio Masuoka, 1980s).
Key product linesT1100, Satellite, Tecra, Portégé, Libretto, Qosmio, Dynabook.
StatusPC business sold to Sharp (2018) → renamed Dynabook Inc. Memory spun off as Kioxia.

Fun fact: Toshiba was the world's top laptop seller through much of the 1990s.

#Psion

Founded 1980 · UK Acquired / merged
Known forPocket organisers and palmtops: the Organiser (1984), Series 3 and the beloved Series 5 (1997) with its sliding keyboard. Its EPOC OS became Symbian.
Key product linesOrganiser, Series 3/3a/3mx, Series 5/5mx, Revo, netBook, Workabout.
StatusAcquired by Motorola Solutions in 2012.

Fun fact: Psion coined the term 'netBook' in 1999, long before the 2007 netbook craze.

#Laptop & PC brands

The major notebook and desktop makers today. Apple, Fujitsu, NEC and Toshiba are in Pioneers above, and Samsung, Huawei and Xiaomi laptops are listed under their phone entries.

#Lenovo

Founded 1984 (as Legend) · China Active
HQBeijing & Morrisville, North Carolina (HQ registered in Hong Kong)
Known forThe world's largest PC maker by units. Bought IBM's PC division (2005), which brought ThinkPad with it, plus Motorola Mobility (2014) and a majority of Fujitsu's PC unit.
Key product linesThinkPad, ThinkCentre, ThinkStation, IdeaPad, Yoga, Legion (gaming), LOQ, Legion Go, Lenovo Tab.

Fun fact: ThinkPads have flown on the International Space Station since the 1990s.

#Dell Technologies

Founded 1984 · USA Active
HQRound Rock, Texas
Known forMichael Dell started it from his University of Texas dorm room (as PCs Limited). Pioneered build-to-order direct sales. Owns Alienware.
Key product linesXPS, Inspiron, Latitude, Precision, OptiPlex, Vostro, Alienware, PowerEdge servers. In 2025 consumer and business lines began moving to Dell / Dell Pro / Dell Pro Max naming.

Fun fact: Dell went private in 2013 in a ~$25 billion buyout and returned to the stock market in 2018.

#HP (HP Inc.)

Founded 1939 · USA Active
HQPalo Alto, California
Known forStarted in a Palo Alto garage (the 'birthplace of Silicon Valley'). Merged with Compaq (2002). Split into HP Inc. (PCs, printers) and HPE (enterprise) in 2015.
Key product linesPavilion, Envy, Spectre, OmniBook, EliteBook, ProBook, ZBook, Omen and Victus (gaming), HyperX (bought 2021), LaserJet/DeskJet printers.

#ASUS

Founded 1989 · Taiwan Active
HQTaipei
Known forStarted as a motherboard maker, now a top-5 PC brand. Launched the netbook era with the Eee PC (2007). Its ROG brand is a gaming giant.
Key product linesROG (Strix, Zephyrus, Flow, Ally), TUF Gaming, Zenbook, Vivobook, ProArt, ExpertBook, Chromebooks, motherboards, GPUs, routers, ROG Phone, Zenfone.

#Acer

Founded 1976 (as Multitech) · Taiwan Active
HQNew Taipei City
Known forA major global PC maker that owns the Gateway, Packard Bell and eMachines brands.
Key product linesAspire, Swift, Spin, Predator (gaming), Nitro, TravelMate, Chromebook, ConceptD, Predator Helios.

Fun fact: Acer was briefly the world's #2 PC maker around 2009–2011 on the back of netbooks.

#MSI (Micro-Star International)

Founded 1986 · Taiwan Active
HQNew Taipei City
Known forMotherboards and graphics cards, then gaming laptops and handhelds.
Key product linesTitan, Raider, Vector, Stealth, Katana, Cyborg, Prestige, Modern, MEG/MPG/MAG boards, Ventus/Gaming X GPUs, MSI Claw.

#Razer

Founded 2005 (brand from 1998) · USA / Singapore Active
HQIrvine, California & Singapore
Known for'For Gamers. By Gamers.' Gaming mice, keyboards and headsets, plus the Razer Blade, the thin, all-metal gaming laptop sometimes called the 'MacBook of gaming laptops'.

Founded 2012 (Microsoft 1975) · USA Active
HQRedmond, Washington
Known forMicrosoft's own hardware line, started to show off Windows 8. The Surface Pro defined the detachable 2-in-1.

#LG gram

#Framework

Known forThe rugged laptop and tablet benchmark for military, police and field use. Also Let's Note ultraportables (Japan).

HQNew Taipei City
Known forMotherboards and GPUs, with AORUS as the gaming brand.

Known forSony's stylish laptops (VAIO 505, X505, Z, Type P). Sold off as an independent company in 2014.

Sources: GIGAZINE: VAIO acquired by Nojima (2024) · MLex: Nojima to buy Vaio, completion 6 Jan 2025

#Medion

Known forFamous for Aldi supermarket PCs. Erazer gaming line.

HQDenver, Colorado
Known forLinux-first laptops and desktops, maker of Pop!_OS and the COSMIC desktop.
Key product linesLemur, Galago, Oryx, Thelio desktop, Launch keyboard.

Fun fact: Its Thelio desktops are designed and built in Denver, Colorado.

#Chuwi

Founded 2004 · China Active
HQShenzhen
Known forBudget laptops, tablets and mini PCs, popular on Amazon and AliExpress.
Key product linesHeroBook, CoreBook, Hi10 tablets, LarkBox mini PC.

Fun fact: Chuwi was known for cheap dual-boot Windows/Android tablets in the mid-2010s.

#Prebuilt desktop & mini-PC brands

Companies that sell ready-built gaming and workstation PCs. Dell, HP, Lenovo (Legion), ASUS, Acer, MSI and Apple (iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro) also sell prebuilts.

#Alienware

Founded 1996 · USA Active
Known forPremium gaming PCs and laptops with sci-fi styling and an alien-head logo.
Key product linesAurora desktops, Area-51, m/x-series and Alienware 16/18 laptops, monitors.
StatusAcquired by Dell in 2006.

Fun fact: Founded by Nelson Gonzalez and Alex Aguila in Miami, inspired by The X-Files.

#CyberPowerPC

Founded 1998 · USA Active
HQCity of Industry, California
Known forA high-volume gaming prebuilt maker sold through Amazon, Best Buy, Costco and Walmart.
Key product linesGamer Xtreme, Gamer Supreme, Gamer Master.

Fun fact: One of the biggest system builders by volume in the US.

#iBUYPOWER

Founded 1999 · USA Active
HQCity of Industry, California
Known forValue gaming prebuilts. Its parent also owns the HYTE PC case brand.
Key product linesY40/Y60-based builds, Element, SlateMesh, TraceMesh.

Fun fact: HYTE's Y60 'fish tank' case came out of iBUYPOWER's design team.

#NZXT

Founded 2004 · USA Active
HQLos Angeles area, California
Known forStarted with PC cases and expanded into AIO coolers, peripherals, the CAM software and BLD prebuilts.
Key product linesH-series cases (H510/H5/H6/H9), Kraken AIOs, Player prebuilts, Function keyboards.

Fun fact: NZXT's H1 case had a 2021 recall over a riser screw fire risk.

#Corsair / Origin PC

Founded 1994 / 2009 · USA Active
HQMilpitas, California (Corsair)
Known forCorsair (memory, then everything) acquired boutique builder Origin PC (founded by ex-Alienware staff) in 2019.
Key product linesCorsair Vengeance PCs, Origin Millennium/Neuron/Chronos, Corsair One (compact).

Fun fact: Corsair's first products were cache memory modules for 1990s PCs.

#Maingear

Founded 2002 · USA Active
HQKenilworth, New Jersey
Known forBoutique custom gaming PCs with high-end finishes and custom water cooling.
Key product linesRush, Turbo, MG-1, Vybe.

Fun fact: Maingear has built PCs for celebrities and streamers, and partnered with Ninja (the streamer) on an MG-1 line.

#Falcon Northwest

Founded 1992 · USA Active
HQMedford, Oregon
Known forOne of the oldest boutique gaming PC makers. Known for hand-painted cases.
Key product linesMach V, Talon, FragBox, Tiki (compact).

Fun fact: Falcon Northwest claims to be the first company to build gaming PCs specifically.

#Digital Storm

Founded 2002 · USA Active
HQCalifornia
Known forCustom gaming and workstation PCs with hardline liquid cooling.
Key product linesAventum, Velox, Lynx, Spark.

Fun fact: Its Aventum line uses a custom chassis designed for big multi-radiator loops.

#Puget Systems

Founded 2000 · USA Active
HQAuburn, Washington
Known forWorkstations tuned for creative and scientific software (Adobe, DaVinci, Unreal, AI). Publishes respected benchmarks.
Key product linesGenesis, Spirit, Serenity (quiet), rackmounts.

Fun fact: Puget's hardware articles are widely cited in the content-creation community.

#Velocity Micro

Founded 1992 · USA Active
HQRichmond, Virginia
Known forVirginia-built performance desktops and workstations.
Key product linesRaptor, ProMagix.

Fun fact: One of the longest-running US boutique builders.

#Skytech Gaming

Founded 2010s · USA Active
Known forBudget-to-mid gaming prebuilts, best sellers on Amazon.
Key product linesChronos, Archangel, Shiva, Blaze.

#Velztorm

Founded 2010s · USA Active
Known forGaming prebuilts sold mainly through online retailers.
Key product linesLux, Praetix, Mini.

#Intel NUC → ASUS NUC

Founded 2013 · USA → Taiwan Acquired / merged
Known forIntel's 'Next Unit of Computing' mini PCs (about 10 × 10 cm). Intel exited in 2023 and ASUS took over the line.
Key product linesNUC kits, Skull Canyon/Hades Canyon/Serpent Canyon gaming NUCs, ROG NUC.
StatusLicensed to ASUS since 2023.

Fun fact: Hades Canyon (2018) put an Intel CPU and an AMD Radeon GPU on one package.

#Beelink

Founded 2011 · China Active
HQShenzhen
Known forAffordable mini PCs with Intel N-series and Ryzen chips.
Key product linesSER, EQ, GTi series.

Fun fact: Popular for home servers, Plex and Home Assistant boxes.

#Minisforum

Founded 2012 · China Active
HQShenzhen
Known forMini PCs and mini-ITX boards with mobile CPUs, including high-end Ryzen models.
Key product linesUM/HX/MS series, AtomMan, BD790i.

Fun fact: Its BD790i board put a 16-core mobile Ryzen 9 on a Mini-ITX desktop board.

#GMKtec

Founded 2019 · China Active
Known forValue mini PCs, including Ryzen AI Max+ 'Strix Halo' machines.
Key product linesNucBox series, EVO-X2.

Fun fact: The EVO-X2 was one of the first mini PCs with AMD's large-iGPU 'Strix Halo' chip (Ryzen AI Max+ 395).

#Zotac

Founded 2006 · Hong Kong / Macau Active
Known forNVIDIA graphics cards plus ZBOX mini PCs and 'MAGNUS' compact gaming boxes.
Key product linesAMP!, Trinity, Twin Edge GPUs, ZBOX, Zone handheld.

#Raspberry Pi

Founded 2012 · UK Active
HQCambridge, England
Known forCredit-card-sized single-board computers, originally for teaching kids programming. Now used in hobby projects, robotics and industry.
