Fun fact: More than 60 million Raspberry Pis had been sold by 2024.

#Component brands

Chip designers, board and graphics-card partners, memory and storage, cooling, cases, power supplies and peripherals. ASUS, MSI, Gigabyte, Zotac and Corsair are listed above.

#Intel

Founded 1968 · USA Active
HQSanta Clara, California
Known forFounded by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore (Moore's Law). Invented the first commercial microprocessor and created x86.
Key product linesCore, Core Ultra, Xeon, Celeron/Pentium (retired), Atom, Arc GPUs, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth chips, Optane (ended), Intel Foundry.

Fun fact: Intel's 'Intel Inside' campaign (1991) and its five-note jingle made a component a consumer brand.

#AMD (Advanced Micro Devices)

Founded 1969 · USA Active
HQSanta Clara, California
Known forIntel's long-time x86 rival. Created AMD64. Bought ATI (2006) and Xilinx (2022). Ryzen, Radeon and EPYC.
Key product linesRyzen, Threadripper, EPYC, Radeon, Instinct (AI GPUs), console chips for PlayStation and Xbox.

Fun fact: In 2009 AMD spun off its factories as GlobalFoundries and became a fabless chip designer.

#NVIDIA

Founded 1993 · USA Active
HQSanta Clara, California
Known forCo-founded by Jensen Huang. GeForce graphics, CUDA (2006) for GPU computing, and the data-centre GPUs behind the AI boom.
Key product linesGeForce RTX, RTX PRO, H100/H200/B200 data-centre GPUs, Jetson, Tegra (Nintendo Switch), DGX.

Fun fact: NVIDIA became the first company to reach a $4 trillion market value (July 2025).

#ARM Holdings

Founded 1990 · UK Active
HQCambridge, England
Known forDesigns and licenses the ARM architecture used in nearly all phones, Apple Silicon and many servers.
Key product linesCortex-A/R/M cores, Neoverse (servers), Mali/Immortalis GPUs.

Fun fact: NVIDIA's $40 billion bid to buy ARM collapsed in 2022 under regulatory pressure. SoftBank owns most of it.

#Qualcomm

Founded 1985 · USA Active
HQSan Diego, California
Known forCDMA cellular technology and Snapdragon chips. Its modems sit in most premium phones.
Key product linesSnapdragon 8/7/6/4, Snapdragon X (PCs), X-series modems, FastConnect Wi-Fi, Quick Charge.

Fun fact: Qualcomm earns a large share of profit from patent licensing on nearly every phone sold.

#MediaTek

Founded 1997 · Taiwan Active
HQHsinchu
Known forThe world's highest-volume phone chip supplier, also in TVs, Chromebooks, routers and Amazon devices.
Key product linesDimensity, Helio, Kompanio, Filogic Wi-Fi.

Fun fact: MediaTek began making optical-drive chips for CD-ROM players.

#TSMC

Founded 1987 · Taiwan Active
HQHsinchu
Known forThe world's largest contract chipmaker (foundry). It builds chips for Apple, NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm and MediaTek.
Key product linesN7, N5, N3, N2 process nodes, CoWoS packaging.

Fun fact: Morris Chang founded TSMC at age 55 and pioneered the 'pure-play foundry' business model.

#ASRock

Founded 2002 · Taiwan Active
Known forA motherboard maker spun off from ASUS, known for value and odd boards. Now also makes Radeon graphics cards.
Key product linesTaichi, Steel Legend, Phantom Gaming, Challenger, DeskMini.

Fun fact: ASRock once sold boards supporting both AGP and PCIe, or DDR and DDR2, on one board.

#Biostar

Founded 1986 · Taiwan Active
Known forBudget motherboards and graphics cards.
Key product linesRacing, Value series.

Fun fact: One of the oldest Taiwanese motherboard brands.

#EVGA

Founded 1999 · USA Active
HQBrea, California
Known forA beloved NVIDIA graphics-card partner known for customer service, Step-Up upgrades and its K|NGP|N overclocking cards. Also PSUs.
Key product linesFTW3, Classified, K|NGP|N, SuperNOVA PSUs.
StatusStill sells PSUs and peripherals, no longer graphics cards.

Fun fact: In September 2022 EVGA quit the GPU business entirely, citing its relationship with NVIDIA.

#Sapphire

Founded 2001 · Hong Kong Active
Known forAMD-exclusive Radeon graphics-card partner.
Key product linesNitro+, Pulse, Toxic, Vapor-X.

Fun fact: Sapphire was ATI's main card manufacturer and is often seen as AMD's 'EVGA'.

#PowerColor

Founded 1997 · Taiwan Active
Known forAMD Radeon card brand from TUL Corporation.
Key product linesRed Devil, Hellhound, Red Dragon, Fighter.

Fun fact: Red Devil cards came with a tiny devil figurine in some editions.

#XFX

Founded 1989 (XFX brand 2002) · USA / Hong Kong Active
Known forA former NVIDIA partner that became AMD-only around 2010.
Key product linesSpeedster MERC, QICK, SWFT.

Fun fact: XFX's 'Double Lifetime Warranty' was a selling point in the 2000s.

#PNY

Founded 1985 · USA Active
Known forMemory, flash drives and graphics cards. NVIDIA's distributor for professional (Quadro/RTX PRO) cards in many regions.
Key product linesXLR8 GPUs, flash drives, SSDs, NVIDIA RTX PRO.

Fun fact: The name is commonly said to come from 'Paris, New York', where its founders traded memory.

#Palit / Gainward

Founded 1988 · Taiwan Active
Known forOne of the largest NVIDIA board partners by volume. Owns Gainward.
Key product linesGameRock, JetStream, Phantom.

Fun fact: Many brands' 'reference' NVIDIA cards are actually built by Palit.

#GALAX / KFA2

Founded 1994 · Hong Kong Active
Known forNVIDIA partner known for HOF (Hall of Fame) white cards used in world-record overclocks.
Key product linesHOF, EX Gamer, SG.

Fun fact: Sold as KFA2 in Europe.

#Corsair (memory & components)

Founded 1994 · USA Active
Known forRAM, PSUs, cases, coolers and peripherals. Owns Elgato (2018), SCUF and Drop.
Key product linesVengeance, Dominator, RMx/HXi PSUs, iCUE, 4000D cases, K70 keyboards.

Fun fact: Corsair went public on Nasdaq in 2020.

#G.Skill

Founded 1989 · Taiwan Active
Known forPerformance memory known for record-breaking DDR overclocks.
Key product linesTrident Z, Trident Z5, Ripjaws, Flare X.

Fun fact: G.Skill kits are regularly used for world DDR5 frequency records (10,000+ MT/s).

#Kingston

Founded 1987 · USA Active
HQFountain Valley, California
Known forThe world's largest independent DRAM module maker. Sold HyperX gaming to HP (2021) and moved memory to Kingston FURY.
Key product linesFURY Beast/Renegade, ValueRAM, KC3000/NV3 SSDs, DataTraveler flash drives.

Fun fact: Its founders shared $100 million of an acquisition payout with employees in 1996.

#Micron / Crucial

Founded 1978 / 1996 · USA Defunct brand
HQBoise, Idaho
Known forMicron makes DRAM and NAND. Crucial was its consumer brand for upgrade RAM and SSDs.
Key product linesCrucial Pro RAM, MX500, P5 Plus, T700/T705 SSDs.
StatusOn 3 December 2025 Micron announced it would exit the Crucial consumer business to focus on AI and data-centre memory. Crucial shipments to shops ended in February 2026, and Micron says it keeps honouring Crucial warranties. Micron-branded enterprise products continue.

Fun fact: Micron co-developed 3D XPoint (Optane) with Intel.

Sources: Micron press release: exit from Crucial consumer business · StorageReview: Micron exits Crucial consumer business

#SK hynix

Founded 1983 (as Hyundai Electronics) · South Korea Active
Known forThe #2 memory maker and leader in HBM memory for AI GPUs. Bought Intel's NAND business, now Solidigm.
Key product linesDDR5, LPDDR5X, HBM3E, Platinum P41/P51 SSDs.

Fun fact: SK hynix's HBM supplies a large share of NVIDIA's AI accelerators.

#Samsung Semiconductor

Founded 1974 (semis) · South Korea Active
Known forThe world's largest memory maker (DRAM & NAND), plus Exynos chips and a foundry.
Key product lines990/9100 Pro, 870 EVO, T7/T9 portable SSDs, EVO/PRO microSD, DDR5, HBM.

Fun fact: Samsung shipped the first mass-produced 3D V-NAND in 2013.

#Western Digital (WD)

Founded 1970 · USA Active
HQSan Jose, California
Known forHard drives, plus controller chips in the PC's early days. Bought HGST (2012) and SanDisk (2016), then spun SanDisk off again in 2025.
Key product linesWD Blue / Black / Red / Purple / Gold, Ultrastar, My Book, My Passport.

Fun fact: WD made the WD1003 controller card that set the standard for early PC hard-disk controllers.

Founded 1979 (as Shugart Technology) · USA Active
HQDublin, Ireland (registered) / Fremont, California
Known forBuilt the ST-506 (1980), the first 5.25" hard drive. Bought Maxtor (2006) and Samsung's HDD unit (2011).
Key product linesBarraCuda, IronWolf, SkyHawk, Exos, FireCuda, Mozaic HAMR.

Fun fact: Co-founder Al Shugart also led the team behind the 8" floppy at IBM and later founded Shugart Associates.

#SanDisk

Founded 1988 (as SunDisk) · USA Active
Known forFlash-memory pioneer: CompactFlash, SD (co-created), microSD/TransFlash, USB drives.
Key product linesExtreme, Ultra, Extreme PRO cards, SanDisk SSDs.
StatusOwned by WD 2016–2025, independent again since Feb 2025.

Fun fact: SanDisk co-founder Eli Harari holds key patents on floating-gate flash.

#Kioxia (ex-Toshiba Memory)

Founded 2017 / 2019 · Japan Active
Known forToshiba's spun-off memory business. Toshiba engineer Fujio Masuoka invented flash memory in the 1980s.
Key product linesExceria, BiCS FLASH, enterprise SSDs.

Fun fact: The name blends Japanese 'kioku' (memory) and Greek 'axia' (value).

#Solidigm

Founded 2021 · USA Active
Known forSK hynix's purchase of Intel's NAND/SSD business.
Key product linesP44 Pro, P41 Plus, D5 (QLC data-centre).

Fun fact: Makes some of the largest-capacity SSDs (122 TB-class QLC).

Founded 2001 · Taiwan Active
Known forMemory and SSDs with XPG as the gaming brand.

Founded 1997 · Taiwan Active
Known forMemory and SSDs.

Fun fact: Its T-Force kits have held DDR5 overclocking records.

#Patriot / Viper

Founded 1985 · USA Active
Known forMemory, SSDs and flash drives.

Fun fact: Viper is Patriot's enthusiast sub-brand.

Founded 1996 · USA → China Active
Known forMemory cards and SSDs. Owned by Micron (2006–2017), now by Longsys (China).

Fun fact: Lexar was one of the first CompactFlash card makers.

#Quantum

Founded 1980 · USA Active

Fun fact: Quantum sold its hard-drive business to Maxtor in 2001.

Fun fact: Conner reached $1 billion in revenue faster than any US manufacturer of its time (fourth year).

Fun fact: Some IBM Deskstar 75GXP drives failed so often (2001) that they were nicknamed 'Deathstar'.

Fun fact: Noctua developed its own liquid-crystal polymer fan blades for tighter tolerances.

Fun fact: The HAF X case was a 2010s favourite for huge airflow.

#Phanteks

Founded 2007 · Netherlands Active

#More chip & component makers

The companies whose chips are inside almost everything, even if their names aren't on the box. Intel, AMD, NVIDIA, ARM, Qualcomm, MediaTek, TSMC, Samsung, SK hynix and Micron are with components.

HQVeldhoven
Known forThe only company that makes EUV lithography machines, needed for every top-end chip. Each machine costs well over $150 million.

Fun fact: An EUV machine is shipped in about 40 containers and needs several planes.

Known forChina's biggest chip factory (foundry).
Key product lines7 nm-class and older processes; makes chips for Huawei and many others.

Current phone brands, historic and defunct phone brands (Nokia, BlackBerry, Palm, LG…), and tablet and e-reader brands.

#Phone brands (current)

Who makes the world's smartphones. Apple is in Pioneers, and ASUS (ROG Phone), Lenovo (Motorola) and Razer are covered above.

#Samsung Electronics

Founded 1969 (Samsung Group 1938) · South Korea Active
HQSuwon, South Korea
Known forThe world's largest phone maker by shipments for most of the last decade. Galaxy phones, foldables, TVs, memory and displays.
Key product linesGalaxy S, Galaxy Z Fold / Flip, Galaxy A/M, Galaxy Note (2011–2020), Galaxy Tab, Galaxy Book, Galaxy Watch/Buds.

Fun fact: Samsung started in 1938 as a trading company selling dried fish, noodles and produce.

#Google Pixel

Founded 2016 (Google 1998) · USA Active
HQMountain View, California
Known forGoogle's own phones, known for computational photography and a clean Android. The Nexus line came before them (2010–2016, built by HTC, Samsung, LG, Motorola and Huawei).
Key product linesPixel, Pixel a-series, Pixel Pro / Pro XL, Pixel Fold / Pro Fold, Pixel Tablet, Pixel Watch, Pixelbook (ended).

Fun fact: Google owned Motorola from 2012 to 2014 and bought part of HTC's phone team in 2018 for $1.1 billion.

#Xiaomi

Founded 2010 · China Active
HQBeijing
Known forFounded by Lei Jun. It grew on high-spec, low-price phones and now makes nearly everything, cars included (SU7).
Key product linesXiaomi number series, Redmi, POCO, Xiaomi Pad, HyperOS (formerly MIUI), Mi Band, SU7 EV.

Fun fact: Xiaomi sold its first phones online in flash sales that sold out in minutes.

#OPPO

Founded 2004 · China Active
HQDongguan
Known forA BBK Electronics brand known for fast charging (VOOC) and camera tech. OnePlus merged into it in 2021.
Key product linesFind X, Find N (foldable), Reno, A-series, ColorOS.

Fun fact: OPPO's SuperVOOC hit 240 W charging (in the realme GT3, a sibling brand).

#OnePlus

Founded 2013 · China Active
Known forFounded by Pete Lau and Carl Pei: 'flagship killer' phones with the slogan 'Never Settle'.
Key product linesOnePlus number series, Nord, Open (foldable), OnePlus Pad, OxygenOS.
StatusMerged into OPPO in 2021, still sold as its own brand.

Fun fact: The OnePlus One (2014) at first required an invite to buy.

#vivo

Founded 2009 · China Active
HQDongguan
Known forBBK sibling of OPPO. Shipped the first in-display fingerprint phone (X20 Plus UD, 2018) and strong camera phones (X series, ZEISS optics).
Key product linesX, V, Y, T series, iQOO (gaming sub-brand), X Fold, OriginOS/Funtouch OS.

Fun fact: vivo was an official FIFA World Cup sponsor in 2018 and 2022.

#realme

Founded 2018 · China Active
Known forBudget/performance brand spun out of OPPO by Sky Li. One of the fastest-growing phone brands ever.
Key product linesrealme number series, GT, C, Narzo.

Fun fact: realme reached 50 million phones shipped in about two years.

#Honor

Founded 2013 · China Active
Known forStarted as Huawei's online sub-brand and became independent in 2020 (sold to a Shenzhen consortium) to escape US sanctions.
Key product linesMagic series, Magic V (foldable), Honor number series, X series, MagicOS.

Fun fact: Honor kept Google services because the split removed it from Huawei's sanctions.

#Huawei

Founded 1987 · China Active
HQShenzhen
Known forFounded by Ren Zhengfei. A telecom-equipment giant whose phones briefly passed Samsung (Q2 2020). Built HarmonyOS after US sanctions in 2019.
Key product linesMate (incl. Mate X / XT tri-fold), Pura (formerly P series), nova, Enjoy, MatePad, MateBook, Watch, Kirin chips.

Fun fact: After losing Google services in 2019, Huawei built an app ecosystem from scratch and in 2024 released HarmonyOS NEXT, which drops Android code entirely.

#Motorola

Founded 1928 · USA (now Lenovo) Active
HQChicago
Known forMade the first handheld cellphone (DynaTAC, 1983), the StarTAC, the RAZR and the Droid. Today it's known for value Moto G phones and the razr foldables.
Key product linesDynaTAC, MicroTAC, StarTAC, RAZR V3, Droid, Moto X/G/E, Edge, razr (2019→).
StatusMotorola Mobility: owned by Google (2012–2014), then Lenovo (2014→). Motorola Solutions is a separate company.

Fun fact: Motorola engineer Martin Cooper made the first handheld cellular call in 1973, to a rival at Bell Labs.

#Sony (Xperia)

Founded 2001 (as Sony Ericsson) / 2012 · Japan Active
Known forXperia phones focused on camera, audio and display enthusiasts, the last flagships with headphone jacks and microSD.
Key product linesXperia 1, 5, 10 series, Xperia Z (earlier).

Fun fact: Sony Xperia 1 phones had 4K OLED screens and a two-stage physical shutter button.

#Nothing

Founded 2020 · UK Active
HQLondon
Known forFounded by OnePlus co-founder Carl Pei. Transparent design with LED 'Glyph' lights on the back.
Key product linesPhone (1)/(2)/(3), Phone (a) series, CMF by Nothing, Ear buds.

Fun fact: Nothing's first product was the Ear (1) earbuds in 2021.

#ZTE / Nubia / RedMagic

Founded 1985 · China Active
Known forTelecom-equipment maker with phones under ZTE, Nubia and the gaming brand RedMagic.
Key product linesAxon, Blade, Nubia Z, RedMagic.

Fun fact: ZTE nearly collapsed in 2018 after a US export ban, which was lifted after a $1 billion fine.

#Transsion (TECNO / Infinix / itel)

Founded 2006 · China Active
HQShenzhen
Known forAfrica's #1 phone seller, with big presences in South Asia and the Middle East.
Key product linesTECNO Camon/Spark/Phantom, Infinix Note/Zero/Hot, itel feature and budget phones.

Fun fact: TECNO tunes camera software for darker skin tones, a key reason for its popularity in Africa.

#Fairphone

Founded 2013 · Netherlands Active
Known forEthical, repairable phones with conflict-free minerals, user-replaceable parts and long software support.
Key product linesFairphone 1–5, Fairbuds.

Fun fact: The Fairphone 5 (2023) launched with a promise of software support until at least 2031.

#HMD Global (Nokia phones)

Founded 2016 · Finland Active
HQEspoo, Finland
Known forLicensed the Nokia brand for Android phones and feature phones (2016–2024), then launched its own HMD-branded phones.
Key product linesNokia X/G/C series, Nokia 3310 (2017 remake), HMD Skyline, HMD Fusion.

Fun fact: HMD's remade Nokia 3310 brought back Snake in 2017.

#TCL / Alcatel

Founded 1981 · China Active
HQHuizhou
Known forTV giant TCL made phones under Alcatel (licensed), BlackBerry (2016–2020) and Palm (2018) brands, plus TCL NXTPAPER phones.
Key product linesTCL 50/40 series, NXTPAPER, Alcatel, BlackBerry KEYone/KEY2 (licensed).

Fun fact: TCL's BlackBerry KEYone revived the physical-keyboard Android phone in 2017.

#Sharp (AQUOS)

Founded 1912 · Japan Active
Known forMade the first camera phone sold commercially (J-SH04, Japan, 2000). AQUOS phones, displays and Zaurus PDAs.
Key product linesAQUOS R/sense/wish, Zaurus, Sidekick (built some).
StatusMajority-owned by Foxconn (Hon Hai) since 2016.

Fun fact: Sharp's name comes from its founder's first invention, the Ever-Sharp mechanical pencil (1915).

#Meizu

Founded 2003 · China Active
Known forStarted as an MP3 player brand, then sleek phones with the Flyme OS.
Key product linesMX, Pro, Meizu 21.

Fun fact: Meizu's M8 (2009) was widely compared to the original iPhone.

#Historic & defunct phone brands

Phone giants that fell, exited or merged.

#Nokia

Founded 1865 · Finland Active
Known forThe world's biggest phone maker from 1998 to 2011. Indestructible candybars, Snake, Symbian smartphones and the N-series.
Key product lines3310, 1100, 6110, 8110 'banana', N95, E71, N8, 808 PureView, Lumia (Windows Phone).
StatusSold its phone division to Microsoft (2014). Today Nokia makes network equipment, and the brand was licensed to HMD for phones.

Fun fact: Nokia started as a paper mill, then made rubber boots, tyres and cables before phones.

#BlackBerry (RIM)

Founded 1984 · Canada Active
HQWaterloo, Ontario
Known forResearch In Motion's email phones with physical QWERTY keyboards ruled business and politics in the 2000s. BBM was an early mass-market messaging app.
Key product linesBlackBerry 850 pager, Pearl, Curve, Bold, Storm (touch), Torch, Z10, Passport, Priv (Android).
StatusStopped making phones (2016). Licensed the brand to TCL (until 2020). Now a cybersecurity and auto-software company.

Fun fact: BlackBerry OS services were shut down on 4 January 2022, bricking old devices' data functions.

#Palm

Founded 1992 · USA Defunct brand
Known forThe Palm Pilot (1996) defined the PDA with Graffiti handwriting, then the Treo smartphones and the elegant webOS Palm Pre (2009).
Key product linesPilot, PalmPilot, Palm III/V/VII, Tungsten, Zire, Treo, Centro, Pre, Pixi.
StatusBought by HP (2010). HP killed webOS hardware (2011). The brand reappeared on a tiny TCL phone in 2018.

Fun fact: Jeff Hawkins carried a wooden block in his shirt pocket to test the Pilot's size before building it.

#HTC

Founded 1997 · Taiwan Active
Known forBuilt many early Windows Mobile phones as an ODM (O2 XDA, i-mate, Qtek, T-Mobile MDA), then the first Android phone (T-Mobile G1, 2008), the Nexus One and the HTC One. Later Vive VR.
Key product linesDream/G1, Hero, Desire, Nexus One, EVO 4G, One M7/M8, U series, Vive.
StatusSold much of its phone R&D team to Google in 2018. Now mostly focused on VR.

Fun fact: HTC was briefly the #1 smartphone vendor in the US (Q3 2011, per Canalys).

#LG Mobile

Founded 1958 (as GoldStar) · South Korea Defunct brand
Known forPhones from the Chocolate and Prada to the G/V series and the swivel LG Wing. Made the Nexus 4 and 5 for Google.
Key product linesChocolate, Prada, enV, Optimus, G2–G8, V10–V60, Velvet, Wing.
StatusLG exited phones in July 2021. LG Electronics continues in TVs, appliances and laptops.

Fun fact: LG showed a rollable phone prototype in early 2021 just before shutting the phone business down.

#Sony Ericsson

Founded 2001–2012 · Sweden / Japan Acquired / merged
Known forJoint venture known for Walkman music phones, Cyber-shot camera phones, the T68i and the P-series UIQ smartphones.
Key product linesT610, K750i, W800i, P900, Xperia X1, Xperia Arc.
StatusSony bought out Ericsson in 2012 to form Sony Mobile.

Fun fact: The K750i (2005) had a 2 MP autofocus camera with a lens cover, a hit in camera-phone history.

#Ericsson (phones)

Founded 1876 · Sweden Active
Known forA telecom pioneer whose handsets (GH388, T28, R380 smartphone) were popular before the Sony merger.
Key product linesGH337, GA628, T28, T39, R380.
StatusMoved its handsets into Sony Ericsson (2001). Now makes network equipment only.

Fun fact: Ericsson's R380 (2000) was one of the first devices marketed as a 'smartphone'.

#Siemens (mobile)

Founded 1847 (phones 1985) · Germany Defunct brand
Known forSiemens phones (S35, C35, SL45, the first phone with an MP3 player and memory card) were big in Europe.
Key product linesS, C, M (rugged), SL series.
StatusSold to BenQ in 2005 (BenQ-Siemens), which went bankrupt in 2006.

Fun fact: The SL45 (2001) is widely credited as the first phone with an MP3 player and expandable storage.

#Alcatel (original)

Founded 1898 (as CGE) · France Acquired / merged
Known forFrench telecom firm with One Touch phones.
Key product linesOne Touch.
StatusThe phone brand passed to TCL in 2004. Alcatel merged with Lucent in 2006, then Nokia bought Alcatel-Lucent (2016).

Fun fact: The One Touch Easy was one of the first phones aimed at mainstream consumers in France.

#Kyocera

Founded 1959 · Japan Active
Known forRugged phones (DuraForce, DuraXV) and early smartphones like the Kyocera 6035 (2001, Palm OS).
Key product linesDuraForce, DuraXV, Torque, Echo (dual-screen).
StatusHas been winding down consumer phones (announced 2023) and focusing on rugged/business devices.

Fun fact: The Kyocera Echo (2011) was a dual-screen Android phone, about a decade before Microsoft's Surface Duo.

#Danger (Hiptop / Sidekick)

Founded 2000 · USA Defunct brand
Known forCo-founded by Andy Rubin, later the creator of Android. Made the swivel-screen T-Mobile Sidekick, a teen and celebrity icon.
Key product linesHiptop / Sidekick, Sidekick 3, Sidekick LX.
StatusAcquired by Microsoft (2008).

Fun fact: Microsoft bought Danger in 2008. A 2009 server failure wiped many users' contacts, and the Kin phones that followed lasted only about 48 days.

#Essential Products

Founded 2015 · USA Defunct brand
Known forAndy Rubin's comeback: the Essential Phone (2017) with a titanium frame and an early camera notch.
Key product linesEssential Phone PH-1.
StatusShut down in 2020.

Fun fact: The PH-1 helped popularise the small 'teardrop' camera cutout.

#Handspring

Founded 1998 · USA Acquired / merged
Known forFounded by Palm's creators. The Visor PDA with a Springboard expansion slot and the first Treo.
Key product linesVisor, Treo 180/270/300.
StatusMerged back into Palm in 2003.

Fun fact: Springboard modules turned the Visor into a phone, a GPS or a camera.

#Microsoft Mobile (Lumia)

Founded 2014–2017 · USA / Finland Defunct brand
Known forMicrosoft's Nokia-acquired phone division making Windows Phone Lumias.
Key product linesLumia 640, 950/950 XL, Nokia 3310-era feature phones.
StatusPhones discontinued by 2017.

Fun fact: Microsoft wrote off about $7.6 billion on the Nokia deal in 2015.

#Pantech / Sagem / Sendo / i-mate

Founded 1990s–2010s · Korea / France / UK / UAE Defunct brand
Known forMid-2000s brands: Pantech (Korean flip phones, US AT&T models), Sagem (French phones), Sendo (UK, a famous Microsoft fallout), i-mate (Dubai-based Windows Mobile phones).
Key product linesPantech Breeze, Sagem myX, Sendo X, i-mate JASJAR.

Fun fact: i-mate, based in Dubai, was one of the biggest Windows Mobile device brands in the mid-2000s.

Apple (iPad), Samsung (Galaxy Tab), Microsoft (Surface), Lenovo, Xiaomi, Huawei, OnePlus and Google appear above. These brands are mainly known for tablets, e-readers or pen tablets.

#Huion & XP-Pen

#Archos

#Teclast

Smartwatches, fitness bands and rings. Apple Watch, Galaxy Watch and Pixel Watch are with their phone brands.

Founded 1989 · USA Active

Known forGPS pioneer, now the king of sports and adventure watches with batteries that last weeks.
Key product linesForerunner, Fenix, Epix, Venu, Instinct, Edge bike computers, aviation and marine GPS, dashcams.

Known forMade step counting a daily habit with clip-on trackers and bands.

HQHefei
Known forCheap watches with long batteries. The company (then Huami) built the original Xiaomi Mi Band.
Key product linesGTR, GTS, T-Rex, Balance, Active, Helio ring, Zepp OS.

#Polar

HQKempele
Known forInvented the wireless heart-rate monitor for athletes (1982).
Key product linesVantage, Grit X, Pacer, Ignite, H10 chest strap.

#Suunto

Founded 1936 · Finland Active
HQVantaa
Known forCompasses, then dive computers and rugged outdoor watches.
Key product linesRace, Vertical, Ocean, compasses, dive computers.
StatusOwned by Chinese firm Liesheng since 2022.

#COROS

Founded 2014 · China Active
Known forLightweight running and mountain watches with huge batteries.
Key product linesPACE, APEX, VERTIX, DURA bike computer.

#WHOOP

Founded 2012 · USA Active
HQBoston
Known forA screenless strap that tracks recovery and sleep, sold by subscription.
Key product linesWHOOP 4.0, WHOOP 5.0 / MG.

#Oura

Founded 2013 · Finland Active
HQOulu
Known forThe smart ring that made sleep scores popular.
Key product linesOura Ring Gen3, Oura Ring 4.

#Pebble

Known forThe e-paper smartwatch that raised a record $10 million on Kickstarter in 2012, years before the Apple Watch.
Key product linesPebble, Pebble Time, Pebble 2.
StatusBought by Fitbit in 2016 and shut down; revived as a small company in 2025.

Fun fact: Google open-sourced PebbleOS in 2025, and the original founder started selling new PebbleOS watches again.

▸Networking, smart home & makers4 sections · Everyoneclick to open / close

Routers and firewalls, smart-home devices, NAS boxes, microcontrollers (ESP32, Arduino) and 3D printers.

1. Networking brands2. Smart-home brands3. NAS & external storage brands4. Maker, microcontroller & 3D-printing brands

#Networking brands

Routers, switches, Wi-Fi and firewalls, from home mesh kits to the gear that runs the internet. Huawei and ZTE are under phones, ASUS under laptops.

#Cisco Systems

Founded 1984 · USA Active
HQSan Jose, California
Known forThe giant of enterprise networking: routers, switches, firewalls and Webex. Its CCNA is the best-known networking certificate.
Key product linesCatalyst & Nexus switches, ISR routers, Meraki (cloud-managed), Webex, Splunk (bought 2024), Linksys (2003–2013).

Fun fact: The name comes from San Francisco, and the logo is a stylised Golden Gate Bridge.

#TP-Link

Founded 1996 · China Active
HQShenzhen (TP-Link Systems: Irvine, California)
Known forHuge range of affordable home networking: one of the biggest Wi-Fi brands in the world by units shipped. Its US business became the separate TP-Link Systems in 2024.
Key product linesArcher routers, Deco mesh, Omada (business), Tapo & Kasa (smart home and cameras), Mercusys (budget brand).

Fun fact: TP stands for 'twisted pair', the kind of copper cable inside an Ethernet lead.

#Netgear

Founded 1996 · USA Active
HQSan Jose, California
Known forHome and small-business networking, famous for big spider-shaped gaming routers.
Key product linesNighthawk routers, Orbi mesh, ProSAFE / Insight switches, Meural frames. Arlo cameras were spun off in 2018.

#Linksys

Founded 1988 · USA Acquired / merged
Known forHome routers. The WRT54G (2002) ran Linux, and its released source code started the custom-firmware scene (DD-WRT, OpenWrt).
Key product linesWRT54G, Velop mesh, Hydra, E-series.
StatusOwned by Cisco (2003–2013), then Belkin (2013), which Foxconn bought in 2018.

Fun fact: The blue-and-black WRT54G is still the most famous home router ever made: people install OpenWrt on its descendants today.

#D-Link

Founded 1986 · Taiwan Active
HQTaipei
Known forBudget routers, switches and cameras sold everywhere.
Key product linesDIR routers, DGS switches, Eagle Pro AI, mydlink cameras.
StatusCheck support dates: several old D-Link routers are end-of-life and won't get security fixes.

#Ubiquiti

Founded 2005 · USA Active
HQNew York
Known forPro-looking networking at prosumer prices. UniFi turned home labs and small offices into tidy, centrally managed networks.
Key product linesUniFi (Dream Machine, access points, switches, Protect cameras), airMAX (outdoor links), EdgeRouter, AmpliFi.

Fun fact: Founded by a former Apple engineer; Ubiquiti's slick UniFi controller is a big reason home labbers rack gear in cupboards.

#MikroTik

Founded 1996 · Latvia Active
HQRiga
Known forVery cheap, very powerful routers running RouterOS. Loved by ISPs and network engineers, feared by beginners (thousands of settings).
Key product lineshAP, RB, CCR and CRS (switches), Chateau (LTE/5G), RouterOS, MTCNA certification.

Fun fact: Many small ISPs in the Middle East, Africa and Asia run on MikroTik boxes.

#Juniper Networks

Founded 1996 · USA Acquired / merged
HQSunnyvale, California
Known forCarrier and data-centre routers and switches; Cisco's main rival at the high end.
Key product linesMX & PTX routers, EX & QFX switches, SRX firewalls, Mist AI Wi-Fi, Junos OS.
StatusBought by Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) in 2025.

#Aruba Networks

Founded 2002 · USA Acquired / merged
Known forEnterprise Wi-Fi for campuses, hospitals and malls.
Key product linesAruba Instant On (small business), Aruba Central, ClearPass.
StatusBought by HPE in 2015; now called HPE Aruba Networking.

#Fortinet

Founded 2000 · USA Active
HQSunnyvale, California
Known forFirewalls (FortiGate) that are everywhere in Gulf offices, banks and schools.
Key product linesFortiGate, FortiWiFi, FortiSwitch, FortiClient VPN, FortiAnalyzer.

#Palo Alto Networks

Founded 2005 · USA Active
HQSanta Clara, California
Known for'Next-generation firewall' pioneer: firewalls that understand apps, not just ports.
Key product linesPA-series firewalls, Prisma (cloud security / SASE), Cortex XDR, GlobalProtect VPN.

#Zyxel

Founded 1989 · Taiwan Active
HQHsinchu
Known forDSL and fibre modems handed out by ISPs, plus business firewalls and switches.
Key product linesVMG/EX modems and routers, USG firewalls, Nebula cloud.

#Tenda

Founded 1999 · China Active
HQShenzhen
Known forLow-cost routers and mesh kits, common in budget shops.
Key product linesAC and AX routers, Nova mesh, 4G routers.

Lights, plugs, sensors, doorbells and cameras. Google Nest, Amazon Echo and Apple Home sit with their parent companies. Matter and Zigbee are explained in Part 24.

#Shelly

Key product linesShelly Plus / Pro relays, Shelly plugs, energy meters.

#Tuya

HQHangzhou
Known forThe cloud platform behind thousands of no-name 'smart' plugs and bulbs. If your app is 'Smart Life', it's probably Tuya.

#SwitchBot

Founded 2015 · China Active
HQShenzhen
Known forLittle robots that physically press old buttons, plus curtain motors and hubs.
Key product linesSwitchBot Bot, Curtain, Hub, Lock.

Founded 2017 · USA Active
HQSeattle
Known forVery cheap home cameras and gadgets.
Key product linesWyze Cam, Wyze Lock, Wyze plugs.

Founded 2014 · USA Active
Known forWire-free security cameras.
Key product linesArlo Pro, Ultra, Essential, Video Doorbell.
StatusSpun off from Netgear in 2018.

#ecobee

Founded 2007 · Canada Acquired / merged
HQToronto
Known forSmart thermostats with room sensors.
Key product linesSmartThermostat, room sensors, SmartCamera.
StatusBought by Generac in 2021.

#NAS & external storage brands

Network storage boxes for home labs and offices, plus external-drive makers. Drive and SSD makers (WD, Seagate, Samsung, Crucial…) are with components.

#Synology

Founded 2000 · Taiwan Active
HQTaipei
Known forThe easiest NAS for most people, thanks to its DSM software and apps (Photos, Drive, Surveillance Station).
Key product linesDiskStation (DS), RackStation, BeeStation, DSM, Active Backup.

Fun fact: In 2025 it required its own branded hard drives in new Plus models, then reversed the rule in DSM 7.3 (October 2025) after sales dropped and users complained.

Source: Tom's Hardware: Synology walks back drive policy with DSM 7.3

#QNAP

Founded 2004 · Taiwan Active
HQTaipei
Known forFeature-packed NAS boxes with more hardware for the money (2.5/10 GbE, PCIe slots).
Key product linesTS and TVS series, QTS / QuTS hero, QuMagie.

Fun fact: QNAP boxes were hit by ransomware like DeadBolt (2022): never expose a NAS's admin page directly to the internet.

#TerraMaster

Founded 2010 · China Active
HQShenzhen
Known forBudget NAS boxes, also popular for installing Unraid or TrueNAS on.
Key product linesF2/F4 series, TOS.

#ASUSTOR

Founded 2011 · Taiwan Active
Known forNAS maker spun off from ASUS.
Key product linesDrivestor, Lockerstor, Flashstor (all-SSD), ADM.

#Buffalo

Founded 1975 · Japan Active
HQNagoya
Known forExternal drives, routers and NAS, very common in Japan.
Key product linesLinkStation, TeraStation, MiniStation drives.

#LaCie

Founded 1987 · France Acquired / merged
HQParis
Known forDesigner external drives, including the orange rubber Rugged drives.

#OWC (Other World Computing)

Founded 1988 · USA Active
Known forMac upgrades, Thunderbolt docks and fast external SSDs.
Key product linesEnvoy SSDs, ThunderBay, Thunderbolt docks, Mac RAM.

#Drobo

Founded 2005 · USA Defunct brand
Known forEasy 'BeyondRAID' storage boxes where you could mix different drive sizes.
Key product linesDrobo 5N, 5D, 8D.
StatusWent bankrupt in 2023, leaving owners without support: a reason to choose storage that uses standard RAID or ZFS.

#Maker, microcontroller & 3D-printing brands

The boards, kits and printers behind home-lab projects and DIY electronics. Raspberry Pi is under prebuilt & mini PCs.

#Espressif Systems

Founded 2008 · China Active
HQShanghai
Known forMakes the cheap Wi-Fi + Bluetooth chips that power millions of smart plugs and DIY projects: the ESP8266 (2014) and ESP32 (2016).
Key product linesESP8266, ESP32, ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3/C6 (RISC-V), ESP-IDF.

Fun fact: The ESP8266 cost about $2 and accidentally started a hobbyist revolution after makers translated its Chinese datasheet.

#Arduino

Founded 2005 · Italy Acquired / merged
Known forThe board that made electronics easy for students and artists, with a simple coding app.
Key product linesArduino Uno, Nano, Mega, Nano ESP32, Arduino IDE.
StatusQualcomm announced it was buying Arduino in October 2025; Arduino keeps its own brand and still supports other companies' chips.

Fun fact: Arduino was born in Ivrea, Italy, and named after a bar there (Bar di Re Arduino).

Source: Reuters via The Star: Qualcomm buys Arduino (Oct 2025)

HQNew York
Known forKits, breakout boards and the best free tutorials; created CircuitPython.
Key product linesFeather boards, QT Py, CircuitPython, NeoPixels.

HQBoulder, Colorado
Known forOpen-source hardware boards and sensors.
Key product linesRedBoard, Qwiic connector system, breakout boards.

Known forGrove sensor kits and tiny XIAO boards.
Key product linesXIAO ESP32 / RP2040, Grove, reTerminal, SenseCAP.

HQSheffield

Key product linesHATs, Pico boards, displays, Picade.

#Prusa Research

HQPrague

#Bambu Lab

#Creality

Key product linesEnder-3, K1, CR-series, Halot (resin).

Known forPro and education 3D printers. MakerBot put early 3D printers in schools.

Part 6

Timeline & Reference

Master timeline, comparison tables, a quick visual ID guide, commonly confused pairs, an A–Z glossary, abbreviations decoded, and an Arabic–English tech glossary.

#Master timeline of computing

Key moments from the 1930s to today. Bold rows are turning points for personal computing.

#Comparison tables

Generations side by side.

#Quick identification guide

Look at the part and use this table to work out what it is.

#Commonly confused pairs

Things that look the same or have similar names but aren't.

#mSATA vs M.2

Storage Current

mSATA: 30 mm wide, 52-pin Mini PCIe-shaped edge, SATA only, two screw corners, 2009–2015. M.2: 22 mm wide, 75-position keyed edge, SATA or NVMe, one end screw, 2013→. They are not interchangeable without an adapter.

#mSATA vs Mini PCIe

Storage Current

The same physical card and connector. mSATA carries SATA (storage), Mini PCIe carries PCIe + USB (Wi-Fi, modems). A slot only works with the type it's wired for, though some laptops wire one slot for both.

#2.5" SATA SSD vs mSATA SSD

Storage Current

Same protocol and same ~550 MB/s ceiling. A 2.5" drive has a case and SATA data and power connectors, while mSATA is a bare card.

#M.2 SATA vs M.2 NVMe

Storage Current

Same shape, very different speed (~550 vs 3,500–14,000 MB/s). SATA M.2 is usually B+M keyed, NVMe is usually M-keyed. Check what your slot supports.

#SATA vs PATA (IDE)

Storage Current

PATA uses a wide 40-pin ribbon and Master/Slave jumpers, SATA a thin 7-pin cable with one device per port.

#SATA vs SAS

Storage Current

SAS (servers) controllers accept SATA drives, but SATA controllers can't run SAS drives. SAS connectors join data and power with a plastic bridge.

#eSATA vs USB-A port

Ports Current

eSATA has no inner plastic tongue and is slightly differently shaped. eSATAp combo ports accept both.

#DVI-I vs DVI-D

Ports Current

DVI-I has four extra analog pins around the flat blade, so passive VGA adapters work. DVI-D is digital only.

#USB-C vs Thunderbolt

Ports Current

USB-C is a connector shape. Thunderbolt 3/4/5 is a protocol that uses that shape. Look for the lightning-bolt icon.

#USB 3.0 vs 3.1 Gen 1 vs 3.2 Gen 1

Ports Current

All three are the same 5 Gb/s, renamed twice. Check for 'Gbps' numbers instead.

#Lightning vs USB-C

Ports Current

Lightning is Apple's flat solid tab (2012–2023). USB-C is a hollow oval with a tongue inside, standard on iPhone since 2023.

#HDMI vs DisplayPort

Ports Current

HDMI is symmetrical and standard on TVs. DisplayPort has one clipped corner and a latch, and is standard on PC monitors with daisy-chaining.

#RJ-45 vs RJ-11

Ports Current

RJ-45 (8-pin) is Ethernet, RJ-11 (4/6-pin, narrower) is telephone/DSL. An RJ-11 plug fits loosely in an RJ-45 jack.

#RGB vs ARGB headers

Motherboards Current

RGB: 12 V, 4-pin, whole strip one colour. ARGB: 5 V, 3-pin, per-LED control. Plugging ARGB into 12 V can burn out the LEDs.

#8-pin EPS (CPU) vs 8-pin PCIe (GPU)

Power Current

Similar plugs with different keying and pinouts. Forcing one into the other can short the 12 V rail.

#LGA vs PGA

CPUs Current

LGA has the pins in the motherboard socket, PGA has them on the CPU. Both bend if handled carelessly.

#Chipset vs socket

Motherboards Current

The socket decides which CPUs fit. The chipset decides features (overclocking, USB, PCIe lanes). Same socket, different chipsets.

#DDR4 vs DDR5

Memory Current

Both are 288-pin, but the notch is in a different place and they aren't compatible. DDR5 has an on-stick PMIC and two sub-channels.

#DDR5 vs LPDDR5 vs GDDR6

Memory Current

DDR5 is desktop/laptop system RAM, LPDDR5 is low-power (soldered, phones and thin laptops), GDDR6 is graphics VRAM. They're completely separate standards.

#RAM vs storage

Basics Current

RAM (e.g. 16 GB) is temporary working memory. Storage (e.g. 1 TB) keeps files permanently. Phone ads that say '256 GB memory' mean storage.

#Integrated vs dedicated GPU

GPUs Current

Integrated graphics share system RAM inside the CPU. A dedicated card has its own chip and VRAM. Plug your monitor into the GPU, not the motherboard.

#Laptop RTX vs desktop RTX

GPUs Current

Same names, much lower power and performance in laptops. Check the GPU wattage (TGP).

#x86 vs x64 vs ARM64

CPUs Current

x86 = 32-bit Intel/AMD, x64 = 64-bit Intel/AMD (AMD64), ARM64 = Apple Silicon, Snapdragon and phones. Software must match (or be emulated).

#Itanium IA-64 vs Intel 64

CPUs Current

IA-64 was Itanium's separate architecture (dead). Intel 64 is Intel's implementation of AMD64 / x86-64.

#TDP vs maximum power draw

CPUs Current

TDP is a cooling guideline. Boosting CPUs and GPUs often draw far more than their rated TDP.

#PCI vs PCI-X vs PCIe

Buses Current

PCI (1992 parallel bus), PCI-X (64-bit server PCI), PCIe (2004+ serial lanes). Physically and electrically different.

#Hub vs switch vs router

Networking Current

A hub repeats everything to all ports (obsolete), a switch delivers only to the right port, a router connects different networks (your LAN ↔ the internet).

#Wi-Fi 6 vs 6E

Networking Current

Same 802.11ax technology. 6E adds the uncrowded 6 GHz band, and both your router and device need to support it.

#Modem vs router

Networking Current

The modem talks to your ISP's line (DSL, cable, fibre ONT). The router builds your home network and Wi-Fi. Many ISP boxes combine both.

#eSIM vs iSIM

Phones Current

eSIM is a separate embedded chip, iSIM is built into the main SoC. Both replace the physical SIM card.

#OLED vs QLED

Displays Current

OLED: self-lit pixels, true blacks. QLED (Samsung marketing): an LCD with a quantum-dot layer, still backlit.

#Resolution vs refresh rate

Displays Current

Resolution is how many pixels (sharpness), refresh rate is how many redraws per second (smoothness).

#Mbps vs MB/s

Basics Current

Megabits vs megabytes: 8 bits = 1 byte, so a 1,000 Mbps connection ≈ 125 MB/s. ISPs quote bits, downloads show bytes.

#GB vs GiB

Basics Current

Drive makers use GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes, while Windows shows GiB = 1,073,741,824 (labelled 'GB'). That's why a '1 TB' drive shows as ~931 GB.

#Apple 'MagSafe' (Mac) vs 'MagSafe' (iPhone)

Phones Current

The Mac's MagSafe is a magnetic charging plug, the iPhone's is a magnetic wireless-charging ring system.

#Chromebook vs Chromebox vs ChromeOS Flex

Laptops Current

Chromebook is a laptop, Chromebox a mini desktop. ChromeOS Flex is a free version you can install on old PCs and Macs.

#Glossary A–Z (318 terms)

Quick definitions of the jargon used throughout this book.

#Abbreviations decoded (235 short forms)

What the letters stand for, in plain words. Tip: anywhere in this book, hover over (or tap) a short form with a dotted underline to see what it means.

#Arabic–English tech glossary · مسرد المصطلحات التقنية (148 terms)

Each term in English, formal Arabic (الفصحى, used in textbooks, official documents and Arabic software menus), and the way people in Saudi Arabia usually say it day to day, which is often the English word written in Arabic letters. Useful for school, repair shops, customer support, and switching your phone between Arabic and English.

Part 7

Cable Guide

Every cable and connector you're likely to meet: mains cords and wall plugs, USB-C grades, video, network and fibre, internal PC cables, audio, charging (including Apple Watch and AirPods tricks), charging life hacks and myths, legacy, safety, and a 'which cable do I need?' table.

#How to read a cable

Every cable is three things: the connector (its shape), the protocol (USB, HDMI, Ethernet...) and the rating (speed, power, length). Two cables can look identical and differ in all three.

#Connector vs protocol vs rating

Current

A USB-C cable might carry USB 2.0 at 60 W, or 80 Gb/s at 240 W. An RJ-45 cable might be Cat5e or Cat8. The shape only tells you what it plugs into, not what it can do.

Identify it: Read the printing on the jacket (e.g. 'CAT6 23AWG UTP', 'USB4 40Gbps 240W', 'Ultra High Speed HDMI') and the logo on the plug.

#Male, female & gender

Current

Male plugs have exposed pins, female sockets have holes. 'Gender changers' swap one for the other. Power always comes from the female side, so live pins are never exposed (that's why mains cords end in female C13 plugs).

#Passive vs active cables

Current

Passive cables are just copper wires. Active cables contain chips (redrivers, retimers, or optical transceivers) that boost the signal so it can travel further or faster. Active cables are often directional, so they have a 'source' end and a 'display' end.

Commonly confused with: An active optical HDMI cable plugged in backwards gives no picture, and that's not a fault.

#Wire gauge (AWG)

Current

American Wire Gauge: smaller number = thicker wire. Ethernet is usually 23–26 AWG, USB power wires 20–28 AWG, speaker wire 12–18 AWG, mains cords 16–18 AWG (or 0.75–1.5 mm²).

Fun fact: Thin 28 AWG power wires in cheap USB cables cause slow charging, because voltage drops along the cable.

#Shielding (UTP, STP, FTP, braided)

Current

Shielding blocks interference: UTP (unshielded twisted pair), FTP/F/UTP (foil around all pairs), STP/S/FTP (braid + foil per pair). Braided jackets on USB cables are mostly about durability, not shielding.

#Length limits

Current

Every protocol has a maximum length before signals fail: USB 2.0 ~5 m, USB 3.x ~2–3 m, 40/80 Gb/s USB-C ~0.8–1 m passive, HDMI 2.1 ~3–5 m passive, Ethernet 100 m, SATA 1 m, DisplayPort 1.4 ~2–3 m (check each cable's rating). Go longer with active, optical or repeater cables.

#Keyed & polarised connectors

Current

Notches, clipped corners and odd shapes stop you plugging things in the wrong way round: SATA's L-shape, DisplayPort's clipped corner, the M.2 notch. If a plug won't go in, don't force it.

#Hot-plugging

Current

Plugging in while powered on. Fine for USB, HDMI, DisplayPort, SATA (with AHCI enabled), Ethernet and Thunderbolt. Not safe for PS/2 (older systems), internal power plugs, IDE, or anything inside a running PC.

#Which cable do I need?

Common jobs and the cable that does them.

#Mains power cords & wall plugs

The cords between the wall and your device: a country-specific wall plug on one end, and an international IEC connector on the other.

Wall plug types (plug face, schematic)

Saudi Arabia standardised on Type G (UK-style) at 230 V. A plug adapter changes the shape, not the voltage, so check that the device label says 100–240 V.

IEC 60320 appliance cords (device end, face view)

Odd numbers (C5, C7, C13, C19) are the female cord ends. The matching even numbers (C6, C8, C14, C20) are the sockets on the device.

#IEC 60320 C13 / C14

1970→ Current

The standard computer power cord, nicknamed the 'kettle lead' in the UK even though true kettles use the hotter-rated C15. Desktop PSUs, monitors, printers, consoles (PS5, Xbox Series X). Rated 10 A.

Pins3 (live, neutral, earth)
Rating10 A, 70 °C
Device endC14 inlet (male)

Identify it: A three-hole rectangular plug with two angled top corners.

Commonly confused with: C15 has an extra notch for hot appliances (kettles). It fits C14 inlets, but C13 doesn't fit C16 inlets.

#C5 / C6 'cloverleaf' ('Mickey Mouse')

Current

A three-lobed earthed connector used on many laptop power bricks (Dell, HP, Lenovo) and projectors. Rated 2.5 A.

Identify it: Three round lobes, like a mouse head or a cloverleaf.

#C7 / C8 'figure-8'

Current

A two-pin unearthed cord shaped like an '8'. Found on PS4, Xbox One S, many TVs, Apple TV and Mac minis. A polarised version has one flat side.

Commonly confused with: Unpolarised C7 cords fit both round and flat-sided figure-8 inlets, but polarised plugs only fit polarised inlets.

#C19 / C20

Current

Bigger 16 A connectors for servers, large UPSs, PDUs and some high-wattage PSUs and mining rigs.

#C1 / C2, C9, C17 & others

Legacy

Less common IEC shapes: C1/C2 (tiny shavers), C9 (old radio and tape gear), C17 (unearthed C13-like, some TVs and monitors).

#NEMA plugs (USA)

Current

North American plug standards: NEMA 1-15 (Type A, 2-pin), 5-15 (Type B, 3-pin household), 5-20 (20 A with a T-shaped slot), L5/L6 twist-locks for data centres.

#Plug types A–N

Current

The IEC lists about 15 wall plug types worldwide. Most common: A/B (Americas, Japan), C/E/F (Europe, Middle East), G (UK, Ireland, Saudi Arabia, Gulf states, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia), I (Australia, China), D/M (India, South Africa).

Fun fact: Type G plugs contain their own fuse (commonly 3 A, 5 A or 13 A) and have insulated sleeves on the live and neutral pins.

#Saudi Arabia plugs & voltage

Current

Saudi Arabia runs at 230 V, 60 Hz and has standardised on Type G (British-style) sockets, with SASO as the electrical safety regulator. Older buildings may still have Type A/B/C or universal sockets from the 127 V era.

Commonly confused with: 60 Hz is unusual for a 230 V country (Europe is 50 Hz). It rarely matters for electronics, but it can affect clocks and some motors.

Sources: WorldStandards: plugs & voltage in Saudi Arabia · TÜV SÜD: Saudi Arabia market access (Type G, SASO)

#Travel adapter vs voltage converter

Current

An adapter only changes the plug shape. A converter/transformer changes the voltage. Most laptop and phone chargers say '100–240 V ~ 50/60 Hz' and only need an adapter. Hair dryers and kettles don't.

Identify it: Check the device's label: '100–240V' = worldwide; '120V only' or '230V only' = needs a converter abroad.

#Power strips & surge protectors

Current

A power strip just adds sockets. A surge protector absorbs spikes (rated in joules, with MOV components that wear out). Neither replaces a UPS for outages.

Commonly confused with: Daisy-chaining power strips (plugging one into another) is a fire risk, and it's banned by many building codes.

#PDUs

Current

Power Distribution Units: rack-mounted strips for servers, often using C13/C19 outlets, with metering and remote switching.

#Laptop DC cables

Current

From the brick to the laptop: barrel plugs (common sizes 5.5×2.5 mm, 4.5×3.0 mm with centre ID pin, 7.4×5.0 mm), Lenovo rectangular 'slim tip', Surface Connect, MagSafe, and now USB-C PD.

#USB & Thunderbolt cables in depth

Why one USB-C cable charges your laptop at 100 W and another can't, and why some don't carry video. See Part 1 → Ports for USB versions.

USB & phone connector shapes (face view, not to scale)

The connector shape tells you nothing about speed. A USB-C port can be anything from USB 2.0 to USB4 / Thunderbolt 5.

#USB 2.0 vs SuperSpeed cables

Current

USB 2.0 cables have 4 wires (power, ground, D+, D−). USB 3.x adds extra twisted pairs for SuperSpeed. A USB 2.0-only cable caps you at 480 Mb/s however fast the ports are.

Identify it: USB-A plugs with a blue tongue or 'SS' logo are SuperSpeed cables.

#USB-C cable types

2014→ Current

USB-C cables come in a few grades: USB 2.0 (60 W or 240 W), 5/10 Gb/s, 20 Gb/s, 40 Gb/s (USB4 / TB3 / TB4), and 80 Gb/s (USB4 v2 / TB5). Power: 60 W (3 A) standard, 100 W (5 A, needs e-marker), 240 W (EPR, 48 V).

Commonly confused with: Most cables bundled with phones are USB 2.0 data. They charge fine, but an external SSD or monitor connected through one will be slow or won't work.

#E-marker chip

Current

A tiny chip inside some USB-C cables that tells devices the cable's speed and current rating. It's required for 5 A (100 W+) and 40 Gb/s+. Without it, chargers cap at 3 A (60 W).

#USB-IF logos (2022→)

2022→ Current

New certified-cable logos print the speed and wattage on the plug or box: e.g. 'USB 40Gbps · 240W'. Older 'SuperSpeed+' and 'Hi-Speed' logos are being phased out.

#Thunderbolt cables

Current

TB3: passive 40 Gb/s up to ~0.8 m, active for longer. TB4: universal 40 Gb/s up to 2 m (active). TB5: 80/120 Gb/s, 1 m passive. TB4/TB5 cables also work as top-tier USB-C cables.

Identify it: A lightning-bolt icon with the number (4 or 5) printed on the plug.

#Charge-only cables

Current

Some cheap cables leave out the data wires completely. Your phone charges but the PC never detects it. Common with freebie micro-USB cables and gadget accessories.

#USB-A to USB-C (legacy) cables

2014→ Current

They need a 56 kΩ pull-up resistor inside to tell the phone it may draw only standard USB current. Early cheap cables used the wrong value and could damage chargers or ports.

Fun fact: Google engineer Benson Leung reviewed dozens of USB-C cables on Amazon in 2015–2016 and named the dangerous ones. One faulty cable destroyed his laptop.

#USB OTG (On-The-Go) adapters

2001→ Current

Lets a phone or tablet act as a USB host for flash drives, keyboards, game controllers. Micro-USB OTG cables have a special ID pin wiring. USB-C phones handle it automatically.

#USB extension cables & active repeaters

Current

Plain A-male to A-female extensions aren't allowed by the USB spec, but they're everywhere. They work for short runs. For long runs use an active repeater cable (USB 2.0 ~5 m per hop) or a USB-over-Ethernet/fibre extender.

#Lightning cables (MFi)

2012→ Legacy

Apple MFi-certified Lightning cables include an authentication chip. Uncertified cables may show 'This accessory may not be supported'. Lightning is USB 2.0 speed on most iPhones (the USB-C iPhone 15 Pro and later support up to USB 3 10 Gb/s with the right cable).

#Video cables

Getting a picture from a computer to a screen, and which cable grade you need for 4K, 8K or high refresh rates.

Video connectors (face view, schematic)

DVI-I has the four extra analog pins around the flat blade. DVI-D doesn't. A DisplayPort plug has one clipped corner, while HDMI is symmetrical.

#HDMI cable grades

2002→ Current

Cables are certified by grade, not by version number: Standard (1080i), High Speed (1080p/4K30, 10.2 Gb/s), Premium High Speed (4K60 HDR, 18 Gb/s), Ultra High Speed (4K120/8K60, 48 Gb/s), Ultra96 (HDMI 2.2, 96 Gb/s, 2025).

Identify it: Certified Ultra High Speed cables carry a hologram label you can scan with the HDMI Cable Certification app.

Commonly confused with: There's no such thing as an 'HDMI 2.1 cable' officially. Look for 'Ultra High Speed'. Counterfeit '8K' labels are common.

#Mini HDMI (Type C) & Micro HDMI (Type D)

2006 / 2009 Current

Smaller HDMI plugs for cameras, tablets, Raspberry Pi 4/5 (micro HDMI) and graphics cards (mini on some small GPUs).

#HDMI with Ethernet / ARC / eARC

Current

HDMI 1.4+ cables can carry Ethernet (rarely used) and Audio Return Channel. eARC (HDMI 2.1) needs a High Speed with Ethernet cable or better, for lossless Dolby Atmos to a soundbar.

#DisplayPort cable certifications

Current

DP 1.2/1.4 cables (HBR2/HBR3, up to 32.4 Gb/s), then VESA's newer DP40 and DP80 certified cables for DP 2.x UHBR modes (40/80 Gb/s). Older 'DP8K' cables cover up to HBR3.

Fun fact: DisplayPort cables should not connect pin 20 (DP_PWR) end to end. Cheap non-compliant cables that do can back-feed power and cause boot problems.

#Mini DisplayPort cables

2008→ Legacy

Apple-originated mini DP plugs on older MacBooks, Surface Pros and pro GPUs (Quadro, Radeon Pro).

#USB-C to HDMI / DisplayPort

Current

Works only if the laptop's USB-C port supports DisplayPort Alt Mode (or Thunderbolt/USB4). Look for a DP icon or lightning bolt next to the port. HDMI output needs an active converter chip, usually built into the cable.

#Passive vs active video adapters

Current

DP++ (dual-mode) ports can feed HDMI and DVI through cheap passive adapters, though usually only up to 4K30 or 4K60. HDMI → DisplayPort, and anything → VGA (digital to analog), need active adapters with a converter chip.

Commonly confused with: VGA → HDMI needs a powered converter box (analog to digital). A plain cable can't do it.

#Active Optical HDMI/DP cables (AOC)

Current

Fibre inside, electronics in the plugs. They carry 4K/8K over 10–100 m and are thin and light. Directional: the 'Source' end goes to the PC or console.

#VGA cables

1987→ Legacy

Analog DE-15 cables. Quality matters: thicker cables with ferrite beads give a sharper image at high resolutions. Some cables leave out the DDC (EDID) pins, which breaks auto-resolution.

#DVI cables

1999→ Legacy

Single-link DVI-D cables have gaps in the pin grid. Dual-link cables have all 24 pins and are needed for 2560×1600 or 1080p 144 Hz on DVI monitors.

Identify it: Count the pin grid: full 3×8 = dual-link; two blocks of 3×3 = single-link.

#Apple Display Connector (ADC)

2000–2004 Obsolete

Apple's single cable carrying DVI video, USB and up to 100 W of power to Cinema Displays and Studio Displays of that era. Using one on a non-ADC Mac needed an adapter brick.

Fun fact: ADC was an early attempt at the one-cable-for-everything idea that USB-C and Thunderbolt later delivered.

#Composite / component / S-Video cables

Obsolete

Analog RCA (yellow; red/green/blue for component) and 4-pin mini-DIN S-Video leads for old consoles, VCRs and GPU TV-out.

#Network cables

Ethernet, fibre, coax and phone lines. Ethernet speed ratings (Cat5e–Cat8) are in Part 1 → Networking.

RJ-45 Ethernet wiring: T568A vs T568B (clip facing away, pins pointing up)

The same standard on both ends gives a straight-through cable. T568A on one end and T568B on the other gives a crossover cable, which modern auto-MDI-X ports rarely need.

#Solid vs stranded Ethernet

Current

Solid-core cable is for in-wall runs (punched into keystone jacks). Stranded cable is for flexible patch cords. Don't crimp RJ-45 plugs onto solid cable with stranded-type plugs, because it gives intermittent connections.

#T568A vs T568B

1991→ Current

Two colour orders for the 8 wires in an RJ-45 plug. T568B is most common in commercial installs, T568A in US homes and government. Either works if both ends match.

Identify it: Look through the clear plug at pin 1 (clip facing away): white-orange = B, white-green = A.

#Straight-through vs crossover cables

Legacy

Straight-through cables connect PC → switch. Crossover cables (A on one end, B on the other) linked two PCs or two switches directly. Auto-MDI-X, standard on gigabit ports, made crossovers mostly unnecessary.

#Patch cables vs flat & slim cables

Current

Round patch cables are the norm. Flat 'ribbon' Ethernet and ultra-slim 28 AWG cables are easy to hide but have shorter safe lengths and more crosstalk.

#PoE (Power over Ethernet)

2003→ Current

Power and data over one Ethernet cable for Wi-Fi access points, IP cameras and VoIP phones. 802.3af (15.4 W), 802.3at PoE+ (30 W), 802.3bt PoE++ (60/90 W). Needs a PoE switch or injector.

Commonly confused with: 'Passive PoE' (fixed 24 V, used by some Ubiquiti and MikroTik gear) isn't the same as 802.3af/at and can damage non-PoE devices.

#Console / rollover cable

Current

Light-blue Cisco console cable: RJ-45 to DB-9 serial (or USB) for configuring routers and switches. The wiring is reversed end to end ('rollover').

#Fibre: single-mode vs multimode

Current

Single-mode (OS2, yellow jacket): 9 µm core, long distance (km). Multimode (OM1–OM5, 50/62.5 µm core): shorter runs inside buildings. OM3/OM4 (aqua) handle 10–100G in data centres.

Identify it: Yellow = single-mode. Orange = OM1/OM2. Aqua = OM3/OM4. Lime green = OM5. Violet/erika is sometimes used for OM4.

#Fibre connectors (LC, SC, ST, MPO)

Current

LC (small, latching, used on SFP modules), SC (square push-pull, FTTH ONTs), ST (bayonet twist, older), MPO/MTP (multi-fibre for 40/100/400G).

Commonly confused with: UPC (blue body, flat polish) vs APC (green body, 8° angled polish). Mating them damages the fibre ends and kills the signal.

#SFP / SFP+ / SFP28 / QSFP modules

2001→ Current

Hot-swappable transceiver cages on switches and NICs: SFP (1G), SFP+ (10G), SFP28 (25G), QSFP+/QSFP28/QSFP-DD (40/100/400G). The module decides the media (fibre type or copper).

Commonly confused with: Some switches only accept their own brand's 'coded' modules.

#DAC & AOC (direct-attach cables)

Current

DAC (Direct Attach Copper twinax) has SFP plugs moulded onto a copper cable: cheap and low-power for runs up to ~5–7 m. AOC (Active Optical Cable) is fibre with fixed transceivers for longer runs.

#Coax: F-type (RG6 / RG59)

Current

Screw-on F connectors for TV aerials, satellite dishes and cable internet (DOCSIS). RG6 is thicker and better for modern cable internet and satellite. RG59 suits older CCTV and short runs. Also used for MoCA home networking.

#BNC

1940s→ Current

Bayonet coax connector: 10BASE2 'thinnet' Ethernet (RG58, 50 Ω), CCTV/SDI video (75 Ω), lab equipment, old Sun/SGI monitor cables (RGB via 5 BNC).

Commonly confused with: 50 Ω and 75 Ω BNC look almost the same but aren't interchangeable for high-frequency signals.

#Phone cables: RJ11 / RJ12 / RJ14 / RJ9

Legacy

6-position modular plugs for landlines and DSL: RJ11 (2 wires, 1 line), RJ14 (4 wires, 2 lines), RJ12 (6 wires). RJ9/RJ10 (4P4C) is the tiny coiled handset cord plug.

#DSL filters / microfilters

Legacy

Small boxes that split a phone line into a filtered phone port and a DSL modem port, so voice calls don't disrupt the broadband signal.

Fibre-optic connectors (schematic)

Jacket colour tells the fibre type: yellow = single-mode, orange = OM1/OM2 multimode, aqua = OM3/OM4, lime green = OM5. A blue connector body is UPC, green is APC.

#Inside the PC: internal cables

Every cable inside a desktop case. The PSU plugs themselves are covered in Part 1 → Power supplies.

SATA connectors (face view, schematic)

A 2.5" or 3.5" SATA drive takes two plugs: the narrow L-shaped data plug and the wide L-shaped power plug. mSATA and M.2 cards get both through their edge connector, so they need no cables.

#SATA data cables

2003→ Current

Flat 7-pin cables up to 1 m. Variants: straight, right-angle (for tight spaces behind GPUs), and latching (a metal clip stops them falling out).

Commonly confused with: Very old 'SATA I' cables work fine for SATA III. Cable quality matters more than the label.

#SATA power splitters & adapters

Current

One SATA power lead split into 2–4. Fine for SSDs and fans. Don't hang many 3.5" HDDs off one cable. Molex → SATA adapters with moulded plastic are notorious for shorting and melting.

Fun fact: 'Molex to SATA, lose all your data' is a real PC-builder saying.

#PCIe riser cables

Current

Ribbon or twinax extensions that let you mount the GPU vertically or sandwich-style in SFF cases. A PCIe 3.0 riser can cause crashes with a PCIe 4.0/5.0 GPU, so match the generation or set the slot speed lower in BIOS.

#Front-panel connectors

Current

Tiny 1-pin or 2-pin plugs for power switch, reset, power LED (+/−) and HDD LED that go onto the F_PANEL header. Many cases now use a single block connector.

Identify it: Labels read POWER SW, RESET SW, POWER LED+, POWER LED−, H.D.D LED. LED polarity matters, but the switches don't care which way round they go.

#Internal USB cables

Current

USB 2.0 9-pin header (10-pin position, 1 blocked), USB 3.x 19/20-pin blue header (fragile, so pull it out straight), USB-C front panel 'Key-A' 20-pin small connector (10/20 Gb/s).

#HD Audio / AC'97 front audio

Current

9-pin front audio cable for the headphone and mic jacks. HD Audio (2004+) replaced AC'97, and most cases have an HD Audio plug.

#Fan cables, splitters & hubs

Current

3-pin (DC) and 4-pin (PWM) fan cables. Splitters send one header's signal to several fans, but only one fan should report RPM. Hubs draw power from SATA so the header isn't overloaded (most headers are ~1 A).

#RGB & ARGB cables

Current

12 V 4-pin RGB and 5 V 3-pin ARGB leads, with daisy-chain pass-throughs. Brands often use their own ARGB controller plugs. See Part 6 → Confused pairs.

#Mini-SAS internal: SFF-8087 & SFF-8643

2006 / 2013 Current

Server and NAS cables from a RAID/HBA card: SFF-8087 (Mini-SAS, 6 Gb/s era) and SFF-8643 (Mini-SAS HD, 12 Gb/s). Each port carries 4 drive lanes.

Identify it: SFF-8087 is a wide plug with a pull tab. SFF-8643 is smaller and squarer.

#Breakout cables: forward vs reverse

Current

Mini-SAS to 4× SATA cables come in two kinds. Forward goes from an HBA (Mini-SAS end) to drives (SATA ends). Reverse goes from motherboard SATA ports to a Mini-SAS backplane. They look identical but aren't interchangeable.

Fun fact: A wrong-direction breakout is one of the most common home-server mistakes.

#Mini-SAS external: SFF-8088 & SFF-8644

Current

External versions for connecting disk shelves (JBODs) to servers.

#U.2 / OCuLink / SlimSAS cables

Current

Cables that carry NVMe: SFF-8639 (U.2) to SFF-8643 or OCuLink (SFF-8611), and SlimSAS (SFF-8654). Used for U.2 SSDs and some high-density motherboards.

#IDE ribbon cables (40 vs 80 conductor)

1986–2008 Obsolete

40-pin connectors with either 40 wires (ATA-33 max) or 80 wires (extra grounds for UDMA/66+). Colour-coded plugs on 80-wire cables: blue = motherboard, grey = slave, black = master (at the end).

Identify it: Red stripe = pin 1. 80-wire cables have visibly finer ridges.

#Floppy ribbon cable (with twist)

1980s–2000s Obsolete

34-pin ribbon with a twist in wires 10–16. The drive after the twist became A:. A wrongly connected floppy cable makes the drive light stay on permanently.

#Internal audio CD cable

1990s–2000s Obsolete

Thin 4-pin cable from the CD-ROM's analog audio output to the sound card, needed to play audio CDs on old PCs.

#Audio & music cables

From earbuds to studio gear.

Audio plugs (side views + XLR face)

Count the black insulating rings: 1 ring = TS (mono), 2 = TRS (stereo or balanced), 3 = TRRS (headset with mic).

#Balanced vs unbalanced

Current

Unbalanced (TS, RCA): 2 conductors, picks up hum over long runs. Balanced (XLR, TRS): two signal copies with opposite polarity, so noise cancels out. Good for long stage and studio runs.

#3.5 mm (1/8") TS / TRS / TRRS

Current

The headphone jack. TRS = stereo, TRRS = stereo + mic (phones, gaming headsets). PCs with separate green and pink jacks need a TRRS splitter for headset mics.

#6.35 mm (1/4") jack

1870s→ Current

The big jack, originally from telephone switchboards. TS for guitars and instruments (unbalanced), TRS for studio headphones and balanced line.

Fun fact: The 1/4" jack is often called a 'phone' connector because operators used it in telephone switchboards from the 1870s.

#XLR

1950s→ Current

Locking circular connector, usually 3-pin, for balanced microphones, mixers, PA speakers and phantom power (48 V for condenser mics). Also XLR-4 and XLR-5, used for DMX stage lighting.

#RCA (phono)

1940s→ Current

Unbalanced line-level audio (red = right, white = left), plus subwoofer out, turntables (with a ground wire) and coax digital audio (orange).

#Speaker wire & binding posts

Current

Two-conductor wire, usually 12–16 AWG. Ends: bare wire, banana plugs, spade lugs or pin connectors. Match + to + (one side often has a stripe or ridge).

Commonly confused with: Reversing polarity on one speaker won't damage anything, but bass will sound thin because the speakers cancel each other out.

#Speakon

1987→ Current

Neutrik's locking speaker connector for pro amps and PA speakers. Safer and sturdier than 1/4" for high-power speaker lines.

#Optical (Toslink) & mini-Toslink

1983→ Current

Fibre-optic digital audio (S/PDIF): Toslink square plug, and mini-Toslink built into some 3.5 mm jacks (old MacBooks, some portable DACs). It can't carry lossless Dolby Atmos (use HDMI eARC).

#Coaxial digital (S/PDIF RCA)

Current

Digital audio over a 75 Ω RCA cable, often with an orange plug. Carries the same data as Toslink.

#MIDI cables (5-pin DIN & USB)

1983→ Current

5-pin DIN MIDI cables (In/Out/Thru) connect keyboards and synths. USB-MIDI is common now. TRS MIDI (Type A/B 3.5 mm) appears on compact gear.

Fun fact: The MIDI 1.0 spec from 1983 is still in use on new instruments today, with MIDI 2.0 arriving in 2020.

#Ground loop isolators

Current

Fix buzzing or hum caused by gear plugged into different power outlets (common with car audio and PC-to-speaker setups).

#Device charging cables

Phones, watches, earbuds and gadgets.

#USB-C (universal)

2014→ Current

The standard charging cable for phones, tablets, laptops and accessories. Required for new phones, tablets and many electronics in the EU since Dec 2024 (laptops from April 2026).

#Lightning

2012–2023 Legacy

Apple's 8-pin cable for iPhone 5–14, older iPads, AirPods and Magic accessories. Still common on older devices.

#Micro-USB

2007–~2020 Legacy

The old Android standard. Still on budget gadgets, older Kindles, power banks and Bluetooth speakers.

#Mini-USB

2000–2012 Obsolete

Older cameras, GPS units, MP3 players and PS3 controllers.

#Apple 30-pin

2003–2012 Obsolete

The wide iPod/iPhone/iPad dock cable. What the pins carry, FireWire charging and adapters: 30-pin dock connector, Part 22.

#Proprietary watch & fitness chargers

Current

Magnetic pucks and pogo-pin clips that only fit their own devices: Apple Watch puck, Samsung Galaxy Watch, Garmin's 4-pin clip, Fitbit, Whoop, Oura ring dock. Apple Watch charging (and charging AirPods on the Watch charger) has its own section below.

Identify it: Usually a USB-A or USB-C plug on one end and a magnetic disc or clip on the other.

#Pogo-pin & magnetic tip cables

Current

Spring-loaded contacts on rugged phones, tablets with keyboard docks, and aftermarket 'magnetic USB' tips that stay in the phone's port.

#Power bank cables & pass-through

Current

Short cables bundled with power banks. Pass-through charging lets the bank charge a device while it charges itself, which suits some banks better than others.

#Game controller & console cables

Current

PS5 DualSense and Switch Pro use USB-C, PS4 and Xbox One use Micro-USB, PS3 uses Mini-USB, Wii remotes have no cable (AA batteries).

#Apple Watch, AirPods & iPhone charging

Which Apple charger works with what, and the useful tricks hidden in them.

#Apple Watch fast charging

2021→ Current

Supported on Apple Watch Series 7 and later, SE 3, and Ultra and later. You need the USB-C Magnetic Fast Charging Cable (the one with the aluminium ring) plus an Apple 18 W or higher USB-C adapter, or any third-party USB-C Power Delivery adapter of 5 W or more. Series 7–9 charge from 0 to 80% in about 45 minutes, and Series 10 and later in about 30 minutes.

Commonly confused with: The old white USB-A puck still charges new watches, just at normal speed. Ordinary Qi wireless pads don't charge an Apple Watch: it needs an Apple Watch charger.

Sources: Apple Support: About fast charge on Apple Watch · MacRumors: Series 7 fast charging needs a 5 W+ USB-C PD adapter

#Life hack: charge AirPods on the Apple Watch charger

2022→ Guide

Apple says you can place these AirPods cases on an Apple Watch charger: AirPods Pro 2 (MagSafe case, Lightning or USB-C), AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods 4 with Active Noise Cancellation. Put the case lid closed, status light facing up, flat and centred on the puck, and it starts charging (newer cases play a sound). One charger on your nightstand or in your travel bag then handles watch and earbuds.

Commonly confused with: Older cases (AirPods 1, 2 and 3, the original AirPods Pro, and AirPods 4 without ANC) won't charge on the Apple Watch puck. Use Qi or MagSafe for the older wireless cases, or a cable.

Sources: Apple Support: Charge your AirPods · Apple AirPods User Guide: Charge AirPods

#Life hack: your iPhone is a power bank for your Watch & AirPods

2023→ Guide

iPhone 15 and later (USB-C) can charge an Apple Watch, an AirPods case or another small device at up to 4.5 W. Plug the Watch's USB-C charging puck straight into the iPhone, or use a USB-C cable to the AirPods case. It's slow, but it can rescue a flat watch before a run or a flight. Lightning iPhones can't do this.

Sources: Apple Support: Charge and connect with the USB-C connector on your iPhone · MacRumors: iPhone 15 USB-C gives 4.5 W to accessories

#Life hack: one charger for everything

Guide

Since the iPhone 15, Apple Watch, AirPods, iPad and MacBook Air all charge over USB-C. A single multi-port USB-C (GaN) charger of 65 W or more can replace a drawer of bricks while travelling. Any USB-C Power Delivery charger works, because the devices negotiate only the power they need (see USB-C Power Delivery in Part 1).

#Battery-saving settings worth turning on

Guide

iPhone: Optimised Battery Charging learns your routine and waits at 80% overnight. iPhone 15 and later also offer a fixed charge limit. AirPods and Apple Watch have the same optimised charging. Android: most brands offer 'Protect battery' or an 85% limit. Heat is a battery's worst enemy, so don't charge under a pillow or on a hot car dashboard.

#Charging & cable life hacks (and myths)

Small tricks that save money and cables, plus the 'tips' that are wrong.

#Cable hacks

Guide

Label cables with coloured tape or bread-bag clips, so you know which is the fast or data cable. Clip binder clips to the edge of a desk to stop cables falling behind it. Use Velcro ties instead of zip ties so you can re-route them. Coil cables loosely (or with the roadie 'over-under' method), and never wrap them tightly round the charger, which breaks the wires at the plug. A short cable in your bag charges just as well and tangles less.

#Is this cable data or charge-only?

Guide

Plug a phone into a computer with it. If the phone only charges and never asks 'Trust this computer?' or shows file transfer, it's a charge-only cable. Mark it so you don't waste time with it for backups or CarPlay/Android Auto. USB-C cables often show their speed and wattage on the plug (see How to read a cable).

#Charging from the wrong port

Guide

Car USB-A ports, TV ports and old laptop ports often give only 0.5–1.5 A (2.5–7.5 W), so a phone may barely charge while you use maps. A small USB-C PD car adapter fixes that. A laptop's USB-C port, a monitor with USB-C, or a power bank all work in a pinch.

#Travel kit

Guide

One multi-port USB-C charger, one USB-C to USB-C cable (plus USB-C to Lightning if you have older gear), your Apple Watch puck (which can also charge AirPods Pro 2/3 and AirPods 4 ANC), a power bank under 100 Wh (the airline carry-on limit without approval), and a Type G adapter for Saudi Arabia, the UK and the Gulf.

#Legacy & vintage cables

For retro computers and old hardware.

#Null-modem serial cable

1970s→ Legacy

Serial cable with the transmit/receive lines crossed, so two computers can talk directly (file transfer, multiplayer DOS games, server consoles).

Commonly confused with: A plain serial extension cable (straight-through) won't link two PCs. It has to be a null-modem.

#Parallel printer cable (IEEE 1284)

1970s–2000s Obsolete

DB-25 male (PC) to Centronics 36 (printer). IEEE 1284 bidirectional cables were needed for ECP/EPP modes, scanners and Zip drives.

#LapLink cable

1980s–1990s Obsolete

Special serial or parallel cable used with LapLink software to transfer files between PCs before networks were common.

#SCSI cables & terminators

1986–2000s Obsolete

Internal 50-pin and 68-pin ribbons with multiple drive connectors. External Centronics-50, DB-25 (Mac), HD50 and HD68 cables. A terminator plug (active or passive) must close the chain at both ends.

#FireWire cables

1995–2010s Obsolete

6-pin (powered FW400), 4-pin (unpowered, Sony i.LINK, camcorders), 9-pin (FW800, 'bilingual' cables connect to FW400). macOS 26 Tahoe removed FireWire support. Full guide, adapters and DV-tape rescue: FireWire in depth, Part 22.

#AT ↔ PS/2 keyboard adapters

Obsolete

Passive DIN-5 ↔ mini-DIN-6 adapters. Also PS/2 ↔ USB adapters, which only work with keyboards and mice that support both protocols.

#Mac DB-15 & ADB cables

1986–1998 Obsolete

Old Macs used a 2-row DB-15 video port (not VGA), so they needed a Mac-to-VGA adapter with DIP switches. ADB cables (4-pin mini-DIN) daisy-chained keyboards and mice.

#Joystick Y-cable & MIDI game-port adapter

1980s–1990s Obsolete

Y-splitters for two joysticks on one game port, and game-port-to-MIDI breakout cables for sound cards.

#AUI & transceivers (10BASE5)

1980s Obsolete

15-pin AUI cables connected a PC to a 'vampire tap' transceiver clamped onto thick yellow coax Ethernet (10BASE5).

#Cassette & TV RF cables

1977–1980s Obsolete

Home computers used RF modulator cables to an aerial input (tune to channel 3/36) and 3.5 mm audio cables to cassette recorders for storage.

#Adapters, fakes & dangers

Cables that can damage hardware or start fires, and how to avoid them.

#Moulded Molex → SATA adapters

Current

Cheap injection-moulded adapters can short internally and melt. Use crimped-pin adapters or a native SATA power cable from the PSU.

#Mixing modular PSU cables

Current

Using a modular cable from a different PSU brand or model, even if it fits, can send 12 V to a 5 V pin and destroy drives and boards. Use only the PSU's own cables.

#Out-of-spec USB-C cables

Current

Wrong resistors, missing e-markers and thin wires can lead to overheating, slow charging or damaged ports. Buy USB-IF-certified or reputable brands for 100 W+.

#Counterfeit 'HDMI 2.1' and '8K' cables

Current

Many cables claim 8K but fail at 48 Gb/s, which shows up as flickering, black screens or no 4K120. Look for the official Ultra High Speed certification label.

#Long adapter chains

Current

USB-C → HDMI → DVI → VGA chains often fail. Each conversion adds limits. Use one direct cable or a single active converter.

#Damaged or frayed cables

Current

Exposed wires, a hot plug, or a melted/brown connector means replace it immediately. Never wrap tape around mains cords as a fix.

#Cable management basics

Current

Velcro ties (not tight zip ties on data cables), avoiding sharp bends (fibre and 12VHPWR especially), labelling both ends, and keeping power and data cables apart to cut interference.
