With strict types on, passing text to a float parameter stops the program with a TypeError, which is much better than silently computing garbage.

PHP
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
function vat(float $amount): float { return $amount * 0.15; }
echo "before\n";
echo vat("abc");
Output
before
Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError: vat(): Argument #1 ($amount) must be of type float, string given, called in main.php on line 5 and defined in main.php:3

#PHP tutorial 4: Forms, sessions, databases & security

What PHP is really for: handling requests safely.

#Superglobals: $_GET, $_POST, $_SESSION…

Concept

PHP fills special arrays for every request: $_GET (URL parameters like ?city=Riyadh), $_POST (submitted form fields, see the forms chapter of the HTML & CSS folder), $_FILES (uploads), $_COOKIE, $_SESSION and $_SERVER (request info). Treat everything in them as untrusted user input.

#Handling a form submission

Concept

Here $_POST is filled by hand to simulate a submitted sign-up form. Validate every field, collect errors, and use filter_var for emails.

PHP
<?php
$_POST = ["name" => "  Sarah ", "email" => "sarah@example", "city" => "Riyadh"];

$name = trim($_POST["name"] ?? "");
$email = trim($_POST["email"] ?? "");
$errors = [];
if ($name === "") $errors[] = "Name is required";
if (!filter_var($email, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) $errors[] = "Email is not valid";

if ($errors) {
    echo "Please fix:\n- " . implode("\n- ", $errors) . "\n";
} else {
    echo "Welcome, $name!\n";
}
Output
Please fix:
- Email is not valid

#Preventing XSS with htmlspecialchars

Concept

Never print user input straight into HTML. A comment containing a <script> tag would run in every visitor's browser (cross-site scripting). htmlspecialchars turns special characters into harmless text.

PHP
<?php
$comment = '<script>alert("hacked")</script> Great laptop!';
echo "Unsafe: <p>$comment</p>\n";
echo "Safe:   <p>" . htmlspecialchars($comment) . "</p>\n";
Output
Unsafe: <p><script>alert("hacked")</script> Great laptop!</p>
Safe:   <p>&lt;script&gt;alert(&quot;hacked&quot;)&lt;/script&gt; Great laptop!</p>

#Databases with PDO & prepared statements

Concept

PDO talks to MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite and others with the same code. Prepared statements (? placeholders) keep user input separate from SQL, which blocks SQL injection. This uses a real in-memory SQLite database. (SQL itself is covered in the SQL folder.)

PHP
<?php
$db = new PDO("sqlite::memory:");
$db->setAttribute(PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE, PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION);
$db->exec("CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER, city TEXT, amount REAL)");
$insert = $db->prepare("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?)");
foreach ([[101, "Riyadh", 150], [102, "London", 45], [103, "Riyadh", 300]] as $row) {
    $insert->execute($row);
}

$userInput = "Riyadh' OR '1'='1";          // an injection attempt
$stmt = $db->prepare("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE city = ?");
$stmt->execute([$userInput]);
echo "rows for the attack string: ", $stmt->fetchColumn(), "\n";

$stmt->execute(["Riyadh"]);
echo "rows for Riyadh: ", $stmt->fetchColumn(), "\n";
foreach ($db->query("SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY city ORDER BY city") as $r) {
    echo "{$r['city']}: {$r['total']}\n";
}
Output
rows for the attack string: 0
rows for Riyadh: 2
London: 45
Riyadh: 450

#Storing passwords safely

Concept

Never store plain passwords. password_hash creates a salted bcrypt/argon2 hash (different every time), and password_verify checks a login attempt against it.

PHP
<?php
$hash = password_hash("MyS3cret!", PASSWORD_DEFAULT);
echo "hash starts with: ", substr($hash, 0, 4), " (", strlen($hash), " characters)\n";
var_dump(password_verify("MyS3cret!", $hash));
var_dump(password_verify("wrong", $hash));
Output
hash starts with: $2y$ (60 characters)
bool(true)
bool(false)

#Sessions: remembering a logged-in user

Concept

HTTP forgets everything between requests. A session stores data on the server and gives the browser a cookie with the session ID. (Shown only, since it needs a web server and browser.)

PHP (needs a web server, not run)
<?php
session_start();                      // must come before any output

if (password_verify($_POST["password"], $userFromDb["hash"])) {
    session_regenerate_id(true);      // prevents session fixation attacks
    $_SESSION["user_id"] = $userFromDb["id"];
    header("Location: /dashboard.php");
    exit;
}

// on every protected page:
if (empty($_SESSION["user_id"])) {
    header("Location: /login.php");
    exit;
}

#PHP tutorial 5: Object-oriented & modern PHP

Classes, interfaces, enums and the PHP 8 features used by Laravel and Symfony.

#Classes & constructor promotion

Concept

PHP 8 lets you declare properties right in the constructor. readonly properties can't change after creation, and -> calls methods.

PHP
<?php
class Product {
    public function __construct(
        public readonly string $name,
        private float $price,
        private int $stock = 0,
    ) {}

    public function priceWithVat(): float { return round($this->price * 1.15, 2); }
    public function sell(int $qty): bool {
        if ($qty > $this->stock) return false;
        $this->stock -= $qty;
        return true;
    }
    public function __toString(): string { return "{$this->name} ({$this->stock} in stock)"; }
}

$m = new Product("Monitor", 300, 5);
echo $m->priceWithVat(), "\n";
var_dump($m->sell(10), $m->sell(2));
echo $m, "\n";
Output
345
bool(false)
bool(true)
Monitor (3 in stock)

#Inheritance & interfaces

Concept

extends inherits, implements promises to follow an interface, and abstract methods must be filled in by child classes.

PHP
<?php
interface Payable { public function amountDue(): float; }

abstract class Document implements Payable {
    public function __construct(protected string $ref) {}
    public function label(): string { return static::class . " " . $this->ref . ": " . number_format($this->amountDue(), 2); }
}
class Invoice extends Document {
    public function __construct(string $ref, private float $net) { parent::__construct($ref); }
    public function amountDue(): float { return $this->net * 1.15; }
}
class Refund extends Document {
    public function amountDue(): float { return -45; }
}

foreach ([new Invoice("INV-1", 1000), new Refund("RF-7")] as $doc) {
    echo $doc->label(), "\n";
}
Output
Invoice INV-1: 1,150.00
Refund RF-7: -45.00

#Enums (PHP 8.1)

Concept

A fixed set of values. Backed enums have a string or int value, which is handy for database columns.

PHP
<?php
enum Status: string {
    case Pending = "pending";
    case Completed = "completed";
    case Returned = "returned";

    public function label(): string {
        return match ($this) {
            Status::Completed => "✅ Completed",
            Status::Returned => "↩️ Returned",
            Status::Pending => "⏳ Pending",
        };
    }
}
$s = Status::from("returned");
echo $s->name, " | ", $s->value, " | ", $s->label(), "\n";
echo count(Status::cases()), " statuses\n";
Output
Returned | returned | ↩️ Returned
3 statuses

#Exceptions

Concept

throw an exception when something is wrong, and try/catch it where you can handle it.

PHP
<?php
function withdraw(float $balance, float $amount): float {
    if ($amount > $balance) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException("Insufficient funds: balance $balance, requested $amount");
    }
    return $balance - $amount;
}
try {
    echo withdraw(500, 100), "\n";
    echo withdraw(500, 900), "\n";
} catch (InvalidArgumentException $e) {
    echo "Error: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
} finally {
    echo "transaction finished\n";
}
Output
400
Error: Insufficient funds: balance 500, requested 900
transaction finished

#PHP tutorial 6: Projects, ecosystem & roadmap

Put it together, then build real websites.

#Project: store receipt with VAT

Concept

Arrays, a loop, printf and str_repeat. It's the same cart as the Python, JavaScript and Java projects, so you can compare all four languages.

PHP
<?php
$prices = ["Keyboard" => 150, "Monitor" => 300, "Headset" => 120, "Mousepad" => 45];
$cart = ["Monitor" => 1, "Keyboard" => 2, "Mousepad" => 1];

$subtotal = 0;
foreach ($cart as $item => $qty) {
    $cost = $prices[$item] * $qty;
    $subtotal += $cost;
    printf("%-10s x%d %10.2f\n", $item, $qty, $cost);
}
echo str_repeat("-", 24), "\n";
printf("%-13s %10.2f\n%-13s %10.2f\n%-13s %10.2f\n",
    "Subtotal", $subtotal, "VAT 15%", $subtotal * 0.15, "TOTAL SAR", $subtotal * 1.15);
Output
Monitor    x1     300.00
Keyboard   x2     300.00
Mousepad   x1      45.00
------------------------
Subtotal          645.00
VAT 15%            96.75
TOTAL SAR         741.75

#Project: a tiny JSON API

Concept

Many PHP apps are APIs that return JSON to a JavaScript front-end or a mobile app. Here a 'request' for completed orders in a city is answered as JSON.

PHP
<?php
$orders = [
    ["id" => 101, "city" => "Riyadh", "amount" => 150, "status" => "Completed"],
    ["id" => 102, "city" => "London", "amount" => 45,  "status" => "Completed"],
    ["id" => 103, "city" => "Riyadh", "amount" => 300, "status" => "Completed"],
    ["id" => 104, "city" => "Riyadh", "amount" => 600, "status" => "Pending"],
];
$_GET = ["city" => "Riyadh"];               // simulates /api/orders.php?city=Riyadh

$city = $_GET["city"] ?? null;
$result = array_values(array_filter($orders, fn($o) => $o["city"] === $city && $o["status"] === "Completed"));
// header("Content-Type: application/json");   (in a real web request)
echo json_encode(["city" => $city, "count" => count($result), "total" => array_sum(array_column($result, "amount")),
                  "orders" => array_column($result, "id")], JSON_PRETTY_PRINT), "\n";
Output
{
    "city": "Riyadh",
    "count": 2,
    "total": 450,
    "orders": [
        101,
        103
    ]
}
▸Git & GitHub tutorial6 chapters · Every programmer needs thisclick to open / close

Save every version of your work and collaborate: commits, undoing mistakes, branches and merge conflicts, GitHub, push/pull and pull requests. Every command really ran.

1. What Git and GitHub are2. Your first repository3. Undoing things safely4. Branches & merging5. GitHub: remotes, push, pull & pull requests6. Workflows, tools & cheat sheet

#Git tutorial 1: What Git and GitHub are

Git remembers every version of your project. GitHub keeps a copy online so you can share and work together.

#Git in one minute

Concept

Git is a version control system: it takes snapshots (commits) of a project folder so you can see what changed, when and by whom, go back to any earlier version, and work on several ideas at once (branches). Linus Torvalds wrote it in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel. Today almost all software, plus many websites, documents and configuration files, is kept in Git.

Fun fact: Torvalds named it 'git', British slang for an unpleasant person, joking that he names all his projects after himself.

#Git vs GitHub

Concept

Git is the program on your computer, and it works fully offline. GitHub (2008, owned by Microsoft since 2018) is a website that hosts Git repositories and adds teamwork features: pull requests, code review, issues, Actions (automation) and Pages (free websites). Alternatives: GitLab, Bitbucket, Codeberg, or self-hosted Gitea / Forgejo (see the Home Lab part).

Commonly confused with: GitHub is not Git. You can use Git without GitHub, and GitHub Desktop is just one of many apps that run Git for you.

#Install Git and introduce yourself (once per computer)

Concept

Windows: install Git for Windows (git-scm.com), which includes Git Bash. macOS: run git --version and accept the Command Line Tools prompt, or brew install git. Linux: sudo apt install git (or dnf/pacman). Then set the name and email that will appear on your commits. Use the same email as your GitHub account.

Terminal (run on your computer)
git --version
git config --global user.name "Sarah Ahmed"
git config --global user.email "sarah@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main    # new repos start on 'main'
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"  # VS Code for commit messages (optional)
git config --list                              # check your settings

#Git tutorial 2: Your first repository

init, status, add, commit, log: the five commands you'll use every day.

#Create a repo and make the first commit

Concept

git init turns a folder into a repository. git status tells you what Git sees. git add stages files and git commit -m saves the snapshot. Read the status messages: Git usually tells you the next command to run.

Terminal (bash + git)
mkdir my-site
cd my-site
git init -q
echo "<h1>Hello</h1>" > index.html
git status
git add index.html
git commit -m "Add home page"
git log
Output
$ mkdir my-site
$ cd my-site
$ git init -q
$ echo "<h1>Hello</h1>" > index.html
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	index.html

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
$ git add index.html
$ git commit -m "Add home page"
[main (root-commit) 0128767] Add home page
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 index.html
$ git log
commit 0128767686d61cb5e0df83e5565660c83bc176aa
Author: Sarah Ahmed <sarah@example.com>
Date:   Mon Jan 5 09:00:00 2026 +0300

    Add home page

#Change, check, commit again

Concept

git diff shows exactly which lines changed (- removed, + added) before you stage them. git log --oneline gives a compact history, newest first.

Terminal (bash + git)
echo "<p>Welcome to my site</p>" >> index.html
echo "body { font-family: sans-serif; }" > style.css
git status --short
git diff
git add .
git commit -m "Add welcome text and styles"
git log --oneline
Output
$ echo "<p>Welcome to my site</p>" >> index.html
$ echo "body { font-family: sans-serif; }" > style.css
$ git status --short
 M index.html
?? style.css
$ git diff
diff --git a/index.html b/index.html
index 986a4a1..c63c6db 100644
--- a/index.html
+++ b/index.html
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 <h1>Hello</h1>
+<p>Welcome to my site</p>
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Add welcome text and styles"
[main c2e34a3] Add welcome text and styles
 2 files changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 style.css
$ git log --oneline
c2e34a3 Add welcome text and styles
0128767 Add home page

#Reading `git status --short`

Concept

?? untracked (Git has never seen it), A added (staged new file), M modified. The left column is the staging area and the right column is the working tree, so M means changed but not staged, and M means staged.

#Ignore files with .gitignore

Concept

Never commit passwords, API keys, .env files, node_modules, build output or big videos. List patterns in a .gitignore file and Git won't show or add them.

Terminal (bash + git)
printf 'SECRET_KEY=abc123\n' > .env
mkdir node_modules && touch node_modules/huge.js
touch notes.log app.js
printf '.env\nnode_modules/\n*.log\n' > .gitignore
cat .gitignore
git status --short
Output
$ printf 'SECRET_KEY=abc123\n' > .env
$ mkdir node_modules && touch node_modules/huge.js
$ touch notes.log app.js
$ printf '.env\nnode_modules/\n*.log\n' > .gitignore
$ cat .gitignore
.env
node_modules/
*.log
$ git status --short
?? .gitignore
?? app.js

#Good commit messages

Concept

Write the subject as a short command, about 50 characters: 'Add login page', 'Fix VAT rounding on invoices', not 'stuff' or 'changes'. One commit = one logical change. Many teams use Conventional Commits: feat: add search, fix: correct total, docs: update README.

Fun fact: Commit messages are a letter to your future self. In six months 'fix bug' will tell you nothing.

#Look back in history

Concept

git show displays one commit and its changes. HEAD~1 means 'one commit before the current one'. git log --stat lists the files each commit touched.

Terminal (bash + git)
git log --oneline
git show --stat HEAD
git log --oneline -- prices.py
git show HEAD~1:README.md
Output
$ git log --oneline
cf5282f Add prices
7253f9d Start the shop project
$ git show --stat HEAD
commit cf5282f2db86ab56de1652dadc2ada80ed29c7dd
Author: Sarah Ahmed <sarah@example.com>
Date:   Mon Jan 5 09:00:00 2026 +0300

    Add prices

 prices.py | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
$ git log --oneline -- prices.py
cf5282f Add prices
$ git show HEAD~1:README.md
# Shop
A tiny online store.

#Git tutorial 3: Undoing things safely

Almost every mistake in Git can be fixed, as long as you committed first.

#restore: throw away an edit

Concept

Oops, you broke a file and want the last committed version back.

Terminal (bash + git)
echo 'PRICE = -5   # oops' > prices.py
git diff --stat
git restore prices.py
cat prices.py
git status --short
Output
$ echo 'PRICE = -5   # oops' > prices.py
$ git diff --stat
 prices.py | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
$ git restore prices.py
$ cat prices.py
PRICE = 100
$ git status --short

#amend: fix the last commit

Concept

Forgot a file? Stage it and amend. The commit gets a new ID because it is a new snapshot, which is why you shouldn't amend commits you have already pushed.

Terminal (bash + git)
echo "Saudi VAT is 15%" > vat.txt
git add vat.txt
git commit -qm "Add VAT note"
git log --oneline -1
echo "VAT = 0.15" > vat.py
git add vat.py
git commit -q --amend -m "Add VAT note and constant"
git log --oneline -1
git show --stat --format=%s HEAD
Output
$ echo "Saudi VAT is 15%" > vat.txt
$ git add vat.txt
$ git commit -qm "Add VAT note"
$ git log --oneline -1
6ec7253 Add VAT note
$ echo "VAT = 0.15" > vat.py
$ git add vat.py
$ git commit -q --amend -m "Add VAT note and constant"
$ git log --oneline -1
41ca64c Add VAT note and constant
$ git show --stat --format=%s HEAD
Add VAT note and constant

 vat.py  | 1 +
 vat.txt | 1 +
 2 files changed, 2 insertions(+)

#revert: undo a shared commit safely

Concept

git revert doesn't delete history. It adds a new commit that does the opposite, so it's safe on branches other people use.

Terminal (bash + git)
echo 'PRICE = 999' > prices.py
git commit -qam "Raise price"
git log --oneline
git revert --no-edit HEAD
git log --oneline
cat prices.py
Output
$ echo 'PRICE = 999' > prices.py
$ git commit -qam "Raise price"
$ git log --oneline
5e3d0af Raise price
cf5282f Add prices
7253f9d Start the shop project
$ git revert --no-edit HEAD
[main 7f0952d] Revert "Raise price"
 Date: Mon Jan 5 09:00:00 2026 +0300
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
$ git log --oneline
7f0952d Revert "Raise price"
5e3d0af Raise price
cf5282f Add prices
7253f9d Start the shop project
$ cat prices.py
PRICE = 100

#stash: park your work

Concept

Your manager needs an urgent fix, but you're halfway through something. git stash saves the unfinished edits and gives you a clean folder. git stash pop brings them back.

Terminal (bash + git)
echo 'print("half-finished feature")' >> app.py
git stash
git status --short
git stash list
git stash pop
git status --short
Output
$ echo 'print("half-finished feature")' >> app.py
$ git stash
Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: cf5282f Add prices
$ git status --short
$ git stash list
stash@{0}: WIP on main: cf5282f Add prices
$ git stash pop
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   app.py

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
Dropped refs/stash@{0} (2af360ec6c9e1b571f868f06a608dfc5c2bfd284)
$ git status --short
 M app.py

#reset and reflog: the safety net

Concept

reset --hard moves the branch back and discards work, so it feels scary. But Git keeps a diary of where HEAD has been for about 90 days: git reflog. Find the ID and reset back to it.

Terminal (bash + git)
git log --oneline
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git log --oneline
git reflog -3
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
git log --oneline
Output
$ git log --oneline
cf5282f Add prices
7253f9d Start the shop project
$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
HEAD is now at 7253f9d Start the shop project
$ git log --oneline
7253f9d Start the shop project
$ git reflog -3
7253f9d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
cf5282f HEAD@{1}: commit: Add prices
7253f9d HEAD@{2}: commit (initial): Start the shop project
$ git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
HEAD is now at cf5282f Add prices
$ git log --oneline
cf5282f Add prices
7253f9d Start the shop project

#Git tutorial 4: Branches & merging

Work on a new idea without touching the working version, then join it back in.

#Why branches?

Concept

main should always work. For every feature or fix, create a branch, commit there, and merge it when it's ready. If the idea fails, delete the branch. A branch is just a tiny label pointing at a commit, so creating one is instant.

#Create a branch, commit, merge

Concept

git switch -c name creates a branch and moves to it (older guides use git checkout -b). When main hasn't moved, the merge is a fast-forward: Git just slides the main label forward.

Terminal (bash + git)
git switch -c discount
echo 'DISCOUNT = 0.10' >> prices.py
git commit -qam "Add 10% discount"
git log --oneline
git switch main
cat prices.py
git merge discount
cat prices.py
git branch -d discount
Output
$ git switch -c discount
Switched to a new branch 'discount'
$ echo 'DISCOUNT = 0.10' >> prices.py
$ git commit -qam "Add 10% discount"
$ git log --oneline
ecef779 Add 10% discount
cf5282f Add prices
7253f9d Start the shop project
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ cat prices.py
PRICE = 100
$ git merge discount
Updating cf5282f..ecef779
Fast-forward
 prices.py | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
$ cat prices.py
PRICE = 100
DISCOUNT = 0.10
$ git branch -d discount
Deleted branch discount (was ecef779).

#Two branches moved: a merge commit

Concept

If both branches got new commits, Git combines them with a merge commit that has two parents. git log --graph draws the shape.

Terminal (bash + git)
git switch -q -c search
echo 'def search(q): return q' > search.py
git add search.py
git commit -qm "Add search"
git switch -q main
echo 'Contact: info@shop.sa' >> README.md
git commit -qam "Add contact email"
git merge --no-edit search
git log --oneline --graph --all
Output
$ git switch -q -c search
$ echo 'def search(q): return q' > search.py
$ git add search.py
$ git commit -qm "Add search"
$ git switch -q main
$ echo 'Contact: info@shop.sa' >> README.md
$ git commit -qam "Add contact email"
$ git merge --no-edit search
Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 search.py | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 search.py
$ git log --oneline --graph --all
*   2a481ed Merge branch 'search'
|\  
| * caf5289 Add search
* | 7ad41a8 Add contact email
|/  
* cf5282f Add prices
* 7253f9d Start the shop project

#A merge conflict, and how to fix it

Concept

If both branches changed the same lines, Git can't decide and stops. It marks the file: your version between <<<<<<< and =======, theirs between ======= and >>>>>>>. Edit the file to the final version, delete the markers, then git add and git commit.

Terminal (bash + git)
git switch -q -c sale
echo 'PRICE = 80' > prices.py
git commit -qam "Sale price"
git switch -q main
echo 'PRICE = 120' > prices.py
git commit -qam "New price"
git merge sale || true
git status --short
cat prices.py
echo 'PRICE = 80   # sale wins until Friday' > prices.py
git add prices.py
git commit -qm "Merge sale branch, keep sale price"
git log --oneline --graph
Output
$ git switch -q -c sale
$ echo 'PRICE = 80' > prices.py
$ git commit -qam "Sale price"
$ git switch -q main
$ echo 'PRICE = 120' > prices.py
$ git commit -qam "New price"
$ git merge sale || true
Auto-merging prices.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in prices.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
$ git status --short
UU prices.py
$ cat prices.py
<<<<<<< HEAD
PRICE = 120
=======
PRICE = 80
>>>>>>> sale
$ echo 'PRICE = 80   # sale wins until Friday' > prices.py
$ git add prices.py
$ git commit -qm "Merge sale branch, keep sale price"
$ git log --oneline --graph
*   e11a62d Merge sale branch, keep sale price
|\  
| * c5835a1 Sale price
* | 3dbbab8 New price
|/  
* cf5282f Add prices
* 7253f9d Start the shop project

#Avoiding painful conflicts

Concept

Keep branches short-lived (days, not months), pull main into your branch often, make small focused commits, and agree on formatting (Prettier, Black) so tools don't reformat whole files. VS Code shows conflicts with buttons: Accept Current, Accept Incoming, Accept Both.

#Tags: mark a release

Concept

A tag is a permanent name for a commit, usually a version number. GitHub turns tags into downloadable Releases.

Terminal (bash + git)
git tag -a v1.0 -m "First public version"
git tag
git log --oneline --decorate
Output
$ git tag -a v1.0 -m "First public version"
$ git tag
v1.0
$ git log --oneline --decorate
cf5282f (HEAD -> main, tag: v1.0) Add prices
7253f9d Start the shop project

#Git tutorial 5: GitHub: remotes, push, pull & pull requests

Sharing your repository and working as a team.

#Remotes, push and clone (with a pretend GitHub)

Concept

Here a local 'bare' repository plays the role of GitHub so the commands really run. On real GitHub the URL looks like https://github.com/you/shop.git or git@github.com:you/shop.git.

Terminal (bash + git)
git init -q --bare ../github-shop.git
git remote add origin ../github-shop.git
git remote -v
git push -u origin main
cd ..
git clone -q github-shop.git laptop-copy
ls laptop-copy
Output
$ git init -q --bare ../github-shop.git
$ git remote add origin ../github-shop.git
$ git remote -v
origin	../github-shop.git (fetch)
origin	../github-shop.git (push)
$ git push -u origin main
To ../github-shop.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
$ cd ..
$ git clone -q github-shop.git laptop-copy
$ ls laptop-copy
README.md
app.py
prices.py

#pull: get your teammate's work

Concept

Your teammate (on another computer, the clone ahmed) pushes a commit. You run git pull, which is git fetch (download) + git merge.

Terminal (bash + git)
cd ../ahmed
echo 'SHIPPING = 25' >> prices.py
git commit -qam "Add shipping fee"
git push -q
cd ../shop
git pull
git log --oneline -3
Output
$ cd ../ahmed
$ echo 'SHIPPING = 25' >> prices.py
$ git commit -qam "Add shipping fee"
$ git push -q
$ cd ../shop
$ git pull
From ../hub
   cf5282f..3a3ddcb  main       -> origin/main
Updating cf5282f..3a3ddcb
Fast-forward
 prices.py | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
$ git log --oneline -3
3a3ddcb Add shipping fee
cf5282f Add prices
7253f9d Start the shop project

#Push rejected? Pull first

Concept

Ahmed pushed a commit a minute ago, and you haven't pulled it yet. GitHub refuses your push so you don't overwrite his work. Pull (here with --rebase, which puts your commit on top of his), then push again. Never fix this with git push --force on a shared branch.

Terminal (bash + git)
echo "y" > b.txt
git add b.txt
git commit -qm "My change"
git push || true
git pull --rebase
git push
git log --oneline -3
Output
$ echo "y" > b.txt
$ git add b.txt
$ git commit -qm "My change"
$ git push || true
To ../hub.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to '../hub.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing to
hint: the same ref. If you want to integrate the remote changes, use
hint: 'git pull' before pushing again.
hint: See the 'Note about fast-forwards' in 'git push --help' for details.
$ git pull --rebase
From ../hub
   cf5282f..a2bd8b4  main       -> origin/main
Rebasing (1/1)
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/main.
$ git push
To ../hub.git
   a2bd8b4..95e8f8c  main -> main
$ git log --oneline -3
95e8f8c My change
a2bd8b4 Ahmed's change
cf5282f Add prices

#Connect to GitHub with an SSH key (once per computer)

Concept

GitHub no longer accepts your account password on the command line. Use SSH keys (below), the GitHub CLI (gh auth login), or a personal access token. Git for Windows and GitHub Desktop also handle login for you.

Terminal (run on your computer)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "sarah@example.com"   # press Enter for the defaults, set a passphrase
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub                        # copy this public key
# GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → paste
ssh -T git@github.com                            # test: "Hi sarah! You've successfully authenticated"
git clone git@github.com:sarah/shop.git

Commonly confused with: Share only the .pub file. The file without .pub is your private key: never upload or send it.

#Security: committed a secret by mistake?

Concept

Treat it as leaked, even if you delete it in the next commit, because it stays in history and bots scan GitHub for keys within minutes. 1. Revoke/rotate the key or password immediately. 2. Then clean history if needed (git filter-repo or BFG). 3. Add the file to .gitignore. GitHub's push protection blocks many known key formats automatically.

Commonly confused with: Making the repo private afterwards doesn't fix it. The key may already have been copied.

#Git tutorial 6: Workflows, tools & cheat sheet

How teams use Git day to day, and the commands on one page.

▸Linux command line & distros7 chapters · Beginner → intermediateclick to open / close

Pick a distro, then master the terminal: files, pipes, grep/awk/sed, permissions, packages, processes, SSH and bash scripts. Every command really ran.

1. Linux & distros2. Moving around & managing files3. Reading files, pipes & text tools4. Permissions, users & sudo5. Software, processes, disks & network6. Shell scripting7. Cheat sheet & roadmap

#Linux tutorial 1: Linux & distros

Linux is the kernel. A distro is the complete operating system built around it.

#What Linux is

Concept

Linux is an operating-system kernel started by Linus Torvalds in 1991 as a student hobby project. Combined with GNU tools, a desktop and an app store, it becomes a distribution (distro) such as Ubuntu or Fedora. Linux runs almost every web server, all of the top 500 supercomputers, most cloud servers, Android phones, routers, smart TVs, the Steam Deck and many cars. On desktops it's a smaller share, but it's free, private and great for learning.

Fun fact: Android uses the Linux kernel, which makes Linux the most-used operating-system kernel in the world.

#Ways to try Linux without risk

Concept

1. WSL on Windows 10/11: wsl --install in PowerShell gives you a real Ubuntu terminal in minutes, which is perfect for this tutorial. 2. A virtual machine (VirtualBox, VMware, Hyper-V, UTM on Mac). 3. A live USB: flash the ISO with Rufus, balenaEtcher or Ventoy and boot from it without installing. 4. A cloud server (a few dollars a month) or a Raspberry Pi. 5. Dual-boot when you're ready, but back up first.

#The terminal, the shell and the prompt

Concept

The terminal is the window. The shell is the program inside that reads your commands. Most Linux distros use bash, macOS uses zsh (almost the same for daily use). A prompt like sarah@laptop:~/shop$ means user sarah on computer laptop, in folder ~/shop (~ is your home folder). $ means a normal user, # means root (admin). Every example below really ran. The lines starting with $ are the commands, and everything else is what they printed.

Fun fact: Part 18 shows the same everyday commands side by side in Bash, PowerShell and Windows cmd.

#Linux tutorial 2: Moving around & managing files

pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, cp, mv, rm: the commands you'll type a hundred times a day.

#Where am I, and what's here?

Concept

pwd prints the current folder, ls lists it, cd changes folder. ls -l shows the long format (permissions, owner, size, date) and -a also shows hidden files that start with a dot.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
pwd
ls
ls -l
cd data
ls -la
cd ..
Output
$ pwd
shop
$ ls
data
docs
scripts
$ ls -l
total 12
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jan  5  2026 data
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jan  5  2026 docs
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jan  5  2026 scripts
$ cd data
$ ls -la
total 16
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jan  5  2026 .
drwxr-xr-x 5 root root 4096 Jan  5  2026 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  264 Jan  5  2026 app.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  220 Jan  5  2026 orders.csv
$ cd ..

#Create, copy, move, rename, delete

Concept

mkdir -p makes folders (including parents), touch makes an empty file, cp copies (-r for folders), mv moves and renames, rm deletes (-r for folders). There is no recycle bin in the terminal: rm is permanent.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
mkdir -p backup/2026
cp data/orders.csv backup/2026/
mv docs/README.md docs/NOTES.md
touch todo.txt
ls -R backup docs
rm todo.txt
rm -r backup
ls
Output
$ mkdir -p backup/2026
$ cp data/orders.csv backup/2026/
$ mv docs/README.md docs/NOTES.md
$ touch todo.txt
$ ls -R backup docs
backup:
2026

backup/2026:
orders.csv

docs:
NOTES.md
$ rm todo.txt
$ rm -r backup
$ ls
data
docs
scripts

#Find files

Concept

find searches by name, type, size or date. * is a wildcard meaning 'anything'.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
find . -name "*.csv"
find . -type d
ls data/*.log
du -sh data
Output
$ find . -name "*.csv"
./data/orders.csv
$ find . -type d
.
./scripts
./data
./docs
$ ls data/*.log
data/app.log
$ du -sh data
12K	data

#Tab completion and history (huge time-savers)

Concept

Press Tab to finish a file or command name, and Tab twice to see the choices. ↑ / ↓ scroll through previous commands, Ctrl+R searches them, !! repeats the last command. Ctrl+C stops a running command, Ctrl+L clears the screen, clear does too.

Commonly confused with: Ctrl+C in a terminal means stop, not copy. Use Ctrl+Shift+C / Ctrl+Shift+V to copy and paste in most Linux terminals.

#Getting help

Concept

man ls opens the manual (press q to quit, /word to search). ls --help gives a shorter summary. tldr ls (install the tldr app) shows practical examples, and is often the fastest.

#Linux tutorial 3: Reading files, pipes & text tools

Linux treats everything as text, and small tools joined with pipes do big jobs.

#Look inside files

Concept

cat prints a whole file, head/tail the first or last lines, wc -l counts lines. For long files use less (scroll with arrows, q quits). tail -f follows a log live as it grows.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
cat docs/README.md
head -3 data/orders.csv
tail -2 data/app.log
wc -l data/orders.csv data/app.log
Output
$ cat docs/README.md
# Shop
Notes for the team.
$ head -3 data/orders.csv
order_id,customer,city,product,qty,price
101,Sarah,Riyadh,Keyboard,2,150
102,Liam,Jeddah,Monitor,1,900
$ tail -2 data/app.log
2026-01-05 09:07:55 ERROR payment timeout order=106
2026-01-05 09:09:10 INFO  backup done
$ wc -l data/orders.csv data/app.log
  7 data/orders.csv
  6 data/app.log
 13 total

#Write to files: > and >>

Concept

> sends a command's output into a file, replacing it. >> adds to the end. echo prints text.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
echo "Buy cables" > todo.txt
echo "Call supplier" >> todo.txt
cat todo.txt
echo "Oops" > todo.txt
cat todo.txt
Output
$ echo "Buy cables" > todo.txt
$ echo "Call supplier" >> todo.txt
$ cat todo.txt
Buy cables
Call supplier
$ echo "Oops" > todo.txt
$ cat todo.txt
Oops

#grep: search inside files

Concept

grep word file prints matching lines. -i ignores case, -c counts, -v inverts (lines that don't match), -r searches every file in a folder, -n shows line numbers.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
grep ERROR data/app.log
grep -c ERROR data/app.log
grep -i riyadh data/orders.csv
grep -rn "Shop" .
Output
$ grep ERROR data/app.log
2026-01-05 09:05:40 ERROR payment timeout order=103
2026-01-05 09:07:55 ERROR payment timeout order=106
$ grep -c ERROR data/app.log
2
$ grep -i riyadh data/orders.csv
101,Sarah,Riyadh,Keyboard,2,150
103,Noura,Riyadh,Mouse,3,60
105,Sarah,Riyadh,Headset,1,250
$ grep -rn "Shop" .
./docs/README.md:1:# Shop

#Pipes: chain small tools

Concept

The pipe | sends one command's output into the next command. Here: which cities have the most orders? cut picks a column, sort sorts, uniq -c counts duplicates, sort -rn sorts by the count, biggest first.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
cut -d, -f3 data/orders.csv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
grep ERROR data/app.log | grep -o "order=[0-9]*"
ls data | wc -l
Output
$ cut -d, -f3 data/orders.csv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      3 Riyadh
      2 Jeddah
      1 Dammam
$ grep ERROR data/app.log | grep -o "order=[0-9]*"
order=103
order=106
$ ls data | wc -l
2

#awk and sed: quick reports and replacements

Concept

awk is a mini-language for columns: here it adds up qty × price per order to get total sales. sed finds and replaces text (s/old/new/g).

Terminal (bash on Linux)
awk -F, 'NR>1 {total += $5*$6} END {print "Total sales:", total, "SAR"}' data/orders.csv
awk -F, 'NR>1 && $3=="Riyadh" {print $2, $4}' data/orders.csv
sed 's/Keyboard/Mechanical keyboard/' data/orders.csv | head -3
sort -t, -k6 -n -r data/orders.csv | head -2
Output
$ awk -F, 'NR>1 {total += $5*$6} END {print "Total sales:", total, "SAR"}' data/orders.csv
Total sales: 1900 SAR
$ awk -F, 'NR>1 && $3=="Riyadh" {print $2, $4}' data/orders.csv
Sarah Keyboard
Noura Mouse
Sarah Headset
$ sed 's/Keyboard/Mechanical keyboard/' data/orders.csv | head -3
order_id,customer,city,product,qty,price
101,Sarah,Riyadh,Mechanical keyboard,2,150
102,Liam,Jeddah,Monitor,1,900
$ sort -t, -k6 -n -r data/orders.csv | head -2
102,Liam,Jeddah,Monitor,1,900
105,Sarah,Riyadh,Headset,1,250

#Linux tutorial 4: Permissions, users & sudo

Who can read, change or run each file, and how to do admin tasks safely.

#Read the permission string

Concept

-rw-r--r-- = file type, then three groups of read, write, execute for the owner, the group, and everyone else. A script needs x to run. chmod +x adds it.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
ls -l scripts/backup.sh
./scripts/backup.sh || echo "Not allowed to run it yet"
chmod +x scripts/backup.sh
ls -l scripts/backup.sh
./scripts/backup.sh
Output
$ ls -l scripts/backup.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 33 Jan  5  2026 scripts/backup.sh
$ ./scripts/backup.sh || echo "Not allowed to run it yet"
bash: ./scripts/backup.sh: Permission denied
Not allowed to run it yet
$ chmod +x scripts/backup.sh
$ ls -l scripts/backup.sh
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 33 Jan  5  2026 scripts/backup.sh
$ ./scripts/backup.sh
Backing up...

#chmod with numbers

Concept

Set the permissions for owner, group and others in one go: make the customer file private (only the owner can read it).

Terminal (bash on Linux)
chmod 600 data/orders.csv
chmod 755 scripts
ls -ld data/orders.csv scripts
Output
$ chmod 600 data/orders.csv
$ chmod 755 scripts
$ ls -ld data/orders.csv scripts
-rw------- 1 root root  220 Jan  5  2026 data/orders.csv
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jan  5  2026 scripts

#Users, root and sudo

Concept

root is the all-powerful admin account. Instead of logging in as root, normal users put sudo in front of one command to run it as admin, and type their own password. chown changes who owns a file.

Terminal (needs admin rights, not run here)
whoami                      # which user am I?
sudo apt update             # run one command as admin
sudo adduser ali            # create a user (Debian/Ubuntu)
sudo usermod -aG docker ali # add ali to the docker group
sudo chown ali:ali report.pdf
id ali                      # show ali's user and groups

Commonly confused with: Don't paste commands with sudo from random websites. sudo rm -rf / (or a script that does it) can wipe the whole system.

#Linux tutorial 5: Software, processes, disks & network

Installing apps, seeing what's running, and checking the machine.

#Disk, memory and system info

Concept

df -h shows free disk space (-h = human-readable sizes), du -sh the size of a folder, uname -r the kernel version, nproc the number of CPU threads. (Numbers here come from the build computer.)

Terminal (bash on Linux)
df -h /
du -sh data docs
uname -s
date -d "2026-01-05 09:00" "+%A %d %B %Y"
Output
$ df -h /
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/vda        252G   13G   30G  29% /
$ du -sh data docs
12K	data
8.0K	docs
$ uname -s
Linux
$ date -d "2026-01-05 09:00" "+%A %d %B %Y"
Monday 05 January 2026

#Processes: what's running, and how to stop it

Concept

Every running program is a process with an ID (PID). htop is the friendly task manager. kill asks a process to stop, and kill -9 forces it.

Terminal (live system info, not run here)
ps aux | grep python        # find a process
htop                        # live task manager (q to quit)
kill 4321                   # politely stop PID 4321
kill -9 4321                # force stop
pkill -f "python server.py" # stop by name
free -h                     # memory in use
uptime                      # how long it has been on, and load

#Services with systemd

Concept

Servers run in the background as services. systemctl starts, stops and enables them at boot. journalctl reads their logs.

Terminal (needs a real Linux machine, not run here)
sudo systemctl status ssh
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo systemctl enable --now docker   # start now and at every boot
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"

#Network commands

Concept

Check your IP, test a connection, download files and log in to other machines.

Terminal (needs a network, not run here)
ip a                       # your network interfaces and IP addresses
ping -c 4 1.1.1.1          # can I reach the internet?
curl -I https://example.com   # fetch just the headers of a web page
wget https://example.com/file.zip
ss -tulpn                  # which ports are listening
ssh sarah@192.168.1.50     # log in to another computer
scp report.pdf sarah@192.168.1.50:~/   # copy a file to it

Fun fact: SSH is how almost every cloud server and home lab is managed. See the Home Lab part for keys and safe remote access.

#Linux tutorial 6: Shell scripting

Save commands in a file and let the computer do the boring work.

#Variables, if and for

Concept

A script is a text file of commands. Variables have no spaces around =, and you read them with $. [ ... ] tests a condition. $(...) captures a command's output.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
name="Sarah"
count=$(grep -c ERROR data/app.log)
echo "Hello $name, the log has $count errors"
if [ "$count" -gt 0 ]; then
  echo "Check the payment system!"
fi
for f in data/*; do
  echo "$f has $(wc -l < "$f") lines"
done
Output
$ name="Sarah"
$ count=$(grep -c ERROR data/app.log)
$ echo "Hello $name, the log has $count errors"
Hello Sarah, the log has 2 errors
$ if [ "$count" -gt 0 ]; then
>   echo "Check the payment system!"
> fi
Check the payment system!
$ for f in data/*; do
>   echo "$f has $(wc -l < "$f") lines"
> done
data/app.log has 6 lines
data/orders.csv has 7 lines

#A real script with arguments

Concept

Here cat > file <<'EOF' writes everything up to EOF into the file (in real life you'd use an editor). $1 is the first argument, $# the number of arguments, and exit 1 reports failure. The first line #!/bin/bash (the shebang) says which program runs the script.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
cat > sales.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# total sales for one city: ./sales.sh Riyadh
city="$1"
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "Usage: ./sales.sh CITY"
  exit 1
fi
awk -F, -v c="$city" '$3==c {s += $5*$6} END {print c ": " s+0 " SAR"}' data/orders.csv
EOF
chmod +x sales.sh
./sales.sh Riyadh
./sales.sh Jeddah
./sales.sh || echo "exit code: $?"
Output
$ cat > sales.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> # total sales for one city: ./sales.sh Riyadh
> city="$1"
> if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
>   echo "Usage: ./sales.sh CITY"
>   exit 1
> fi
> awk -F, -v c="$city" '$3==c {s += $5*$6} END {print c ": " s+0 " SAR"}' data/orders.csv
> EOF
$ chmod +x sales.sh
$ ./sales.sh Riyadh
Riyadh: 730 SAR
$ ./sales.sh Jeddah
Jeddah: 1020 SAR
$ ./sales.sh || echo "exit code: $?"
Usage: ./sales.sh CITY
exit code: 1

#Functions and exit codes

Concept

Every command returns an exit code: 0 = success, anything else = failure. && runs the next command only if the first succeeded, || only if it failed.

Terminal (bash on Linux)
backup() {
  mkdir -p "backup/$1" && cp data/*.csv "backup/$1/" && echo "Backed up to backup/$1"
}
backup 2026-01-05
ls backup/2026-01-05
ls nothing-here 2>/dev/null || echo "ls failed, exit code $?"
Output
$ backup() {
>   mkdir -p "backup/$1" && cp data/*.csv "backup/$1/" && echo "Backed up to backup/$1"
> }
$ backup 2026-01-05
Backed up to backup/2026-01-05
$ ls backup/2026-01-05
orders.csv
$ ls nothing-here 2>/dev/null || echo "ls failed, exit code $?"
ls failed, exit code 2

#Run it automatically with cron

Concept

crontab -e opens your schedule. Five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. (Modern systems can also use systemd timers.)

crontab (not run here)
# m  h  dom mon dow  command
0   2  *   *   *    /home/sarah/shop/scripts/backup.sh     # every day at 02:00
*/15 *  *   *   *    /home/sarah/check-site.sh              # every 15 minutes
0   9  *   *   0    /home/sarah/weekly-report.sh           # Sundays at 09:00

Fun fact: crontab.guru explains any schedule in plain English.

#Script safety tips

Concept

Start scripts with set -euo pipefail to stop on errors and unset variables. Always quote variables ("$file") so names with spaces don't break. Test on copies first. For anything long or complicated, Python is usually a better choice than bash.
