Part 10

Software & Operating Systems

Kernels, file systems, virtualisation and containers. The history of DOS, Windows, macOS, Unix, Linux and mobile OSes. Licensing, open source and how software is built.

#Operating systems — core concepts

The operating system manages hardware, runs programs and gives you an interface.

#Operating system (OS)

Concept

System software that sits between hardware and apps: it manages the CPU, memory, storage and devices, and provides files, security and the user interface. Examples: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS.

#Kernel (monolithic, micro, hybrid)

Concept

The core of the OS that runs with full hardware access. Monolithic kernels put everything in one big program (Linux). Microkernels keep only the minimum and run drivers as separate processes (MINIX, QNX, seL4). Hybrid kernels mix both (Windows NT, macOS XNU).

Fun fact: Andrew Tanenbaum and Linus Torvalds had a famous 1992 Usenet argument over monolithic vs micro kernels.

#Shell, CLI & GUI

Concept

The shell is the program you talk to: a command line (Bash, zsh, cmd, PowerShell) or a graphical interface (Windows Explorer, macOS Finder, GNOME, KDE).

Fun fact: Xerox PARC → Apple Lisa/Macintosh → Windows: the desktop/window/icon/mouse GUI is often called WIMP (windows, icons, menus, pointer).

#Device drivers

Concept

Small programs that let the OS control specific hardware (GPU, printer, Wi-Fi). Bad drivers are a top cause of crashes and blue screens.

#Processes, threads & multitasking

Concept

A process is a running program with its own memory. Threads are parallel paths inside it. Pre-emptive multitasking (OS decides who runs) replaced cooperative multitasking (Windows 3.x, classic Mac OS), where one frozen app could hang the whole system.

#Virtual memory & paging

Concept

The OS gives each process its own address space and moves rarely used memory pages to disk (page file / swap). This lets apps use more memory than physically exists, at the cost of speed.

#File systems

Concept

How data is organised on a drive: FAT12/16/32 (DOS, USB sticks), exFAT (SD cards), NTFS (Windows), HFS+ → APFS (Apple), ext4, Btrfs, XFS, ZFS (Linux/servers).

Commonly confused with: FAT32 can't store a single file larger than 4 GB, so big videos fail to copy onto old-format USB sticks. Use exFAT.

#Boot process

Concept

Power on → firmware (BIOS/UEFI) → POST → bootloader (Windows Boot Manager, GRUB, iBoot) → kernel → services → login screen.

#Users, permissions & admin rights

Concept

Accounts, file permissions and privilege levels (Administrator, root, sudo, UAC prompts) stop programs damaging the system.

#Services & daemons

Concept

Background programs that run without a window, such as print spoolers and web servers. Unix calls them daemons (e.g. sshd, ending in 'd'), Windows calls them services.

#Virtualization & hypervisors

Concept

Running multiple operating systems on one machine as virtual machines. Type 1 hypervisors run on bare metal (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, Xen). Type 2 run as apps (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels). This is the foundation of cloud computing.

#Containers (Docker, Kubernetes)

Concept

Lightweight isolation that shares the host kernel: a container packages an app with its libraries. Docker (2013) made it popular, and Kubernetes (Google, 2014) orchestrates thousands of them.

Commonly confused with: Containers are not VMs. A VM has its own full OS kernel, while a container shares the host's.

#Emulation & compatibility layers

Concept

Emulators imitate other hardware (DOSBox, MAME, console emulators, QEMU). Compatibility layers translate system calls instead: Wine/Proton (Windows games on Linux/Steam Deck), Rosetta 2 (x86 on Apple Silicon), WSL (Linux on Windows).

#Real-time OS (RTOS)

Concept

An OS that guarantees response times, used in cars, medical devices, aircraft and microcontrollers: FreeRTOS, VxWorks (Mars rovers), QNX, Zephyr.

#Firmware & embedded OS

Concept

Software built into devices: router firmware (OpenWrt), printer firmware, smart TV OSes (Tizen, webOS, Android TV/Google TV), car infotainment.

#Operating systems through history

#CP/M

1974–1980s Obsolete

Gary Kildall's OS for 8-bit Intel/Zilog micros. The standard before MS-DOS, which copied its command style.

Fun fact: IBM first approached Kildall's Digital Research for the PC's OS. The deal fell through, and Microsoft got the job.

#MS-DOS / PC DOS

1981–2000 Obsolete

Microsoft's text-mode OS for the IBM PC, bought from Seattle Computer Products' 86-DOS. Commands like DIR, CD and COPY, and C:\> prompts. Windows 95/98/ME still started on top of DOS.

Fun fact: Its 640 KB conventional-memory limit spawned a whole industry of memory managers (HIMEM, EMM386, QEMM).

#Microsoft Windows

1985→ Current

From a graphical shell on DOS (1.0–3.11), to Windows 95's Start menu, to the NT-based XP, 7, 10 and 11. Runs on roughly 70% of desktop PCs worldwide.

Fun fact: Windows 95's launch used the Rolling Stones song Start Me Up, reportedly licensed for millions of dollars.

#OS/2

1987–2006 Obsolete

An IBM–Microsoft joint OS meant to replace DOS. After the partners split, IBM's OS/2 Warp lost to Windows. It lived on in ATMs and train systems, and ArcaOS still sells it.

#Classic Mac OS (System 1 – Mac OS 9)

1984–2001 Obsolete

The original Macintosh GUI system: menu bar, Finder, trash can, single-button mouse. No protected memory, so one app crash could freeze the Mac.

Fun fact: System 1's 'Sad Mac' and the startup chime became Apple icons.

#macOS (Mac OS X)

2001→ Current

Built on NeXTSTEP with a Unix (BSD/Mach 'Darwin') core and the Aqua interface. Releases were named after big cats (Cheetah to Mountain Lion), then California places (Mavericks onward). Version numbers jumped to 26 'Tahoe' in 2025 to match the year.

#Unix

1969→ Legacy

Bell Labs' multi-user OS by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie. Its philosophy is small tools that do one thing well, connected with pipes. Commercial versions: Solaris, AIX, HP-UX. macOS is a certified Unix.

Fun fact: Unix time counts seconds from 1 January 1970 and overflows 32-bit counters on 19 January 2038 (the 'Y2038 problem').

#BSD (FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD)

1977→ Current

Berkeley's Unix branch. FreeBSD runs Netflix's streaming servers and is the base of PlayStation 4/5 system software. OpenBSD is known for security, and parts of BSD live inside macOS.

#Linux

1991→ Current

Linus Torvalds's free kernel combined with GNU tools. It runs nearly all servers and supercomputers, Android, ChromeOS, routers, TVs and cars. Mascot: Tux the penguin.

Commonly confused with: Strictly, 'Linux' is the kernel. A full OS is a distribution (distro) like Ubuntu.

#Linux distributions

1993→ Current

Bundles of the kernel, tools and desktop: Debian, Ubuntu (beginner-friendly), Linux Mint, Fedora / Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Arch ('I use Arch, by the way'), openSUSE, Alpine (containers), SteamOS (Steam Deck), Kali (security testing).

#ChromeOS & ChromeOS Flex

2011→ Current

Google's lightweight Linux-based OS built around the Chrome browser, with Android and Linux app support. Flex revives old PCs.

#Android

2008→ Current

Google's open-source mobile OS on a Linux kernel, the world's most-used OS. Versions had dessert names (Cupcake 1.5 to Pie 9), then plain numbers from Android 10.

#iOS & iPadOS

2007→ Current

Apple's mobile OS (called iPhone OS until 2010). iPadOS split off in 2019. Version numbers jumped to 26 in 2025 to match the year.

#HarmonyOS

2019→ Current

Huawei's OS for phones, tablets, watches and cars. HarmonyOS NEXT (2024) dropped Android compatibility entirely.

#BeOS / Haiku

1995–2001 / 2002→ Legacy

BeOS was a fast, media-focused OS that Apple nearly bought in 1996 (it bought NeXT instead). Haiku is its open-source revival.

#AmigaOS, RISC OS, GEOS & others

1985→ Legacy

Beloved alternative systems: AmigaOS (pre-emptive multitasking in 1985), RISC OS (Acorn, still updated for Raspberry Pi), GEOS (a GUI for the Commodore 64), NeXTSTEP, Solaris, Plan 9, ReactOS (open Windows clone), FreeDOS.

#Software types, licensing & engineering

#System vs application software

Concept

System software runs the computer (OS, drivers, firmware, utilities). Application software does user tasks (browsers, games, Office, Photoshop).

#Open source & free software

Concept

Source code anyone can read, change and share. 'Free software' (Stallman's GNU) stresses user freedom, 'open source' (1998 term) stresses development benefits. Examples: Linux, Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, Blender, Python.

#Software licences

Concept

Copyleft (GPL: changes must stay open), permissive (MIT, BSD, Apache: almost anything goes), proprietary (EULA, closed source), public domain. Creative Commons covers content rather than code.

#Shareware, freeware, freemium & abandonware

Concept

Shareware (try before you buy, e.g. Doom episode 1, WinRAR), freeware (free, closed source), freemium (free core, paid extras), abandonware (old software no longer sold or supported).

Fun fact: WinRAR's '40-day trial' famously never actually expires.

#SaaS & subscriptions

Concept

Software as a Service runs in the cloud and is paid monthly: Microsoft 365, Adobe Creative Cloud, Google Workspace, Salesforce. It replaced boxed CDs with a version number.

#App stores

Concept

Curated software marketplaces: Apple App Store (2008), Google Play (2008 as Android Market), Microsoft Store, Steam (games, 2003), Mac App Store (2011).

#Software development life cycle (SDLC)

Concept

Requirements → design → implementation → testing → deployment → maintenance. Waterfall does these in sequence, iterative methods loop through them.

#Agile, Scrum & Kanban

Concept

The Agile Manifesto (2001) values working software and feedback over big upfront plans. Scrum works in sprints with stand-ups and retrospectives, Kanban in a flowing board of cards.

#DevOps, CI/CD

Concept

Developers and operations working together. Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery automatically builds, tests and ships code on every change (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI).

#Software testing

Concept

Unit tests (single functions), integration tests, end-to-end/UI tests, regression tests, load testing, beta testing with users. Test-driven development (TDD) writes tests first.

#Design patterns

Concept

Reusable solutions to common design problems, catalogued in the 1994 'Gang of Four' book: Singleton, Factory, Observer, Model-View-Controller (MVC), and more.

#Release stages & versioning

Concept

Pre-alpha → alpha → beta → release candidate (RC) → stable/GA → LTS (long-term support) → EOL (end of life). Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g. 2.4.1).

#Internationalisation & localisation (i18n / l10n)

Concept

Building software to support any language (i18n, 18 letters between i and n), then translating and adapting it for each market (l10n): right-to-left layout for Arabic and Hebrew, date and number formats, Hijri calendars, fonts.

#Unicode & character encoding

Concept

ASCII (1963) covered 128 English characters. Code pages and Windows-1256 (Arabic) followed. Unicode (1991) aims to cover every writing system plus emoji, and UTF-8 (1992) is the encoding used by about 98% of websites.

Fun fact: 'Mojibake' (Japanese for character transformation) is the garbled text you see when encodings get mixed up.

#Software bloat & legacy code

Concept

Programs growing slower and bigger over time, and old code that's risky to change but still critical (much of it in COBOL).

#Y2K problem

Concept

Old software stored years as two digits, so 2000 would read as 1900. Billions were spent fixing it before 1 January 2000, and few failures happened. Its successor is the Unix Y2038 problem.

Fun fact: Some argue Y2K was 'overhyped', but most engineers say little broke because the fixes worked.

Part 11

Internet & Web

How the internet works (packets, IP, DNS, HTTP, TLS), its history from ARPANET to the cloud, web technologies, and the services that run on it.

#Internet history

From a four-computer research network to billions of users.

#ARPANET

1969–1990 Obsolete

The US Defense Department's ARPA-funded packet-switched network. Its first link was UCLA → Stanford Research Institute (29 Oct 1969), and it grew to four nodes by December (adding UCSB and Utah).

Fun fact: A popular myth says ARPANET was built to survive nuclear war. Its builders say the main goal was sharing scarce computers.

#TCP/IP flag day

1 Jan 1983 Legacy

ARPANET switched from NCP to TCP/IP, often called the internet's birthday.

#Bulletin board systems (BBS)

1978–1990s Obsolete

Dial-up message boards run from home PCs with modems. Users left messages, played 'door' games and swapped files, one caller at a time per phone line. FidoNet linked them worldwide.

#Usenet & newsgroups

1980→ Legacy

Worldwide threaded discussion groups (comp., rec., alt.*). Gave us FAQs, 'flame wars' and netiquette. Linus Torvalds announced Linux on Usenet in 1991.

Fun fact: The first known commercial spam was a 1994 Usenet post advertising a 'Green Card lottery' service.

#Gopher

1991–late 1990s Obsolete

The University of Minnesota's menu-based document system, briefly more popular than the web until 1993 licence-fee worries.

#NSFNET & commercial internet

1985–1995 Obsolete

The US National Science Foundation's backbone replaced ARPANET. Commercial traffic was allowed from the early 1990s, and NSFNET was retired in 1995 as ISPs took over.

#World Wide Web

1989/1991→ Current

Tim Berners-Lee's system of linked hypertext pages (HTML) delivered over HTTP and found by URLs. The first website, info.cern.ch, went live in 1991.

Commonly confused with: The internet is the network of networks. The web is one service running on it, like email or gaming.

#Browser wars

1995–2001 / 2008→ Legacy

First war: Netscape Navigator vs Internet Explorer, which Microsoft bundled with Windows and won (leading to a US antitrust case). Second: Firefox (2004) and Chrome (2008) beat IE. Chrome's engine (Chromium/Blink) now dominates.

#Dot-com bubble

1995–2001 Obsolete

A frenzy of internet stock investment. The Nasdaq fell about 78% from its 2000 peak. Pets.com and Webvan collapsed, while Amazon and eBay survived.

#Web 2.0 & social media

2004→ Current

The shift to user-created content: blogs, wikis, YouTube (2005), Facebook (2004), Twitter (2006), plus Ajax web apps like Gmail and Google Maps.

#Mobile internet & apps

2007→ Current

The iPhone, App Store and 3G/4G moved most internet use to phones. Mobile passed desktop web traffic around 2016–2017.

#Cloud era

2006→ Current

Renting computing over the internet: AWS (2006), Azure (2010), Google Cloud. Most apps now run in hyperscale data centres.

#How the internet works

The protocols and pieces behind every web page and message.

#Packet switching

Concept

Data is cut into small packets that travel independently across the network and are reassembled at the destination. This is more efficient and resilient than reserving a whole circuit, as old phone networks did.

#OSI & TCP/IP models

Concept

Layered descriptions of networking. The 7-layer OSI model: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. The practical 4-layer TCP/IP model: Link, Internet (IP), Transport (TCP/UDP), Application (HTTP, DNS...).

Fun fact: Mnemonic for OSI from the bottom: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away'.

#IP addresses (IPv4 & IPv6)

Concept

Every device on the internet needs an address. IPv4 (e.g. 192.168.1.10) has about 4.3 billion addresses, and they ran out from 2011. IPv6 (e.g. 2001:db8::1) has 340 undecillion (3.4×10^38).

#Private IPs, NAT & DHCP

Concept

Home networks use private ranges (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x). The router's NAT shares one public IP among all devices. DHCP hands out addresses automatically.

#TCP vs UDP

Concept

TCP guarantees ordered, complete delivery with acknowledgements (web, email, files). UDP is fire-and-forget: faster but lossy (gaming, video calls, DNS). QUIC (2021 standard) runs reliable streams over UDP for HTTP/3.

#Ports

Concept

Numbers that route traffic to the right program: 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 22 (SSH), 25/587 (SMTP mail), 53 (DNS), 3389 (Remote Desktop), 25565 (Minecraft).

#DNS (Domain Name System)

Concept

The internet's phone book. It translates names like example.com into IP addresses through a hierarchy of root servers, TLD servers (.com, .sa) and authoritative servers. Public resolvers include 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare) and 8.8.8.8 (Google).

Fun fact: There are 13 named root server identities (A to M), served by more than 1,500 machines worldwide.

#Domain names & TLDs

Concept

Top-level domains: generic (.com, .org, .net, .ai), country codes (.sa Saudi Arabia, .uk, .de), and internationalised Arabic-script TLDs such as .السعودية. Managed globally by ICANN and sold through registrars.

#URLs

Concept

Uniform Resource Locator: https://www.example.com:443/path/page?query=1#section = scheme, host, port, path, query string, fragment.

#HTTP & HTTPS

Concept

The web's request/response protocol: GET, POST, status codes like 200 OK, 301 moved, 404 not found, 500 server error. HTTPS wraps it in TLS encryption, and browsers now warn on plain HTTP.

Fun fact: HTTP 418 'I'm a teapot' began as a 1998 April Fools' joke spec and survives in many web frameworks.

#TLS/SSL & certificates

Concept

Encryption for HTTPS, email and more. Sites prove their identity with certificates signed by a Certificate Authority. Let's Encrypt (2015) made certificates free and pushed HTTPS to the majority of sites. SSL is the old name: TLS 1.2/1.3 is what's used now.

#Routing & BGP

Concept

Routers forward packets hop by hop. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is how the internet's ~75,000+ networks announce which addresses they can reach.

Fun fact: A BGP misconfiguration took Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp offline for about six hours in October 2021.

#ISPs, backbones & submarine cables

Concept

Internet Service Providers connect homes. Tier-1 backbones and internet exchange points (IXPs) interconnect them. About 95%+ of intercontinental traffic travels through undersea fibre cables, not satellites.

#CDN (content delivery network)

Concept

Copies of sites and videos cached on servers near users (Cloudflare, Akamai, Amazon CloudFront, Netflix Open Connect), which cuts delay and load.

#Latency, ping, jitter & bandwidth

Concept

Bandwidth = how much data per second. Latency/ping = round-trip delay (ms). Jitter = variation in latency. Gamers care most about ping, streamers about bandwidth.

#VPN & proxy

Concept

A VPN encrypts your traffic and tunnels it through another server (privacy, remote work, region access). A proxy relays requests without necessarily encrypting them.

Commonly confused with: A VPN hides your traffic from your ISP but not from the VPN company, so it's not full anonymity.

#Satellite internet

Concept

Geostationary satellites (high latency, ~600 ms) vs low-Earth-orbit constellations like Starlink (2019→, ~20–50 ms) and Amazon's Kuiper.

#Internet governance

Concept

No single owner. ICANN coordinates names and numbers, IETF writes protocol standards (RFCs), W3C writes web standards, regional registries assign IPs, and national regulators handle local rules.

#Web technologies

What web pages and web apps are made of.

#HTML

Concept

HyperText Markup Language: the structure of web pages (<h1>, <p>, <a href>, <img>). HTML5 (2014) added video, audio, canvas and semantic tags. XHTML was a stricter XML variant that faded.

#CSS

Concept

Cascading Style Sheets control layout and appearance: colours, fonts, Flexbox and Grid layouts, animations, responsive design for phones (media queries). Frameworks: Bootstrap, Tailwind.

#JavaScript & the DOM

Concept

JavaScript makes pages interactive by changing the DOM (Document Object Model, the page's live tree of elements). Front-end frameworks: React (Meta), Vue, Angular (Google), Svelte.

#Ajax, JSON & XML

Concept

Ajax (term coined 2005) lets pages fetch data without reloading. Data formats: XML (tag-based, older) and JSON (lightweight, now dominant).

#Web browsers & engines

Concept

Browsers: Chrome, Safari, Edge, Firefox, Opera, Brave, Samsung Internet. Engines: Blink (Chrome, Edge, Opera, Brave), WebKit (Safari, all iOS browsers historically), Gecko (Firefox).

Fun fact: The first browser, Berners-Lee's WorldWideWeb (1990), was also an editor. You could write pages in it.

#Web servers

Concept

Software that answers HTTP requests: Apache (1995), Nginx (2004), Microsoft IIS, LiteSpeed, Caddy, Node.js servers.

#Front end vs back end vs full stack

Concept

Front end runs in the browser (HTML/CSS/JS). Back end runs on servers (databases, APIs, logic in Python, PHP, Java, Node, Go, C#). Full stack = both.

#REST, GraphQL & web APIs

Concept

How apps exchange data over HTTP. REST uses URLs and verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE), GraphQL (Meta, 2015) lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs.

#Cookies & local storage

Concept

Small data files a site stores in your browser for logins, carts and tracking. Third-party cookies for ad tracking are being restricted (Safari and Firefox block them by default).

#CMS (content management systems)

Concept

Tools for building sites without coding every page: WordPress (powers a large share of websites), Drupal, Joomla, Wix, Squarespace, Shopify (stores), Ghost.

#Web hosting

Concept

Renting server space: shared hosting, VPS, dedicated servers, cloud and 'serverless' platforms (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages).

#WebAssembly (Wasm)

Concept

A fast binary format (2017) that runs C, C++ and Rust code in the browser at near-native speed. Used for Figma, Photoshop on the web and browser games.

#Progressive web apps (PWA)

Concept

Websites that install like apps, work offline and send notifications.

#Web accessibility (a11y)

Concept

Making sites usable by people with disabilities: alt text for images, keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels (ARIA), contrast. Guided by the W3C's WCAG standards.

#SEO

Concept

Search Engine Optimisation: improving pages to rank higher in Google and others (content, links, speed, structured data).

#RSS & Atom feeds

Concept

XML feeds that let readers and podcast apps follow sites without visiting them. Podcasts still depend on RSS.

#Mashups & embeds

Concept

Combining data and services from several sites (e.g. a Google Maps embed with listings), a hallmark of the Web 2.0 era.

#Internet services & culture

#Email (SMTP, IMAP, POP3)

Concept

SMTP sends mail, IMAP syncs mailboxes across devices, POP3 downloads and usually deletes from the server. Webmail: Hotmail (1996), Yahoo Mail, Gmail (2004, 1 GB free storage when rivals offered a few MB).

#Search engines

Concept

Early: Archie (1990), AltaVista (1995), Yahoo! Directory, Ask Jeeves. Google (1998) won with PageRank. Others: Bing, Baidu (China), Yandex (Russia), DuckDuckGo. Now joined by AI answer engines.

#Instant messaging & chat

Concept

IRC (1988), ICQ (1996, 'Uh-oh!'), AIM, MSN Messenger, BlackBerry Messenger, then WhatsApp (2009), WeChat, Telegram, Signal, iMessage, Discord, Slack.

#Social networks

Concept

SixDegrees (1997), Friendster, MySpace (2003), Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter/X, Instagram (2010), Snapchat (2011), TikTok (2016/2018), Reddit, plus decentralised Mastodon and Bluesky.

#Video & music streaming

Concept

RealPlayer (1995) → YouTube (2005) → Netflix streaming (2007) → Spotify (2008) → Twitch (2011), Disney+, Shahid (MENA). Adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS, DASH) adjusts quality to your connection.

#Wikis & Wikipedia

Concept

Collaboratively edited sites. Wikipedia (2001) has 60+ million articles across 300+ languages, including Arabic Wikipedia.

#Blogs, forums & podcasts

Concept

Blogger (1999), WordPress, LiveJournal; forums like phpBB and vBulletin; Reddit; podcasts (the word came from 'iPod + broadcast', 2004).

#Peer-to-peer (P2P) & file sharing

Concept

Napster (1999) shared MP3s and was shut down in 2001 by lawsuits. Gnutella, Kazaa and LimeWire followed. BitTorrent (2001) splits files among many peers and is also used legitimately (Linux ISOs, game updates).

#E-commerce & online payments

Concept

Amazon (1995), eBay (1995), PayPal (1998), Alibaba (1999), Shopify (2006); mobile wallets (Apple Pay, Google Pay, STC Pay, mada Pay); buy-now-pay-later (Tabby, Tamara, Klarna).

#Cloud computing (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS)

Concept

IaaS rents raw servers (AWS EC2), PaaS rents a managed platform (Heroku, Google App Engine), SaaS rents finished software (Gmail, Microsoft 365). Big providers: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Alibaba, Oracle.

Fun fact: Joke: 'There is no cloud, it's just someone else's computer.'

#Internet of Things (IoT) & smart home

Concept

Everyday devices online: smart speakers (Alexa, Google Home), bulbs, plugs, cameras, thermostats. Matter (2022) is a cross-brand smart-home standard over Wi-Fi, Ethernet and Thread.

#Blockchain & cryptocurrency

Concept

A shared append-only ledger secured by cryptography. Bitcoin (2009, Satoshi Nakamoto, identity unknown), Ethereum (2015, smart contracts), stablecoins and NFTs. Highly volatile and regulated differently by each country.

#Dark web & Tor

Concept

Tor (onion routing, originally US Naval Research) hides users' locations by bouncing traffic through relays. '.onion' sites form the 'dark web'. Also used by journalists and dissidents.

#Net neutrality

Concept

The principle that ISPs should treat all traffic equally and not block, slow or charge extra for particular sites. Rules vary widely by country and keep changing in the US.

#Digital divide

Concept

The gap between people with fast, affordable internet and those without, between and within countries.

#Netiquette & internet slang

Concept

Etiquette for online life (don't type in ALL CAPS, it reads as shouting) and slang that started online: LOL, BRB, AFK, FTW, 'lurker', 'troll', memes, emoticons :-) (proposed by Scott Fahlman, 1982) and emoji (Shigetaka Kurita, NTT Docomo, 1999).

Part 12

Security & Privacy

Malware, attacks and scams, and how passwords, MFA, encryption, updates and backups defend against them. Plus the people and cases that shaped cybersecurity.

#Malware & attacks

The main kinds of threat, explained so you can recognise them.

#Malware

Concept

Malicious software: the umbrella term for viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware, spyware, adware, rootkits and more.

#Computer virus

Concept

Code that attaches to other programs or files and spreads when they run. Early viruses travelled on floppy disks: Elk Cloner (Apple II, 1982), Brain (first PC virus, 1986, from Lahore, Pakistan).

Fun fact: The Brain virus included its authors' real names, address and phone number in the code.

#Worm

Concept

Self-spreading malware that needs no user action. Morris worm (1988, infected ~10% of the then-internet), ILOVEYOU (2000, email), Code Red, SQL Slammer (2003, spread worldwide in ~10 minutes), WannaCry (2017).

#Trojan horse

Concept

Malware disguised as something useful: a cracked game, a fake update, a 'free' tool. It doesn't self-replicate. RATs (remote access trojans) give attackers full control.

#Ransomware

Concept

Encrypts your files and demands payment, often with a threat to leak stolen data. WannaCry (2017) hit hospitals worldwide. NotPetya (2017) caused about $10 billion in damage. Attacks on Colonial Pipeline (2021) and Saudi Aramco's Shamoon wiper (2012, destroyed ~30,000 PCs) were landmark incidents.

Commonly confused with: Shamoon was a wiper: it destroyed data rather than holding it for ransom.

#Spyware, adware & stalkerware

Concept

Software that secretly collects data or shows unwanted ads. Stalkerware is installed on a partner's or family member's phone to track them. Commercial spyware like Pegasus can target journalists' phones.

#Rootkits & bootkits

Concept

Malware that hides deep in the OS or firmware to avoid detection. Secure Boot and TPM help block them.

Fun fact: In 2005 Sony BMG music CDs secretly installed a rootkit on PCs as copy protection, causing a major scandal and recall.

#Botnets & DDoS

Concept

Networks of infected devices ('zombies') controlled together. DDoS attacks flood a target with traffic. The Mirai botnet (2016) used hacked cameras and routers to knock major sites offline.

#Phishing, smishing & vishing

Concept

Fake emails (phishing), texts (smishing) and calls (vishing) that trick you into giving passwords or money. Spear phishing targets one person, whaling targets executives.

Identify it: Red flags: urgency ('account suspended!'), mismatched sender or link domains, requests for codes or passwords, prizes you didn't enter for.

#Social engineering

Concept

Manipulating people rather than hacking machines: pretending to be IT support, tailgating through secure doors, baiting with USB sticks left in car parks.

#Identity theft & SIM swapping

Concept

Stealing personal data to open accounts or take over existing ones. SIM swapping tricks a carrier into moving your number to the attacker's SIM, so they receive your SMS login codes.

#Scams & online fraud

Concept

Fake shops, investment and crypto scams, romance scams, tech-support scams ('Microsoft calling'), advance-fee ('Nigerian prince') emails, fake delivery texts.

#Zero-day & exploits

Concept

A vulnerability is a bug that can be abused, an exploit is code that abuses it, and a zero-day is a flaw unknown to the vendor, with zero days to patch. CVE numbers catalogue public vulnerabilities.

#Buffer overflow & memory bugs

Concept

Writing past the end of a memory buffer can overwrite code and data. It's the classic way into C/C++ programs and a major reason for moving to memory-safe languages like Rust.

#SQL injection & XSS

Concept

Web attacks: SQL injection sneaks database commands through input fields. Cross-site scripting (XSS) injects scripts into pages other users see.

Fun fact: The famous 'Little Bobby Tables' xkcd comic is about SQL injection.

#Man-in-the-middle (MITM)

Concept

An attacker secretly relays and alters communication, for example on a fake public Wi-Fi hotspot. HTTPS and certificate checks defend against it.

#Supply-chain attacks

Concept

Compromising software or hardware before it reaches you: SolarWinds (2020) shipped backdoored updates to thousands of organisations. The xz Utils backdoor (2024) was caught just before reaching major Linux distros.

#Hardware & side-channel attacks

Concept

Spectre and Meltdown (2018) abused CPU speculative execution to read secrets. Rowhammer flips RAM bits by hammering neighbouring rows. Also cold-boot attacks and malicious USB devices.

#Cyberwarfare & APTs

Concept

State-sponsored attacks: Stuxnet (discovered 2010) physically damaged Iranian centrifuges, often called the first cyberweapon. Ukraine's power grid attacks (2015, 2016). Advanced persistent threats (APTs) quietly spy for years.

#Defences & cryptography

How systems and people stay safe.

#Passwords & password managers

Concept

Long, unique passwords for every site. A password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password, Apple Passwords, built-in browser managers) remembers them. Reusing passwords lets one breach unlock everything.

Fun fact: '123456' and 'password' still top lists of the most common leaked passwords every year.

#Multi-factor authentication (MFA / 2FA)

Concept

Something you know (password) + something you have (phone, security key) + something you are (fingerprint). Strongest: hardware keys and authenticator apps. Weakest: SMS codes (because of SIM swapping).

#Passkeys

Concept

Passwordless logins (FIDO2/WebAuthn) using a key stored on your device, unlocked with biometrics or PIN. Phishing-resistant, backed by Apple, Google and Microsoft since 2022.

#Biometrics

Concept

Fingerprint, face (Face ID), iris, voice and palm recognition. Convenient, but unlike a password you can't change your fingerprint if it leaks.

#Encryption

Concept

Scrambling data so only key holders can read it. Symmetric (one shared key: AES) and asymmetric / public-key (a public key to encrypt, a private key to decrypt: RSA, elliptic curve). End-to-end encryption (Signal, WhatsApp, iMessage) means even the service can't read messages.

#Public-key cryptography

Concept

Invented publicly by Diffie and Hellman (1976) and made practical by RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 1977). It lets strangers exchange secrets over open networks and powers HTTPS and digital signatures.

Fun fact: British GCHQ researchers (Ellis, Cocks, Williamson) discovered similar methods earlier, but it was classified until 1997.

#Hashing

Concept

One-way fingerprints of data (SHA-256, older MD5/SHA-1 are broken). Used to store passwords safely (with salt, via bcrypt/Argon2), verify downloads and build blockchains.

#Digital signatures & certificates

Concept

Prove who sent something and that it wasn't changed. Used for HTTPS certificates, signed software updates, PDF signatures and national digital IDs.

#Post-quantum cryptography

Concept

New algorithms (e.g. ML-KEM / Kyber, standardised by NIST in 2024) designed to resist future quantum computers that could break RSA and elliptic-curve crypto. Already being rolled into browsers and messaging apps.

#Full-disk encryption

Concept

Encrypting the whole drive so a stolen laptop is unreadable: BitLocker (Windows), FileVault (macOS), LUKS (Linux), built in on modern phones.

#Firewalls

Concept

Filter network traffic by rules. Network firewalls (in routers and appliances) and host firewalls (Windows Defender Firewall). Next-gen firewalls inspect applications, not just ports.

#Antivirus & EDR

Concept

Antivirus scans for known malware signatures and behaviour (Microsoft Defender is built into Windows). EDR/XDR (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne) monitors and responds across company devices.

Fun fact: A faulty CrowdStrike update in July 2024 crashed about 8.5 million Windows PCs, grounding flights and disrupting hospitals.

#Updates & patching

Concept

Most attacks exploit known, already-fixed bugs. Keeping the OS, browser, router firmware and apps updated is the single most effective defence. Microsoft's monthly 'Patch Tuesday' started in 2003.

#Backups (3-2-1 rule)

Concept

3 copies of data, on 2 different media, 1 off-site (or offline). Offline or immutable backups beat ransomware.

#Zero trust

Concept

A security model of 'never trust, always verify': every user, device and request is authenticated, even inside the company network. It replaces the old 'castle and moat' model.

#Penetration testing & bug bounties

Concept

Hiring ethical hackers to attack your own systems. Bug bounty programs (HackerOne, Bugcrowd, vendor programs) pay finders for responsibly reported flaws.

#Hackers: white, black & grey hat

Concept

White hat: ethical security researchers. Black hat: criminal. Grey hat: in between. 'Hacker' originally (1960s MIT) meant a clever, playful programmer.

#CAPTCHA

Concept

'Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart': squiggly text, image grids, or invisible behaviour checks (reCAPTCHA, Cloudflare Turnstile).

Fun fact: Old reCAPTCHA puzzles helped digitise books and newspapers, because users were transcribing words OCR couldn't read.

#Privacy & data protection laws

Concept

Rules on how organisations handle personal data: EU GDPR (2018), California CCPA, and Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL), in force since 14 September 2023 and fully enforceable since 14 September 2024, after a one-year grace period, with SDAIA as the regulator.

Sources: Clyde & Co: Saudi PDPL becomes enforceable (2024) · Herbert Smith Freehills: Saudi PDPL, what you need to know

#Computer forensics

Concept

Recovering and analysing digital evidence for investigations: disk images, deleted files, logs, phone extractions. Chain of custody keeps evidence admissible in court.

#Security figures & landmark cases

#Whitfield Diffie & Martin Hellman

1944– / 1945– Person

Published 'New Directions in Cryptography', which introduced public-key key exchange. Turing Award 2015.

NationalityAmerican
Known forPublic-key cryptography (1976)

#Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir & Leonard Adleman

1947– / 1952– / 1945– Person

Created RSA at MIT. Turing Award 2002.

NationalityAmerican / Israeli / American
Known forRSA algorithm (1977)

#Phil Zimmermann

1954– Person

Released PGP for free and was investigated by the US government under arms-export rules, which treated strong crypto as a munition. The case was dropped in 1996.

NationalityAmerican
Known forPGP encryption (1991)

#Kevin Mitnick

1963–2023 Person

Once the FBI's most-wanted hacker, mostly through social engineering. After prison (1995–2000) he became a respected security consultant and author.

NationalityAmerican
Known forFamous hacker turned consultant

#Clifford Stoll

1950– Person

A Berkeley astronomer who traced a 75-cent accounting error to a KGB-linked hacker in 1986 and wrote the classic book about it.

NationalityAmerican
Known forThe Cuckoo's Egg

#Robert Tappan Morris

1965– Person

His experimental worm accidentally crippled thousands of internet computers. He was the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Later an MIT professor and Y Combinator co-founder.

NationalityAmerican
Known forMorris worm (1988)

#Eugene Spafford

1956– Person

Purdue professor who wrote a key analysis of the Morris worm and founded the CERIAS research centre.

NationalityAmerican
Known forSecurity education, Morris worm analysis

Links for checking facts and reading further. Facts that change over time (laws, company news, product support) link to their source right on the card.

Part 13

Computer Science Fundamentals

Binary and hex, logic gates, algorithms and data structures, the theory of computation (Turing, P vs NP), quantum computing, and databases. The full SQL course is in Part 9.

#Bits, bytes & number systems

How computers represent everything as numbers.

#Binary (base 2)

Concept

Computers store everything as 0s and 1s, because transistors are either off or on. Place values double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... so binary 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.

Fun fact: There are 10 types of people: those who understand binary and those who don't.

#Bits, nibbles, bytes & words

Concept

Bit = one 0/1. Nibble = 4 bits. Byte = 8 bits (one character in ASCII, 0–255). Word = the CPU's natural chunk (16/32/64 bits).

#Hexadecimal (base 16)

Concept

Digits 0–9 then A–F. One hex digit = 4 bits, so a byte is two hex digits (FF = 255). Used for colours (#FF8800), memory addresses and MAC addresses. Often written with 0x (0x1F).

#Octal (base 8)

Concept

Digits 0–7, one digit = 3 bits. Used in Unix file permissions (chmod 755).

#Signed numbers & two's complement

Concept

How computers store negatives: flip the bits and add one. An 8-bit signed value runs from −128 to +127.

Fun fact: Civilization's 'Nuclear Gandhi' legend claims an aggression value wrapped from 0 to 255. Its creator says this is a myth, though the story spread so widely that later games added it on purpose.

#Overflow

Concept

When a result is too big for its storage: 255 + 1 in an 8-bit byte wraps to 0. It caused the Ariane 5 loss, the 'Gangnam Style' YouTube counter upgrade (2014), and the Y2038 problem.

#Floating-point numbers

Concept

Decimals stored in scientific-notation form (IEEE 754): sign, exponent, fraction. Fast, but inexact for many decimals.

Fun fact: In most languages 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004.

#Storage units: KB vs KiB

Concept

Decimal: kB = 1,000 bytes, MB = 10^6, GB = 10^9, TB = 10^12. Binary: KiB = 1,024, MiB = 1,048,576, GiB = 2^30. Windows labels binary values 'GB', which is why drives look smaller than advertised.

#Characters & text encoding

Concept

Text is stored as numbers: ASCII (A = 65), then Unicode and UTF-8 for every language and emoji (see Part 10).

#Boolean logic & logic gates

Concept

Boolean algebra (George Boole): AND, OR, NOT, XOR, NAND, NOR. Transistors form logic gates, gates form adders and memory, and those form CPUs.

Fun fact: Every possible logic circuit can be built from NAND gates alone.

#Bitwise operations

Concept

Operating on individual bits: AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~), shifts (<< >>). Used in graphics, encryption, compression and flags.

#Algorithms & data structures

#Algorithm

Concept

A precise, step-by-step procedure for solving a problem (named after al-Khwarizmi, see Part 8). Recipes, directions and sorting a deck of cards are all algorithms.

#Big-O notation

Concept

How an algorithm's time or memory grows with input size: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), O(n²) quadratic, O(2ⁿ) exponential.

#Searching: linear vs binary search

Concept

Linear search checks every item (O(n)). Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted list (O(log n)): 1 million items need only ~20 checks.

#Sorting algorithms

Concept

Bubble sort and insertion sort (simple, O(n²)), merge sort (O(n log n), stable), quicksort (Tony Hoare, 1959, fast on average), heapsort. Real languages use hybrids like Timsort (Python, Java).

#Arrays & lists

Concept

Array: items in consecutive memory, with instant access by index. Linked list: nodes pointing to the next, so inserting is easy but finding by position is slow.

#Stacks & queues

Concept

Stack: last in, first out (undo history, function calls). Queue: first in, first out (print jobs, message queues).

Fun fact: A 'stack overflow' happens when too many nested function calls fill the call stack, and the famous Q&A website is named after it.

#Hash tables (dictionaries)

Concept

Store key → value pairs with near-instant lookup by hashing the key: Python dicts, JavaScript objects and maps.

#Trees & heaps

Concept

Hierarchical structures: binary search trees, balanced trees (B-trees power databases and file systems), heaps (priority queues), tries (autocomplete).

#Graphs

Concept

Nodes connected by edges: road maps, social networks, the web. Algorithms: BFS/DFS search, Dijkstra's shortest path, A* (games, GPS), PageRank.

#Recursion & divide-and-conquer

Concept

Solving a problem by solving smaller versions of itself (merge sort, the Tower of Hanoi, tree traversal).

#Dynamic programming & greedy algorithms

Concept

Dynamic programming stores answers to subproblems to avoid recomputing (shortest paths, spell-check edit distance). Greedy algorithms pick the best-looking step each time (coin change, Huffman coding).

#Data compression

Concept

Lossless (ZIP/DEFLATE, PNG, FLAC, 7z: exact restoration) vs lossy (JPEG, MP3, H.264/AV1: discards detail you won't notice). Huffman coding (1952) and LZ77/78 (Lempel–Ziv) are classic building blocks.

#Error detection & correction

Concept

Parity bits, checksums, CRC, and error-correcting codes (Hamming, Reed–Solomon) let data survive noise. Used in RAM ECC, QR codes, CDs, SSDs and deep-space radio.

#Random number generation

Concept

Computers generate pseudo-random numbers from formulas (fine for games). Security needs cryptographically secure randomness from hardware noise.

Fun fact: Cloudflare uses a wall of lava lamps filmed by a camera as one source of randomness.

#Theory of computation & big ideas

#Turing machine

Concept

Turing's 1936 abstract machine: an infinite tape, a read/write head, and rules. Anything computable can be computed by one. A language that can simulate it is Turing-complete.

Fun fact: Microsoft Excel formulas, Minecraft redstone and Magic: The Gathering have all been shown to be Turing-complete.

#Church–Turing thesis

Concept

The idea that anything 'effectively computable' can be computed by a Turing machine (or lambda calculus). Not provable, but universally accepted.

#Halting problem

Concept

Turing proved no program can decide, for every program and input, whether it will eventually stop. Some problems are fundamentally uncomputable.

#Complexity: P vs NP

Concept

P: problems solvable quickly. NP: problems whose answers can be checked quickly (sudoku, scheduling, the travelling salesman). Whether P = NP is the biggest open question in computer science, with a $1 million Clay Millennium Prize for an answer.

#Finite state machines

Concept

Systems with a set number of states and transitions: traffic lights, vending machines, regex engines, game AI.

#Von Neumann architecture vs Harvard

Concept

Von Neumann: one memory for program and data (most PCs). Harvard: separate memories (many microcontrollers and DSPs). Modern CPUs mix both via split L1 caches.

#Parallel & distributed computing

Concept

Splitting work across many cores or machines: multithreading, GPUs, clusters, grid computing (SETI@home, Folding@home), cloud. Limited by Amdahl's law.

#Information theory

Concept

Shannon's mathematics of communication: entropy (information content), channel capacity and the limits of compression and error correction.

#Cybernetics & control systems

Concept

Feedback loops in machines and organisms (Norbert Wiener): thermostats, cruise control, autopilots, robotics.

#Quantum computing

Concept

Uses qubits that can be in superpositions and entangled, to attack certain problems (factoring, chemistry simulation) far faster than classical computers. Today's machines (IBM, Google, Quantinuum and others) are still small and error-prone.

Commonly confused with: Quantum computers won't speed up everyday tasks like gaming or browsing. They target specific problem types.

#Molecular, DNA & optical computing

Concept

Experimental approaches: computing with DNA strands (Adleman, 1994), photonic (light-based) chips for AI, neuromorphic chips modelled on brains (Intel Loihi, IBM TrueNorth).

#Moore's law & its slowing

Concept

Transistor counts doubled roughly every two years from the 1960s. Physical limits have slowed it, so progress now comes from 3D stacking, chiplets, specialised accelerators and new transistor designs (GAAFET).

#Databases & data

#Database & DBMS

Concept

Organised data plus software to store and query it. Relational databases (tables, rows, SQL): Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite. E. F. Codd's 1970 relational model is the foundation.

Fun fact: SQLite is likely the most deployed database in the world. It's inside every smartphone, browser and many apps.

#NoSQL databases

Concept

Non-relational stores for scale and flexibility: document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j).

#ACID transactions

Concept

Guarantees that keep data correct: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. That's why a bank transfer can't half-happen.

#Data warehouse, data lake & big data

Concept

Warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) hold cleaned data for analysis. Lakes hold raw data. 'Big data' tools: Hadoop, Spark, Kafka.

#Data mining & analytics

Concept

Finding patterns in large datasets: clustering, association rules ('people who bought X also bought Y'), dashboards and business intelligence (Power BI, Tableau).

#SQL

Concept

The standard language for querying relational databases. See the SQL tutorial in Part 9 for the full hands-on guide with runnable examples.

#Spreadsheets

Concept

VisiCalc (1979) → Lotus 1-2-3 (1983) → Excel (1985 Mac, 1987 Windows) → Google Sheets. The most widely used data tool in the world.

#Vector databases

Concept

Store AI 'embeddings' (number arrays representing meaning) for similarity search, a core piece of AI apps (Pinecone, pgvector, Weaviate).

Part 14

AI & Robotics

Artificial intelligence from the Turing test to large language models, how machine learning works, and robots from Unimate to humanoids. To use AI today (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, HUMAIN Chat, API prices, and running models offline), see Part 23.

#AI history

From the 1956 Dartmouth workshop to large language models.

#Turing test

1950 Legacy

Turing's 'imitation game': if a human judge can't tell a machine from a person in text conversation, the machine 'thinks'. Modern chatbots have made the test a subject of fresh debate.

#Dartmouth workshop

1956 Obsolete

The summer project where John McCarthy coined the term artificial intelligence, with Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester.

#Perceptron

1958 Obsolete

Frank Rosenblatt's single-layer neural network that learned to recognise simple patterns. Minsky and Papert's 1969 book on its limits helped trigger an AI winter.

#ELIZA

1966 Obsolete

Joseph Weizenbaum's chatbot at MIT that imitated a psychotherapist by rephrasing users' statements. People confided in it, which disturbed Weizenbaum.

Fun fact: The 'ELIZA effect' is the tendency to read human understanding into simple programs.

#Shakey the robot

1966–1972 Obsolete

SRI's first mobile robot that reasoned about its actions. It introduced the A* search algorithm.

#AI winters

1974–1980 / 1987–1993 Obsolete

Periods when hype outran results and funding collapsed, after the 1973 UK Lighthill Report and the 1980s expert-system bust.

#Expert systems

1970s–1990s Legacy

Rule-based programs encoding specialists' knowledge: MYCIN (medical diagnosis), XCON (configured DEC computers and saved millions). Brittle and hard to maintain.

#Deep Blue vs Kasparov

1997 Obsolete

IBM's chess computer beat world champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match, mostly through brute-force search of ~200 million positions per second.

#Watson wins Jeopardy!

2011 Obsolete

IBM's question-answering system beat champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter on TV.

#Deep learning breakthrough (AlexNet)

2012 Legacy

A neural network trained on GPUs by Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton won the ImageNet image-recognition contest by a large margin, launching the modern deep learning era.

#AlphaGo

2016 Legacy

DeepMind's program beat Go champion Lee Sedol 4–1, about a decade earlier than many experts predicted. 'Move 37' in game 2 stunned professionals.

#Transformers

2017 Current

The 'Attention Is All You Need' paper (Google) introduced the transformer architecture behind nearly all modern language models: GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.

#AlphaFold

2020 Current

DeepMind's system predicted protein 3D structures with near-lab accuracy. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (with David Baker).

#ChatGPT & the generative AI boom

2022→ Current

OpenAI's ChatGPT (Nov 2022) reached about 100 million users in two months. Image generators (DALL·E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion) and assistants like Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), Copilot, Llama (Meta) and DeepSeek followed.

#AI agents & AI PCs

2024→ Current

Models that use tools, browse, write code and complete multi-step tasks, plus on-device AI running on NPUs in phones and Copilot+ PCs.

#AI concepts explained

#Artificial intelligence (AI)

Concept

Computer systems doing tasks that normally need human intelligence: understanding language, recognising images, planning, learning. Narrow AI does specific tasks, AGI (general AI) would match humans broadly and doesn't exist yet.

#Machine learning (ML)

Concept

Systems that learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules. Supervised (labelled examples), unsupervised (find structure), reinforcement (learn by reward, as in game-playing AIs).

#Neural networks & deep learning

Concept

Layers of simple artificial 'neurons' with adjustable weights, trained by backpropagation on large datasets. 'Deep' means many layers. Types: CNNs (images), RNNs/LSTMs (sequences), transformers (language and almost everything now).

#Large language models (LLMs)

Concept

Huge transformer networks trained on vast text to predict the next token, then refined with human feedback (RLHF) to follow instructions. They can write, translate, summarise and code, but can also confidently make things up ('hallucinate').

#Tokens, parameters & context window

Concept

Tokens are word-pieces the model reads (roughly ¾ of a word in English). Parameters are the learned weights (billions to trillions). The context window is how much text the model can consider at once.

#Training vs inference

Concept

Training builds the model (weeks on thousands of GPUs, very expensive). Inference runs the trained model to answer a request. GPUs, TPUs and NPUs accelerate both.

#Generative AI

Concept

AI that creates new content: text (LLMs), images (diffusion models), audio and voice, music, video (Sora, Veo, Runway), code and 3D.

#Computer vision

Concept

Teaching machines to see: image classification, object detection (YOLO), face recognition, OCR, medical imaging, self-driving perception.

#Natural language processing (NLP)

Concept

Understanding and generating human language: translation (Google Translate, with Arabic among its early languages), sentiment analysis, chatbots, speech.

#Speech recognition & synthesis

Concept

Speech-to-text (Siri 2011, Alexa 2014, Whisper 2022) and text-to-speech, now with near-human AI voices and voice cloning.

#Optical character recognition (OCR) & handwriting recognition

Concept

Turning images of text into editable text. Arabic OCR is harder because letters join and change shape by position, and modern deep-learning models handle it far better.

#Fuzzy logic

Concept

Reasoning with degrees of truth (0.7 'warm') instead of just true/false, by Lotfi Zadeh (1965). Used in washing machines, rice cookers and camera autofocus.

#Genetic & evolutionary algorithms

Concept

Solve problems by 'breeding' and mutating candidate solutions over generations. Used in antenna design (a NASA antenna was evolved this way), scheduling and game AI.

#Knowledge representation & ontologies

Concept

Encoding facts and relationships so machines can reason: semantic networks, knowledge graphs (Google's Knowledge Graph), the Semantic Web.

#Bias, alignment & AI safety

Concept

AI can reflect biases in its training data and act in unintended ways. Alignment research tries to make AI systems helpful, honest and safe. Rules are emerging, such as the EU AI Act (2024).

#Technological singularity

Concept

The speculative idea (Vernor Vinge, Ray Kurzweil) that AI could improve itself so fast that the future becomes unpredictable. Kurzweil has predicted it for around 2045.

#Cellular automata & artificial life

Concept

Simple rules on grids producing complex behaviour: John Conway's Game of Life (1970), Wolfram's rule 30. 'Artificial life' studies evolution in simulation.

#Robotics

#Robot

Concept

A machine that senses, decides and acts in the physical world. The word comes from Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. (Czech robota, 'forced labour').

Fun fact: Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics (1942) appear in fiction, not in real robot design.

#Unimate

1961 Obsolete

The first industrial robot arm, built by George Devol and Joseph Engelberger. It worked on a General Motors die-casting line. Engelberger is called the 'father of robotics'.

#Industrial robots

Concept

Robot arms for welding, painting and assembly (FANUC, ABB, KUKA, Yaskawa). Car factories use thousands of them. Cobots (collaborative robots) work safely beside people.

#Mobile & service robots

Concept

Warehouse robots (Amazon's Kiva, acquired 2012), robot vacuums (Roomba, iRobot, 2002), delivery robots, hospital robots, lawn mowers.

#Humanoid robots

Concept

Human-shaped robots: Honda ASIMO (2000), Boston Dynamics Atlas, Tesla Optimus, Figure, Unitree, UBTech. Saudi Arabia granted citizenship to Hanson Robotics' Sophia in 2017, a world first.

Fun fact: Boston Dynamics' Atlas videos (parkour, dancing) became viral showcases of robot agility.

#Autonomous vehicles

Concept

Self-driving levels 0–5 (SAE). Robotaxis from Waymo, Baidu Apollo, Zoox and others operate in some cities. Driver-assist systems (Tesla Autopilot/FSD, GM Super Cruise) still need human supervision.

#Drones (UAVs)

Concept

Uncrewed aerial vehicles: consumer camera drones (DJI), delivery drones, agricultural spraying and military UAVs.

#Space robots & rovers

Concept

Mars rovers Sojourner (1997), Spirit and Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance (2021, with the Ingenuity helicopter), Canadarm on the ISS.

#Telepresence & surgical robots

Concept

Remote-controlled robots that extend human presence: the da Vinci surgical system (2000), telepresence robots for offices and hospitals, bomb-disposal robots.

#Robot sensors & control

Concept

LiDAR, cameras, IMUs, force sensors, SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping), PID control loops, ROS (Robot Operating System).

#AI & robotics pioneers

#John McCarthy

1927–2011 Person

Organised the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, invented Lisp and time-sharing ideas. Turing Award 1971.

NationalityAmerican
Known forCoined 'artificial intelligence', Lisp

#Marvin Minsky

1927–2016 Person

AI pioneer who wrote The Society of Mind and co-wrote Perceptrons.

NationalityAmerican
Known forMIT AI Lab co-founder

#Herbert Simon & Allen Newell

1916–2001 / 1927–1992 Person

Built early reasoning programs (1956). Simon also won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Economics.

NationalityAmerican
Known forLogic Theorist, General Problem Solver

#Joseph Weizenbaum

1923–2008 Person

Created ELIZA and later became a leading critic of over-trusting computers (Computer Power and Human Reason, 1976).

NationalityGerman-American
Known forELIZA, AI ethics

#Edward Feigenbaum

1936– Person

'Father of expert systems'. Turing Award 1994.

NationalityAmerican
Known forExpert systems

#Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun & Yoshua Bengio

1947– / 1960– / 1964– Person

The 'godfathers of deep learning'. Turing Award 2018. Hinton also shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics (with John Hopfield).

NationalityBritish-Canadian / French / Canadian
Known forDeep learning

#Fei-Fei Li

1976– Person

Created the ImageNet dataset that fuelled the deep-learning breakthrough in computer vision.

NationalityChinese-American
Known forImageNet

#Demis Hassabis

1976– Person

Former chess prodigy and game designer who co-founded DeepMind (Google). 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

NationalityBritish
Known forDeepMind, AlphaGo, AlphaFold

#Ray Kurzweil

1948– Person

Invented an early omni-font OCR reading machine for blind people and the Kurzweil synthesizer. Popularised the singularity idea.

NationalityAmerican
Known forOCR, speech, singularity

#Rodney Brooks & Cynthia Breazeal

1954– / 1967– Person

Brooks co-founded iRobot (Roomba) and Rethink Robotics. Breazeal built Kismet, an early social robot, at MIT.

NationalityAustralian / American
Known forBehaviour-based robotics, social robots

#Seymour Papert

1928–2016 Person

Co-created Logo and argued children learn best by building things with computers (Mindstorms, 1980). LEGO named its robotics kits after his book.

NationalitySouth African-American
Known forLogo, constructionism
Part 15

Games, Media, Apps & Society

Game consoles and game tech, file formats and codecs, graphics and creative software, everyday productivity apps, and computing's effect on society.

#Game consoles & handhelds

Gaming hardware generation by generation.

#Magnavox Odyssey

1972 Obsolete

The first home video game console (Ralph Baer). No sound, no score display, and plastic TV overlays for 'graphics'.

#Atari 2600 (VCS)

1977 Obsolete

Cartridge console that brought arcade hits home (Space Invaders, Pac-Man).

Fun fact: Atari's rushed E.T. game (1982) became a symbol of the 1983 video game crash. Unsold cartridges were buried in a New Mexico landfill and dug up in 2014.

#Nintendo Entertainment System (NES / Famicom)

1983 JP / 1985 US Obsolete

Revived the industry after the 1983 crash with Super Mario Bros., Zelda and Metroid. Nintendo's 'Seal of Quality' controlled third-party games.

#Sega Master System & Mega Drive / Genesis

1985 / 1988 Obsolete

Sega's challengers. The 16-bit Genesis and Sonic the Hedgehog fought the SNES in the 1990s 'console wars'. Sega quit hardware after the Dreamcast (1998/1999).

#Game Boy

1989 Obsolete

Nintendo's monochrome handheld with Tetris bundled. Game Boy + Game Boy Color sold about 119 million.

Fun fact: A Game Boy damaged in a Gulf War bombing still works and has been displayed at Nintendo's New York store.

#Super Nintendo (SNES)

1990 JP / 1991 US Obsolete

16-bit Nintendo with Mode 7 pseudo-3D and classics like Super Mario World, Zelda: A Link to the Past and Street Fighter II.

#Sony PlayStation (PS1)

1994 JP / 1995 Obsolete

CD-based 3D console that made Sony a gaming giant. It was born from a cancelled Nintendo–Sony CD add-on.

#Nintendo 64

1996 Obsolete

Cartridge-based 3D console with an analog stick: Super Mario 64, GoldenEye 007, Ocarina of Time.

#PlayStation 2

2000 Obsolete

The best-selling home console ever, at roughly 160 million units. It also played DVDs, which helped the format spread.

#Microsoft Xbox

2001 Obsolete

Microsoft's first console, essentially a PC inside (Pentium III, NVIDIA GPU, hard drive). Halo and Xbox Live online play.

#Nintendo GameCube & Game Boy Advance

2001 Obsolete

Mini-disc cube console with a handle, and the 32-bit GBA handheld.

#Nintendo DS & Sony PSP

2004 Obsolete

Dual-screen touch handheld (~154 million sold, the best-selling handheld ever) vs Sony's media-rich PSP with UMD discs.

#Xbox 360 / PS3 / Wii

2005 / 2006 / 2006 Obsolete

The HD and online generation. The Wii's motion controls reached non-gamers (~101 million sold). The PS3 included a Blu-ray drive and the Cell processor.

Fun fact: The Xbox 360's 'Red Ring of Death' hardware failures cost Microsoft over $1 billion in extended warranties.

#PlayStation 4 / Xbox One

2013 Legacy

x86 AMD-based consoles: PCs in all but name. Digital game sales boomed. The PS4 sold over 117 million.

#Nintendo Switch

2017 Current

A hybrid home/handheld console with detachable Joy-Con controllers, one of the best-selling consoles ever (150+ million).

#PlayStation 5 / Xbox Series X|S

2020 Current

Fast NVMe SSD storage, ray tracing, 4K. Chip shortages and scalpers made them hard to buy at launch.

#Nintendo Switch 2

2025 Current

Bigger screen, magnetic Joy-Con 2, mouse-style controls, NVIDIA chip with DLSS. It became the fastest-selling console in history at launch.

#PC handhelds & cloud gaming

2022→ Current

Steam Deck, ROG Ally and Legion Go run PC games portably (see Part 2). Cloud services stream games from data centres: Xbox Cloud Gaming, GeForce NOW, PlayStation Plus. Google Stadia closed in 2023.

#VR & AR headsets

2016→ Current

Oculus Rift and HTC Vive (2016), PlayStation VR, standalone Meta Quest (2019→), Apple Vision Pro (2024, 'spatial computing'), plus AR glasses (Ray-Ban Meta, HoloLens).

#Video game technology & culture

#Arcade games

Concept

Coin-operated cabinets: Computer Space (1971), Pong (1972), Space Invaders (1978), Pac-Man (1980), Street Fighter II (1991). Their golden age was about 1978–1983.

#Early computer games

Concept

Tennis for Two (1958, oscilloscope), Spacewar! (1962, PDP-1), text adventures like Colossal Cave Adventure (1976) and Zork, and MUDs, the ancestors of MMOs.

#Game engines

Concept

Reusable foundations for making games: Unreal Engine (Epic, 1998→), Unity (2005→), Godot (open source), id Tech (Doom/Quake), Source (Valve), RAGE (Rockstar), Frostbite (EA).

#PC gaming milestones

Concept

Doom (1993, shareware 3D shooter), Myst, Half-Life, StarCraft, World of Warcraft (2004, MMO), Minecraft (2009/2011, best-selling game ever with 300+ million copies), the Steam store (2003).

#Esports

Concept

Competitive gaming with pro leagues and prize pools: StarCraft in South Korea, League of Legends, Dota 2, Counter-Strike, Valorant. Riyadh hosts the Esports World Cup (2024→), one of the biggest prize pools in esports.

#Game distribution models

Concept

Cartridges → discs → digital downloads → subscriptions (Game Pass, PS Plus) → free-to-play with in-game purchases (Fortnite), battle passes and microtransactions.

#Mobile gaming

Concept

Snake (Nokia, 1997) → Angry Birds (2009) → Candy Crush, Clash of Clans, PUBG Mobile, Genshin Impact. Now the largest part of the games market by revenue.

#File formats & codecs

What's inside the files you open every day.

#Image formats (raster)

Concept

BMP (uncompressed), GIF (1987, 256 colours, animation), JPEG (1992, lossy photos), PNG (1996, lossless with transparency), TIFF (print), WebP (Google), HEIC/HEIF (iPhone default), AVIF, JPEG XL, and camera RAW files.

Fun fact: GIF's creator, Steve Wilhite, said it's pronounced with a soft g, 'JIF'. The debate continues.

#Vector graphics

Concept

Images made of shapes and curves that scale to any size without blurring: SVG (web), EPS, AI (Illustrator), PDF. Logos and icons are usually vector.

Commonly confused with: Raster images (photos, pixels) lose sharpness when enlarged. Vector images don't.

#Audio formats

Concept

WAV/AIFF (uncompressed), MP3 (1993, Fraunhofer, lossy, launched the digital music era), AAC (iTunes, YouTube), FLAC/ALAC (lossless), Ogg Vorbis, Opus (calls, Discord), MIDI (notes, not sound).

#Video codecs

Concept

Compression methods: MPEG-2 (DVD, TV), H.264/AVC (2003, everywhere), H.265/HEVC (4K, Apple), VP9 (YouTube), AV1 (2018, royalty-free, Netflix/YouTube), H.266/VVC. GPUs and phones include hardware encoders and decoders.

Commonly confused with: A codec compresses the video, a container holds it. An .mp4 file is a container that usually holds H.264 or H.265 video.

#Video containers

Concept

MP4, MOV (Apple QuickTime), MKV (Matroska, many tracks and subtitles), AVI (old Windows), WebM, FLV (old Flash video), TS (broadcast).

#Document formats

Concept

TXT, RTF (Microsoft, 1987), DOC → DOCX (Office Open XML, 2007), ODT (OpenDocument), PDF (Adobe, 1993, ISO standard since 2008), EPUB (e-books), Markdown (2004, plain text with simple formatting), CSV/XLSX (tables).

#PostScript & PDF

Concept

Adobe's PostScript (1984) page-description language powered laser printers and desktop publishing. PDF (1993) became the universal 'looks the same everywhere' document format.

#Archives & compression formats

Concept

ZIP (Phil Katz, 1989), RAR (Eugene Roshal, 1993), 7z, tar.gz (Unix), ISO (disc images), DMG (Mac disk images).

#Fonts & typography

Concept

Bitmap fonts → outline fonts: PostScript Type 1 (1984), TrueType (Apple/Microsoft, 1991), OpenType (1996), variable fonts (2016). Arabic fonts need contextual shaping, ligatures and right-to-left support (e.g. Noto Naskh/Kufi, Dubai, IBM Plex Sans Arabic).

Fun fact: Steve Jobs credited a calligraphy class at Reed College for the Mac's multiple typefaces.

#Colour models

Concept

RGB (screens: red, green, blue light), CMYK (printing inks), HSL/HSV (hue-based picking), hex codes for the web (#RRGGBB), colour spaces sRGB, Display P3, Adobe RGB.

#Graphics, media & creative computing

#Computer graphics & CGI

Concept

Raster vs vector, 3D modelling, texturing, lighting and rendering (rasterisation in games, ray/path tracing in films). Milestones: Tron (1982), Terminator 2's liquid metal (1991), Jurassic Park (1993), Toy Story (1995, the first fully computer-animated feature film).

#3D & animation software

Concept

Blender (free, open source), Autodesk Maya and 3ds Max, Cinema 4D, Houdini (effects), ZBrush (sculpting), Pixar's RenderMan.

#Image editing

Concept

Adobe Photoshop (1990), GIMP, Affinity Photo, Paint.NET, Lightroom (photo workflows), mobile editors, plus AI generative fill.

#Desktop publishing (DTP)

Concept

Laying out pages on a computer. Aldus PageMaker (1985) + Mac + LaserWriter + PostScript started the DTP revolution. Then QuarkXPress, Adobe InDesign, Affinity Publisher, Canva.

#CAD/CAM

Concept

Computer-aided design and manufacturing: AutoCAD (1982), SolidWorks, CATIA, Fusion 360, Revit (architecture/BIM). CAM drives CNC machines and 3D printers.

#Digital photography

Concept

Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built the first digital camera in 1975 (0.01 MP, 23 seconds per image, saved to cassette tape). Phones have since replaced most compact cameras.

#Digital audio & music production

Concept

DAWs (Digital Audio Workstations): Pro Tools, Logic Pro, Ableton Live, FL Studio, GarageBand, plus MIDI controllers, plug-ins (VST) and Auto-Tune (1997).

#Video editing

Concept

From tape-to-tape to non-linear editing: Avid (1989), Final Cut Pro, Adobe Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, iMovie, CapCut.

#Digital rights management (DRM) & copy protection

Concept

Technical locks on media and software: dongles, CD keys, online activation, Widevine/FairPlay video DRM, game DRM (Denuvo). Apple dropped DRM from iTunes music in 2009.

#Digital music & video distribution

Concept

MP3 players → iPod (2001) + iTunes Store (2003) → streaming (Spotify, Apple Music, Anghami in the Middle East, YouTube Music) and video streaming.

#E-books & digital libraries

Concept

Project Gutenberg (1971, the first e-book project), Kindle (2007), EPUB, Internet Archive, Google Books.

#Productivity & business software

#Word processors

Concept

Electric Pencil (1976), WordStar (1978), WordPerfect (DOS king of the 1980s), Microsoft Word (1983), Google Docs (2006), Pages, LibreOffice Writer.

Fun fact: George R. R. Martin famously writes his books on an old DOS PC running WordStar 4.0.

#Office suites

Concept

Microsoft Office / Microsoft 365 (1990→), Google Workspace, Apple iWork, LibreOffice (free, forked from OpenOffice in 2010), WPS Office, Zoho.

#Presentation software

Concept

PowerPoint (1987, made by Forethought and bought by Microsoft the same year), Keynote, Google Slides, Prezi, Canva.

#Spreadsheets

Concept

VisiCalc (1979, the Apple II's killer app) → Lotus 1-2-3 → Excel → Google Sheets. See Part 13.

#Email clients & personal information managers

Concept

Outlook, Apple Mail, Thunderbird, Gmail apps. PIMs organise contacts, calendars and notes, from the Psion organisers and Palm to Outlook and Notion.

#ERP, CRM & business systems

Concept

ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) runs finance, HR and supply chains (SAP 1972, Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics, Odoo). CRM manages customers (Salesforce, HubSpot).

#Project management & collaboration

Concept

Microsoft Project, Trello, Asana, Jira, Notion, Monday.com, plus team chat (Slack, Teams) and video calls (Zoom, Teams, Google Meet).

#Maps, GPS & GIS

Concept

GPS satellites (US, fully operational 1995), plus GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou. Consumer maps: MapQuest (1996), Google Maps (2005), Waze. GIS software (Esri ArcGIS, QGIS) analyses geographic data.

#Educational software & e-learning

Concept

The Oregon Trail (1971), Math Blaster, encyclopedias on CD (Encarta), and now learning platforms (Moodle, Blackboard, Google Classroom, Khan Academy, Coursera, Saudi Arabia's Madrasati).

#Accounting & finance software

Concept

Peachtree, QuickBooks, Xero, Zoho Books, online banking and investing apps, and VAT-compliant e-invoicing systems (Saudi ZATCA 'Fatoorah').

#Computing & society

How technology affects people, law and the world.

#Intellectual property & software

Concept

Copyright protects code and content automatically. Patents protect inventions (software patents are controversial). Trademarks protect names and logos. Open licences and Creative Commons grant permissions.

#Privacy in the digital age

Concept

Tracking, data brokers, location data, facial recognition. Laws like GDPR and Saudi Arabia's PDPL give people rights over their data (see Part 12).

#E-government

Concept

Government services online. Saudi examples: Absher (Ministry of Interior services), Nafath (national digital identity login), Tawakkalna, plus Estonia's well-known digital state.

#Accessibility & assistive technology

Concept

Screen readers (JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack), braille displays, eye tracking, switch access, captions, voice control. Stephen Hawking communicated via a cheek-sensor speech system.

#Digital literacy & computer education

Concept

Teaching people to use computers, judge online information and code. National coding initiatives and school computer-science curricula have expanded worldwide.

#Women in computing

Concept

Ada Lovelace, the ENIAC programmers, Grace Hopper, Margaret Hamilton, Katherine Johnson, Radia Perlman and many more (Part 8). The share of women in computer science degrees fell from about 37% in the mid-1980s in the US and is slowly recovering.

#Remote work & telecommuting

Concept

Working from home via the internet. Video calls, VPNs and cloud apps made it mainstream during COVID-19 (2020) and many roles stayed hybrid.

#Gig economy & platforms

Concept

Work through apps: ride-hailing (Uber, Careem), delivery (Jahez, HungerStation, Talabat), freelancing (Upwork, Fiverr).

#Misinformation & deepfakes

Concept

False information spreads fast online. AI deepfakes can convincingly fake faces and voices, which drives work on detection, content credentials (C2PA) and media literacy.

#E-waste & environmental impact

Concept

Discarded electronics contain toxic materials and valuable metals (~62 million tonnes generated in 2022, under a quarter properly recycled). Data centres and AI also use large amounts of electricity and water.

#Digital wellbeing & screen time

Concept

Built-in tools (Screen Time, Digital Wellbeing) and parental controls help manage device use. Research on social media and mental health remains debated.

#Electronic voting

Concept

Voting machines and online voting raise accuracy and security concerns. Many experts recommend paper ballots or paper trails for audits.

#Science fiction & computing

Concept

Fiction that shaped tech culture: HAL 9000 (2001, 1968), Neuromancer (1984, coined 'cyberspace'), WarGames (1983), The Matrix (1999), Her (2013).

Fun fact: 'Cyberspace' was coined by William Gibson in a 1982 short story, Burning Chrome, before Neuromancer made it famous.

Part 16

Build, Repair & Troubleshoot

Hands-on guides: tools and safety, building a PC step by step, BIOS settings, troubleshooting PCs, laptops and phones, upgrades and maintenance. Based on and linked to iFixit's free repair guides.

#Before you open anything: tools & safety

Most repairs fail because of rushing, lost screws or static, not difficulty. iFixit's free guides (ifixit.com) cover thousands of devices with photos for every step. Find your exact model first.

#A basic repair toolkit

Guide

You don't need much to start. Buy a decent precision driver set rather than a cheap one, because soft bits strip screws.

Step 1Screwdrivers: Phillips #000/#00/#0/#1/#2, Torx T3–T10, Pentalobe P2/P5 (iPhones, MacBooks), Tri-wing (Nintendo), Torx Security (game consoles)
Step 2Opening tools: plastic spudgers, thin guitar-pick openers, a suction cup, plastic cards. They're safer than metal near batteries and flex cables
Step 3Handling: anti-static tweezers, a magnetic project mat or ice-cube tray for screws
Step 4Heat & cleaning: a hair dryer or heat pad to soften adhesive, 90%+ isopropyl alcohol, lint-free cloths, compressed air
Step 5Nice to have: headlamp or flashlight, zip ties, thermal paste, a multimeter, a USB-C power meter

Fun fact: iFixit's Pro Tech Toolkit and Essential Electronics Toolkit are popular all-in-one kits, but any quality precision set with the bits above does the job.

#Static electricity (ESD)

Guide

Electrostatic discharge is the tiny spark you feel touching a door handle. It's usually harmless to modern parts, but it can still kill or weaken chips, and that damage is hard to diagnose later. Prevention is easy. → iFixit: ESD explained

Step 1Work on a hard table, not carpet, and avoid polyester clothes, which build up static
Step 2Touch a bare metal part of the PC case (or wear a grounded anti-static wrist strap) before handling parts
Step 3Hold cards and RAM by the edges and keep parts in their anti-static bags until needed
Step 4Unplug the power cable, then press the power button once to drain leftover charge

Commonly confused with: ESD precautions do not protect you from high voltage. Never open a power supply or an old CRT monitor, because their capacitors can hold a dangerous charge long after unplugging.

#Swollen & damaged batteries

Guide

A swelling lithium battery is a fire risk. Signs: a lifted trackpad, a rocking laptop, a screen pushed out of a phone, a bulging case, a sweet chemical smell. → iFixit: What to do with a swollen battery

Step 1Stop using and charging it. Don't press on it, puncture it or bend it
Step 2If the device is very hot, smoking or smells strongly, don't open it. Move it away from flammable things, outdoors if possible, and avoid the fumes
Step 3If you do replace it yourself: drain it as low as possible first, wear eye protection and gloves, and work somewhere ventilated
Step 4Loosen glued batteries with heat or an adhesive solvent (isopropyl alcohol) rather than prying hard, which can puncture the cell
Step 5Put the old battery in a fire-safe container and take it to an e-waste or battery collection point. Never put it in household trash

#Screw management & photos

Guide

Laptops and phones use screws of different lengths that look identical. A too-long screw in the wrong hole can pierce a circuit board or battery.

Step 1Take a photo before and after every step
Step 2Lay screws out on a mat in the same pattern as they came out, or label them by step
Step 3Never force a screw. If it won't turn, check the bit size and that it isn't hidden under a sticker or rubber foot
Step 4Disconnect the battery first on any device where the guide says to

#Before any repair: backup, warranty, parts

Guide

A few minutes of preparation saves the expensive mistakes.

Step 1Back up your data: repairs can go wrong, and drives fail
Step 2Check the warranty: opening a device under warranty may affect coverage, so a free official repair might be better
Step 3Find the exact model number (the sticker underneath, Settings → About, or the serial number lookup) and follow a guide for that exact model
Step 4Get quality parts: cheap batteries and screens are a common cause of repeat failures

#Know when to stop

Concept

Some jobs need specialist tools or skills: board-level microsoldering, BGA chip rework, OLED screen refurbishing, water-damage board repair. Phone screens and Face ID / Touch ID parts may also be 'paired' to the original device by the maker. A good independent repair shop is often the right call for these.

#Building a desktop PC, step by step

Building a PC is mostly careful plugging-in. Expect 2–4 hours for a first build. iFixit's PC build walkthrough on Make: has photos of every stage. See Part 1 for what each part does.

#1. Plan & check compatibility

Guide

Most build problems are compatibility problems. Check these before buying (PCPartPicker checks many automatically).

Step 1CPU ↔ motherboard: same socket (e.g. AM5, LGA1851), and a chipset/BIOS that supports that CPU generation
Step 2RAM ↔ motherboard: DDR4 or DDR5 (they aren't interchangeable), and a capacity and speed listed by the board
Step 3Case ↔ parts: motherboard size (ATX/mATX/ITX), GPU length, CPU cooler height, radiator mounts
Step 4PSU ↔ everything: enough watts with 30–40% headroom, the right GPU connectors (8-pin or 12V-2x6), ATX 3.x for modern GPUs
Step 5Storage: M.2 slot type (NVMe vs SATA) and how many slots, which may disable SATA ports when used

#2. Prepare the workspace

Guide

A clear table, good light, the motherboard manual open, and the motherboard box to build on (it makes a handy non-conductive work surface).

Step 1Keep every box and bag until the PC boots: spare screws and adapters hide in them
Step 2Ground yourself on the case before touching parts
Step 3Find the front-panel, USB and fan headers in the manual now. They're easier to plan before the case gets crowded

#3. Install the CPU

Guide

Do this with the motherboard outside the case.

Step 1Lift the socket's retention arm (and load plate on LGA sockets)
