Step 2Match the small gold triangle on the CPU corner to the marked corner of the socket
Step 3Lower the CPU straight down, with no pressure and no sliding, then close the arm. The plastic cover on LGA sockets pops off by itself
Step 4If it doesn't sit flat, lift and re-align. Never press. Bent pins are the most expensive beginner mistake

#4. Install M.2 SSD & RAM

Guide

Still outside the case: these are easier to reach now.

Step 1M.2: remove the slot's heatsink if present (peel the film off its thermal pad), insert the SSD at about 30°, press it flat and fix it with the screw or latch
Step 2RAM: open the slot clips and use the slots the manual recommends for two sticks (usually the 2nd and 4th from the CPU, A2/B2)
Step 3Line up the notch and press firmly on both ends until the clips click. It needs more force than people expect

#5. Mount the CPU cooler

Guide

Stock and aftermarket coolers come with mounting brackets, and some need a backplate fitted behind the board. → iFixit: How to apply thermal paste

Step 1If the cooler has pre-applied paste, don't add more. Otherwise put a pea-sized dot in the CPU centre
Step 2Remove any plastic film from the cooler base (an easy step to forget)
Step 3Tighten screws a little at a time in a cross pattern so the pressure stays even
Step 4Plug the cooler fan into CPU_FAN (or the AIO pump into AIO_PUMP / PUMP_FAN)

#6. (Optional) Test outside the case

Guide

Experienced builders often 'breadboard': boot with just the board, CPU, cooler, one RAM stick and the PSU on the box to confirm the parts work before installing them.

Step 1Connect the 24-pin and the CPU 8-pin power
Step 2Start the board by briefly touching the two PWR_SW header pins with a screwdriver, or use the board's power button if it has one
Step 3Check for a BIOS screen (through the GPU or motherboard video output) or the debug LEDs

#7. Prepare the case & install the motherboard

Guide

Step 1Make sure the standoffs line up with every board hole, and that no extra standoff sits where there's no hole (it can short the board)
Step 2Fit the I/O shield first if the board doesn't have one built in (it snaps in from inside)
Step 3Lower the board at an angle so the ports enter the I/O cut-out, then screw it down. Snug, not tight

#8. Power supply & cables

Guide

Step 1Mount the PSU with its fan facing a filtered vent (usually down, if the case has a bottom vent)
Step 2Connect the 24-pin motherboard cable and the 8-pin EPS CPU cable(s) at the top-left corner of the board
Step 3With modular PSUs, use only that PSU's own cables. Mixing brands can destroy parts

#9. Graphics card

Guide

Step 1Remove the matching rear slot covers
Step 2Press the card into the top full-length PCIe slot until the latch clicks, then screw it to the case
Step 3Plug in the GPU power cables fully. 12VHPWR / 12V-2x6 plugs must sit flush with no gap. Use separate PSU cables for each 8-pin socket where possible
Step 4Support heavy cards with the included bracket to stop the slot sagging

#10. Front panel, fans, USB & storage cables

Guide

Step 1Front-panel pins (power switch, reset, power LED +/−, HDD LED): follow the manual's diagram. The switches don't care about polarity, the LEDs do
Step 2USB 3 header (blue, fragile, push straight in), USB-C Key-A header, HD Audio
Step 3Fans: front fans pull air in, rear and top fans push air out. Plug them into SYS_FAN headers or a fan hub
Step 4SATA drives: data cable to the board, SATA power from the PSU

#11. First boot & BIOS checks

Guide

Close the side panel later. First, power on and check.

Step 1Enter BIOS/UEFI (usually Del or F2) and confirm the CPU, all RAM and all drives are detected
Step 2Turn on XMP / EXPO so RAM runs at its rated speed
Step 3Check CPU temperature at idle (roughly 30–50 °C is normal depending on cooler and room)
Step 4Update the BIOS if the board's site lists fixes for your CPU. Never cut power during an update

#12. Install the operating system & drivers

Guide

Step 1Make a Windows install USB with Microsoft's Media Creation Tool (8 GB+ stick) on another PC, or a Linux USB with Rufus / balenaEtcher
Step 2Boot from it via the boot menu key (often F8/F11/F12) and install to the NVMe drive
Step 3Install chipset drivers from the motherboard maker, and GPU drivers from NVIDIA / AMD / Intel
Step 4Run Windows Update, then a short stress test (e.g. a game or benchmark) while watching temperatures

#BIOS / UEFI settings guide

The firmware setup screen that runs before Windows. Most settings can stay on default, but these are worth knowing.

#Boot order & boot menu

Concept

The boot order sets which drive starts first. Use the one-time boot menu to start from a USB installer without changing it. Windows Boot Manager should be first for normal use.

#XMP / EXPO (memory profiles)

Concept

One switch that runs your RAM at its advertised speed rather than the slower default. If the PC becomes unstable, choose a lower profile or turn it off.

#Secure Boot, TPM & Windows 11

Concept

Windows 11 needs UEFI mode, Secure Boot capability and TPM 2.0. On AMD it's called fTPM, on Intel PTT. Usually it's on by default on modern boards. Turning off CSM (legacy boot) is often needed for Secure Boot.

#Virtualization (VT-x / AMD-V / SVM)

Concept

Needed for virtual machines, WSL2, Android emulators and Docker. Intel calls it VT-x / VT-d, AMD calls it SVM Mode.

#Resizable BAR / Smart Access Memory

Concept

Lets the CPU access the whole GPU memory at once, giving small gains in many games. It needs UEFI mode with CSM off. Required for good performance on Intel Arc GPUs.

#Fan curves & power limits

Concept

Set fans to speed up as temperatures rise (quiet at idle, cool under load). Power limits (PL1/PL2, PBO on AMD) trade performance against heat and noise.

#Clearing CMOS (resetting the BIOS)

Concept

Resets every setting to default, which fixes most failed overclocks and RAM issues. Methods: the Clear CMOS button on the rear I/O, the CLR_CMOS jumper (short two pins for ~10 s), or remove the CR2032 coin battery for a few minutes with the PSU unplugged.

#Updating the BIOS safely

Concept

Only update for a reason: new CPU support, a stability fix or a security fix. Use the motherboard's built-in flash tool (EZ Flash, M-Flash, Q-Flash) or BIOS Flashback from a USB stick, which works even without a CPU. Never switch off during an update.

#Troubleshooting computers

iFixit's computer troubleshooting principles: check easy and likely causes first, then easy but unlikely ones, and only then hard ones. Suspect cables and configuration before blaming a 'dead' part. Truly dead-on-arrival parts are the least likely cause.

#PC won't turn on (no lights, no fans)

Guide

Work from the wall towards the motherboard. → iFixit: Desktop PC troubleshooting

Step 1Test the wall outlet with a lamp. Bypass power strips and the UPS
Step 2Check the PSU rocker switch is on (I) and the power cable is fully in. Try a known-good cable (monitors often use the same C13 cable)
Step 3Unplug every USB device and try again
Step 4Re-seat the 24-pin and CPU 8-pin cables. Check the case's power button wires on the PWR_SW header
Step 5Start the board by shorting the PWR_SW pins with a screwdriver. If that works, the case button is the problem
Step 6If still dead, test with another PSU. A failed PSU is the most common hardware cause

#Turns on, but no picture

Guide

The PC runs (fans, lights) but the screen stays black. Often it's the display chain, not the PC.

Step 1Make sure the monitor is on, set to the right input, and plugged into the graphics card (not the motherboard)
Step 2Try another cable and port (HDMI vs DisplayPort) or another monitor or TV
Step 3Watch the debug LEDs (CPU / DRAM / VGA / BOOT) or beep codes. They point at the failing part
Step 4Re-seat the RAM and try one stick at a time. Re-seat the GPU and its power cables
Step 5Clear CMOS to undo bad settings

#Blue screens (BSOD) & random crashes

Guide

Write down the stop code (e.g. MEMORY_MANAGEMENT, IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL). The last change you made is usually the cause.

Step 1Undo recent changes: new drivers, overclocks, XMP, new hardware
Step 2Update or roll back the GPU and chipset drivers. Run Windows Update
Step 3Test RAM: Windows Memory Diagnostic, or MemTest86 from USB
Step 4Check the drive's health (CrystalDiskInfo, or PowerShell Get-PhysicalDisk | Select FriendlyName, HealthStatus) and run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
Step 5Check temperatures (HWiNFO, HWMonitor). Crashes under load often mean heat or an overloaded PSU

#Overheating, loud fans & throttling

Guide

Laptops and PCs slow down to protect themselves when hot. Dust is the usual culprit. → iFixit: How to repaste a laptop

Step 1Give it room: leave space around the vents, and don't run laptops on beds or cushions
Step 2Clean dust from filters, fans and heatsinks with compressed air. Hold fans still so they don't spin and generate current
Step 3Check fan curves in BIOS, and make sure case fans actually spin
Step 4Replace dried-out thermal paste (often after 3–5+ years) on the CPU/GPU

#Slow PC

Guide

The cause is usually software, not worn-out hardware.

Step 1Check Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) for what is using the CPU, RAM or disk
Step 2Disable unneeded startup apps (Task Manager → Startup apps)
Step 3Free up storage. A drive over ~90% full slows down noticeably
Step 4Scan for malware with Microsoft Defender
Step 5Biggest hardware wins: replace a hard drive with an SSD, and go from 8 GB to 16 GB+ RAM

#Windows won't start (but the hardware works)

Guide

Windows has built-in repair tools in the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE).

Step 1Interrupt startup 3 times in a row (power off at the logo) to reach WinRE automatically
Step 2Troubleshoot → Advanced options → Startup Repair
Step 3Try Safe Mode (Startup Settings → Restart → 4/5) to remove a bad driver or app
Step 4Use System Restore or Uninstall Updates to roll back
Step 5Last resort: Reset this PC (keep or remove files) or reinstall from USB, after backing up data

#No internet / Wi-Fi problems

Guide

Find out whether the problem is the device, the router or the internet provider.

Step 1Check whether other devices can connect. If none can, restart the modem/router (unplug for 30 seconds)
Step 2On one device: toggle Wi-Fi, forget and re-join the network, update the Wi-Fi driver
Step 3Run ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew and ipconfig /flushdns (Windows)
Step 4Test with an Ethernet cable to rule out Wi-Fi interference
Step 5Windows: Settings → Network & internet → Advanced → Network reset

#No sound, USB or drive not detected

Guide

Quick checks for common hardware 'it's not working' problems.

Step 1Sound: check the output device (taskbar speaker icon), mute and volume, the cable in the green jack, and the audio driver
Step 2USB: try another port (rear ports connect straight to the board), another cable, and Device Manager for errors
Step 3New drive not showing in File Explorer: open Disk Management and initialise (GPT) and format it. New drives come blank
Step 4Drive missing in BIOS: check SATA data and power cables or re-seat the M.2, and check M.2 / SATA lane sharing

#Laptop won't turn on

Guide

iFixit's order of checks, simplest first: → iFixit: Laptop won't turn on

Step 1Force-restart: hold the power button for about 10 seconds
Step 2Charge for 15+ minutes with a known-good charger and outlet
Step 3Drain stuck charge: unplug the charger and peripherals, remove the battery if you can, then hold power for 60 seconds
Step 4Lights and fans but no picture? Connect an external monitor, or press Win + Ctrl + Shift + B to restart the graphics driver
Step 5Listen for beep codes and watch the status LEDs, then look up the meaning for your model
Step 6Re-seat the RAM, then suspect the battery, screen cable or motherboard
Step 7'No bootable device' means the storage drive or boot order (check BIOS or reinstall the OS)

#Laptop upgrades & repairs

Many laptops can still be upgraded or repaired at home. Check the iFixit guide for your exact model first.

#Check what you can upgrade

Guide

Before buying parts, find out what's soldered.

Step 1Look up your model's spec sheet or service manual (Dell, HP and Lenovo publish them free)
Step 2RAM: SO-DIMM slots = upgradeable. 'Onboard' / LPDDR = soldered. Some have both
Step 3Storage: most have an M.2 slot (check 2230 / 2242 / 2280 length and NVMe vs SATA). Some have a spare second slot
Step 4Tools like Crucial System Scanner or CPU-Z show your current RAM and slots
Step 5Check iFixit's laptop repairability scores when buying your next laptop

#Upgrade or replace the SSD

Guide

The single best upgrade for an older laptop.

Step 1Back up, then clone the old drive to the new one with a USB-to-NVMe/SATA enclosure and cloning software (Macrium Reflect, Clonezilla, or the SSD maker's tool), or do a fresh OS install
Step 2Unplug the charger, open the bottom panel, and disconnect the battery if the guide says so
Step 3Remove the M.2 screw, slide the old drive out, insert the new one at an angle, press it down and screw it in
Step 4Boot. If you cloned, extend the partition in Disk Management to use the extra space

#Add or upgrade RAM

Guide

Match the type (DDR4 vs DDR5 SO-DIMM) and ideally the speed. Install pairs for dual-channel.

Step 1Release the side clips. The stick pops up at an angle
Step 2Insert the new stick at about 30° with the notch aligned, then press down until the clips lock
Step 3First boot may take longer while the memory trains. Check the total in Task Manager → Performance

#Replace a laptop battery

Guide

Batteries are consumables. Expect noticeably reduced capacity after about 300–1,000 cycles. → iFixit: Swollen battery safety

Step 1Check wear first: run powercfg /batteryreport in Windows (compare Full Charge Capacity with Design Capacity) or System Information on a Mac
Step 2Buy a battery matching the exact part number. Avoid unbranded ultra-cheap cells
Step 3Disconnect the old battery connector before anything else, then remove its screws or adhesive
Step 4If it's swollen, follow the swollen-battery safety steps

#Clean & repaste a laptop

Guide

Restores cooling on laptops that run hot and loud after a few years. → iFixit: How to repaste a laptop

Step 1Open the bottom panel and blow dust out of fans and heatsink fins (hold the fan still)
Step 2For repasting: remove the heatsink screws in the numbered order printed next to them
Step 3Clean old paste off with isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free cloth
Step 4Apply a small rice-grain-sized drop on each chip and refit the heatsink, tightening in number order

#Other common laptop repairs

Concept

Keyboard (sometimes riveted to the top case, which makes it harder), screen panel (match the panel part number and connector type, eDP 30/40-pin), hinges, charging port / DC jack, fans, Wi-Fi card (M.2 E-key). The difficulty varies hugely by model, so check the guide first.

#Phone & tablet fixes

Software fixes first, then the simple hardware ones, and leave board-level work to specialists.

#Phone won't charge

Guide

Most 'broken charging port' cases are lint in the port. → iFixit: iPhone not charging

Step 1Try another cable and charger, and a wireless charger if the phone supports it. If wireless works, it's the cable or port
Step 2Shine a light into the port. Gently remove packed lint with a non-metal tool (wooden toothpick or plastic pick), with the phone off
Step 3Restart and update the phone. Pixels: try turning off Adaptive Charging
Step 4Give a fully drained phone up to 30 minutes on the charger before deciding it's dead
Step 5Still nothing? Battery, then charging port, then board, in that order

Fun fact: iFixit also has a dedicated Pixel not charging page.

#Battery health & replacement

Guide

Phone batteries usually need replacing after 2–4 years.

Step 1iPhone: Settings → Battery → Battery Health (Apple considers below 80% worn). Many Androids show it under Battery or Device care
Step 2Signs: sudden shutdowns at 20–30%, slowdowns, the phone getting warm, a swelling case
Step 3Battery swaps involve heat, adhesive pull-tabs and care around the battery. Follow a model-specific guide, or use an authorised or reputable shop

#Cracked screen

Guide

Step 1Small cracks: a screen protector stops shards and slows spreading, but replace it soon
Step 2OLED screens are expensive, and cheap replacements are often lower-quality LCD or 'incell' panels with worse colours and battery life
Step 3Some makers pair parts to the phone. Third-party screens may show warnings or lose features like True Tone
Step 4Back up the phone before any screen repair

#Water damage

Guide

Act fast and skip the myths.

Step 1Power it off immediately. Don't charge it
Step 2Wipe it dry and leave it in a ventilated place with the ports facing down
Step 3Don't use rice (Apple's own advice): grains and dust get into ports. Don't use hair dryers on high heat
Step 4Saltwater, sugary drinks or a phone that won't turn on: get it professionally cleaned soon, because corrosion spreads over days
Step 5IP67/IP68 ratings fade with age and drops, and liquid damage usually isn't covered by warranty

#Clean the speaker, mic & ports

Guide

Step 1Use a soft dry brush or toothbrush on speaker grilles
Step 2Use painter's tape or blue-tack to lift dust from grilles
Step 3Never push needles or SIM tools hard into speaker or mic holes. The membranes behind them tear easily

#Repairability scores

Concept

iFixit rates devices from 0 (unrepairable) to 10 (easiest) after its teardowns, based on how easy priority parts (battery, screen) are to replace and whether parts and manuals are available. See the smartphone scores and laptop scores. France and the EU also run official repairability indexes.

#Maintenance & making devices last

Small habits that add years to your gear.

#Battery care habits

Concept

Lithium batteries age fastest when hot, at 100%, or near 0% for long periods. Use built-in charge limits or optimised charging (iPhone Optimized/80% Limit, Samsung Protect Battery, Lenovo Conservation Mode, ASUS 80%), avoid charging under pillows or in hot cars, and store devices at about 50% if unused for months.

#Cleaning schedule

Concept

Desktops: dust filters monthly, inside every 6–12 months (more often in dusty climates like Riyadh's). Laptops: vents every few months. Keyboards and screens: microfibre cloth with a little isopropyl alcohol or water, never sprayed straight onto the device.

#Drive health monitoring

Concept

Check SSD/HDD health with CrystalDiskInfo (Windows), smartctl (Linux/macOS) or the drive maker's tool. Rising 'reallocated sectors' or a health % dropping fast is a warning to back up now.

#Software hygiene

Concept

Keep the OS, browser and drivers updated, uninstall what you don't use, use the built-in antivirus, and keep 15–20% of storage free. Follow the 3-2-1 backup rule (Part 12).

#Power protection

Concept

A surge protector for everything plugged in, and a UPS for desktops if your area has outages or voltage dips. That protects data mid-save and the PSU.

#Recycling & e-waste

Concept

Wipe devices before selling or recycling them (factory reset, sign out of iCloud / Google, remove the SIM). Recycle batteries and electronics at proper collection points, and many brands and retailers run take-back schemes. Selling or donating a working device is even better.

#Sources & further reading

Links for checking facts and reading further. Facts that change over time (laws, company news, product support) link to their source right on the card.

  1. iFixit repair guideshttps://www.ifixit.com/
Part 17

Buying Guides

How to choose laptops, phones, tablets, PC parts, monitors, storage, chargers and networking gear by need and budget, with what to look for and what to avoid.

#How to buy tech without regret

Model names change every year, but these rules don't. Price bands are rough SAR ranges (late 2026), so check current prices before buying.

#Start from what you'll actually do

Guide

List your top 3 tasks (e.g. browsing + Office + video calls, or 1440p gaming, or 4K video editing). Buy for those, not for specs you'll never use.

✓ 1Write down must-haves (weight, battery, a specific app or game)
✓ 2Set a budget including accessories, warranty and software
✓ 3Decide what matters more: portability, performance or price. You usually get two

#Read reviews the right way

Guide

Specs on paper don't show heat, noise, screen quality or battery life. Reviews do.

✓ 1Look for measured results (battery-life tests, display brightness in nits, benchmark charts)
✓ 2Watch for problems that appear after months: user reviews and forums
✓ 3Compare the exact configuration, since the same laptop name can have very different CPUs, GPUs or screens

#Software support & longevity

Guide

How long a device gets security updates matters as much as its hardware.

✓ 1Phones: recent Samsung Galaxy S and Google Pixel models promise up to 7 years of OS/security updates, and many Galaxy A models about 6. iPhones typically get about 6–7 years. Check the maker's current policy
✓ 2Chromebooks: check the Auto Update Expiration (AUE) date before buying
✓ 3Laptops: upgradeable RAM and storage add years of life

#Warranty, returns & where to buy

Guide

✓ 1Buy from official stores or authorised retailers (in Saudi Arabia: brand stores, Jarir, eXtra, Amazon.sa, noon and others) so the local warranty applies
✓ 2Grey imports may be cheaper but can lack local warranty, Arabic keyboards, or the right plugs and network bands
✓ 3Check the return window and keep the box and receipt
✓ 4Extended warranties are worth it mainly for expensive, fragile, hard-to-repair devices

#New vs refurbished vs used

Guide

Refurbished (by the maker or a reputable seller) often gives last year's flagship with a warranty for much less.

✓ 1Used phones: check battery health, that it's not iCloud / Google locked, and the IMEI isn't blacklisted
✓ 2Used laptops: check battery wear, keyboard, ports, screen, hinge, and that BIOS / Windows aren't locked by a company (MDM)
✓ 3Used GPUs: ask about mining use, test under load, check temperatures
✓ 4Meet in safe public places and test before paying

#Avoid these common traps

Guide

✓ 1'Up to' speeds and 'GB of memory' meaning storage, not RAM
✓ 28 GB RAM laptops in 2026, which will struggle soon
✓ 3eMMC '128 GB' storage sold as if it were an SSD
✓ 4Very old CPUs in a new-looking laptop (check the generation number)
✓ 5Huge mAh power banks with no brand, which often have far less real capacity

#Laptops

The most common purchase and the easiest to get wrong. See Part 2 for laptop classes and parts.

#Students & everyday use

Guide

Browsing, Office, Teams/Zoom, streaming. Approx. SAR 1,800–3,500.

✓ 1Thin and light, 16 GB RAM, 512 GB SSD, a bright IPS screen
✓ 2Strong options: MacBook Air (M-series, quiet, long battery), mid-range Windows ultrabooks, Chromebook Plus models for school
✓ 3Arabic/English keyboard printing if you type in both languages

#Programmers & data analysts

Guide

Many browser tabs, IDEs, Docker, databases, Python. Approx. SAR 4,000–8,000.

✓ 132 GB RAM if you use VMs, Docker or large datasets
✓ 2A good keyboard and a 14–16" screen with higher resolution
✓ 3macOS or Linux-friendly hardware (ThinkPad, Framework, Dell) for dev work, or Windows + WSL2

#Gaming laptops

Guide

Approx. SAR 4,000–12,000+ depending on GPU tier.

✓ 1The GPU and its wattage (TGP) decide performance. The same GPU name at 80 W vs 140 W can differ by 30%+
✓ 2A 1080p/1440p screen at 144–240 Hz matched to the GPU
✓ 3Good cooling (check noise and thermals in reviews), 16 GB+ RAM, a spare M.2 slot
✓ 4Accept the trade-offs: weight, short battery life, a big charger

#Creators (photo / video / 3D)

Guide

Approx. SAR 6,000–15,000+.

✓ 1A colour-accurate screen (100% DCI-P3, factory calibrated)
✓ 232 GB+ RAM, a fast 1–2 TB SSD, plus external storage
✓ 3Apple M Pro/Max for video editing efficiency, or Windows with an RTX GPU for 3D, CUDA and AI tools
✓ 4Thunderbolt for fast external drives and displays

#Windows vs macOS vs ChromeOS vs Linux

Guide

Choose the ecosystem first.

✓ 1Windows: widest software and games, most hardware choice
✓ 2macOS: excellent battery and build, iPhone integration, creative apps. Fewer games, no upgrades
✓ 3ChromeOS: cheap, simple, secure, good for schools. Limited offline and pro software
✓ 4Linux: free, private, great for developers. Check hardware support and the apps you need

#Phones & tablets

#What matters most in a phone

Guide

✓ 1Update policy (years of security updates) for longevity and safety
✓ 2Battery & charging: 4,500–6,000 mAh plus fast charging (check whether a charger is included)
✓ 3Camera: look at sample photos at night and with zoom, not megapixel counts
✓ 4Storage: 256 GB is the comfortable minimum without microSD. Check whether it has a microSD slot
✓ 5Local factors: network bands for your carrier, eSIM / dual SIM, Arabic support

#iPhone vs Android

Guide

✓ 1iPhone: long updates, resale value, Apple ecosystem (Mac, Watch, AirPods), privacy features
✓ 2Android: more choice at every price, customisation, often faster charging, USB-C file transfer to PCs, Samsung DeX desktop mode
✓ 3Switching later: both have migration tools, but chat history and app purchases may not move easily

#Tablets

Guide

Approx. SAR 600–6,000+.

✓ 1Media and reading: entry iPad, a mid-range Samsung Tab, Amazon Fire (cheapest)
✓ 2Note-taking and study: a tablet with stylus support (Apple Pencil, S Pen included on many Galaxy Tab S models)
✓ 3Laptop replacement: iPad Pro/Air + keyboard, Galaxy Tab S + DeX, or a Surface Pro (full Windows)
✓ 4Pure reading: an E-ink e-reader (Kindle, Kobo) is lighter and easier on the eyes

#Smartwatches & earbuds

Guide

✓ 1Watches only fully work with their own phone ecosystem (Apple Watch needs an iPhone)
✓ 2Fitness first: Garmin, or Huawei/Amazfit for long battery life
✓ 3Earbuds: check ANC (noise cancelling), codec support (AAC for iPhone, LDAC/aptX for Android), fit and call quality

#Desktop PCs & PC parts

Build or buy prebuilt? Building saves money and gives full control, while prebuilts save time and include one warranty for everything.

#Where to spend & where to save

Guide

✓ 1Spend on: GPU (gaming), CPU (workstation), a quality PSU (a cheap PSU can take everything else with it), an SSD instead of an HDD
✓ 2Save on: RGB, flagship motherboards (mid-range chipsets are fine), cases (good airflow beats looks), more than 32 GB RAM for gaming
✓ 3Plan for upgrades: a newer socket (AM5 has a promised long life), a PSU with headroom, an extra M.2 slot

#Monitors

Guide

Match the monitor to the GPU and use.

✓ 1Office: 24–27" 1080p/1440p IPS, adjustable stand, USB-C if your laptop supports it
✓ 2Gaming: 1080p 144–240 Hz (entry GPU), 1440p 165–240 Hz (sweet spot), 4K 144 Hz (high-end GPU), OLED for contrast and speed
✓ 3Creators: IPS or OLED with wide colour gamut, factory calibration, 4K for detail
✓ 4Check ports (DisplayPort for high refresh) and VESA mount support

#Storage

Guide

✓ 1Main drive: a 1–2 TB NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD with DRAM or a good HMB controller. PCIe 5.0 matters little for gaming yet
✓ 2Mass storage: a large HDD for media and backups, or a big QLC SSD
✓ 3External: a portable SSD (USB 10–20 Gb/s) for speed, an HDD for cheap backup space
✓ 4Always keep backups. One drive is not a backup

#Keyboards, mice & headsets

Guide

✓ 1Keyboard: mechanical or Hall-effect for typing feel and gaming. Choose the size (full, TKL, 75%, 65%) and the Arabic/English legends
✓ 2Mouse: shape and size for your hand matter more than DPI. Wireless low-latency is now as good as wired
✓ 3Headset or mic: a separate USB mic beats most headset mics for calls and streaming

#Chargers, power banks & cables

Small accessories, big safety impact. See Part 7 for cable details.

#Wall chargers (USB-C PD & GaN)

Guide

✓ 1Pick USB-C Power Delivery (PD) chargers. One charger can then serve your phone, tablet and laptop
✓ 2GaN (gallium nitride) chargers are smaller and run cooler at the same wattage
✓ 3Wattage: phones 20–45 W, tablets 30–45 W, ultrabooks 65 W, larger laptops 100–140 W+
✓ 4Multi-port chargers split power between ports, so check the per-port rating
✓ 5Buy reputable brands with safety certifications. Unbranded chargers are a fire risk

#Power banks

Guide

✓ 1Real capacity is lower than the label (about 60–70% reaches your device after conversion losses)
✓ 2Airline rules: banks up to 100 Wh (~27,000 mAh at 3.7 V) are generally allowed in carry-on. 100–160 Wh usually need airline approval. Never put them in checked bags
✓ 3Wh = mAh × 3.7 ÷ 1000, so 20,000 mAh ≈ 74 Wh
✓ 4For laptops you need PD 60–100 W+ output. Phones are fine with 20–30 W
✓ 5Check whether the airline also limits using power banks on board (several airlines now do)

#Cables

Guide

✓ 1For laptops: USB-C cables rated 100 W or 240 W (e-marked)
✓ 2For data or SSDs: the cable must support the speed (USB 3.2 / USB4 / Thunderbolt). Most phone cables are only USB 2.0
✓ 3Braided cables last longer, and it's best to buy certified ones

#Networking & smart home

#Routers & mesh Wi-Fi

Guide

✓ 1Apartment: a single Wi-Fi 6/6E router is usually enough. Larger villas: mesh (2–3 nodes) or access points wired with Ethernet
✓ 2Wi-Fi 7 helps if your devices support it and you have very fast fibre
✓ 3Wire the important devices (PC, console, TV) with Ethernet for stable gaming and streaming
✓ 4Change the default admin password and keep the firmware updated

#Smart home basics

Guide

✓ 1Pick one ecosystem (Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, SmartThings) and check Matter support for cross-brand compatibility
✓ 2Start with simple wins: smart plugs, lights, a doorbell or camera
✓ 3Choose cameras with local storage or end-to-end encryption options for privacy
Part 18

Practical Skills

Command line, keyboard shortcuts, Excel & Google Sheets formulas, Python for data analysis, and tech careers & certifications. Formulas, Python and terminal examples were actually run, and their real results are shown.

#The command line (terminal)

Typing commands is often faster than clicking, and it's essential for servers, developers and IT support. Windows has Command Prompt (cmd) and PowerShell, while macOS and Linux use a Unix shell (zsh/bash). The examples below use a small CSV export of the store orders from the SQL tutorial (Part 9). Use the Bash / PowerShell / Command Prompt / All buttons on any example to switch shells: your choice applies to every example and is remembered. The Bash versions were actually run, and the Windows versions are equivalents written for Windows (PowerShell 7 also runs on macOS and Linux). For a full hands-on course, see the 📁 Linux command line tutorial in Part 9.

#Look at a file: head & wc

Concept

head -n shows the first lines. wc -l counts lines (here: 1 header + 16 orders).

Bash / zsh (Linux, macOS)
head -n 4 orders.csv
wc -l orders.csv
PowerShell (Windows) · not run here
Get-Content orders.csv -TotalCount 4
(Get-Content orders.csv).Count
Command Prompt (cmd) · not run here
rem cmd has no "head", so page through the file instead
more orders.csv
find /c /v "" orders.csv
Output (from the Bash run. PowerShell and cmd show the same data, with slightly different layout)
order_id,order_date,customer,city,product,category,quantity,amount,status
101,2026-01-05,Sarah Ahmed,Riyadh,Keyboard,Accessories,1,150,Completed
102,2026-01-09,Liam Smith,London,Mousepad,Accessories,1,45,Completed
103,2026-02-14,Sarah Ahmed,Riyadh,Monitor,Displays,1,300,Completed
17 orders.csv

#Search with grep

Concept

grep prints lines containing a pattern. -c counts matches, -i ignores case.

Bash / zsh (Linux, macOS)
grep Returned orders.csv
grep -c Riyadh orders.csv
PowerShell (Windows) · not run here
Get-Content orders.csv | Select-String Returned
(Select-String Riyadh orders.csv).Count
Command Prompt (cmd) · not run here
findstr Returned orders.csv
find /c "Riyadh" orders.csv
Output (from the Bash run. PowerShell and cmd show the same data, with slightly different layout)
106,2026-02-25,Yousef Al-Qahtani,Riyadh,Webcam,Accessories,1,95,Returned
114,2026-04-12,Aisha Rahman,Dubai,Mousepad,Accessories,2,90,Returned
8

#Pipes: chain small tools together

Concept

| sends one command's output into the next. Here: take column 4 (city), drop the header, then count each city. That's the Unix philosophy in action.

Bash / zsh (Linux, macOS)
cut -d, -f4 orders.csv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
PowerShell (Windows) · not run here
Import-Csv orders.csv | Group-Object city |
    Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
Command Prompt (cmd) · not run here
rem cmd has no built-in tools for this. Use the PowerShell version,
rem or type  wsl  to open Linux inside Windows and run the Bash version there.
Output (from the Bash run. PowerShell and cmd show the same data, with slightly different layout)
      8 Riyadh
      3 Dammam
      2 London
      2 Dubai
      1 Jeddah

#Calculate with awk

Concept

awk processes columns. Here: total amount per status, the same answer as SQL's GROUP BY.

Bash / zsh (Linux, macOS)
awk -F, 'NR>1 {sum[$9]+=$8} END {for (s in sum) print s, sum[s]}' orders.csv | sort
PowerShell (Windows) · not run here
Import-Csv orders.csv | Group-Object status | Sort-Object Name |
    ForEach-Object { '{0} {1}' -f $_.Name, ($_.Group | Measure-Object amount -Sum).Sum }
Command Prompt (cmd) · not run here
rem cmd can't add up columns on its own. Use the PowerShell version,
rem or type  wsl  to open Linux inside Windows and run the Bash version there.
Output (from the Bash run. PowerShell and cmd show the same data, with slightly different layout)
Completed 2910
Pending 280
Returned 185

#Redirect output to a file

Concept

> writes to a file (overwrites), >> appends. Here we save completed Riyadh orders and count them.

Bash / zsh (Linux, macOS)
grep Riyadh orders.csv | grep Completed > riyadh_completed.csv
wc -l < riyadh_completed.csv
PowerShell (Windows) · not run here
Get-Content orders.csv | Where-Object { $_ -match 'Riyadh' -and $_ -match 'Completed' } > riyadh_completed.csv
(Get-Content riyadh_completed.csv).Count
Command Prompt (cmd) · not run here
findstr Riyadh orders.csv | findstr Completed > riyadh_completed.csv
find /c /v "" < riyadh_completed.csv
Output (from the Bash run. PowerShell and cmd show the same data, with slightly different layout)
7

#File permissions (Linux / macOS)

Concept

ls -l shows permissions like -rwxr-xr--: owner / group / others × read / write / execute. Change them with chmod (e.g. chmod 755 script.sh or chmod +x script.sh) and the owner with chown.

#sudo & administrator rights

Concept

sudo runs one command as the administrator (root) on Linux/macOS. On Windows, open Terminal with Run as administrator. Be careful: commands like rm -rf with sudo can destroy a system instantly, so read before you press Enter.

#Tab completion & history

Concept

Press Tab to auto-complete file and folder names. Press ↑ for previous commands, Ctrl+R to search history (bash/zsh, PSReadLine), Ctrl+C to stop a running command.

#Windows Terminal, PowerShell & WSL

Concept

Windows Terminal hosts cmd, PowerShell and Linux tabs. PowerShell pipes objects, not text (Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5). WSL runs real Linux distros inside Windows (wsl --install).

#SSH: control remote computers

Concept

ssh user@server opens a secure terminal on another machine (servers, Raspberry Pi, routers). Use key-based login (ssh-keygen, then copy the public key) instead of passwords.

#Keyboard shortcuts

The highest-value shortcuts by platform. On a Mac, ⌘ (Command) usually replaces Ctrl.

#Excel & Google Sheets formulas

Spreadsheets are the world's most-used data tool and the natural partner to SQL (Part 9). Every formula below runs against the practice sheet. Classic formulas were calculated by LibreOffice Calc, and Excel 365-only functions were checked with equivalent Python. Formulas work the same in Excel and Google Sheets unless noted.

#Cell references: relative, absolute & mixed

Concept

A1 is relative: it shifts when copied. $A$1 is absolute: it never shifts. $A1 and A$1 are mixed. Press F4 (Windows) to cycle through them. Absolute references are essential for things like a fixed tax rate cell.

Fun fact: Saudi VAT is 15%. Put 0.15 in a cell, name it or reference it as $K$1, and multiply amounts by it.

#SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX

Concept

The basic aggregates. Here: total revenue across all orders.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=SUM(H2:H17)
Output
3375

#AVERAGE

Concept

Average order value (all statuses).

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=AVERAGE(H2:H17)
Output
210.9375

#COUNT vs COUNTA vs COUNTBLANK

Concept

COUNT counts numbers, COUNTA counts non-empty cells, COUNTBLANK counts empty ones. Here: how many customer names there are.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=COUNTA(C2:C17)
Output
16

#COUNTIF

Concept

Count cells meeting one condition: returned orders.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=COUNTIF(I2:I17,"Returned")
Output
2

#SUMIF

Concept

Sum where one condition is met: revenue from Riyadh customers.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=SUMIF(D2:D17,"Riyadh",H2:H17)
Output
1350

#SUMIFS (several conditions)

Concept

Sum with several conditions (all must be true): completed Riyadh revenue. Note that SUMIFS puts the sum range first, unlike SUMIF.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=SUMIFS(H2:H17,D2:D17,"Riyadh",I2:I17,"Completed")
Output
1255

#COUNTIFS with a date range

Concept

Orders placed in March 2026. Build date criteria with ">="&DATE(...).

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=COUNTIFS(B2:B17,">="&DATE(2026,3,1),B2:B17,"<"&DATE(2026,4,1))
Output
5

#AVERAGEIFS

Concept

Average order value for Accessories products.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=AVERAGEIFS(H2:H17,F2:F17,"Accessories")
Output
130.5556

#IF

Concept

If/else for one cell. Row 5 (order 104) is 120 SAR.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=IF(H5>=300,"Large","Small")
Output
Small

#IFS (several conditions)

Concept

Checks conditions in order, like SQL's CASE. Row 6 (order 105) is 560.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=IFS(H6>=300,"Large",H6>=120,"Medium",TRUE,"Small")
Output
Large

#AND / OR inside IF

Concept

Is row 11 (order 110) a completed order of 3+ items?

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=IF(AND(I11="Completed",G11>=3),"Bulk order","Normal")
Output
Bulk order

#VLOOKUP (exact match)

Concept

Look up a value in the first column of a range and return a column to its right. Always use FALSE for exact matches. Here: the amount of the first Monitor order.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=VLOOKUP("Monitor",E2:H17,4,FALSE)
Output
300

Commonly confused with: VLOOKUP can only look to the right and breaks if columns are inserted. INDEX/MATCH and XLOOKUP don't have those problems.

#INDEX + MATCH

Concept

The flexible classic lookup: MATCH finds the position, INDEX returns the value at that position. Here: which customer placed the largest order?

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=INDEX(C2:C17,MATCH(MAX(H2:H17),H2:H17,0))
Output
Fatimah Al-Harbi

#IFERROR

Concept

Replace errors with something friendly, e.g. when a lookup finds nothing.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=IFERROR(VLOOKUP("Tablet",E2:H17,4,FALSE),"Not sold")
Output
Not sold

#XLOOKUP (Excel 365 / Google Sheets)

Concept

The modern replacement for VLOOKUP: looks in any direction, exact match by default, built-in 'not found' value. Here: Noura's first order amount.

Formula (Excel 365 / Google Sheets, result checked with Python)
=XLOOKUP("Noura Al-Futtaim",C2:C17,H2:H17,"none")
Output
120

#SUMPRODUCT

Concept

Multiplies arrays and sums them. It's an old-school way to do multi-condition maths before SUMIFS. Here: total items sold in Riyadh.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=SUMPRODUCT((D2:D17="Riyadh")*G2:G17)
Output
9

#Text: LEFT, MID, FIND, LEN

Concept

Extract the first name: everything before the first space in C2.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=LEFT(C2,FIND(" ",C2)-1)
Output
Sarah

#Text: UPPER, PROPER, TRIM, SUBSTITUTE

Concept

Clean and reformat text. Here: product name in capitals with spaces replaced by dashes (row 6: Portable SSD 1TB).

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=SUBSTITUTE(UPPER(E6)," ","-")
Output
PORTABLE-SSD-1TB

#Joining text: & and TEXTJOIN

Concept

& joins pieces, and TEXTJOIN joins a whole range with a separator (skipping blanks).

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=C2&" ("&D2&")"
Output
Sarah Ahmed (Riyadh)

#TEXT: format numbers & dates

Concept

Turns values into formatted text, for example a month label from a date.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=TEXT(B9,"YYYY-MM")
Output
2026-03

#Dates: YEAR, MONTH, EOMONTH

Concept

End of the month for order 101's date (5 Jan 2026), useful for monthly reports. Format the cell as a date, or you'll see a serial number like 46053.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=EOMONTH(B2,0)
Output
2026-01-31

#DATEDIF: time between dates

Concept

Days between the first and last order. Units: "d", "m", "y".

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=DATEDIF(MIN(B2:B17),MAX(B2:B17),"d")
Output
112

#NETWORKDAYS.INTL with a Saudi weekend

Concept

Working days between two dates with a Friday–Saturday weekend (weekend code 7). Here: working days in March 2026.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=NETWORKDAYS.INTL(DATE(2026,3,1),DATE(2026,3,31),7)
Output
23

Fun fact: Weekend code 1 is Saturday–Sunday (the default), code 7 is Friday–Saturday, used in Saudi Arabia and most of the Gulf.

#ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN

Concept

Round the average order value to 2 decimals.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=ROUND(AVERAGE(H2:H17),2)
Output
210.94

#RANK.EQ

Concept

Rank order 105's amount among all orders (1 = highest).

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=RANK.EQ(H6,H2:H17,0)
Output
1

#MEDIAN & PERCENTILE

Concept

The middle value, which a few huge orders can't skew the way they skew the average.

Formula (result calculated by LibreOffice)
=MEDIAN(H2:H17)
Output
155

#UNIQUE (Excel 365 / Sheets)

Concept

Returns a list of distinct values that 'spills' into cells below. Here: every city with orders.

Formula (Excel 365 / Google Sheets, result checked with Python)
=SORT(UNIQUE(D2:D17))
Output
Dammam
Dubai
Jeddah
London
Riyadh

#FILTER (Excel 365 / Sheets)

Concept

Returns all rows matching a condition as a live, spilling table. Here: Riyadh orders of 150 or more (order, customer, amount).

Formula (Excel 365 / Google Sheets, result checked with Python)
=FILTER(CHOOSECOLS(A2:H17,1,3,8),(D2:D17="Riyadh")*(H2:H17>=150))
Output
101  Sarah Ahmed  150
103  Sarah Ahmed  300
108  Noura Al-Futtaim  160
113  Yousef Al-Qahtani  150
116  Noura Al-Futtaim  280

#SORTBY + TAKE (Excel 365)

Concept

Top 3 orders by amount, customer and amount.

Formula (Excel 365 / Google Sheets, result checked with Python)
=TAKE(SORTBY(CHOOSECOLS(A2:H17,3,8),H2:H17,-1),3)
Output
Fatimah Al-Harbi  560
Khalid Al-Otaibi  360
Sarah Ahmed  300

#LET: name parts of a formula

Concept

Gives names to intermediate values, making long formulas readable (Excel 365 / Sheets). Here: completed revenue divided by number of orders.

Formula (Excel 365 / Google Sheets, result checked with Python)
=LET(done,SUMIFS(H2:H17,I2:I17,"Completed"),n,COUNTA(A2:A17),ROUND(done/n,2))
Output
181.88

#PivotTables

Concept

Drag-and-drop summaries: rows (e.g. city), columns (e.g. month), values (sum of amount), filters. They're the fastest way to do GROUP BY in a spreadsheet. Excel: Insert → PivotTable. Sheets: Insert → Pivot table.

#Tables (Ctrl+T) & structured references

Concept

Format data as a Table and formulas auto-fill and use names like =SUM(Orders[amount]). Charts and pivots then grow automatically as rows are added.

#Conditional formatting & data validation

Concept

Conditional formatting colours cells by rules (e.g. red if returned, colour scales for amounts). Data validation restricts input to dropdown lists, dates or number ranges, which prevents typos at the source.

#Charts that work

Concept

Line charts for trends over time, bar charts for comparing categories, avoid 3D and pie charts with many slices, and always label axes and units (SAR, %).

#Power Query (Get & Transform)

Concept

Excel's built-in tool for importing and cleaning data from files, folders, databases and the web, with recorded, repeatable steps. It's the same engine as in Power BI.

#Google Sheets extras

Concept

QUERY() runs SQL-like queries inside Sheets (=QUERY(A1:I17,"select D, sum(H) group by D")), IMPORTRANGE pulls data from other sheets, GOOGLEFINANCE fetches market data, plus real-time collaboration.

#Python for data analysis

Python is the most popular language for data work (Part 9). Once data is too big or messy for spreadsheets, or you want automation, charts and machine learning, Python with pandas is the next step after SQL. Every example below was executed, and the output shown is real.

#Setting up

Concept

Easiest start: Google Colab (free, in the browser, nothing to install) or Jupyter notebooks. On your PC: install Python from python.org or use Anaconda, then code in VS Code with the Python and Jupyter extensions. Install libraries with pip install pandas.

#Python basics: variables, lists, loops

Concept

Lists hold ordered values, for loops repeat, and f-strings format text.

Python
cities = ["Riyadh", "Jeddah", "Dammam"]
vat = 0.15
for city in cities:
    print(f"{city}: VAT rate {vat:.0%}")
print(len(cities), "cities")
Output
Riyadh: VAT rate 15%
Jeddah: VAT rate 15%
Dammam: VAT rate 15%
3 cities

#Dictionaries & functions

Concept

A dictionary maps keys to values. Functions package reusable logic.

Python
prices = {"Keyboard": 150, "Monitor": 300, "Headset": 120}

def with_vat(amount, rate=0.15):
    return round(amount * (1 + rate), 2)

for product, price in prices.items():
    print(product, price, "->", with_vat(price))
Output
Keyboard 150 -> 172.5
Monitor 300 -> 345.0
Headset 120 -> 138.0

#Load data into a pandas DataFrame

Concept

A DataFrame is a table in Python. In real work you'd use pd.read_csv('orders.csv') or pd.read_excel(...). Here we build it from the same store orders used in the SQL part.

Python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame(FLAT, columns=COLS)
df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"])
print(df.shape)          # (rows, columns)
print(df.head(3).to_string(index=False))

#Select & filter rows

Concept

Boolean masks work like SQL WHERE. Combine with & (and) or | (or), each condition in brackets.

Python
big_riyadh = df[(df["city"] == "Riyadh") & (df["amount"] >= 150)]
print(big_riyadh[["order_id", "customer", "amount"]].to_string(index=False))

#Sort & new columns

Concept

Create calculated columns and sort, like SQL's ORDER BY.

Python
df["amount_with_vat"] = (df["amount"] * 1.15).round(2)
top = df.sort_values("amount", ascending=False).head(3)
print(top[["customer", "product", "amount", "amount_with_vat"]].to_string(index=False))

#groupby: totals per group

Concept

pandas' version of SQL GROUP BY. .agg() computes several summaries at once.

Python
done = df[df["status"] == "Completed"]
summary = (done.groupby("city")
               .agg(orders=("order_id", "count"), revenue=("amount", "sum"))
               .sort_values("revenue", ascending=False))
print(summary.to_string())
Output
        orders  revenue
city                   
Riyadh       7     1255
Dammam       3     1100
Jeddah       1      360
Dubai        1      150
London       1       45

#Monthly trend with dates

Concept

.dt.to_period('M') buckets dates by month, like DATE_TRUNC in SQL.

Python
monthly = (done.groupby(done["order_date"].dt.to_period("M"))["amount"]
               .sum())
growth = (monthly.pct_change() * 100).round(1)
print(pd.DataFrame({"revenue": monthly, "growth_%": growth}).to_string())
Output
            revenue  growth_%
order_date                   
2026-01         195       NaN
2026-02         980     402.6
2026-03         970      -1.0
2026-04         765     -21.1

#pivot_table: a spreadsheet pivot in code

Concept

Rows × columns × values, with zeros filled in.

Python
pivot = df.pivot_table(index="category", columns="status",
                       values="amount", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
print(pivot.to_string())
Output

category                                 
Accessories        990        0       185

#merge: joining tables

Concept

pd.merge works like SQL JOIN. how='left' keeps all rows from the left table.

Python
targets = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Riyadh", "Jeddah", "Dammam"],
                        "target": [900, 400, 600]})
actual = done.groupby("city", as_index=False)["amount"].sum()
report = targets.merge(actual, on="city", how="left").fillna(0)
report["hit_target"] = report["amount"] >= report["target"]
print(report.to_string(index=False))
Output
  city  target  amount  hit_target
Riyadh     900    1255        True
Jeddah     400     360       False
Dammam     600    1100        True

#Missing values

Concept

Find and handle blanks: isna(), fillna(), dropna().

Python
emails = pd.Series(["sarah@example.com", None, "omar@example.com", None])
print("missing:", emails.isna().sum())
print(emails.fillna("(no email)").tolist())
Output
missing: 2
['sarah@example.com', '(no email)', 'omar@example.com', '(no email)']

#Charts with matplotlib

Concept

One line turns a Series into a chart. In notebooks it appears inline, and savefig writes a PNG.

Python
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                  # no screen needed
ax = monthly.plot(kind="bar", title="Completed revenue by month (SAR)")

#Run SQL from Python

Concept

Python's built-in sqlite3 (or DuckDB) lets you combine SQL with pandas.

Python
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
df.drop(columns=["amount_with_vat"]).assign(order_date=df["order_date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")).to_sql("orders", con)
q = "SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status"
