▸FireWire, 30-pin & classic ports3 sections · Cables & connectorsclick to open / close

FireWire 400/800 explained, the 30-pin dock connector, FireWire charging, and every old Mac port with its modern adapter.

1. FireWire (IEEE 1394) in depth2. The Apple 30-pin dock connector3. Other classic Mac ports

#FireWire (IEEE 1394) in depth

Apple's fast cable of the 1990s and 2000s, used for camcorders, audio interfaces, hard drives and the first iPods.

#What FireWire is

1995–2025 Obsolete

A high-speed serial bus that Apple developed and the IEEE standardised as IEEE 1394 in 1995. FireWire was Apple's name. Sony called it i.LINK and Texas Instruments called it Lynx. Unlike USB it is peer-to-peer: a camcorder can copy straight to a tape deck or a hard drive with no computer in between. It also guarantees bandwidth for audio and video (isochronous transfer), hot-plugs, and daisy-chains up to 63 devices.

StandardIEEE 1394 (1995), 1394a (2000), 1394b (2002)
Speeds100 / 200 / 400 / 800 Mbit/s
Max cable4.5 m per hop (FW400)
Devices per bus63

Identify it: A 'Y'-shaped logo with three prongs, or the words FireWire / i.LINK / IEEE 1394 next to the port.

Fun fact: The original iMac DV (1999) put FireWire and iMovie together, which made home video editing mainstream: plug in a MiniDV camcorder and edit.

#Why FireWire beat USB 2.0 in practice

Concept

USB 2.0 is rated 480 Mbit/s, higher than FireWire 400 on paper, but FireWire drives were usually faster in real copies and used less CPU, because FireWire does not need the computer to manage every transfer. Its guaranteed bandwidth meant video capture never dropped frames, so DV camcorders, pro audio interfaces and studio gear stayed on FireWire for years.

#Target Disk Mode

Concept

Hold T while starting a FireWire Mac and it becomes a plain external hard drive for another Mac. It's perfect for rescuing files or migrating to a new Mac. Later Macs do the same over Thunderbolt and USB-C.

#Why FireWire died

2008–2025 Obsolete

Per-port royalties and pricier chips, USB 2.0 being on every PC, then USB 3.0 (2008) and Thunderbolt (2011). Apple dropped it from the aluminium MacBook in 2008. The last Mac with a built-in FireWire port was released in 2012. Apple then sold a Thunderbolt-to-FireWire adapter for many years. macOS 26 Tahoe (2025) removed FireWire support completely: FireWire drives, camcorders and the first iPods no longer appear even through adapters. macOS 15 Sequoia and earlier still work. On Linux, the FireWire maintainer plans to keep support going until 2029.

Commonly confused with: Thunderbolt (2011) used the same plug shape as Mini DisplayPort, not FireWire. Thunderbolt 1/2 is a different technology that can carry FireWire through an adapter.

#Connecting FireWire to a modern computer

Guide

Mac (macOS 15 or earlier only): USB-C/Thunderbolt 3–5 port → Apple Thunderbolt 3 (USB-C) to Thunderbolt 2 adapter → Apple Thunderbolt to FireWire adapter → FireWire 800 cable, or a 9-to-6-pin cable for FireWire 400. The FireWire adapter can't power large bus-powered devices. Windows/Linux desktop: fit a PCIe FireWire card. Cards with a Texas Instruments chipset are the most compatible for DV capture. Laptops without Thunderbolt: use an old FireWire computer instead.

Commonly confused with: Cheap 'USB to FireWire' cables don't transfer data. They're usually just a power lead or a fake. Real USB-to-FireWire adapters basically don't exist.

#Rescuing MiniDV tapes before it's too late

Guide

Capture DV tapes over FireWire while working camcorders and FireWire computers still exist. A Mac on macOS 15 or older with iMovie or Final Cut, or Windows with a capture tool such as WinDV, copies the tape as an exact digital file. Expect about 13 GB per hour of DV video (25 Mbit/s). Keep the original DV files, then make MP4 copies for phones and sharing.

#The Apple 30-pin dock connector

The wide, flat plug on every iPod from 2003 to 2012, the iPhone up to the 4S and the iPad 1 to 3, and the reason so many old speaker docks exist.

Classic Apple & FireWire connectors (plug face views, roughly to scale)

FireWire 400 comes in 4-pin and 6-pin, and only the 6-pin carries power. FireWire 800 uses the 9-pin plug, and a 9-pin-to-6-pin or 9-pin-to-4-pin cable connects it to FireWire 400 devices at 400 Mbit/s.

#Apple 30-pin dock connector

2003–2012 Obsolete

Introduced with the 3rd-generation iPod (April 2003) and replaced by Lightning in September 2012 (iPhone 5, iPod touch 5th gen, iPod nano 7th gen). About 21 mm wide with squeeze-release clips on better cables. Its 30 contacts carried far more than charging: data, audio, video and accessory control.

DevicesiPod 3G–classic, iPod mini, nano 1–6, shuffle (no), touch 1–4, iPhone 2007–4S, iPad 1–3
Width≈ 21 mm
Replaced byLightning (2012)

Identify it: A wide flat plug, about three times as wide as Lightning, with a row of tiny gold contacts and a key (it only fits one way, with the logo up).

#'Charging is not supported with this accessory'

2008→ Obsolete

The first iPods charged from the 30-pin connector's 12 V FireWire pins. Many chargers, car kits and docks used them. The original iPhone could charge that way, but the iPhone 3G (2008) dropped FireWire charging, as did later iPods and iPhones. Plug a newer device into an old FireWire-powered accessory and it shows 'Charging is not supported with this accessory'. Music may still play, but the battery won't charge.

Commonly confused with: It isn't a broken cable. The accessory supplies power on pins the device no longer uses.

#The dock ecosystem

Concept

The 30-pin plug created a whole accessory industry: speaker docks (Bose SoundDock, B&W Zeppelin, iHome clock radios), car stereo kits, FM transmitters and Apple's Universal Dock. Apple's 'Made for iPod' licensing programme (2005) certified them, and that is the origin of today's MFi certification for Lightning and other accessories.

#Lightning to 30-pin Adapter

2012 Obsolete

Apple's adapter (a short plug and a 0.2 m cable version) lets Lightning iPhones and iPods use old 30-pin docks. It carries analogue audio, USB audio, syncing and charging, but not video and not old iPod-remote features, so some car kits and video docks won't work.

Commonly confused with: Third-party 'Lightning to 30-pin' adapters that are only a few millimetres long are often charge-only.

#Using 30-pin devices today

Guide

Use a data cable for syncing, because many cheap 30-pin cables only charge. Any USB-A charger works (iPods and iPhones draw 5 V, up to about 1 A, and iPads up to 2 A). With a USB-C charger or laptop, use a USB-C-to-USB-A adapter. For old FireWire-only iPods (1st and 2nd gen) see the iPod folder. Clean fluff from the port with a wooden toothpick, not metal.

#Other classic Mac ports

If you buy an old Mac, these are the sockets you'll meet on the back.

#Mac power: don't mix up MagSafe versions

Guide

MagSafe 1 (2006–2012) and MagSafe 2 (2012–2017) are different sizes. Apple sold a cheap MagSafe-to-MagSafe-2 converter. Match the wattage too (45 W, 60 W or 85 W): a lower-watt charger may charge slowly or not at all while the Mac is busy. Early T-shaped MagSafe 1 cables fray at the plug, so replace them rather than taping them up.

▸iPod3 sections · 2001–2022click to open / close

The iPod story, every model of iPod, mini, nano, shuffle and touch, and how to sync, repair and upgrade one today.

1. The iPod story2. Every iPod model3. Identify, sync & revive an old iPod

#The iPod story

From '1,000 songs in your pocket' to the last iPod touch.

#iPod (1st generation)

2001 Obsolete

Announced 23 October 2001: a 5 GB, 1.8-inch Toshiba hard drive, a mechanical scroll wheel, FireWire for fast syncing and charging, and Mac-only at first. Its pitch, '1,000 songs in your pocket', beat flash MP3 players that held only a few dozen songs.

Storage5 GB (10 GB from 2002)
ConnectorFireWire 6-pin
Battery≈ 10 hours music

#iTunes & the iTunes Store

Concept

iTunes (January 2001) ripped CDs and synced the iPod. The iTunes Store (April 2003) sold songs for 99 cents each and reached Windows in October 2003. That made buying music legally easy after the Napster era, and the iPod plus iTunes became Apple's turnaround story.

#The click wheel

Concept

The scrolling wheel evolved from a mechanical wheel (1G) to a touch wheel (2G), touch buttons above the wheel (3G), and finally the Click Wheel, with the buttons built into the wheel. The Click Wheel debuted on the iPod mini (2004) and then reached the full-size iPod later that year.

#From iPod to iPhone

Concept

The iPod's success funded the iPhone. Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone in 2007 as an iPod, a phone and an internet communicator in one. Phones then absorbed the music player: iPod sales peaked around 2008. Apple discontinued the shuffle and nano in 2017, the classic in 2014, and the iPod touch in May 2022, ending the iPod line.

The iPod family, 2001–2022

Bars run from launch year to the year the line was discontinued. Every iPod line had ended by May 2022.

#Every iPod model

All five iPod lines, generation by generation.

#Identify, sync & revive an old iPod

Old iPods are popular again. Here's how to get one working.

#Identify your iPod

Guide

Check the wheel and buttons first (see the iPod story section), then the model number on the back (it starts with A, e.g. A1238). Apple's support page 'Identify your iPod model' matches numbers to models. A connected iPod also shows its exact model in Finder or iTunes.

#Syncing on a modern computer

Guide

Mac: since macOS Catalina (2019) iPods sync in Finder (click the iPod in the sidebar), not iTunes. Windows: use iTunes. 1st and 2nd gen iPods are FireWire-only, so they need a FireWire Mac on macOS 15 or earlier, or a PC with a FireWire card. The 3rd gen also syncs over USB 2.0 with the right cable, and everything later uses USB.

Commonly confused with: A Windows-formatted iPod (FAT32) works on both Mac and Windows. A Mac-formatted one (HFS+) only works on a Mac, so restore it from iTunes on Windows if you need both.

#Reset, Disk Mode & Diagnostics (Click Wheel iPods)

Guide

Reset: flick the Hold switch on and off, then hold Menu + centre button for 6–8 seconds until the Apple logo appears. Disk Mode (to force it to show up on a computer): right after the reset, hold centre + Play/Pause. Diagnostics: right after the reset, hold centre + Previous. It has hard-drive tests, useful when buying a used iPod.

#'Sad iPod' & the clicking hard drive

Guide

A sad-face iPod icon, or clicking and buzzing sounds, usually means the 1.8-inch hard drive is failing. They're 15–20 years old now and were never meant to last forever. The popular fix is an iFlash adapter, which replaces the drive with SD or CompactFlash cards. For the iPod video and classic, the iFlash-Sata version takes an mSATA SSD (see Part 1's mSATA vs SATA entries): it's silent, shock-proof, lighter and saves battery.

Fun fact: With an SD adapter and large cards, an iPod classic can hold far more music than the 160 GB it shipped with.

#Battery replacement

Guide

After 15+ years most iPod batteries hold little charge, and a swollen battery that bulges the case must be replaced, never charged. Opening the metal-backed iPods needs plastic opening tools and patience, because the clips are tight. iFixit has step-by-step guides and parts for every model (see Part 16).

#Rockbox: free replacement firmware

Guide

Rockbox is open-source firmware for many older iPods (and other players). It adds FLAC and Ogg playback, gapless audio, themes and games, and lets you copy music by drag-and-drop without iTunes. It can be installed alongside Apple's software. Check rockbox.org for your exact model before installing.

▸Old iPhones3 sections · 2007–2025click to open / close

Every iPhone with its plug and last iOS, the famous controversies, and what an old iPhone can still do.

1. Every iPhone, 2007–20252. iPhone milestones & controversies3. Using an old iPhone today

#Every iPhone, 2007–2025

Each model's big change, plug and final iOS version. Part 3 covers phone hardware in general.

#iPhone milestones & controversies

The stories behind the models.

#The original iPhone launch

2007 Obsolete

Announced at Macworld on 9 January 2007, on sale 29 June 2007 in the US for $499 (4 GB) and $599 (8 GB), on AT&T only. It had no App Store (Apple pushed web apps), no 3G, no GPS, and no copy-and-paste until 2009.

Fun fact: People 'jailbroke' it within weeks to install apps, which helped persuade Apple to open the App Store in July 2008 with about 500 apps.

#Antennagate (2010)

Concept

The iPhone 4's steel band was its antenna, and holding it across a gap at the bottom-left could weaken the signal. Apple gave owners free bumper cases. Later iPhones moved the antenna gaps.

#Bendgate (2014)

Concept

Some iPhone 6 Plus phones bent in tight pockets. Apple strengthened the aluminium in later models (7000-series aluminium from the 6s).

#Batterygate (2017)

Concept

Apple admitted that iOS slowed some older iPhones with worn batteries to prevent sudden shutdowns. It cut battery replacement prices for 2018 and added Battery Health in Settings (iOS 11.3). Lesson for old iPhones: a new battery often makes them feel fast again.

#Touch ID → Face ID

Concept

Touch ID (iPhone 5s, 2013) put a fingerprint reader in the Home button. Face ID (iPhone X, 2017) replaced it with a 3D face scan. The iPhone SE (3rd gen, 2022) was the last iPhone with a Home button.

#Lightning → USB-C

Concept

EU rules requiring USB-C on phones pushed Apple to switch with the iPhone 15 (2023). The iPhone 14 and SE (3rd gen) were the last Lightning iPhones sold.

#Using an old iPhone today

What still works, what doesn't, and what to watch out for when buying one.

#Calls on old iPhones: the network problem

Guide

Many countries are switching off 2G and 3G networks. The original iPhone to iPhone 4S have no 4G, and the iPhone 5, 5c and 5s have 4G data but no VoLTE (voice over 4G), so on a network without 2G/3G they may not make calls at all. VoLTE arrived with the iPhone 6. Check with your carrier before relying on an older iPhone as a phone.

#Apps & websites

Guide

Most current apps need a recent iOS. If you previously downloaded an app with your Apple ID, the App Store may offer the last compatible version for an older iPhone. Old Safari versions can't load many modern websites, because they lack current security certificates and encryption.

#Security

Guide

A phone that no longer gets updates shouldn't be used for banking, work email or passwords. Use it offline or for low-risk jobs instead.

#Good uses for an old iPhone

Guide

A dedicated music player (a better iPod), a kids' offline game and video device, an alarm clock, a smart-home remote, a spare camera, or a piece of a collection. Original and early iPhones are now collectible, especially boxed ones.

#Buying a used iPhone: Activation Lock

2013→ Guide

Since iOS 7, Find My links an iPhone to its owner's Apple ID with Activation Lock. A locked phone can't be set up by anyone else, even after a full erase. Before paying, make sure the seller signs out of their Apple ID and erases the phone in front of you, and that it reaches the 'Hello' setup screen.

Commonly confused with: Activation Lock is different from a carrier (SIM) lock. An iCloud-locked phone is effectively a parts-only phone.

#Restoring old iPhones

Guide

Apple stops 'signing' old iOS versions, so a restore in Finder or iTunes installs the newest version Apple still allows for that model, usually its final release. If the phone won't start, use recovery mode (or DFU mode) and restore. Identify the model in Settings → General → About, or from the A-number on the back or the SIM tray.

#Battery & screen repairs

Guide

Old iPhone batteries degrade and can swell. Replace them rather than charging a bulging phone. iFixit guides cover every model, and Apple's Self Service Repair covers newer ones. See Part 16 for tools and safety.

▸Classic Macs4 sections · 1984–2020sclick to open / close

Four processor eras, landmark Macs from the 128K to M1, every Mac OS version, and how to run and repair vintage Macs.

1. The four eras of the Mac2. Landmark Macs3. Mac OS & macOS versions4. Running & repairing vintage Macs

#The four eras of the Mac

The Mac changed processor three times, more than any other popular computer line.

Four processor eras of the Mac

Each switch came with a translator so old apps kept running: a 68k emulator (1994), Rosetta (2006) and Rosetta 2 (2020). macOS 26 Tahoe (2025) is the last version for Intel Macs.

#Landmark Macs

The machines that defined each era.

#Apple Lisa

1983 Obsolete

Apple's first computer with a graphical interface and a mouse. At $9,995 it flopped, but its ideas went straight into the Macintosh.

#Macintosh 128K

1984 Obsolete

Launched 24 January 1984 for $2,495 with the famous '1984' Super Bowl advert. An 8 MHz Motorola 68000, 128 KB of RAM, a 9-inch black-and-white screen and a 400 KB 3.5-inch floppy drive, all in one compact case with a mouse and a graphical desktop.

Fun fact: The original Mac team's signatures are moulded inside the case.

#Macintosh Plus & SE/30

1986 / 1989 Obsolete

The Plus added 1 MB of RAM and SCSI, and stayed on sale until 1990, longer than any other Mac. The SE/30 put a fast 68030 in the compact case and is a collector favourite.

#Macintosh II

1987 Obsolete

The first colour, expandable Mac, with NuBus slots and a separate monitor. It started the 'big box' professional Mac line.

#PowerBook 100 series

1991 Obsolete

Moved the keyboard back and put a trackball and palm rests in front. Almost every laptop since has copied that layout (see Part 2).

#Power Macintosh 6100

1994 Obsolete

The first PowerPC Macs. A built-in emulator ran old 68k software, a trick Apple repeated with Rosetta.

#Mac clones

1995–1997 Obsolete

Apple licensed Mac OS to Power Computing, Umax, Motorola and others. After Steve Jobs returned in 1997, Apple ended the programme.

#iMac G3

1998 Obsolete

The translucent 'Bondi Blue' all-in-one designed under Jony Ive: USB only, no floppy drive and no old Mac ports. It sold hugely and helped make USB the standard (see Part 1).

Fun fact: Later versions came in fruit colours, and the iMac DV (1999) added FireWire and iMovie.

#iBook G3 'clamshell'

1999 Obsolete

A colourful laptop with a carry handle. It was one of the first consumer laptops built for Wi-Fi (Apple AirPort), when wireless networking was still exotic.

#Power Mac G4 Cube

2000–2001 Obsolete

A silent, fanless 20 cm cube. It was a sales failure, discontinued within a year, but is now in New York's Museum of Modern Art collection.

#iMac G4 & eMac

2002 Obsolete

The iMac G4 had a flat screen on a swivel arm above a dome base ('the lamp'). The eMac was a cheaper CRT Mac for schools.

#Power Mac G5

2003 Obsolete

64-bit PowerPC in an aluminium 'cheese grater' case. Its heat problems helped push Apple to Intel in 2006.

#MacBook Air (original)

2008 Obsolete

Pulled out of a paper office envelope on stage. It had no optical drive and one USB port, and set the template for thin laptops ('ultrabooks').

#Mac Pro 2013 'trash can'

2013 Obsolete

A small black cylinder with dual GPUs. It was hard to upgrade, and Apple publicly admitted the design was a mistake before replacing it in 2019.

#Butterfly keyboard & Touch Bar MacBooks

2015–2023 Obsolete

Very thin 'butterfly' keyboards (2015–2019) jammed from dust, which led to a free repair programme. The Touch Bar (2016) replaced function keys with a touch strip and was dropped after 2023. Avoid buying these used without checking the keyboard carefully.

#AirPower (cancelled)

2017–2019 Defunct brand

A charging mat for iPhone, Apple Watch and AirPods together, announced in 2017 and cancelled in March 2019 before it ever went on sale. Apple replaced the idea with MagSafe (2020). The full story is in the gimmicky tech folder.

#M1 Macs

2020 Current

The first Apple silicon Macs (MacBook Air, MacBook Pro 13", Mac mini) were faster, cooler and much longer-lasting on battery than the Intel models they replaced.

#Mac OS & macOS versions

From System 1 to macOS 26, with what each version is remembered for.

#Running & repairing vintage Macs

Keeping 20- to 40-year-old Macs alive safely.

#Dangers inside old Macs

Guide

Compact Macs (128K to Classic) and old CRT iMacs contain a CRT that can hold a dangerous high-voltage charge even when unplugged. Leave CRT work to people trained to discharge it. Old clock batteries ('PRAM' batteries) leak and eat circuit boards, so remove them from Macs in storage. Leaking electrolytic capacitors on many early-1990s boards (SE/30, Classic, LC, PowerBooks) cause no-sound or no-boot faults, and re-capping fixes them.

#Replacing old drives

Guide

Original SCSI and IDE hard drives are failing. SD-card SCSI emulators (BlueSCSI, ZuluSCSI) replace SCSI drives, IDE-to-CompactFlash/SD adapters replace IDE drives, and floppy emulators such as FloppyEmu stand in for disks. Note that 400K/800K Mac floppies use a format PC floppy drives can't read.

#Yellowed plastic

Guide

Beige Macs turn yellow as flame retardants in the plastic react with light and heat. Hobbyists reverse it with hydrogen-peroxide treatments ('Retr0bright') or sunlight. Results vary and it can make plastic brittle, so test on a hidden part first.

#Emulators: old Macs without the old hardware

Guide

Mini vMac (early 68k Macs), Basilisk II (68k, System 7 to Mac OS 8.1), SheepShaver (PowerPC, Mac OS 9), QEMU (PowerPC Mac OS X) and UTM on Apple silicon Macs. Infinite Mac (infinitemac.org) runs classic Mac OS versions right in a web browser.

#Identify an old Mac

Guide

On a working Mac: Apple menu → About This Mac (or 'About This Macintosh' on classic systems). Otherwise check the model number on the bottom or back, Apple's 'Identify your Mac model' pages, or the EveryMac.com specification database.

#Getting files on and off

Guide

The easiest bridges: a USB stick or CD on iMac-era Macs, Ethernet with file sharing or FTP, or an SD-card drive emulator you can also read on a modern computer. Old browsers can't open most HTTPS sites, so download files on a modern computer and transfer them across.

1. Local AI vs cloud AI: the big picture2. What AI really costs: tokens, plans and electricity

#Local AI vs cloud AI: the big picture

The same kind of model can run in a giant data centre or on the phone in your pocket. Here's how to choose.

#What actually happens when you ask a chatbot

Concept

Your message is split into tokens (word pieces), fed to a large language model (LLM), and the model predicts the answer one token at a time. Cloud AI runs that model on thousands of GPUs in a company's data centre and sends you the answer over the internet. Local AI runs a smaller model on your own phone, laptop or home server. For how models are trained, see AI concepts in Part 14. This part is about using AI today.

#What AI really costs: tokens, plans and electricity

Subscriptions, pay-per-token APIs and running it yourself, worked out in riyals.

#Three ways to pay

Concept

1. Free tiers: smaller or limited models, usage caps, sometimes ads. 2. Monthly plans (about $8–20 for most people, $100+ for heavy users) for the chat apps. 3. APIs: developers pay per million tokens, separately for input (what you send) and output (what the model writes, usually 4–5× more expensive). A chat subscription never includes API usage.

Commonly confused with: The Saudi riyal is pegged at 3.75 SAR = 1 USD, so a $20 plan is 75 SAR before VAT.

#Cost calculator: a customer-support chatbot

Concept

A shop's chatbot answers 2,000 questions a day. Each conversation sends about 1,500 tokens (instructions + history + question) and gets about 400 tokens back. Prices are the official per-million-token rates in November 2026. The last lines estimate the electricity for a home GPU doing the same work locally.

Python
prices = {                       # USD per 1M tokens: (input, output)
    "Claude Haiku 5.5":    (0.10, 0.50),
    "Gemini 4 Hydrogen":   (1.50, 7.50),
    "Claude Sonnet 5.5":   (2.00, 10.00),
    "Claude Opus 5.5":     (4.00, 20.00),
    "Gemini 4 Argon*":     (4.00, 20.00),
}
chats = 2000 * 30                # a month
tok_in, tok_out = 1500, 400
SAR = 3.75

print(f"{'Model':<20}{'USD/month':>11}{'SAR/month':>11}{'SAR (batch -50%)':>18}")
for name, (p_in, p_out) in prices.items():
    usd = chats * (tok_in * p_in + tok_out * p_out) / 1_000_000
    print(f"{name:<20}{usd:>11,.0f}{usd * SAR:>11,.0f}{usd * SAR / 2:>18,.0f}")

# Local: one 350 W GPU writing 40 tokens/second, Saudi tariff 0.21 SAR/kWh (from 2027)
seconds = chats * tok_out / 40
kwh = 0.350 * seconds / 3600
print(f"\nLocal GPU: {seconds / 3600:,.0f} hours of generation, {kwh:,.0f} kWh, about {kwh * 0.21:,.0f} SAR of electricity")
print("(plus the GPU itself, and one GPU can only answer a few people at the same moment)")
Output
Model                 USD/month  SAR/month  SAR (batch -50%)
Claude Haiku 5.5             21         79                39
Gemini 4 Hydrogen           315      1,181               591
Claude Sonnet 5.5           420      1,575               788
Claude Opus 5.5             840      3,150             1,575
Gemini 4 Argon*             840      3,150             1,575

Local GPU: 167 hours of generation, 58 kWh, about 12 SAR of electricity
(plus the GPU itself, and one GPU can only answer a few people at the same moment)

Commonly confused with: Gemini 4 Argon's introductory price of $2 / $10 ends on 30 November 2026.

Sources: Claude API pricing (official) · TechJack Solutions: Gemini 4 API prices from Google's pricing page (Nov 2026) · BuildMVPFast: Gemini 4 Argon price doubles on 1 December 2026

#Subscription or API?

Concept

If you just chat, a plan is simpler and usually cheaper. If you're building something (a website feature, an automation in n8n, a bot), you need the API. Many developers start with free API credits or a cheap small model, then move up only when quality demands it.

▸Cloud AI5 sections · Beginner → developerclick to open / close

ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and HUMAIN Chat plans; today's models and API prices; using APIs from code; privacy; Arabic and Saudi AI.

1. Cloud AI apps & plans (November 2026)2. Today's frontier models (November 2026)3. Using cloud AI from code (APIs)4. Privacy, safety & rules for cloud AI5. Arabic & Saudi AI

#Cloud AI apps & plans (November 2026)

The big chat assistants, what the plans cost, and what you get.

#How to pick a plan

Guide

Start free on two or three assistants for a week with your real tasks (homework, emails in Arabic and English, code, summaries). Pay for the one you keep reaching for. Only consider $100+ tiers if you hit the limits every day, usually for heavy coding or research. One paid plan plus free tiers of the others covers most people.

#Today's frontier models (November 2026)

The model behind the app matters more than the app's name.

#Benchmarks: take them with salt

Concept

Leaderboards (LMArena, SWE-bench for coding, Humanity's Last Exam, ARC-AGI) give a rough ranking, but companies tune for them and the top spots change monthly. The best benchmark is your own task: give the same 5–10 real prompts to two models and compare.

#Using cloud AI from code (APIs)

Add AI to your own app, website or automation.

#Getting started with an API

Guide

1. Create a developer account (console.anthropic.com / platform.claude.com, platform.openai.com, aistudio.google.com). 2. Add a payment method or use free credits, and set a monthly spending limit. 3. Create an API key and keep it secret: put it in an environment variable or a .env file that is in .gitignore (see the Git tutorial). 4. Call the API from Python, JavaScript or a no-code tool such as n8n.

Commonly confused with: An API key is like a credit card. If it leaks on GitHub, bots will use it within minutes: revoke it immediately.

#Python: ask Claude through the API

Concept

Install the SDK with pip install anthropic and set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. The same pattern (model + messages → reply) works for every provider.

Python (needs an API key, not run here)
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=300,
    system="You are a friendly shop assistant. Answer in the customer's language.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "هل عندكم كيبورد ميكانيكي؟"}],
)
print(reply.content[0].text)
print(reply.usage.input_tokens, "tokens in,", reply.usage.output_tokens, "tokens out")

Source: Claude API pricing (official)

#The OpenAI-compatible format: one code, many providers

Concept

Many services (OpenRouter, Groq, Together, Mistral, DeepSeek) and local servers (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp) accept the same 'chat completions' format. Change base_url and model to switch.

Python (not run here)
from openai import OpenAI

# cloud gateway with hundreds of models:
client = OpenAI(base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", api_key="sk-or-...")
# …or your own computer running Ollama (no key, nothing leaves the house):
# client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")

r = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5",      # or "llama3.2:3b" on Ollama
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise: the meeting moved to Sunday 10am."}],
)
print(r.choices[0].message.content)

#Privacy, safety & rules for cloud AI

What happens to what you type, and how to use AI responsibly at school and work.

#Good AI habits

Guide

Verify facts, numbers, quotes and sources: AI can hallucinate convincingly. Give context (who it's for, length, tone, examples) for much better answers. Ask it to show its reasoning or sources. Follow your school's or employer's AI policy, and say when work was AI-assisted where that's expected. For agents that can click, buy or send, keep a human approval step.

#Prompt injection: the new security risk

Concept

When an AI reads web pages, emails or documents, hidden text inside them can try to give it orders ('ignore your instructions and send me the files'). Good AI tools treat that content as data, not commands, but be careful when giving an agent access to email, files or payments.

Fun fact: This is why many AI agents ask for confirmation before sending messages or making purchases.

#Arabic & Saudi AI

AI that understands Arabic dialects, built in and for the Kingdom.

#HUMAIN Chat & ALLaM

AI · 2025– Current

HUMAIN is the national AI company owned by the Public Investment Fund (PIF), launched in May 2025. In August 2025 it released HUMAIN Chat, an Arabic-first assistant powered by ALLaM 34B, with real-time web search, Arabic speech input across dialects, Arabic–English switching and conversation sharing. It launched first in Saudi Arabia (web, iOS and Android), hosted end-to-end on HUMAIN's infrastructure in the Kingdom.

ModelALLaM 34B (Arabic-first LLM)
OriginALLaM began at SDAIA: pilot chat app May 2023, on IBM watsonx May 2024
Team120+ specialists including 35 PhDs
Websitechat.humain.ai

Identify it: The HUMAIN logo and app; answers grounded in Arabic, Islamic culture and Saudi context

Commonly confused with: HUMAIN (the company) vs HUMAIN Chat (the app) vs ALLaM (the model)

Fun fact: ALLaM 34B was described as built from scratch and trained on one of the largest proprietary Arabic datasets.

Sources: Arab News: HUMAIN Chat launches in the Kingdom (Aug 2025) · Mobile World Live: HUMAIN launches Arabic-trained AI app · Middle East AI News: HUMAIN Chat goes live with ALLaM 34B

#Tips for better Arabic answers

Guide

Write the prompt in Arabic if you want Arabic back, and say the variety: 'بالعربية الفصحى' or 'باللهجة السعودية'. Give an example sentence of the tone you want. For translations, say who the reader is (a government form, a TikTok caption, a child). For RTL documents, ask for plain text and paste it into your editor, because some apps mix up punctuation direction.

▸Local AI: phone & PC3 sections · Beginner → intermediateclick to open / close

Open-weight models, AI fully offline on your phone, a phone as an AI server, and a local AI server on a PC or Mac.

1. Open-weight models: the engines of local AI2. Your phone as a local AI3. Local AI on a PC, Mac or home server

#Open-weight models: the engines of local AI

Models you can download, run, change and (depending on the licence) use commercially.

#Ollama in five commands

Concept

Install from ollama.com (Windows, macOS, Linux), then use the terminal. Models download once and work offline afterwards.

Terminal (not run here)
ollama pull qwen3:8b          # download a model (≈5 GB)
ollama run qwen3:8b           # chat in the terminal (/bye to exit)
ollama list                   # what's installed
ollama ps                     # what's loaded in memory right now
ollama rm qwen3:8b            # delete it to free space

Commonly confused with: Model tags change. Search ollama.com/library for current names and sizes before pulling.

#Your phone as a local AI

Modern phones can run real language models fully offline: private, free, and working on a plane.

#Why run AI on your phone?

Concept

Privacy (nothing leaves the device), works offline (desert trips, flights, bad signal), free after the model download, and fun to experiment with. The trade-off: phone models are small (about 1–8 billion parameters), so they're good at summarising, rewriting, translation, quick questions and brainstorming, but weaker at complex reasoning and facts than big cloud models. Expect roughly 3–15 words per second (tokens/s), and the phone will get warm and use battery quickly.

Source: PromptQuorum: mobile local LLMs (2026)

#Getting started in 5 minutes

Guide

1. Install PocketPal AI or Google AI Edge Gallery. 2. On Wi-Fi, download a small model (1–4B) that the app recommends for your phone. 3. Switch on airplane mode and chat to prove it's fully offline. 4. Try tasks it's good at: 'summarise this', 'make this email more polite', 'translate to Arabic', 'give me 10 names for…'. Double-check facts, because small models make things up more often than big ones.

#Hack: turn an Android phone into an AI server for your home

Concept

With Termux (most guides recommend installing it from F-Droid or GitHub), an Android phone can run Ollama and answer requests from any device on your Wi-Fi: your PC, Home Assistant, n8n workflows or Open WebUI. Keep it plugged in with a battery charge limit on, and expect it to get warm.

Termux / bash (not run here)
# inside Termux on the Android phone
pkg update && pkg upgrade
pkg install ollama
OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 ollama serve &     # listen on the Wi-Fi network, not just the phone
ollama pull llama3.2:1b                # or another small model that fits the phone's RAM

# from any computer on the same Wi-Fi (replace with the phone's IP address):
curl http://192.168.1.60:11434/api/generate \
     -d '{"model": "llama3.2:1b", "prompt": "Explain VLANs in one sentence", "stream": false}'

Commonly confused with: Only do this on a trusted home network. Ollama has no password, so anyone on the same Wi-Fi can use it. Never port-forward it to the internet.

Sources: Coder Legion: run Ollama on Android without root (pkg install ollama) · Jonathan's Blog: llama.cpp in Termux (pkg install llama-cpp)

#Local AI on a PC, Mac or home server

More memory means bigger, smarter models.

#Local AI server with Docker: Ollama + Open WebUI

Concept

Two containers give you a private ChatGPT-style site at http://server-ip:3000 for everyone at home. On an NVIDIA GPU, add the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and a GPU reservation to the ollama service.

docker-compose.yml (not run here)
services:
  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ollama:/root/.ollama           # downloaded models live here
    ports:
      - "11434:11434"
  open-webui:
    image: ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      - OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://ollama:11434
    ports:
      - "3000:8080"
    volumes:
      - open-webui:/app/backend/data
volumes:
  ollama:
  open-webui:

#Useful local-AI projects

Guide

Private document chat: load PDFs into Open WebUI or AnythingLLM and ask questions. Voice assistant: Home Assistant Assist + Whisper + a local model controls the house without the cloud. Automations: n8n calls the Ollama API to sort emails or summarise RSS feeds. Transcription: whisper.cpp turns lectures into searchable text. Always check each model's licence before commercial use.

▸Hybrid: the best of both1 section · Intermediateclick to open / close

Combine local and cloud models: Open WebUI, routers, automations, and starter kits by budget.

1. Hybrid setups: local + cloud together

#Hybrid setups: local + cloud together

Use local AI for private and simple work, and the cloud for the hard stuff.

#A simple routing rule you can apply by hand

Guide

Private? → local. Needs today's news or web search? → cloud. Hard reasoning, long code, important decision? → the best cloud model, then double-check. Quick rewrite, translation, summary of non-sensitive text? → whichever is closest at hand.

1. Wi-Fi generations: from Wi-Fi 4 to Wi-Fi 82. Routers, mesh, access points & switches

#Wi-Fi generations: from Wi-Fi 4 to Wi-Fi 8

The numbers on the router box, and what they really mean at home.

#Wi-Fi 8 (802.11bn)

Networking · draft → 2028 Concept

Wi-Fi 8 doesn't raise the top speed. Its goal is Ultra High Reliability: about a quarter less lag at the worst moments (the 95th percentile), fewer lost packets, smoother roaming, and neighbouring access points that coordinate instead of fighting for airtime. In July 2026 the IEEE group sent Draft 2.0 to ballot; Wi-Fi Alliance certification is expected around January 2028 and final IEEE approval later in 2028. Early chips were shown at CES 2026, but certified consumer routers aren't expected before then.

Status (Nov 2026)Draft standard
CertificationExpected ~2028
Speed vs Wi-Fi 7Same peak, better consistency

Identify it: Boxes saying 'Wi-Fi 8 ready' before 2028 are pre-standard

Commonly confused with: Wi-Fi 8 (WLAN) vs 5G/6G (mobile networks)

Fun fact: Buying advice for now: a good Wi-Fi 7 (or Wi-Fi 6E) router or mesh is the right choice, and it will stay useful for years.

Sources: Evetech: Wi-Fi 8 in 2026, where the standard actually stands · ABI Research: Wi-Fi 8 Draft 2.0 sent to ballot (July 2026) · Dr. Web: Wi-Fi 8, reliability instead of speed (German)

#Saudi Arabia and the 6 GHz band

Networking · 2021 Concept

On 30 March 2021 the Saudi regulator (then CITC, now CST) opened the entire 6 GHz band (5925–7125 MHz, 1,200 MHz) for licence-free Wi-Fi, the first country in Europe, the Middle East and Africa to do so. That means Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 routers sold in the Kingdom can use all seven 160 MHz channels or three 320 MHz channels in 6 GHz.

RegulatorCST (Communications, Space & Technology Commission), formerly CITC
SpectrumFull 1,200 MHz at 6 GHz

Commonly confused with: Many countries opened only the lower half (500 MHz) of the 6 GHz band, so routers from abroad may be locked to fewer channels

Fun fact: Saudi Arabia ended up with more than 2 GHz of mid-band spectrum for Wi-Fi, among the most of any country.

Sources: RCR Wireless: Saudi Arabia designates the entire 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi (Mar 2021) · Intel: Saudi Arabia opens full 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi

#Wi-Fi names on your devices

Concept

Phones and laptops show the generation as 'Wi-Fi 6', '6E' or '7' in settings or spec sheets. On Windows, netsh wlan show interfaces shows the radio type (802.11ax = Wi-Fi 6, 802.11be = Wi-Fi 7). Your connection runs at the level of the older side: a Wi-Fi 7 router doesn't make a Wi-Fi 5 laptop faster (though it can still help with range and crowding).

#Routers, mesh, access points & switches

The boxes that make a home network, and where to put them.

#Getting great Wi-Fi at home

Guide

1. Put the router or main node central and high, out of cabinets, away from the AC unit and microwave. 2. In a villa, use one mesh node or AP per floor, ideally connected by Ethernet. 3. Wire the things that don't move: TV, PC, console, NAS. 4. Use one network name (SSID) for 2.4/5/6 GHz and let devices choose, unless an old smart device needs 2.4 GHz only. 5. Update the router firmware and change the admin password. 6. Concrete and blockwork walls typical in Saudi homes block Wi-Fi strongly, so plan for more nodes than the box suggests.

#Calculator: Mbps vs MB/s, and how long a download takes

Concept

Internet plans are sold in megabits per second (Mbps). Downloads show megabytes per second (MB/s). 1 byte = 8 bits, so divide by 8, then take off roughly 10% for overheads.

Python
plans_mbps = [100, 200, 500, 1000]
game_gb = 80                                  # a big console/PC game
print(f"{'Plan':>10}{'Real MB/s':>11}{'80 GB game':>13}{'4 GB movie':>12}")
for mbps in plans_mbps:
    mb_per_s = mbps / 8 * 0.9                 # bits → bytes, ~10% overhead
    game_min = game_gb * 1000 / mb_per_s / 60
    movie_min = 4 * 1000 / mb_per_s / 60
    print(f"{mbps:>6} Mbps{mb_per_s:>11.1f}{game_min:>9.0f} min{movie_min:>9.1f} min")
Output
      Plan  Real MB/s   80 GB game  4 GB movie
   100 Mbps       11.2      119 min      5.9 min
   200 Mbps       22.5       59 min      3.0 min
   500 Mbps       56.2       24 min      1.2 min
  1000 Mbps      112.5       12 min      0.6 min

#Troubleshooting checklist

Guide

Everything slow? Run a speed test wired to the router (fast.com, speedtest.net). If wired is fine, the problem is Wi-Fi. One device slow? Forget the network and reconnect, move closer, update drivers. Drops at night? Check for overheating and congestion; try a different channel. Websites won't load but apps do? Try another DNS (1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8). Still bad? Restart ONT → router → mesh in that order, then call the ISP with your wired speed-test results.

1. Home internet in Saudi Arabia

#Home internet in Saudi Arabia

Fibre, 5G home and the providers, plus what to ask before you sign.

#Questions to ask before signing

Guide

1. Is fibre available at my exact address (not just the district)? 2. What are the upload speed and contract length? 3. Can I use my own router (bridge mode / PPPoE details)? 4. Do I get a public IP, or am I behind CGNAT? (5G home and some plans share one public IP between many customers, which blocks port-forwarding; home-labbers can use Tailscale or Cloudflare Tunnel instead, see Part 20.) 5. What happens after the data cap or fair-use limit, if any? 6. Is there an installation fee or a router deposit?

#Who regulates it

Concept

The Communications, Space and Technology Commission (CST), formerly CITC, licenses providers, sets quality rules and handles complaints you can't resolve with the provider (cst.gov.sa). Some content is filtered under Saudi law.

Source: Expat Focus: Saudi Arabia internet guide (reviewed May 2026)

#Smart-home protocols: Wi-Fi, Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread & Matter

How smart devices talk, and why it matters when you buy them.

#Matter

Smart home · 2022– Current

Matter is a royalty-free standard from the Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA), backed by Apple, Google, Amazon and Samsung, so one device works in every major app and is controlled locally (no cloud round trip). Matter 1.4 (Nov 2024) improved home routers and energy devices. Matter 1.5 (20 Nov 2025) finally added cameras and video doorbells (live streams, two-way talk, privacy zones), closures such as blinds and garage doors, soil sensors and more energy management. Maintenance release 1.5.1 followed on 31 March 2026, and SmartThings was the first big platform to support Matter cameras.

Runs overWi-Fi, Thread, Ethernet
ControllersApple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings, Home Assistant
Latest (Nov 2026)Matter 1.5.x

Identify it: The Matter logo on the box, plus a pairing QR code and number on the device or manual

Commonly confused with: Matter (the language) vs Thread (one of the radios it uses)

Fun fact: With 'multi-admin', one Matter device can be in Apple Home and Google Home at the same time.

Sources: CSA: Matter 1.5 introduces cameras, closures and energy management · The Gadgeteer: Matter 1.5 cameras and doorbells (1.5.1 on 31 Mar 2026) · Matter Alpha: SmartThings first to support Matter 1.5 cameras

#Buying rule of thumb

Guide

Prefer Matter devices (over Thread for battery sensors, over Wi-Fi for plugs and cameras), or Zigbee if you run Home Assistant. Avoid devices that only work with one brand's cloud app: if the company shuts the server, the device can stop working.

#Ecosystems, devices & a Saudi smart home

Choosing a platform, what to automate first, and keeping it secure.

#Buying smart devices in Saudi Arabia

Guide

Check the device is rated for 220–240 V, 60 Hz and comes with the Saudi plug or a proper fitting, carries SASO approval where required, and that the app works in the Saudi region. For wall switches, many Saudi homes don't have a neutral wire in the switch box, so look for 'no neutral required' models or ask an electrician. AC-related devices must handle the start-up current of the unit, so use controllers made for ACs rather than ordinary smart plugs.

#Point of sale (POS): the shop counter

Everything that sits on a cash counter, and how it connects.

#What a POS system is

Concept

A point of sale is where a sale is completed. Today it's a small computer running POS software that scans items, totals the bill, adds VAT, takes payment, prints or sends a receipt, updates stock and reports the sale. In Saudi Arabia it must also produce ZATCA-compliant e-invoices (see the receipts folder).

Commonly confused with: People in Saudi Arabia often say 'الشبكة' or 'جهاز الشبكة' for the card machine. The POS is the whole cashier system; the card machine is just the payment part.

#Setting up a small shop counter: a checklist

Guide

1. Pick the software first, then hardware it supports. 2. Put the POS on wired Ethernet if possible, and keep payment devices on a separate network from guest Wi-Fi. 3. Add a small UPS so a power cut doesn't kill a sale halfway. 4. Keep a spare paper roll within reach (and spares in a cool place). 5. Test offline mode: what happens when the internet drops? 6. Train staff on refunds, voids and end-of-day reports. 7. Back up the product list.

#POS terminal ports explained

The colour-coded back panel of a restaurant or shop terminal, port by port. Many of these look like normal PC ports but aren't.

123445678910101112

A real POS terminal's back panel (Oracle MICROS-style restaurant workstation). The numbers match the table above.

#Receipt & label printers

The little printers that never need ink, and the commands that drive them.

#Thermal printing: why receipts need no ink

Concept

Direct thermal printers heat tiny dots on a print head against heat-sensitive paper, which turns black. No ink, no toner, few moving parts, very fast. The catch: the print fades with heat, sunlight and time, and the paper goes black if it gets hot, so a receipt left on a Riyadh car dashboard in summer can turn grey in a day.

Fun fact: Scratch thermal paper with a fingernail: the friction heat leaves a dark line. Normal paper doesn't.

#ESC/POS: how a POS talks to a receipt printer

Concept

Most receipt printers understand ESC/POS, a command language created by Epson: plain text plus short codes that start with ESC (byte 27) or GS (byte 29). This builds the bytes for a tiny receipt, the same bytes a POS app would send over USB or the network to port 9100.

Python
ESC, GS = b"\x1b", b"\x1d"
init        = ESC + b"@"                 # reset the printer
center      = ESC + b"a" + bytes([1])    # align centre
left        = ESC + b"a" + bytes([0])
bold_on     = ESC + b"E" + bytes([1])
bold_off    = ESC + b"E" + bytes([0])
double_size = GS + b"!" + bytes([0x11])  # double width and height
normal_size = GS + b"!" + bytes([0])
cut         = GS + b"V" + bytes([66, 0]) # feed and cut
open_drawer = ESC + b"p" + bytes([0, 25, 250])  # pulse to the cash-drawer port

receipt = (init + center + double_size + b"RIYADH TECH\n" + normal_size
           + b"VAT 310122393500003\n" + left
           + b"1 x USB-C cable        35.00\n"
           + bold_on + b"TOTAL SAR              35.00\n" + bold_off
           + b"\n\n" + cut + open_drawer)

print(len(receipt), "bytes to send to the printer (USB, or TCP port 9100)")
print("First bytes:", receipt[:14].hex(" "))
print("1b 40 = ESC @ (reset), 1b 61 01 = centre, 1d 21 11 = double size")
print("Last bytes: ", receipt[-9:].hex(" "), "= cut paper, then pulse the drawer")
Output
121 bytes to send to the printer (USB, or TCP port 9100)
First bytes: 1b 40 1b 61 01 1d 21 11 52 49 59 41 44 48
1b 40 = ESC @ (reset), 1b 61 01 = centre, 1d 21 11 = double size
Last bytes:  1d 56 42 00 1b 70 00 19 fa = cut paper, then pulse the drawer

#Arabic on receipt printers

Guide

Arabic letters change shape depending on their position, and text runs right to left. Many cheap printers' built-in fonts can't do this properly, so good POS apps draw the receipt as an image (raster) and send that. If Arabic prints as reversed or disconnected letters, switch the app's printer setting to 'image/graphics mode' or use a printer model the POS vendor certifies.

#E-invoicing in Saudi Arabia (ZATCA Fatoora)

Why every Saudi receipt has a QR code, and what's inside it.

#ZATCA e-invoicing (Fatoora)

Business · 2021– Current

Saudi Arabia's Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority made electronic invoices mandatory for VAT-registered businesses. Phase 1 (Generation) started on 4 December 2021: invoices must come from a compliant electronic system (no handwritten or Excel invoices), and simplified invoices to consumers must carry a QR code. Phase 2 (Integration) began on 1 January 2023 in waves by turnover: systems must produce XML (UBL 2.1) invoices with a cryptographic stamp and connect to ZATCA's Fatoora platform. Wave 24 (turnover SAR 375,000–750,000) had to integrate by 30 June 2026, and wave 25 must integrate by 1 February 2027.

AuthorityZATCA (هيئة الزكاة والضريبة والجمارك)
PlatformFatoora (فاتورة)
Format (Phase 2)UBL 2.1 XML + cryptographic stamp
QR codeTLV, Base64

Identify it: A QR code on every simplified tax invoice (receipt)

Commonly confused with: Tax invoice (B2B, cleared by ZATCA before it's sent) vs simplified tax invoice (B2C receipt, reported within 24 hours)

Fun fact: ZATCA notifies each wave at least six months before its deadline.

Sources: ZATCA: E-Invoicing (Fatoora) official page · KPMG: Saudi Arabia wave 25 of e-invoicing integration (Jul 2026) · ClearTax: ZATCA wave 24 (deadline 30 June 2026) · Noqta: Fatoorah guide, phase 1 vs phase 2 and the TLV QR code

#Decode (and build) a ZATCA receipt QR code

Concept

The QR code holds TLV data: for each field, a Tag number, the Length in bytes, then the Value, all joined and Base64-encoded. This builds the five basic fields for the receipt shown below, then decodes it like a scanner app would. (Arabic seller names work too, because the length counts UTF-8 bytes.)

Python
import base64

def tlv(fields):
    raw = b""
    for tag, value in fields:
        v = value.encode("utf-8")
        raw += bytes([tag, len(v)]) + v
    return base64.b64encode(raw).decode()

items = [("USB-C cable 1m", 1, 35.00), ("Thermal paper 80mm x5", 2, 25.00), ("Mouse", 1, 60.00)]
total = sum(q * p for _, q, p in items)          # shelf prices include 15% VAT
vat = round(total * 15 / 115, 2)

qr = tlv([(1, "Riyadh Tech Store"), (2, "310122393500003"), (3, "2026-11-19T16:50:00Z"),
          (4, f"{total:.2f}"), (5, f"{vat:.2f}")])
print("QR text:", qr)

names = {1: "Seller", 2: "VAT number", 3: "Time", 4: "Total incl. VAT", 5: "VAT"}
raw, i = base64.b64decode(qr), 0
while i < len(raw):
    tag, length = raw[i], raw[i + 1]
    print(f"{names[tag]:<16}{raw[i + 2:i + 2 + length].decode()}")
    i += 2 + length
print(f"Price before VAT: {total - vat:.2f} SAR")
Output
QR text: ARFSaXlhZGggVGVjaCBTdG9yZQIPMzEwMTIyMzkzNTAwMDAzAxQyMDI2LTExLTE5VDE2OjUwOjAwWgQGMTQ1LjAwBQUxOC45MQ==
Seller          Riyadh Tech Store
VAT number      310122393500003
Time            2026-11-19T16:50:00Z
Total incl. VAT 145.00
VAT             18.91
Price before VAT: 126.09 SAR

Source: Noqta: Fatoorah guide, phase 1 vs phase 2 and the TLV QR code

Riyadh Tech Store

فاتورة ضريبية مبسطة · Simplified tax invoice
VAT No. 310122393500003
19/11/2026 16:50 · #000123
1 × USB-C cable 1m35.00
2 × Thermal paper 80mm x550.00
1 × Mouse60.00
VAT 15% (incl.)18.91
TOTAL SAR145.00
mada contactless145.00
شكراً لزيارتكم · Thank you!
What this receipt is made of: an 80 mm thermal roll, text sent as ESC/POS commands, the Arabic lines usually printed as an image, and a real ZATCA-style QR code (generated when this book was built). Scan it with any QR app and you'll see Base64 text. The Python decoder above turns it back into the seller name, VAT number, time, total and VAT. A Phase 2 (integration) invoice adds four more tags: the invoice hash, a digital signature, the public key and ZATCA's stamp signature.
▸Card machines & payments1 section · Everyoneclick to open / close

1. Card machines: from the 'old phone' to Android and Tap to Pay

#Card machines: from the 'old phone' to Android and Tap to Pay

How shops take card payments, and how the machines evolved.

#The classic keypad card terminal (the 'old phone')

Business · 1980s–2010s Legacy

The beige or black box with a phone-style keypad, a small screen and a coiled cable into the wall phone socket. Early models had only a magnetic-stripe slot and connected over the telephone line (PSTN) with a built-in modem; later ones added a chip reader, a PIN pad and Ethernet or a SIM card. Verifone (founded 1981) and Ingenico made most of them. Many shops kept these for years because they just worked, but dial-up lines, magnetic stripe and old encryption were retired as networks moved to EMV chip, contactless and IP connections.

InputsMagstripe → chip → contactless
ConnectionPhone line (dial-up) → Ethernet → GPRS/3G/4G
PrinterBuilt-in thermal paper roll
MakersVerifone, Ingenico, Hypercom, PAX

Identify it: Phone-style 12-key keypad, green/yellow/red buttons (OK, clear, cancel), a slot on the side or top, and an RJ11 phone cable

Commonly confused with: A card terminal (talks to the bank) vs a PIN pad (only takes the card and PIN, connected to a terminal or POS)

Fun fact: The coloured buttons (green = enter, yellow = clear, red = cancel) are still on almost every card machine, including Android ones.

#Contactless, chip, PIN: what's secure

Concept

Chip (EMV) and contactless create a one-time code for each payment, so copying a card is much harder than with the old magnetic stripe. Apple Pay / Google Pay / mada Pay add tokenisation: the shop never sees the real card number. Never let a card leave the customer's sight, never write down PINs, and don't use a terminal that looks tampered with (loose parts, extra layers on the slot).

Commonly confused with: 'Tap on phone' (the shop's phone accepts cards) is not the same as paying with your phone (Apple Pay).

#Sejin Electron SWK-865x wireless trackball keyboards (incl. SWK-8657WKD)

Business · 2000s–2010s Legacy

Sejin Electron (Seoul, now SJK Co.) took over Futaba's keyboard business in 1991 and became a major OEM keyboard maker: it builds keyboards that other companies sell under their own names. Its SWK-865x family are compact wireless keyboards with a built-in trackball and mouse buttons, made for video-conference rooms, medical carts, kiosks and industrial PCs. For example, the SWK-8653WT was sold as a Polycom conference-system keyboard, and the SWK-8650RT uses 2.4 GHz frequency-hopping radio. The SWK-8657WKD belongs to this family; its exact specs aren't publicly documented, so check the label on the back (FCC ID starting GJJ) and look that ID up on fccid.io for its manual.

MakerSejin Electron Inc. (FCC grantee code GJJ)
FamilySWK = Sejin wireless keyboard; 865x = compact trackball models
Radio2.4 GHz RF (older models infrared)
NeedsIts matching USB receiver (Sejin SWR-series)

Identify it: Small rectangular keyboard with a trackball on the right and two mouse buttons; a brand like Polycom on the front and 'SEJIN ELECTRON INC' on the rear label

Commonly confused with: SWK (wireless) vs SPR (wired mini keyboards like the SPR-8695) vs SKR/SKM (desktop keyboards)

Fun fact: Without its own receiver dongle these keyboards usually can't connect to anything: they don't use Bluetooth, so a phone or laptop can't pair with them directly.

Sources: Deskthority wiki: Sejin Electron · fccid.io: all Se Jin Electron filings (GJJ) · SWK-8650RT 2.4 GHz RF keyboard manual

#IT basics every small business should have

Guide

1. Business email on your own domain (Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace), with two-factor login for everyone. 2. Backups: the 3-2-1 rule (3 copies, 2 types of storage, 1 off-site). 3. A password manager for shared accounts. 4. Separate Wi-Fi for guests, and a different network for the POS and card machines. 5. Automatic updates on every PC and phone. 6. An asset list: who has which laptop, licence and password. 7. A plan for when someone leaves: disable accounts the same day. See also Security & Privacy (Part 12).

1. Business tech concepts

#Business tech concepts

The jargon you hear in shops, offices and startup meetings.

#Barcodes: check an EAN-13 number

Concept

The last digit of an EAN-13 barcode is a check digit that catches most typing and scanning errors. Multiply the first 12 digits by 1, 3, 1, 3…, add them up, and the check digit makes the total a multiple of 10.

Python
def ean13_check(first12):
    total = sum(int(d) * (3 if i % 2 else 1) for i, d in enumerate(first12))
    return (10 - total % 10) % 10

for code in ["628100123456", "400638133393", "501234567890"]:
    print(code + str(ean13_check(code)), "<- prefix", code[:3])

scanned = "6281001234567"
ok = ean13_check(scanned[:12]) == int(scanned[12])
print(scanned, "valid" if ok else "INVALID: rescan or retype")
Output
6281001234562 <- prefix 628
4006381333931 <- prefix 400
5012345678900 <- prefix 501
6281001234567 INVALID: rescan or retype

Fun fact: GS1 prefix 628 belongs to Saudi Arabia, 400–440 to Germany, 50 to the UK. The prefix shows where the barcode number was registered, not where the product was made.

#Vintage computers (and the Arabic MSX)

The home computers of the 1970s–90s, including the one that taught a generation of Arab kids to code.

#Sakhr MSX (صخر)

Vintage · 1980s Obsolete

Arabic-language MSX home computers sold across the Arab world by Al-Alamiah, the Kuwaiti company founded by Mohammed Al-Sharekh in 1980, which set up Sakhr in 1982. The machines (such as the AX-170, made by Japanese MSX makers like Yamaha and Sanyo and localised for Arabic) had Arabic keyboards, Arabic BASIC and a library of Arabic educational games. For many Gulf and Egyptian children it was their first computer. Sakhr later became an Arabic language-technology company (machine translation, OCR, speech).

PlatformMSX1 / MSX2 standard (Zilog Z80 CPU)
LanguageArabic + English
Loaded fromCartridges, cassette tapes, floppy disks
FounderMohammed Al-Sharekh (1942–2024)

Identify it: Wedge-shaped keyboard computer with Arabic letters on the keys and a صخر logo; plugged into the family TV

Commonly confused with: Sakhr (the Arabic MSX brand) vs MSX (the Japanese/Microsoft standard used by many brands)

Fun fact: Konami's first Metal Gear (1987) was an MSX game, so many Arab players met Solid Snake on a Sakhr.

Sources: Arab News: Arabic software pioneer Mohammed Al-Sharekh dies (Mar 2024) · Generation Amiga: the forgotten Arabic computer of the 1980s home-PC boom (Jun 2026) · Tamatem: Sakhr computers, a forgotten Arab tech legacy

#Arabic on old computers

Concept

Before Unicode, every company stored Arabic differently: code pages like CP-864, ASMO 449 and Windows-1256, plus special Arabic DOS and Windows versions. That's why old Arabic documents and websites often open as gibberish today; converting them with the right code page (or an online converter) usually fixes it.

Fun fact: Unicode now gives every Arabic letter one fixed number, and the computer picks the right joined shape when it displays it.

#Vintage media, TV & games

Tapes, discs, dishes and the consoles everyone called 'Atari'.

#TV in Saudi homes before streaming

Concept

Thick CRT TVs, a rooftop satellite dish pointed at Arabsat or Nilesat, a receiver box with hundreds of channels, and VCRs or VCD players for films. Many homes had the dish installer on speed dial after every sandstorm knocked it out of alignment.

#Myth: blowing into game cartridges

Concept

Millions of kids blew into NES and Sega cartridges to 'fix' them. It seemed to work only because re-inserting the cartridge moved the contacts. The moisture in breath actually helps the contacts corrode. Clean them with isopropyl alcohol instead.

#Collecting & reviving vintage tech

How to buy, store, fix and digitise old gear without ruining it.

#Safety first

Guide

CRT TVs and monitors can hold a dangerous high-voltage charge for a long time after unplugging: don't open them unless you're trained. Old power supplies can have failing capacitors; plug new-old gear into a power strip with a switch and watch it the first time. Check the voltage (Saudi Arabia uses 220–230 V at 60 Hz; Japanese and American gear may expect 100–120 V and need a step-down transformer).

#How many floppy disks would your phone need?

Concept

A 3.5" high-density floppy holds 1.44 MB. Here's what today's files would need, and how tall the stack would be (each disk is about 3.3 mm thick).

Python
floppy_mb = 1.44
things = {
    "One phone photo (4 MB)": 4,
    "A 3-minute song (MP3)": 3.5,
    "Windows 95 (13 floppies, 1995)": 13 * 1.44,
    "A 1-hour 1080p video": 3_500,
    "A 256 GB phone, full": 256_000,
}
for name, mb in things.items():
    disks = -(-mb // floppy_mb)                  # round up
    mm = disks * 3.3
    height = f"{mm / 10:.1f} cm" if mm < 1000 else f"{mm / 1000:,.1f} m"
    print(f"{name:<32}{disks:>10,.0f} floppies{height:>12} tall")
Output
One phone photo (4 MB)                   3 floppies      1.0 cm tall
A 3-minute song (MP3)                    3 floppies      1.0 cm tall
Windows 95 (13 floppies, 1995)          13 floppies      4.3 cm tall
A 1-hour 1080p video                 2,431 floppies       8.0 m tall
A 256 GB phone, full               177,778 floppies     586.7 m tall

Fun fact: The 256 GB stack would be taller than the Kingdom Centre in Riyadh (about 300 m), roughly twice over.

#Where to find vintage tech in Saudi Arabia

Guide

Online classifieds such as Haraj, weekend and second-hand markets, old electronics shops in older districts, and family storerooms. Ask the seller to power it on in front of you, check battery compartments for corrosion, and don't pay collector prices for common items. For games and old software, use legal sources: original discs/cartridges you own, or re-releases on modern consoles and stores like GOG and Steam.

#Gimmick hall of fame: gadgets that flopped

Big promises, big launch events, short lives.

#Humane AI Pin

Gimmick · 2023–2025 Defunct brand

A screenless AI wearable that clipped to your shirt, answered by voice and projected a laser display onto your palm. It cost $699 plus a required $24/month subscription. Reviews were brutal: slow, hot, unreliable. In February 2025 HP bought Humane's technology and team for about $116 million, and the servers were switched off on 28 February 2025, turning every pin into a paperweight.

Price$699 + $24/month
DisplayLaser projection onto the hand
LastedUnder a year after shipping (April 2024 to February 2025)

Identify it: A small square pin on clothing with a camera and a magnetic battery pack

Commonly confused with: Humane AI Pin vs Rabbit R1 (a cheaper handheld AI gadget from the same era that is still sold)

Fun fact: The lesson: a gadget that depends completely on one company's cloud dies when the company does.

Sources: The Decoder: Humane ends its AI Pin, sells technology to HP for $116 million · Layer3 Labs: Humane AI Pin post-mortem ($699 + $24/month)

#Juicero

Gimmick · 2016–2017 Defunct brand

A Wi-Fi-connected juice press that launched at $699 and squeezed proprietary juice packs. In 2017 reporters showed the packs could be squeezed just as well by hand. The company shut down later that year.

Price$699, later $399
GimmickInternet-connected press that scanned a QR code on each pack

Fun fact: It became the classic example of over-engineered 'smart' products.

#More flops & dead gadgets, one by one

Phones, consoles and gadgets that were cancelled, shut down or quietly forgotten.

#Apple AirPower

2017–2019 (never released) Defunct brand

A wireless charging mat that was meant to charge an iPhone, Apple Watch and AirPods at the same time, anywhere on the mat. Apple showed it at the iPhone X event in September 2017 and promised it for 2018. It never shipped. On 29 March 2019 Apple cancelled it, saying it would not 'achieve our high standards', and apologised to people who were waiting. Reports blamed the many overlapping charging coils, which ran too hot and interfered with each other.

Announced12 September 2017 (iPhone X event)
Cancelled29 March 2019
PriceNever announced (analysts guessed $99–199)
IdeaMany overlapping coils so any device works anywhere on the mat

Identify it: Long, white, rounded mat; Apple's photos showed an iPhone, an Apple Watch and AirPods charging on it together

Commonly confused with: MagSafe (2020), the magnetic charger Apple shipped instead, and the 'MagSafe Duo' folding charger

Fun fact: AirPower is Apple's best-known piece of vapourware. The boxes of the second-generation AirPods (2019) even showed an AirPower-style mat. Lesson: don't pre-announce hardware you haven't finished.

Sources: TechCrunch: Apple cancels AirPower (March 2019) · MacRumors: Apple officially cancels AirPower · Engadget: AirPower cancelled after more than a year of delays

#Microsoft Kin

2010 Defunct brand

Two social-media phones for teenagers (Kin ONE and Kin TWO). They had no app store and needed an expensive data plan. Microsoft pulled them about six weeks after launch.

LastedAbout 6 weeks on sale

Fun fact: Many Kin engineers moved on to Windows Phone, which launched later that year.

#Google Stadia

2019–2023 Defunct brand

Cloud gaming: play console games on any screen, streamed from Google's servers. Few games, a confusing business model and doubts that Google would keep it led to shutdown on 18 January 2023. Google refunded players for hardware and games.

GimmickNo console: games streamed from the cloud
Ended18 January 2023

Commonly confused with: Xbox Cloud Gaming and GeForce NOW, which are still running

Fun fact: The Stadia controller's Bluetooth was unlocked by Google before shutdown so it wouldn't become e-waste.

#Google Nexus Q

2012 Defunct brand

A glowing $299 black sphere that streamed music and video from Google's cloud to your TV and speakers. It was delayed before release and never went on general sale.

Price$299
Made inUSA (unusual for a gadget)

#Snap Spectacles (2016)

2016 Legacy

Sunglasses with a camera that recorded 10-second clips for Snapchat, sold from yellow vending machines with long queues. The hype faded fast and Snap wrote off unsold stock.

GimmickCamera sunglasses sold from vending machines ('Snapbots')

Commonly confused with: Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which became a hit later

#Ouya

2013–2019 Defunct brand

A $99 Android game console funded by a huge Kickstarter. Every game had to be free to try. Most people ended up using it to play emulators; the store closed in 2019.

Price$99
Kickstarter≈ $8.6 million raised

#LG Wing

2020 Obsolete

A phone whose main screen swivelled sideways to reveal a second, smaller screen underneath, making a T-shape. A wild idea from LG's last year of phones.

Screens6.8" main + 3.9" second screen
GimmickSwivel 'T' mode and a gimbal-style camera mode

Fun fact: LG left the phone business in 2021, a few months after the Wing launched.

#YotaPhone

2013–2017 Defunct brand

A Russian phone with a normal screen on the front and an e-ink screen on the back for reading and notifications with almost no battery use.

ScreensLCD/AMOLED front + e-ink back

#RED Hydrogen One

2018 Obsolete

A $1,295 phone from a cinema-camera company with a 'holographic' 4-View 3D screen and planned add-on camera modules that never arrived.

Price$1,295 (aluminium) / $1,595 (titanium)
GimmickGlasses-free '4V' 3D screen

Fun fact: RED itself was later bought by Nikon (2024).

#Lytro light-field camera

2012–2018 Defunct brand

A lipstick-shaped camera that let you change the focus after taking the photo. Clever, but the pictures were low resolution. Lytro shut down in 2018.

GimmickRefocus photos afterwards

Commonly confused with: Phone 'portrait mode', which does a similar trick with software

#Jibo

2017–2019 Defunct brand

A cute $899 home robot that turned its head to look at you and chat. It couldn't do much more than a smart speaker, and its servers later shut down.

Price$899

Fun fact: Before the servers went off, Jibo told owners it was shutting down: a sad goodbye that went viral.

#Amazon Halo

2020–2023 Defunct brand

A screenless fitness band that judged your tone of voice and scanned your body fat from phone photos. Amazon shut it down on 31 July 2023 and refunded recent buyers.

GimmickVoice-tone analysis and 3D body-fat scans
Ended31 July 2023

#Microsoft Band

2014–2016 Defunct brand

An early fitness band with lots of sensors (GPS, heart rate, UV) that worked with iPhone, Android and Windows Phone. Microsoft stopped making it after two models.

SensorsGPS, heart rate, UV, skin temperature and more

#Sony PSP Go

2009–2011 Obsolete

A small sliding PSP that dropped the UMD disc drive: download-only games years before that was normal. Players didn't want to buy their games again.

GimmickNo disc drive, slide-out controls

#Facebook Portal

2018–2022 Defunct brand

Smart displays with cameras that followed you around the room during video calls. Privacy worries hurt sales; Meta stopped selling it to consumers in 2022.

GimmickAI camera that pans and zooms to follow you

#Hoverboards (self-balancing scooters)

2015–2016 Legacy

The two-wheeled 'hoverboards' (which don't hover) were the must-have gift of 2015, until cheap batteries started catching fire. In 2016 the US recalled about 500,000 of them.

ProblemCheap lithium batteries and chargers without safety certification

Fun fact: Lesson: always look for a safety certificate (UL 2272 in the US, SASO in Saudi Arabia) on anything with a big battery.

#Rabbit R1

2024 Current

An orange $199 AI gadget with a scroll wheel and a rotating camera. It promised to use apps for you with a 'Large Action Model'; reviewers found most of it could have been a phone app.

Price$199, no subscription

Commonly confused with: Humane AI Pin (above), its pricier rival that shut down

#Microsoft Zune

2006–2012 Defunct brand

Microsoft's iPod rival, famous for its brown colour option and a 'squirt' feature to share songs over Wi-Fi with other Zunes. Its design ideas lived on in Windows Phone.

GimmickWireless song sharing ('squirting')

#HP TouchPad

2011 Obsolete

A webOS tablet that HP cancelled after about seven weeks; the leftover stock was sold off at $99 and suddenly everyone wanted one.

OSwebOS (from Palm)

#BlackBerry PlayBook

2011 Obsolete

BlackBerry's tablet launched without built-in email: you had to tether a BlackBerry phone to get it.

OSBlackBerry Tablet OS (QNX)

#Nintendo Wii U

2012–2017 Obsolete

A console with a tablet-like GamePad controller. People thought it was a Wii accessory; it sold about 13.5 million, Nintendo's worst home console. Many of its games got a second life on the Switch.

GimmickGamePad with its own screen

#Keurig Kold

2015–2016 Defunct brand

A $370 fridge-sized fizzy-drink pod machine. Drinks were small and pods were expensive, and Keurig stopped it within a year.

Price≈ $370

#Gimmick phones & laptops

Real products built around one wild idea.

#Gimmick features (that came with real products)

Good phones and laptops with features nobody ended up using.

#Gimmicks that became normal

Some 'gimmicks' were just early. These were laughed at, then everyone had one.
